title: David Jonsson: the London rising star handpicked to be the new Black Panther | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jonsson has come a long way from east London’s Docklands, winning accolades on stage and screen
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Jonsson has come a long way from east London’s Docklands, winning accolades on stage and screen
Content: David Jonsson has won widespread acclaim for roles in Industry, Rye Lane and Wasteman.Photograph: Dean Chalkley/The ObserverView image in fullscreenDavid Jonsson has won widespread acclaim for roles in Industry, Rye Lane and Wasteman.Photograph: Dean Chalkley/The ObserverMoviesProfileDavid Jonsson: the London rising star handpicked to be the new Black PantherJonsson has come a long way from east London’s Docklands, winning accolades on stage and screenNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 27 Jul 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew characters carry the cultural weight of Black Panther. Since 2018, the Wakandan king has become a global symbol of Black excellence, credited with reshaping expectations of representation on screen.The first film grossed more than $1.3bn (£1bn) worldwide, won three Oscars and became the first superhero movie nominated for best picture.Now, six years after the death of the film’s star, Chadwick Boseman,Marvel has found its next T’Challa: British star David Jonsson, who will play Boseman’s son in Black Panther 3.The character’s grip on fans is so huge that when Jonsson was introduced on stage by director Ryan Coogler at Comic-Con in San Diego at the weekend, the crowd erupted into chants of “Wakanda forever”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Letitia Wright, Winston Duke, Ryan Coogler, David Jonsson and Kevin Feige on stage at Comic-Con.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APAccording to Marvel, Coogler first suggested Jonsson for one of Hollywood’s most coveted blockbuster roles six months ago.“He called me and said: ‘I found him’,”Marvel Studios president, Kevin Feige recalled. “‘He’s this guy, David Jonsson.’”It is a remarkable ascent for an actor who grew up in the east London Docklands, was expelled from school, and, only a few years ago, was best known for his part in the HBO/BBC banking drama Industry.Coogler later told Feige he knew Jonsson was right for the role after meeting him privately following the completion ofSinners. “He’s the guy,” he said. “I felt it in my soul. He’s a good man, and he is the next Black Panther.”View image in fullscreenJonsson earlier this summer at the Goodwood Festival of Speed.Photograph: Jas Lehal/PAJonsson, 32, grew up in Custom House in Newham, the youngest of four children. His father worked as an IT engineer at Heathrow, his mother worked for the Metropolitan police. He describes his heritage as Creole, with roots in Nigeria, Sierra Leone, the Caribbean and Sweden.He has spoken of the upheaval that followed his parents’ separation when he was 11. He pushed boundaries at school and was eventually expelled for fighting as a teenager.“I wasn’t a bad kid at all,” the self-described introverttold the Guardian. “I was just a bit … distracted at the time.”View image in fullscreenChadwick Boseman as Black Panther in the original film.It was around then that Jonsson told his mother – one of the first Black police community support officers in London – that he wanted to be an actor.At a new school in Hammersmith, a 90-minute commute across the city, he began performing in school plays, and at 16 won a scholarship to the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York. Returning to Britain two years later, he joined the National YouthTheatrebefore winning a place the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.Jonsson left drama school early to join a revival of Mary Stuart opposite Juliet Stevenson, which transferred to the West End; his 2021 performance in And Breathe … at the Almeida won him a Black British Theatre Award.Television came alongside his stage work. After early roles in the ITV detective drama Endeavour and the Fox UK espionage thriller Deep State, his breakthrough came as Gus Sackey in Industry, the cult drama about young graduates clawing their way up a London investment bank.To prepare, Jonsson immersed himself in a world of elite schools and Oxbridge privilege far removed from his own upbringing. He left the show in 2022. “Life is short, art is long,” he later told GQ.His ascent since then has been rapid. His first film lead came in Raine Allen-Miller’s acclaimed 2023 romcom Rye Lane,which premiered at Sundance to critical acclaimand earned him a British Independent Film Award (Bifa) nomination.View image in fullscreenJonsson, left, and Vivian Oparah in Rye Lane.Photograph: Chris Harris/APHe became the first Black lead in a television adaptation of Agatha Christie with the BBC’s Murder Is Easy.Then came the sci-fi horror Alien: Romulus in 2024 – which earned him the Bafta Rising Star award, the Stephen King adaptation The Long Walk, and the British prison film Wasteman, which earned him his second Bifa nomination.Jonsson has long been conscious of what his roles represent. “Every character I do, no matter what, I’m going to be a Black man first,” he has said.Accepting his Bafta award last year, he added: “Growing up, I had the Denzel Washingtons and Idris Elbas, but they’re not me.View image in fullscreenJonsson after winning his Bafta Rising Star award.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian / Bafta“There’s not enough space for diverse talent in this industry. I realise I have an important role in defining what Black is.”Paul Roseby, CEO and artistic director of the National Youth Theatre, said: “I remember watching David play the lead in our adaptation of Pigeon English with Bristol Old Vic in 2013. He was electrifying.“His kindness and generosity as a creative and a person continues to shine through. We’re very grateful to him for taking the time in recent years to share his experience with our current generation of talent, and very proud of everything he is going on to achieve.”Interviewers have described him as warm, with “an innate sense of decency” – which would make him the perfect successor to Boseman,who was deeply respected for his humility and grace.The mantle of Black Panther passed once before, to Letitia Wright’s Shuri in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever (2022).Jonsson plays the next generation of Wakanda’s royal family, inheriting both the character’s name and its huge legacy.Explore more on these topicsFilmTelevisionTheatreprofilesShareReuse this content

title: A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that | Benedict Cumberbatch, Alan Cumming and Benedict Wong | The Guardian
description: The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should, say actors led by Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong
Author: Benedict Cumberbatch
Headline: The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should, say actors led by Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionTelevision industryA TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop thatThe Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought in the US and UK. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She shouldBenedict Cumberbatch,Alan CummingandBenedict WongMon 27 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.40 EDTShareView image in fullscreenThough it has yet to become front-page news in the UK, you should know about the proposedParamount-Warner Bros merger. It threatens to inflict immense harm on the British public. As actors and public figures who have spent our careers in the arts in Britain – working with British crews, on British stages and sets – we have a responsibility to the public who support, enjoy and consume the art we make.The UK is being threatened by a media merger that would harm our workers, our culture and the public – but we can stop it. We are encouraged by Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, who recently sent letters toParamount SkydanceandWarner Bros Discovery, as well as a statement toparliament, indicating that she is “minded to intervene” in Paramount’s$110bn takeoverof Warner Bros.She is correct to investigate this major threat to the UK’s public interest. And she will not be acting alone. This month, 12 US states, led by California,sued in federal courtto block the merger, warning that it would raise prices, shrink the number of films made and degrade the quality of what audiences see. And they just won a major victory: on Friday, Paramount agreed todelay the mergeruntil trial, which could be months. These states acted even after Washington’s own justice department – despitethe reported reservationsof career staff –waved the deal through.Their lawsuit confirms the danger; it cannot, however, do the UK’s work for it. US courts fight on the antitrust front for US markets. The EU, which last weekconditionally backed the merger, also makes its own decisions. The UK’s public interest, our public service broadcasting, our news plurality, the plurality of voices British audiences hear, can only be defended here, by our own secretary of state and the Competition and Markets Authority.The fight against this merger now runs on two fronts, and Nandy commands one of them. Should her department decide to intervene, it may prove one of the most important decisions any culture secretary has taken for UK film, television and media in a generation.This is why. We have spent our lives working in this industry. We know what it looks like from the inside: the sound stages at Leavesden, the crews who move from production to production, the editors and camera operators and costume designers whose names scroll past in the credits at the end of a film. These are our cherished friends and colleagues, who create the shows we all love, who produce the news that educates the public and film the sport events we enjoy together. UK film and television are not just images on your screens; they are the lives and livelihoods of thousands of workers and families, whose work supports local economies. The industry supportsmore than 180,000 jobs, generated£6.8bn in production spendlast year alone and adds roughly£12bn a yearin value to our economy. It is one of the things the UK still does better than almost anyone, and a cultural heritage we must protect.We have watched, with growing alarm, what consolidation does to the breadth and depth of the work we produce: independent film acquisitions at the leading independent film festival Sundancefell by halfbetween 2019 and 2025. Award-winning documentaries – films thatwon Oscarsandtopped festival juries– havestruggled to find commercial distributionbecause they touched subjects the remaining handful of buyers found inconvenient. Every merger of this kind narrows the funnel through which stories can reach audiences.That is precisely what makes the Paramount-WBD merger so dangerous. It’s why the intervention of Nandy and her department matters so much.Paramount proposes to swallow Warner Bros Discovery in one of the largest leveraged buyouts ever attempted, loading the combined company withan estimated $84bn in debt. To service it, executives have promised investors around $6bn in “synergies”. In plain English, that means redundancies, cancelled productions, fewer films commissioned and fewer risks taken.We have seen this before. When Discovery merged with WarnerMedia in 2022, it shelved finished films andcut thousands of jobs; when Skydance merged with Paramount last year, itlaid off about 2,000 people. Now the same executives are making the same promise, and UK crews, producers, talent and audiences will pay when the bill comes due.But jobs are mostly a matter for the Competition and Markets Authority,whose reviewshould end in a full phase 2 investigation. The job of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport goes further: to determine whether the merger is in the public interest. It most certainly is not. Inher statement to British MPs, Nandy cited the need for a sufficient plurality of views in news media and a sufficient plurality of individuals controlling media enterprises. She has also highlighted the potential impact on streaming services, content homogenisation and children’s television. TheEnterprise Actprotects something we should all care about: who decides what we get to watch, and what we get to know.Consider the breadth of what this single company would hold. Channel 5, one of our fivepublic service broadcasters, which serves the evening news to people without the cost of a subscription. CNN International, whichOfcom research in 2018 foundUK viewers rated above every other TV news source for quality, accuracy, trustworthiness and impartiality. The CNN and CBS news archives – among the world’s most important broadcast news collections, withmore than 4.25mvideos, images and media spanning nearly half a century of history. If one commercially interested owner controls access to both, they control the raw material of our historical memory.One owner controlling this much of the news, and the truth, endangers the public in a way no ordinary consolidation does. When separate owners run separate newsrooms, a story judged inconvenient by one can still reach audiences through another. Fold those newsrooms into a single company, and one boardroom’s commercial anxieties – or political debts – determine what millions of people see and what they never learn existed.And we know something about this particular proprietor’s intentions. Paramount’s chief executive reportedly told Donald Trump that he would make “sweeping changes” to CNN if the deal went through. When the buyer of the world’s most trusted international news channel makes editorial promises to a politician, a British secretary of state is entitled – and, really, obliged – to ask questions before the ink dries.Nandy has been scrupulous in noting that no final decision has been taken. Good. It is important to take the time to get this right. But the case for a full public interest intervention, with Ofcom assessing plurality and reporting back, is overwhelming.Actors are often told to stay out of legal arguments. We understand the instinct. But we have spent our lives on enough UK sets, worked alongside enough UK crews and watched enough brilliant work from the UK struggle to find a buyer to know that this is not someone else’s argument. It is ours. Nandy has opened the door to intervention. Shemustwalk through it, for the sake of everyone who makes UK television and film – and everyone who watches it. If she does not, we will be left without the ability to protect our industry and our culture from this consolidation. We must not push the public’s interest aside; we must stand up for it and block this merger.Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong are actors working in the UK and Hollywood

title: Bill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBC | Bill Oddie | The Guardian
description: The beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he loved
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he loved
Content: TV’s signature birdwatcher … Bill Oddie at home in his garden.Photograph: Vicki Couchman/Camera PressView image in fullscreenTV’s signature birdwatcher … Bill Oddie at home in his garden.Photograph: Vicki Couchman/Camera PressBill OddieBill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBCThe beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he lovedBill Oddie, naturalist and broadcaster, dies aged 85Bill Oddie – a life in picturesMark LawsonMon 27 Jul 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 21.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Oddie,who has died aged 85, had two separate, substantial TV presences – as a comedy actor and an ornithologist. Both roles brought him fame but also pain. The peak of the former career was 76 episodes from 1970-82 of The Goodies, which he co-wrote and co-starred in with Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor. They played an eccentric trio of investigators and fixers who rode into action on a three-seater bicycle called a “trandem”.As a birdwatcher, his onscreen zenith was Springwatch, which he initially co-hosted with Kate Humble, from 2005. It began a BBC Two natural history franchise marking the change of seasons, its success leading to wintry, autumnal and summery spin-offs. Binoculars lowered to show eyes awed or enthused, and Oddie became TV’s signature birdwatcher.Bill Oddie – a life in picturesRead moreBorn in Rochdale, he came early to both comedy and ornithology. He was a teenager when his sightings first appeared in the annual report of the West Midland Bird Club. In his early 20s, he appeared in the West End and on Broadway in transfers of the Cambridge University revue in which he first worked professionally with Brooke-Taylor and Garden, who is now the only survivor of the three. Oddie wrote the music for the revue and then The Goodies, who released five spin-off singles in 1974-75, spending a combined 38 weeks in the pop charts, with Funky Gibbon, an anthropomorphic jungle dance number, reaching four in the Top 10.Each of Oddie’s TV hits, though, was overshadowed by sadness. In the case of Springwatch, it was personal. Particularly bad incidents of the bipolar condition he experienced throughout his life led him to miss a number of episodes. He returned to the programme, but his departure in 2008 – which he made clear was not voluntary – was triggered, by his account, by another serious depressive downturn.In the case of The Goodies, there was an underlying resentment shared by Brooke-Taylor and Garden relating to the show’s treatment by the BBC. The series attracted 12 million viewers at its mid-70s peak – very high for a BBC Two show – and won the Silver Rose of Montreux, the second prize at Europe’s leading TV festival. The gong was for Kitten Kong, an inspired movie spoof in which a massive moggy terrorises London using some special effects impressive for the period.View image in fullscreenThe Goodies in 1973, from left: Tim Brooke-Taylor, Graeme Garden and Bill Oddie.Photograph: South Coast Press/ShutterstockHowever, The Goodies was never valued by many corporation executives who – due to the relatively high quotient of slapstick, puns and visual gags involving animals – designated it a “children’s show”, which was intended as an insult and taken as such by two of the creators. For what proved to be the final series, the trio moved to London WeekendTelevision.Unlike most hit shows of its period, The Goodies has not been regularly repeated on terrestrial TV, any re-airings by the BBC largely in archive slots. This upset and frustrated Oddie, Brooke-Taylor and Garden. During the home video and DVD boom, when it sometimes seemed that the BBC was systematically releasing all material ever shown, the threesome negotiated a box set release with a commercial outfit, which did something to redress the neglect.A few other shows from the era have also been denied repeats and releases because they contain language or attitudes now considered unacceptable. BBC off-the-record briefers have sometimes suggested that this was why The Goodies has been so difficult to watch or buy. There is an occasion on which the three men start to apply blackface, but it occurred in an extraordinary 1975 episode called South Africa. This begins with the Goodies undertaking an advertising campaign to attract Britons to South Africa and ends in a Britain with a Black Enoch Powell presiding over a regime of reverse apartheid.Although there is some silly wordplay – at one point, a regime of “apart-height” requires the diminutive Oddie to become a slave to his taller colleagues – the broadly progressive politics and complexity of the storyline make the “children’s television” tag seem particularly absurd. Indeed, absurdity is a more fitting label for South Africa and many other editions.In The Goodies, the writer-actors played exaggerations of aspects of their character: Garden (a qualified doctor) professorial and absent-minded, Brooke-Taylor posh and patriotic, and Oddie sulky and scrappy. Those characteristics meant that some colleagues found him hard to work with – which may have contributed to his departure from Springwatch – but some such behaviour was explained, if not entirely excused, by his mental health issues.Oddie was quite right, though, to be annoyed by the diminishment in BBC and TV history of The Goodies, memories of which will make its viewers smile amid the sadness at his death. His admirers will also hope that any afterlife contains a chorus of birdsong.Explore more on these topicsBill OddieTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Swathes of Cairngorms unrecognisable after 12 days of ‘cataclysmic’ wildfires | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: With large areas still burning, damage from national park’s worst blaze could take decades, if not longer, to put right
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: With large areas still burning, damage from national park’s worst blaze could take decades, if not longer, to put right
Content: It could take months for the blaze to be fully extinguished.Photograph: Robyn Vinter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIt could take months for the blaze to be fully extinguished.Photograph: Robyn Vinter/The GuardianWildfiresSwathes of Cairngorms unrecognisable after 12 days of ‘cataclysmic’ wildfiresWith large areas still burning, damage from national park’s worst blaze could take decades, if not longer, to put rightRobyn VinterMon 27 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the jewel in the crown of the Highlands, one of Scotland’s most impressive natural landscapes, but 12 days on from the start of an enormous wildfire that is tearing through moorland and forest, the Cairngorms national park is unrecognisable.Hectares of blackened land were visible as low cloud cleared on Sunday, with smoke billowing into the air from large areas still ablaze. In the evening, the sky glowed an eerie orange.Authorities have warned the danger is far from over in what has been described as the worst fire the Cairngorms has ever seen. It will be weeks, if not months, before the blaze is fully extinguished but emergency services are hoping they can stop it spreading much further. The damage so far has been significant and it will take decades to put right.Flames have claimed areas of the Caledonian pinewood forest, which contains Scots pine trees 300 years old, but most of the older forest has been saved by fire breaks urgently bulldozed into the land in the early days of the fire.“For rare habitat loss, it really is a challenge,” says Ian Allsopp, the Forestry and Land Scotland planning manager for the north region, saying larger animals, such as deer, would have escaped but smaller mammals, lizards, insects and ground-nesting birds would have perished.View image in fullscreenFlames have claimed areas of the Caledonian pinewood forest, which contains 300-year-old Scots pines.Photograph: Robyn Vinter/The GuardianGrant Moir, the chief executive of the Cairngorms national park, told the Guardian it was the worst fire the park had seen. “The fact that this is right in the centre of the Cairngorms, in the actual Cairngorm mountains and Abernethy – it is such a precious place,” he says.A national park bylaw was introduced in April, banning campfires and barbecues over the summer to help reduce ignition points. It is still unknown what caused this fire but the vast majority of UK wildfires have a human origin and can be something as small as a discarded cigarette or abandoned glass bottle.Police Scotland said on Saturday night it was no longer treating the fire as a major incident. However, anxiety is still high, particularly among local people who were told it was “contained” last week, only for strong winds to fan the flames, leading to the evacuation of Nethy Bridge village on Friday night.Residents have been toldthey can return home. Inside Nethy Bridge community centre, which is being used as a makeshift base for the emergency services, a long table against a wall is groaning under the weight of donated food, while the fire service, police and volunteers bustle around, many looking exhausted.“It’s absolutely heartbreaking,” says Sandy McCook, a retired press photographer from the village. “The flames on Friday were cataclysmic.”He is angry too. Many locals feel the fire could have been prevented. McCook shows the Guardian a photo he took of the wildfire when it was only the size of a tennis court.“Had we had a helicopter there on government contract to deal with such incidents, that fire could have been dealt with within two hours of it being reported,” he says. He wants to see a model similar to the Scottish air ambulance, with a specialist firefighting helicopter and crew able to scramble to tackle hard-to-reach fires, and he is not the only one.Three private helicopters have been contracted to provide assistance in the Cairngorms, depositing approximately 750,000 litres of water a day on wildfire hotspots, something that is essential to getting the blaze under control. Allsopp says it was “so lucky” the helicopter companies were able to assist in water-bombing what he says was an “inferno”.View image in fullscreenFirefighters said an ‘intensive operation’ was still under way but better weather conditions had slowed the fire and limited its spread.Photograph: RSPB Scotland/PAThe Cairngorms area is an “extremely challenging landscape”, including steep mountains and forest, “access is so difficult, you just can’t get people up here”.On Monday, the Scottish Green party called for publicly available firefighting aircraft during the wildfire season, saying Scotland “cannot continue to rely on a patchwork of private operators and borrowed resources”.It came after the UK government offered military support on Sunday but said it had no access to specialist firefighting helicopters requested by the Scottish government.Firefighters said an “intensive operation” was still under way but better weather conditions, including heavy rain and low winds, had slowed the fire and limited its spread. More than 75 firefighters remained at the scene, the Scottish fire and rescue service said on Sunday.Light rain has brought some relief but everyone on the ground is anxious in the face of more dry weather to come. “Wet weather is not enough to put out the fire on its own,” says Allsopp. It requires helicopter water-bombing “for days and days and days” to contain it.The operation is a massive coordinated effort between Forestry and Land Scotland, the national park authority, the police, fire service, RSPB, Highland Council and other partners, with assistance being offered from the Scottish and UK governments.Allsopp says each organisation has worked well together, pooled skills and knowledge, and helped each other out. “Even our accountants are here, running errands and getting water and sun cream for people,” he said. “At times, it has been completely overwhelming and we’ve been struggling to keep up. It feels like a war strategy.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresScotlandNational parksnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The greatest album never made’: the untold story of George Michael’s secret, star-packed duets project | George Michael | The Guardian
description: Suing his record label and sick of being a sex symbol, the singer spent 1992 working on the Trojan Souls for stars including Aretha Franklin and Bryan Ferry. Now, newly released studio footage shows him in his creative prime
Author: Dorian Lynskey
Headline: Suing his record label and sick of being a sex symbol, the singer spent 1992 working on the Trojan Souls for stars including Aretha Franklin and Bryan Ferry. Now, newly released studio footage shows him in his creative prime
Content: ‘The best time of our lives’ … Michael at LAX in October 1992.Photograph: Ron Galella Collection/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The best time of our lives’ … Michael at LAX in October 1992.Photograph: Ron Galella Collection/Getty ImagesGeorge Michael‘The greatest album never made’: the untold story of George Michael’s secret, star-packed duets projectSuing his record label and sick of being a sex symbol, the singer spent 1992 working on the Trojan Souls for stars including Aretha Franklin and Bryan Ferry. Now, newly released studio footage shows him in his creative primeWham! special: read Andrew Ridgeley on their bizarre 1985 trip to ChinaDorian LynskeyMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheGeorge Michaelalbum that never was began in defiance and ended in grief. It was 1992. Mired in a toxic dispute with Sony Records, Michael chose to keep busy and declare his independence by making an album of songs to be sung by several of his musical heroes, including Aretha Franklin, Janet Jackson and Sade Adu, under the alias the Trojan Souls. Michael worked on the album for months until his Brazilian boyfriend Anselmo Feleppa died of Aids in March 1993 and he lost interest in music. It was never revived.Tracks from the sessions have since leaked, along with some of the fly-on-the-wall footage filmed by Michael’s close friend and informal adviser Andros Georgiou, who has spent years trying to get unauthorised clips removed from YouTube and TikTok. Now, months before the 10th anniversary of Michael’s death, he is releasing 90 minutes of unedited video as Trojan Souls – not exactly a film but an unfiltered view of Michael in his creative prime. “I thought these fans were making money from my rights so I decided to stop fighting and get it out there,” Georgiou says. He hopes it will open a door on what he calls, with characteristic hyperbole, “the greatest album never made”.Georgiou called his self-published 2012 memoir Rock: The Luckiest Man in Pop, the luck being that his father and Michael’s father were cousins who emigrated to England from Cyprus together in 1953, so he grew up alongside one of the greatest artists of his generation. They remained close until a bitter falling out in 1998, of which more later.View image in fullscreen‘He had a 48-track studio in his mind’ … Michael at work.Photograph: Courtesy Andros GeorgiouEver loyal to his childhood friends (another, David Austin, now runs his estate), Michael gave Georgiou creative opportunities. They first collaborated as Boogie Box High, whose cover of the Bee Gees’ Jive Talkin’ was a Top 10 hit in 1987, and co-founded Aegean Records in 1996. Georgiou was also a regular on-the-road companion. When they were in Tokyo during the Faith tour, Sony gave Georgiou a state-of-the-art Hi8 video camera which enabled him to make high-quality home movies.Georgiou makes the origins of the Trojan Souls sound as a dramatic as a heist. When Michael released Listen Without Prejudice Vol 1 in 1990, he was so sick of his sex-symbol image that he disappeared from view: no appearances in videos or on record sleeves, no interviews, no concerts. “He wanted to make music but he didn’t want to play the lying game any more,” says Georgiou. Michael believed that Sony then punished him by underpromoting the album. The singer felt trapped.double quotation markBeing arrested was the beginning of the end. He laughed it off but it seriously affected himIn January 1992, he and Georgiou flew to LA for some winter sun but Michael soon got bored and suggested going to Dave Stewart’s Chapel Studios in Encino to bang out a quick cover in the spirit of Boogie Box High. The 1979 disco hit Ain’t No Stoppin’ Us Now was a symbolic choice because Gene McFadden and John Whitehead originally wrote it to rebuke their own label, Philadelphia International. Michael decided they should return in July to start an album, recruiting vocalists he had loved growing up. According to Georgiou, only David Bowie politely declined. He says the name came to him in a dream: The Voice of Reason by the Trojan Souls. “From the Trojan horse,” he says. “The soldiers came in and then came down fighting.”Back in London, Georgiou was contractually obliged to offer it to Sony first, despite the bad blood. “Of course they said no. I called George and he said, ‘Fuck Sony!’ I went, ‘I’ll be home in two hours with a deal, trust me.’” Georgiou called an A&R at Warner and dashed over. “Rob Dickins, the chair, was there. He said, ‘What do you want?’ I said a million pounds. He goes, done.” In October, Michaelfiled a lawsuit against Sony, alleging that his contract was unreasonable restraint of trade. “He wanted to get back at Sony any which way he could,” says Georgiou.Despite the project’s bitter origins, the three songs in the film have a sunny, funky dynamism. “He was so happy,” Georgiou says. “For the first couple of months we probably had the best time of our lives making this record.” The lush ballad One Day I’ll Know was destined for Stevie Wonder and the shimmering Maybe It’s Not Your Time for Bryan Ferry. The instrumental track Wendy Melvoin’s Song featured virtuosic rhythm guitar by one half of Wendy and Lisa, in the hope that she would lure her former employer Prince on board.Obsessed with protecting his mystique, Michael was never officially filmed handling an instrument or building a track. “If you’re a fan,” says Georgiou, “this is your first chance to see how he directs everyone in the studio.” It’s fascinating to watch how precisely Michael drills his world-class musicians – Melvoin, keyboardist Chris Cameron, bassist Deon Estus and Lynn Mabry’s backing singers – through take after take, even grabbing Estus’s bass guitar at one point to show him what he means. To the viewer the takes may sound identical but Michael was always chasing the perfect sound he heard in his head.View image in fullscreenCollaboration … Elton John and Michael in the early 1990s.Photograph: Photoshot/Getty Images“He had a 48-track studio in his mind,” says Georgiou. He recalls how, even when they were kids, Michael used to deconstruct songs by their favourite artists and explain how he would have changed this or that. Or how, when they were working at Sarm West in Notting Hill, Michael would get in the car with a cassette of a skeletal backing track and have a melody written by the time he got home to Hampstead.“He was quite a frustrating person to work with because he had quite a strange creative process,” says Sathnam Sanghera, author of Tonight the Music Seems So Loud: The Meaning of George Michael. “He would often sing at musicians and say, ‘This is what I want it to sound like.’ I’ve talked to a lot of musicians who worked with him and almost all of them said the same thing: ‘At the time it drove us fucking mad.’ But looking back they can see that of all the people they’d worked with he was the most talented. He just had these amazing ears.”double quotation markThis is just the beginning of something that could have been amazingThe fragments heard in Trojan Souls are tantalising but only the Elton John collaboration This Kind of Love was ever completed. By the start of 1993, Feleppa was fading fast. “It was terribly difficult for him to finish anything so we went from track to track,” Georgiou says. “And then it got too much for him.” Leaving work unfinished was not unusual for Michael, though. “George had a history of losing interest,” says Sanghera. “A lot of projects never came to fruition: Listen Without Prejudice Vol 2, the Daft Punk collaboration, the duets album …”A few years later, Georgiou’s friendship with Michael ended, too. On 7 April 1998, Michael was arrested for “engaging in lewd conduct” in a public toilet in LA’s Will Rogers Memorial Park and the closeted star was outed to the world. “Basically it all went wrong when he was arrested,” Georgiou says. “He laughed it off but it seriously affected him mentally and that was the beginning of the end.”When I interviewed Michael in 2004, he connected the incident to losing his mother to cancer a year earlier. Having finally worked through the creative drought occasioned by Feleppa’s death to make 1996’s Older, he was poleaxed by grief once again. “Really since 1991, when I found out [Feleppa] was HIV positive, all I’d done was either wait for someone to die or grieve,” he told me. “It was just so easy to feel picked on and angry and nihilistic.”View image in fullscreenClose before a bitter falling out … Georgiou and Michael.Photograph: Courtesy Andros GeorgiouMichael’s compulsive cruising on Hampstead Heath created a rift. Georgiou thought it was self-destructive; Michael resented his friend’s judgment. “I couldn’t understand the risks he was taking,” Georgiou says. “He was loud and proud, which I absolutely respected, but you can’t carry on doing what you’re doing.” He claims that the final straw was Michael suddenly ordering him to drop Aegean’s entire roster. “The next day I was just like, you know what? Fuck you. And I walked out.”An alternative account is that Georgiou crossed a line by telling his story, and giving family photographs, to Hello! magazine. Either way, Michael told me, “losing that relationship absolutely devastated me. Everything I took for granted in my 20s I lost.” Georgiou says that they tentatively reconnected in 2016 and planned to meet up in the new year. “It took a lot. We’re both Greeks at heart and have our arrogance and pride. And then he died. Even talking about it now, I can’t believe it.”The Trojan Souls material wasn’t mothballed entirely. Ain’t No Stoppin’ Us Now was released on Aegean Records in 1998, as one of the first ever commercially available MP3s, and Michael rerecorded This Kind of Love, sans Elton, not long before his death – Sanghera calls it “his one great unreleased song”. As for the rest, we can only imagine. Could The Voice of Reason ultimately have been a triumph?“I think it could have worked as a duets album, because 90% of George was his voice,” Sanghera says. “He was at his creative peak. This could have been Listen Without Prejudice Vol 2 if his lover wasn’t dying, if he hadn’t sued Sony. But I think he would have needed another two years for a fully realised album. This is just the beginning of something that could have been amazing.”Georgiou has often been regarded with suspicion by Michael’s fans for monetising his proximity to pop genius. Now he is preparing a rewritten memoir, an accompanying film, the release of more footage on his website, and even a duet version of This Kind of Love if he can get Elton John’s blessing. Then again, these are his videos and Trojan Souls was his project, too. Given his long estrangement from Michael, the home movies document not just an unfinished album but a much-missed friendship. “It’s my legacy in a way,” he says. “I was there for nearly 40 years. What a time!”Trojan Souls is available for streaming attrojansouls.comExplore more on these topicsGeorge MichaelPop and rockDocumentary filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: He was shot at by ICE, then wrongfully accused. His nightmare had only just begun | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: After masked agents fired on his truck, Francisco Longoria was ambushed, charged and jailed – only for the case against him to fall apart. Now he and his family are seeking justice, and says the harrowing experience is part of a troubling pattern
Author: Hilary Beaumont
Headline: After masked agents fired on his truck, Francisco Longoria was ambushed, charged and jailed – only for the case against him to fall apart. Now he and his family are seeking justice, and says the harrowing experience is part of a troubling pattern
Content: From left: Jonathan Longoria, Francisco Longoria and Daniel Rascon, beside the vehicle they were in when agents fired at them. The bullet holes remain. Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianAfter masked agents fired on his truck, Francisco Longoria was ambushed, charged and jailed – only for the case against him to fall apart. Now he and his family are seeking justice, and says the harrowing experience is part of a troubling patternByHilary Beaumontin San Bernardino, CaliforniaMon 27 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was just after 8am on 16 August and Francisco Longoria, who runs a party supply business, was driving his truck down a suburban southernCaliforniastreet to deliver a jumper for a water slide. But this ordinary Saturday morning turned into a nightmare when, suddenly, three unmarked vehicles stopped his truck and four masked men jumped out.Longoria, who had brought his son Jonathan Longoria and son-in-law Daniel Rascon with him, wondered if they were being abducted.“I see what happens in Mexico,” he said in Spanish. “I thought, are we going to be kidnapped by these masked men?”The masked men were agents withUS immigrationand Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). They wore police gear, but Longoria said they didn’t identify themselves. As the agents walked toward the truck with their guns drawn, the passengers pulled out their phones to record video.One agent pulled on the door handle, knocked on the window, and told Longoria to roll down his window, but the agent didn’t have a warrant. When Longoria didn’t comply, the agent smashed the glass and struck him in the face. Another agent broke the front passenger’s window.With the agents on either side of the truck, and the road ahead clear, Longoria hit the gas. As he drove away, an agent shot three rounds, leaving two bullet holes in the passenger’s side of the truck. One bullet barely missed the back window. Sitting in the back seat, Rascon felt terrified. “One of us is about to get killed,” he thought.“I was afraid for my life,” Longoria said. “I felt like death was imminent.”The whole encounter lasted less than a minute, but it was only the beginning of the family’s harrowing tale.The shooting happened a few blocks away from their home in San Bernardino, about 60 miles east of Los Angeles. When they arrived back at home minutes later, they called the police to report that masked men had shot at them.Instead of receiving help, Longoria found himself in the crosshairs of a US government investigation that culminated in a night-time ambush of the family’s home, a felony charge accusing Longoria of weaponizing his vehicle against officers, and months in ICE detention – only for the case against him to eventually be dropped.View image in fullscreenFrancisco Longoria at home in San Bernardino.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianLongoria is speaking out for the first time as his family seeks justice for the violence they experienced. The family has filed a lawsuit against the federal government and the officers involved, seeking damages for physical injury, psychological injuries including PTSD, lost wages, property damages, wrongful incarceration, public humiliation and reputational harm.The lawsuit alleges the officer “attempted to kill” them by firing shots in violation of CBP’s use of force policy, which directs officers to not shoot at “a moving vehicle merely fleeing from agents”; the only exception is if the agent has a reasonable belief that deadly force is being used against them or others present. “No legitimate law-enforcement purpose justified the use of deadly force under these circumstances,” the lawsuit states. It also alleges that the officers violated a temporary restraining order issued by a California judge that prohibited officers from targeting people solely based on race, language or type of work.Longoria said he didn’t know why the agents stopped his truck, but suspects it was racial profiling. He and his family remain traumatized by their experience. “What I have lived through, I don’t wish that upon others,” he said.The incident came at atense time in their quiet neighborhood in San Bernardino, a predominantly Latino city with a population of more than 200,000 people. About a quarter of residents were born outside the US.Elected on promises of an immigration crackdown, the Trump administration had ordered a string of aggressive immigration raids across the US. Southern California was an early target, as federal agents arrested more than4,000 peoplefrom June to August last year, with immigrant advocates saying people were targeted based on their skin color, accents or jobs. Federal officers have routinely used excessive force, resulting in injuries and deaths, including the killings of Rene Good and Alex Pretti.Shots heard after immigration agents pull over Francisco LongoriaLongoria’s experience is not an isolated one. Since Trump took office last year, ICEhas opened fireon at least 30 people, according to Trace, a US outlet tracking such shootings. However, after its agents act violently, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE and CBP, frequently accuses the victims of weaponizing their vehicles against officers. In many cases, such charges end upbeing dismissed.This month, ICE agentsshot and killed two menin their vehicles in Texas and Maine. Following the shootings, ICE paused most vehicle stops – a moveswiftly reversedby Trump.The Longoria family’s lawyers are calling on the California attorney general, Rob Bonta, to open a criminal investigation.“It was an illegal stop,” said Greg Jackson, partner and managing attorney at the Simon Law Group. “It’s one of those stops where they saw brown people in a truck and decided to exercise their perceived authority over them.”DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s detailed request for comment about the Longoria family’s lawsuit and Longoria’s allegations about the shooting before publication.Longoria, a chatty man with a green thumb who was born in Mexico, has spent the last 24 years planting roots in southern California. He and his wife own a single-story home in San Bernardino, where they live with their children and son-in-law. The walls of their home are decorated with graduation and quinceañera photos, and a crucifix hangs next to the front door. Longoria, a devout Catholic, supported his family with his party rental business, while also working warehouse and restaurant shifts.On the day of the shooting, Longoria arrived home and immediately called 911. When San Bernardino police arrived, he thought they were there to help. But he did not know that before he called, federal officers had already reported to local police that they shot at the truck. Call logs show that San Bernardino police misheard federal agents and believed Longoria had returned fire at them, so local police considered him a suspect, although they knew federal officers were not hit. “Marshal was not struck, med aid will be for a scrape to the arm,” the call logs state.Local police arrived at Longoria’s home and arrested him. “They handcuffed me and put me in the car,” he said. They asked him if he ran over anyone with his truck, and he said no. His family members showed them the videos they had recorded.While Longoria was in the squad car, the masked federal agents who had stopped the truck arrived at the family home. Local police looked up Longoria’s criminal record, but he didn’t have one. They had no reason to hold him.But after local police released Longoria, ICE and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents attempted to arrest him themselves, telling family members to open the metal gate to their front yard. The agents lacked a warrant, so the family refused.View image in fullscreenThe Longoria family pose for a portrait outside their home.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianOn the typically quiet street, neighbors noticed the heavy police presence. They poured out of their homes to defend Longoria and his family, who were known in the community for their contributions to the local church and party business.The standoff between the crowd and police lasted several hours. Police call logs described the crowd as “hostile”. Officers deployed pepper spray and arrested several people.Longoria said it felt good to see the community support: “I am forever indebted to them.”When the officers left, the family felt relieved, but still on edge. They struggled to sleep for weeks after. Rascon noticed vehicles parked nearby that he believed were watching their home. Longoria stayed inside while family members, who are US citizens, picked up groceries and went to work. “We were still looking over our shoulders,” Rascon said.It turned out their fears were justified. On 28 August, a security camera captured the moment at 4.19am when a group of federal officers in helmets, vests and night-vision goggles arrived while the family were still asleep, pointing guns at their door. They announced over a megaphone that they had a warrant for Longoria’s arrest.Immigration agents raid Francisco Longoria’s homeRascon was asleep on the couch when his mother-in-law shook him awake. He stood up and saw the agents outside carrying assault rifles. The family gathered in the living room, wearing the clothes they had been sleeping in, and called their lawyers.The officers broke the locks on the exterior metal door and interior wooden door, and pointed assault rifles at them, the lasers from the guns hitting their bodies. Longoria said the agents told them: “If you move, we will shoot you.”The lasers touched Joana Longoria, Rascon’s fiance, who was five months pregnant. Rascon told the officers: “Don’t shoot, she’s pregnant!”“I was afraid of having a miscarriage [as a result of the stress],” she said.View image in fullscreenJonathan Longoria, Francisco’s son, who was in the car when agents shot at them.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianThe agents wanted to arrest Longoria, but the family shielded him. Longoria told them to step aside, fearing they would be killed. But Rascon said they refused to move until the officers produced a warrant.The agents handed them a piece of paper that alleged Longoria had run over two officers with his vehicle, amounting to a felony charge of assault against federal officers with a dangerous weapon. The family’s lawyers confirmed over the phone that the warrant was legitimate, and they reluctantly allowed the agents to take Longoria. He wore only a muscle shirt and shorts, so they ran to get his clothes as the agents barked at them to hurry up. “I had to leave with my shoes in my hands,” Longoria said.Jackson, the family’s attorney, said the ambush involved “extreme levels of violence that you would see for drug dealers, narco- terrorists, criminals” – an unnecessary amount of force for someone with no criminal history. He said the DHS knew the family were represented by attorneys and could have contacted them with the warrant, avoiding the trauma of arresting him at gunpoint.View image in fullscreenFrancisco Longoria at home in California. He wears an ankle monitor and regularly checks in with authorities.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianThat same day, Longoria had a bond hearing. More than 30 community members filed into the courtroom. He felt blessed to see them, but frustrated about the felony charge. “Why is this happening to me?” he wondered. “I haven’t done anything wrong.”During the hearing, the US attorney acknowledged he couldn’t think of a lawful basis for the officers to stop Longoria’s truck, and he wasn’t aware of any injuries to the officers. The judge said the videos recorded inside the truck were “quite scary”, and granted Longoria bond. But he was still subject to an ICE detainer, a request to hold a person so the agency can assume custody, because the government charged Longoria with being in the US without authorization.The judge allowed him to hug his children before ICE took him. A few days later, he arrived at the Adelanto ICE facility, a huge 2,000-person capacity detention center in southern California’s high desert.The food was awful, the portions were too small, and they weren’t given enough water, Longoria said. He estimated he lost 20lb. The guards watched them constantly, even when they used the bathroom.In Adelanto, he met people who were captured in the southern California raids – car-wash workers, street vendors and day laborers. “The majority of people detained were hard-working people,” he said.People who had been injured by federal agents showed him their broken hands and limbs, and he said they did not receive medical attention. At least two people died in Adelanto while he was there –Gabriel Garcia-Aviles, 56, andIsmael Ayala-Uribe, 39 – after ICE allegedly neglected their medical needs.View image in fullscreenJoana Longoria poses for a portrait with her daughter Delilah.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianThe government dropped the charges against Longoria on 17 September, but he was still held at Adelanto for a total of three months. After his lawyers fought for his release, Longoria returned home in early December – in time to celebrate Christmas and attend the birth of his granddaughter in January.In February, Rascontestifiedbefore a House and Senate hearing examining violent abuses by DHS agents. “They’re terrorizing more than just our neighborhood … They haven’t stopped, to this day,” Rascon told the Guardian. He wants to see the officers face justice: “They should be imprisoned or charged.”The lawsuit alleges officers attempted to “cover up” the truth of the shooting by making false statements that led Francisco to be charged – “part of a wide-ranging pattern of behavior … where ICE and/or CBP officers shoot or otherwise attack innocent people and then manufacture charges … falsely alleging the innocent individual ‘weaponized’ their vehicle, only to later dismiss all charges”.Longoria doesn’t have bad wishes toward the officers – he only asks that they follow the law. “Instead, what they do is they injure people first, or kill them, and then later they figure out that they are good people,” he said.Longoria, who is still facing removal proceedings from the US, wears an ankle monitor and regularly checks in with immigration authorities. He can’t work, so the rest of the family are working longer hours. Longoria is caring for his granddaughter Delilah, a calm baby with big, curious eyes who has brought them a renewed sense of joy.With more time at home, Longoria has planted tomatoes, squash, watermelon, chilis and peas in every available inch of soil. But reminders of the family’s ordeal remain; the front door that was broken in the ambush has been nailed back together. His truck with the bullet holes and smashed windows is parked next to the house, unrepaired.Longoria’s attorneys are fighting to keep him in the US.“We will continue to go to court and see what happens next,” he said. “I want to stay in the country with my family, but I’m not the one to decide that. Only God can decide what happens to my future.”Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US politicsTrump administrationUS immigrationCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needs | Education policy | The Guardian
description: PM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs market
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: PM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs market
Content: Under the plan, mayors and other local leaders will work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyView image in fullscreenUnder the plan, mayors and other local leaders will work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyEducation policyBurnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needsPM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs marketPeter WalkerandJosh HallidayMon 27 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will tell schools across England to adapt their curriculums to the needs of local businesses as part of a devolution drive aimed at tackling the jobs crisis for young people.By moving decision-making to local areas, the PM hopes the plan will make technical and vocational skills as valued as academic qualifications – and help cut the benefits bill.Based in part on the Greater Manchester baccalaureate that Burnham introduced as the region’s mayor, it will task schools with making their curriculums for students aged 14 and above more responsive to the local jobs market, teaching technical skills alongside traditional academic subjects.It would, Burnham said, mean the country could “value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap”.Described by No 10 as “a fundamental change to the education system”, the announcement kicks off a week of policy initiatives by Burnham, expected to also cover adult social care, defence and devolution.After last week’s succession of rapid, consumer-focused policies such as help with electricity bills, Burnham’s team aim to use the coming days to present him as a leader willing to tackle more intractable and complex political problems.Under the plan, intended to begin operating from September 2028, mayors and other local leaders would work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs.In combination, there will be prioritised funding for such technical and vocational qualifications, plus guidance to Ofsted to recognise the value of these as well as more traditional qualifications.In addition to giving local areas more control over education for the 14-16 age group, Burnham said the intention was to redress what he said was an over-simplified focus on academic routes.He said:“For too long in this country, students have been told that you must take the academic path to do well and to be respected. The whole school system has been built around it and that has let down young people seeking technical qualifications.“I want an education system based on parity between academic and technical which gives all young people a clear path in life. From today, Britain will value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap.”The intention is also to help address the worsening problem of young people not in education, employment or training, which was the subjectof a reportpublished in May by Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister.The first part of an ongoing review, Milburn’s report said the issue now affected 1 million young people across the UK, with the numbers rising fast. It cited a number of factors, including a changing job market, inequality and health problems, but also blamed a lack of focus on employability skills and non-academic qualifications.Milburn said in a statement that he welcomed the plans to overhaul and devolve education for 14-plus pupils, calling it “a big step in the right direction and consistent with the findings of my review”.Moves to get more young people into work will also be a key element of wider efforts to tackle the benefits system, due to be guided by both Milburn’s findings and a separatereview by Stephen Timms, the minister for social security, into the personal independence payment disability system.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn an interview with the BBC broadcast on Monday night, Burnham said he believed that many young people had been failed by a system that “pays for failure” rather than “sets people up for success”.Asked if he believed some people received benefits they did not need, he replied: “I wouldn’t necessarily go straight to blaming those people. What I would say is that there are people in the benefit system, young people in their 20s, who have been, I would say, quite seriously let down because the support wasn’t there for them when it should have been there.”This failure included, he said, “an education system that for a very long time has been obsessed on the university route but hasn’t done enough for young people who want technical qualifications and in many ways has treated them as second class students”.The new initiative is firmly based on Burnham’s flagship education policy as Greater Manchester mayor, introduced in September 2024.Known as the Greater Manchester baccalaureate, or MBacc, it was designed to offer courses and work experience for children aged 14 and over in key sectors in the regional economy.Alongside the traditional subjects of English, maths and sciences, schools in Greater Manchester can now offer technical lessons tailored towards employment in industries including financial services, engineering and manufacturing, construction and the green economy. There are also new routes into public services such as health and social care, education and transport.Experts say it is too soon to properly evaluate whether the MBacc has been a success – it was piloted in only 10 schools in its first academic year. However, several other of England’s regional mayors have called for greater power over the school curriculum to link it more closely with their local economy.Some mayors complain that the Department for Education has been one of the most stubborn government bodies when it comes to devolving powers outside Whitehall.Explore more on these topicsEducation policySchoolsEnglandAndy BurnhamYouth unemploymentVocational educationYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew and Tristan Tate to remain in jail until next extradition hearing | Andrew Tate | The Guardian
description: Social media influencers fighting against extradition to UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Social media influencers fighting against extradition to UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegations
Content: Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan speak to the media as they arrive in Romania from US on 22 March 2025.Photograph: Daniel Mihăilescu/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndrew Tate and his brother Tristan speak to the media as they arrive in Romania from US on 22 March 2025.Photograph: Daniel Mihăilescu/AFP/Getty ImagesAndrew TateAndrew and Tristan Tate to remain in jail until next extradition hearingSocial media influencers fighting against extradition to UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegationsAssociated PressMon 27 Jul 2026 16.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 16.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSocial media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail at least two more weeks until their next hearing as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge said on Monday.US magistrate Lauren Louis set a detention hearing for 13 August to determine whether the Tates should stay in jail or be released during what could be a months-long extradition process.The brothers were not in court on Monday or required to be there and have remained in jail since making a brief court appearance two days after their 18 July arrest.The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the US, Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing.Attorneys for the brothers said on Monday that they want the US government to turn over documents that UK officials submitted to secure their arrest.“They don’t have anything but the accusations,” Joseph McBride, an attorney, said after the hearing. “It’s just their word against our word right now.”The UK has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the state department, Alejandra Lopez, a US attorney, said in court.The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes.Jackie Perczek, another one of their attorneys, said the Tates have shown they are not a flight risk by returning to Romania every month after they were accused there of luring women for sexual exploitation.“For three years they have not fled,” she said. “They’ve traveled the world and every month they return to Romania.”The former professional kickboxers, who have dual US and UK citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn’t expect any help from the president.McBride said shortly after the Tates were arrested that “they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit,” he said.McBride said the extradition attempt was politically motivated, though he provided no details.Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in south-eastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”.The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the UK between 2012 and 2015.The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case has not gone forward because of legal and procedural problems.Andrew Tate, 39, became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the UK reality television show Big Brother. He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman.He has amassed more than 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women.Explore more on these topicsAndrew TatenewsShareReuse this content

title: Families in London temporary housing told they cannot use in-built air conditioning | Society | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Two children taken to hospital during heatwaves after residents told units in glass-fronted block ‘not offered as amenity’
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Exclusive: Two children taken to hospital during heatwaves after residents told units in glass-fronted block ‘not offered as amenity’
Content: Some residents at Britannia Point in Colliers Wood, London, experienced such stifling conditions young children became ill.Photograph: Paul Gapper/AlamyView image in fullscreenSome residents at Britannia Point in Colliers Wood, London, experienced such stifling conditions young children became ill.Photograph: Paul Gapper/AlamySocietyFamilies in London temporary housing told they cannot use in-built air conditioningExclusive: Two children taken to hospital during heatwaves after residents told units in glass-fronted block ‘not offered as amenity’Peter WalkerMon 27 Jul 2026 12.21 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHomeless families placed in temporary accommodation inLondonwere told they could not use the in-built air conditioning as it had “not been offered as an amenity” for them, leading to two children being hospitalised during recent heatwaves.Other families placed in Britannia Point in Colliers Wood, south-west London, also experienced such stifling conditions that young children became ill. The company managing some of the tenancies involved told the Guardian households in temporary accommodation had now been told they could use the air conditioning.However, some residents said they were informed that if they used the system they would be billed via a standing charge rather than for how long the air conditioning ran, which could result in bills of up to £500 for the summer.The 19-storey glass-fronted block is owned by Criterion Capital, set up by the billionaire property magnate Asif Aziz. The companywas accusedthis year of trying to mass-evict tenants shortly before no-fault evictions were banned, something it has denied.The temporary accommodation tenancies, in which councils place otherwise homeless households in properties for periods that can last from weeks to years, are managed separately by lettings agencies, one of them London-based Aura Assets Management.After a tenant complained to the building management about their air conditioning not working, they were sent an email, seen by the Guardian, which said that under the tenancy as managed by Aura, air conditioning “has been switched off” for households in emergency accommodation.It went on: “Air conditioning has not been offered as an amenity under these arrangements, and the units cannot be switched back on as a result. You are welcome to use a portable fan or portable air conditioning unit at your own arrangement in the meantime.”Residents say the all-glass construction of the block and the fact that windows open only slightly mean that, without air conditioning, their flats have become unbearably hot.“It is very difficult to cool the flats down,” one person said. “I find that as soon as I enter the building, I become much hotter, start feeling sick and sweat profusely.”Alice Rogers, who lives in Britannia Point with her four-year-old son, Hassan, said they regularly had to leave the block due to the heat. “There is a window that you can open, but there’s not much of a difference that makes,” she said. “Whether you open it or close it, it’s just literally the same.”She added: “My son had a nosebleed the other day and was faint. I’m very much worried about his life.”Stuart Neaverson, a Labour councillor in Merton who has been trying to help people in Britannia Point along with the local MP, Labour’s Siobhain McDonagh, said he had been told about two children being taken to hospital because of the heat, calling the situation “disgraceful”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “With another heatwave imminent, it’s vital that air conditioning is restored immediately to everyone in the tower to help prevent a tragedy.”A statement from Aura Assets Management said the air conditioning was now “fully operational and tenants have been advised that they are welcome to use it”. It went on: “Given the exceptionally warm weather this summer, we have also encouraged sensible, rather than continuous, use, simply to help residents avoid unexpectedly high utility bills – not to discourage use of a service that exists for their comfort.”When asked about the email sent to a resident saying tenants in temporary accommodation were not given access to air conditioning, the company said that this “was issued by the building management based on the information and operational arrangements in place at the time”.This email was sent to a “couple of flats”, they said, adding: “The situation has since changed.”Criterion has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsSocietyHousingCommunitiesLondonHomelessnessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police make inquiries after Farage reports Polanski post for ‘inciting murder’ | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotine
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotine
Content: A Green party spokesperson said that Zack Polanski ‘condemns the image on the T-shirt’.Photograph: Rich McCarthy/PAView image in fullscreenA Green party spokesperson said that Zack Polanski ‘condemns the image on the T-shirt’.Photograph: Rich McCarthy/PANigel FaragePolice make inquiries after Farage reports Polanski post for ‘inciting murder’Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotineSinéad CampbellMon 27 Jul 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are “conducting inquiries” into an image shared by Green party leaderZack Polanskion Instagram after Reform UK reported it for “inciting murder”.The image showed a man wearing a black T-shirt with the words “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, alongside a photograph of a guillotine.AGreen partyspokesperson said that Polanski “condemns the image on the T-shirt” and accepted being tagged in a post with 20 images “without realising there was more to it than he had seen”.Nigel Farage shared a screenshot of the image on X and wrote: “This is what Zack Polanski has just posted on his Instagram.“If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski.”Reform UK’s spokesperson for home affairs, Zia Yusuf, said Polanski was “inciting murder”, and that sharing the image weeks after the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe, who was murdered in her home in Devon, was “staggering”.Last week, prosecutors told a court that a man allegedly hit Widdecombe 21 times over the head with a hammer in a “planned and targeted” attack.A Green party spokesperson said: “The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself [Polanski].“He [Polanski] and the Green party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division.”A spokesperson for the Metropolitan police said: “Earlier today, we received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media.“We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting inquiries into the matter.”Yusuf wrote on social media: “Zack Polanski has posted to his 713kInstagramfollowers a photo of a man in a T-shirt calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage.“Polanski is inciting murder. It must be treated as such by the police.”The image, which has since been removed from Polanski’s Instagram account, was shared in a collaborative post with other accounts, as part of a carousel of images from a Green party event on Sunday.The words on the T-shirt come from Making Plans for Nigel, a song by English rock band XTC, which was released as the lead single from the 1979 album Drums and Wires.A post on a website that appeared to sell the T-shirt for £20 stated: “Whether it’s a nod to old punk music or a sharper bit of political satire, this design is for those who prefer their statements with a side of mystery.”Earlier this month, Andy Burnham said that a serious review is needed into MP security after the murder of Ann Widdecombe. Jess Phillips previouslytold the Guardianthat the threat to MPs must be tackled at source, amid an ongoing refusal by social media platforms to take responsibility for what’s published on their platforms.According to theBBC, Polanski has not been contacted by the police.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageZack PolanskiReform UKGreen partyInstagramnewsShareReuse this content

title: Industrial chicken farming accelerating spread of diarrhoea bacteria, study finds | Chicken | The Guardian
description: Intensive nature of modern chicken farming creates ideal conditions for campylobacter, allowing bacteria to evolve
Author: Hannah Devlin
Headline: Intensive nature of modern chicken farming creates ideal conditions for campylobacter, allowing bacteria to evolve
Content: There are about 27 billion chickens in the world, a seven-fold increase since the 1960s.Photograph: David Tadevosian/AlamyView image in fullscreenThere are about 27 billion chickens in the world, a seven-fold increase since the 1960s.Photograph: David Tadevosian/AlamyChickenIndustrial chicken farming accelerating spread of diarrhoea bacteria, study findsIntensive nature of modern chicken farming creates ideal conditions forcampylobacter, allowing bacteria to evolveHannah DevlinScience correspondentMon 27 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndustrial chicken farming is accelerating the spread of the world’s most common bacterial cause of diarrhoea, scientists have found.The study found a dramatic increase in the exchange ofcampylobacterstrains between wild birds and chickens as farming has intensified, creating the ideal conditions for the bacteria to mix, spread and acquire new traits. There has also been a rise in antimicrobial resistance traits in circulating strains, raising concerns that serious illness in people will be more difficult to treat.“As the chicken population has exploded, they’ve increasingly picked up strains from different wild birds and become a cauldron of bacterial evolution,” said Prof Sam Sheppard of the University of Oxford and senior author of the paper. “Lots of strains come together and hybridise. We do not want that, because that’s where new Frankenstein monster bugs emerge.”Campylobacteris the most common bacterial cause of diarrhoea worldwide, causingmore than three timesas many gastroenteritis cases in the UK each year as all other monitored foodborne bacteria combined. An estimated 60-80% ofcampylobacterinfections are caught from raw chicken.“Cooking kills pathogens, but just a tiny splash and it’s on your lettuce leaves or your hands or your knife,” said Sheppard.Most people will get better without treatment, but sometimes antibiotics are required and infection also raises the risk of irritable bowel syndrome. Rising rates of antimicrobial resistance, which occurs when bacteria resist drugs designed to kill them, mean that some antibiotics that were previously used to treatcampylobacterinfections are no longer effective.The latest work suggests that the evolution of the infection is being fuelled by the unprecedented scale of chicken production.A chart showing the rapid increase of poultry production per capita since the 1960s.Chickens now account for about 70% of all bird biomass on EarthSince the 1960s, global chicken numbers have increased seven-fold toapproximately 27 billion birds, accounting for about 70% of all bird biomass on Earth. Intensive breeding has led to “super growing” chickens that reach adult size and are slaughtered at around five weeks old.
