The industrialisation of chicken farming has led to affordable animal protein at scale, but also presents new health risks.The latest work, published in the journalProceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, analysed nearly 2,800 bacterial genomes collected from chickens and wild birds in 30 countries, including the UK, US and China, between 1979 and 2024.The dataset allowed the scientists to reconstruct the evolutionary trees of the diverse strains, including the rate of exchange between hosts. Prior to domestication of the chicken 5,000 years ago, strains ofcampylobactertended to be tightly linked to individual species of birds, with little cross-infection. But as chicken numbers increased, this picture changed, with an estimated 100-fold increase in transitions of strains between chickens and wild birds since 1900 compared with pre-domestication – a trend that appears to have continued steeply in recent decades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The scale is what’s bad,” said Sheppard. “By adjusting the world’s ecosystems in this dramatic way, it leads to the evolution of pathogens within those birds. That’s a massive risk to us. We can’t continue to produce chickens at this huge capacity.”The researchers also identified genetic changes incampylobacterthat were associated with adaptation to the chicken environment. These included genes involved in antimicrobial resistance, which can help bacteria survive and thrive in modern poultry production systems, where antibiotics are routinely given to encourage rapid growth or to keep disease under control in densely packed sheds.Maya Pardo, legal coordinator at Communities Against FactoryFarming(CAFF), said: “Intensive chicken farming has spread out of control in the UK, and the 100-fold increase in the movement ofcampylobacteris the latest in a long list of devastating consequences. While communities are desperately calling for no more factory farms, the government is absurdly looking to relax planning rules to build yet more of these disease-ridden industrial facilities.”Explore more on these topicsChickenFoodHealthFarmingFarm animalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I would be ashamed to have written any part of this’: Odyssey translator Emily Wilson attacks Nolan blockbuster | Movies | The Guardian
description: Wilson, whose work on Homer’s epic was praised by Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with ‘nothing convincing to say’
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Wilson, whose work on Homer’s epic was praised by Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with ‘nothing convincing to say’
Content: ‘Underdeveloped’ … Matt Damon and Charlize Theron in The OdysseyPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Underdeveloped’ … Matt Damon and Charlize Theron in The OdysseyPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMovies‘I would be ashamed to have written any part of this’: Odyssey translator Emily Wilson attacks Nolan blockbusterWilson, whose work on Homer’s epic was praised by Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with ‘nothing convincing to say’Peter Bradshaw reviews The Odyssey‘At times I felt I’d bitten off more than I could chew’: Christopher Nolan interviewedWhat Nolan’s Odyssey changed, invented – and left outAndrew PulverMon 27 Jul 2026 10.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 21.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmily Wilson, the classicist whose 2017 translation of Homer’s Odysseywas cited by Christopher Nolan in early publicityfor his hugely successful adaptation of the poem, has roundly criticised the film, saying “it has nothing convincing to say” and that it “lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth”.Go woke, get rich: why rightwing hate campaigns don’t affect the box officeRead moreIn a scathing essay for the London Review of Books, Wilson writes: “I had hoped that Nolan’s affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters. But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality … the film’s vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants.”Wilson adds: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great. It has nothing convincing to say about time, memory, history, war, or about the relationship between one warrior’s glorious return and the lives of his family, adversaries, comrades, friends and neighbours. It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth. Its narrative structure is gimmicky. The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.”View image in fullscreen‘And all the food looks horrible’ … Emily Wilson.Photograph: Elijah EllisWilson also noted Nolan’s admiration for the opening line of her Odyssey translation: “Tell me about a complicated man” – but added: “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”Wilson, who is department chair and professor of classical studies at the University of Pennsylvania, also went on the attack inan interview with the Sunday Times, saying: “It didn’t land emotionally for me at all. Which I think is partly about the fact that, unlike Homer, it’s not very well written.”The music in Nolan’s Odyssey is as well-crafted – and bloodlessly forgettable – as the film itselfRead more“The characters don’t have the kind of depth the Homeric characters have. I felt, ‘Do I really care if this guy gets back to his wife?’ You haven’t given me any reason to.”Why is it so hard to translate The Odyssey?Nevertheless, Wilson acknowledged the impact the film is already having on cultural awareness of ancient Greek literature as well as cinema itself. Saying “the release ofThe Odysseyis still an event to celebrate,” she suggests: “This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas … translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves … [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments.”“Nolan,” Wilson says, “is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful.”Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyHomerClassicsChristopher NolannewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia and North Korea finalising first road crossing amid concerns it serves as Ukraine war supply route | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: New bridge makes it easier to dodge satellite surveillance, investigation argues, as Ukrainian president warns Russia is to receive 30,000 more North Korean soldiers
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: New bridge makes it easier to dodge satellite surveillance, investigation argues, as Ukrainian president warns Russia is to receive 30,000 more North Korean soldiers
Content: Satellite imagery from April 2026 shows a newly built bridge that forms the first ever road crossing between North Korea and Russia. Above it is the Friendship bridge, the only rail crossing between the two countries.Photograph: Truth Hounds / Planet Labs PBCView image in fullscreenSatellite imagery from April 2026 shows a newly built bridge that forms the first ever road crossing between North Korea and Russia. Above it is the Friendship bridge, the only rail crossing between the two countries.Photograph: Truth Hounds / Planet Labs PBCUkraineRussia and North Korea finalising first road crossing amid concerns it serves as Ukraine war supply routeNew bridge makes it easier to dodge satellite surveillance, investigation argues, as Ukrainian president warns Russia is to receive 30,000 more North Korean soldiersRaphael RashidandLuke HardingMon 27 Jul 2026 19.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 22.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia andNorth Koreaare close to completing a bridge that will form the first road link ever built between them, amid concerns the two increasingly close allies are creating infrastructure to boost military cooperation in the Ukraine war.The bridge spans the Tumen River, between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, a remote, thinly populated stretch of borderland where the river marks the final few miles of the frontier before it reaches the coast.The crossing is now largely complete. North Korea finished its side of the project, including customs and quarantine facilities, ahead of a planned opening on 19 June, but Russia has fallen behind on its own side of the border, and no new opening date has been confirmed.Russian and North Korean authorities have made no secret of the bridge project, saying it is intended to expand trade and tourism.However, a new investigation by Ukrainian human rights group Truth Hounds and shared with the Guardian suggests it is intended more to provide a discreet military logistics corridor than to boost trade.View image in fullscreenA newly built bridge that spans the Tumen River, forming the first ever road crossing between North Korea and Russia.Photograph: Ministry of Transport of the Russian FederationNazar Myhun, who led the open-source research at Truth Hounds, said a key reason behind its conclusion was the fact that it is much easier to evade satellite monitoring – a surveillance method used by the west to understand Russian and North Korean activities – by using roads compared with a rail network.The new crossing over the Tumen River runs alongside the Friendship Bridge, which is the only rail link between the two countries.Russia and North Korea’s road network is far bigger than their rail network, he said, making it harder to watch in its entirety. Loading and unloading of trucks can also take place much more quickly than for railcars, which are exposed to satellite passes for a longer period of time.“The type of railcar visible in an image reveals a great deal about the cargo, and certain categories of goods are transported in open railcars, which allows them to be identified,” Myhun told the Guardian.map“Trucks, by contrast, almost always look the same in satellite imagery.”Road cargo can also be loaded anywhere, as opposed to trains, which rely on a handful of fixed rail hubs, Myhun said.Russian officials have presented the project as a way to expand trade andtourism. Andrey Nikitin, Russia’s transport minister, said: “The opening of the new road bridge will increase mutual trade, optimise logistics, strengthen cultural ties, and transform border areas into dynamically developing economic hubs.”North Korea’s state media news agency, KCNA, has similarly cast the bridge as a way to boost “travel of persons, tourism and circulation of commodities” between the two countries.However, Truth Hounds argues that the bridge’s economic rationale is weak. The crossing is estimated to have cost more than $100m, versus bilateral trade that was reportedly worthjust $34m in 2024. Tourism from Russia into North Korea remains tightly controlled and largely limited to escorted tours, with around 10,000Russian visitors in 2025. Pyongyang, where most foreign tourists visit, lies over 500km from the crossing.Instead, the investigation concludes that the crossing is better understood as strategic infrastructure: a corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, and for Russian technology and resources to move in the opposite direction.View image in fullscreenSatellite imagery from April 2026 shows construction under way on a border checkpoint on the Russian side of the only road bridge connecting Russia and North Korea. New buildings and building materials are visible on site. The checkpoint, reported to be 40% complete as of April, is planned to be 10 lanes wide.Photograph: Truth Hounds / Planet Labs PBCMyhun said Truth Hounds monitors Russia-North Korea cooperation closely because it considers it “one of the key factors affecting Russia’s strength in this war” onUkraine.The deepening relationship has also made the two-way exchange of weapons and technology between the two countries “easier and less transparent”, he said, which also poses a threat to North Korea’s neighbours.The Kremlin has been contacted about the claims made in the investigation but has yet to respond.A growing military allianceThe bridge over the Tumen River is about 1km long and seven metres wide, with two lanes, part of a wider 4.7km crossing that includes approach roads. Satellite imagery also shows supporting infrastructure being built on the Russian side, including a helicopter landing pad.However, the rail line is hobbled by a mismatch in rail gauge between Russia and North Korea, meaning wheelsets must be changed to allow trains to travel further into either country’s network, a limitation the new road bridge does not share.mapOpen-source researchers have previously relied on satellite imagery of the rail crossing to monitor suspected weapons transfers between the two countries.Construction of the bridge began after Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong-un signed a comprehensivestrategic partnership pactin June 2024, cementing military ties that have since seen North Korea provide troops, artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles to support Russia’s war in Ukraine.It forms a small part of a much broader military relationship. More than14,000 North Korean troopshave fought alongside Russian forces in the Kursk region, after Ukraine staged a surprise counter-invasion in August 2024. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy hasnow warnedthat Russia is preparing to receive a further 30,000 soldiers. Moscow and Pyongyang have expanded cooperation on weapons, military technology and reconstruction.In 2023,Reuters reportedthat satellite images showed an estimated 2,000 containers exported from the North Korean port of Rason to Russia, believed to have contained artillery shells and possibly short-range missiles.Kim haspraised North Korean soldierswho fought and died for Russia and unveiledhousing for the families of those killed. At least 2,000 North Korean servicemen are believed to have died fighting in Russia’s war, with two badly wounded soldiers taken prisoner.Explore more on these topicsUkraineNorth KoreaRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham’s Ukraine gambit is a symbolic start for PM who wants to look inward | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: New prime minister wants to focus at home, but his first week already suggests the world has other plans
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: New prime minister wants to focus at home, but his first week already suggests the world has other plans
Content: Andy Burnham told Volodymyr Zelenskyy: ‘We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.’Photograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham told Volodymyr Zelenskyy: ‘We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.’Photograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APAndy BurnhamAnalysisBurnham’s Ukraine gambit is a symbolic start for PM who wants to look inwardPippa CrerarPolitical editorNew prime minister wants to focus at home, but his first week already suggests the world has other plansMon 27 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.37 EDTShareIt took just seven days in office forAndy Burnhamto meet his first world leader. As he welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday, the new prime minister told the Ukrainian president it was “no accident” he was his first international visitor since entering No 10.“It is intended to send a very clear message,” Burnham told him. “We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” In short, the UK’s support for Kyiv would continue despite the change in leadership.ForKeir Starmer, the relationship with Zelenskyy became one of the defining ones of his premiership. He visited Ukraine four times over his two years in office, inviting the Ukrainian president back to the UK on another four occasions. They also met regularly at international summits.In a symbolic move, Starmer travelled to Ukraine during his final week in office, receiving the order of freedom medal for his role leading the coalition of the willing and helping to persuade Donald Trump back to the table on Ukraine after he flirted with siding with Putin.But over the course of his premiership, the formerLabourleader faced accusations of spending too much time on international issues instead of domestic ones, with his critics nicknaming him “never here Keir” and even his own Downing Street team complaining that he “needs to get off a plane”.View image in fullscreenZelenskyy talks to Burnham. The UK prime minister said: ‘It is intended to send a very clear message.’Photograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APBurnham, in contrast, has always been clear he would prioritise what was happening at home, reflecting his own political instincts as well as his wariness of not falling into the same trap as his predecessor. But it led some in the Labour party to worry that he would be unprepared for the global stage.“It’s a frustrating characterisation because not many incoming prime ministers, including Keir, have any experience of international affairs,” one of his inner circle said. “Andy has said that his priority will be domestic, but of course there will be moments where he’ll need to be more outward facing.”Day to day, Burnham’s allies have suggested that he will rely on delegating responsibility to his team – including his foreign secretary in Ed Miliband and senior diplomatic adviser in Jonathan Powell, whom he persuaded to stay on in No 10 from the Starmer administration.Labour MPs point out that Yvette Cooper, Miliband’s predecessor, was often left fighting for influence as there were so many other senior figures who saw themselves as the de facto foreign secretary, including the deputy prime minister, David Lammy, Powell, and Starmer himself.One senior MP said: “I suspect that Ed may be in a fortunate position where he is actually given more freedom than other foreign secretaries in the past. As long as Ed is known to have the authority of the PM and to be trusted to speak for him, then this may be his moment.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APOther Labour figures suggested that strong prime ministers should be able to delegate and rely on their teams. One said: “I don’t think Andy is particularly interested in foreign affairs. He’ll need to front some things up, but as long as he’s well briefed and charming, he doesn’t need to make the day-to-day decisions like Keir did.”But they warned there would inevitably be moments where complex international issues “crash land” on UK domestic policy – as Starmer found to his cost when dealing with Trump – and he would have no choice but to intervene.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham has already indicated he will not shy away from standing up to the US president. “Obviously, the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything that they say,”he told the Guardianlast month.There are some with experience of foreign affairs in government who believe that Starmer has already done the hard yards on foreign policy – on Ukraine, the European Union and the US in particular – so Burnham just has to stick to the same course.In his final interview in office, Starmer told his successor that he should not spend less time focusing on international affairs, in order to prioritise the situation at home. “It’s not sensible to think you can just separate these two things out,” he said.“If you’re PM and you care what bills are going to be like in any household around the country, you have to care about finding a lasting solution to the situation in Ukraine, you have to care about what happens in the strait of Hormuz.”But those around Burnham believe he can better balance them. At least for now. They have been watching events in Iran closely, mindful of the potential to cause yet more global economic upheaval should Trump take further action.“Andy has a bit of space now to prioritise policy at home – but it could all be blown off course by Iran,” one Foreign Office insider said. “He has to seize this moment to talk about the domestic, because this window might not come again.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamForeign policyLabourKeir StarmeranalysisShareReuse this content

title: How to create the perfect women’s holiday capsule wardrobe: 12 pieces worth packing | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Too many outfits and not enough suitcase space? Whether it’s sightseeing or sundowners, our fashion writer shares her secrets for packing smarter
Author: Charlotte Gornall
Headline: Too many outfits and not enough suitcase space? Whether it’s sightseeing or sundowners, our fashion writer shares her secrets for packing smarter
Content: Pack smart … a well-planned wardrobe saves space without sacrificing style.Photograph: d3sign/GettyView image in fullscreenPack smart … a well-planned wardrobe saves space without sacrificing style.Photograph: d3sign/GettyThe FilterFashionHow to create the perfect women’s holiday capsule wardrobe: 12 pieces worth packingToo many outfits and not enough suitcase space? Whether it’s sightseeing or sundowners, our fashion writer shares her secrets for packing smarterThe travel essentials that made your holiday betterDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereCharlotte GornallMon 27 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.When you hear the words capsule wardrobe, you probably picture beige knits and minimalist tailoring. A capsule isn’t just about dressing neutrally, though: it’s about choosing a handful of pieces that work together in countless combinations.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.There is no time that skill is more important than when you’re packing for a holiday. I have streamlined my approach by sticking to a simple rule of thumb: instead of packing for every possible scenario, I focus on versatile staples that can be dressed up or down and worn more than once.Every holiday capsule should include three essentials: a dependable basic, one statement piece, and shoes that can take you from sightseeing to dinner. Build everything else around those foundations and you’ll find yourself wearing every item you pack.Theultimate whiteteeView image in fullscreenAirism T-shirt£14.90 at UniqloThe cornerstone of any wardrobe. I love this T-shirt because of its boxy silhouette and subtle side slits that create a slightly flared shape. Plus, the Airism cotton fabric is sweat-wicking and feels cool against the skin. I wear mine with pretty much everything from denim shorts during the day to a statement skirt for dinner.A pair of statement earringsView image in fullscreenMinerva bow-drop beaded earrings£50 at SelfridgesYou only really need a few pieces of jewellery: something understated and everyday, and something to transform an outfit in seconds. These sculptural earrings will lift even the most minimal outfit.Shoes that doit allView image in fullscreenTeva mid-form sandals£44.99 at SchuhI often travel with one pair of shoes, so need a pair that does it all. These strappysandalsare comfortable enough for long days exploring, but smart enough to wear for dinner thanks to their minimal design.A skirt that becomes a dressView image in fullscreenMulti-way skirt£59 at Omnes£59.99 at John LewisMultifunctional clothing is the holy grail of holiday packing. A smocked waist maxi skirt can also be worn as a bandeau midi dress thanks to its stretchy waistband. It’s two outfits in one, saving valuable suitcase space. This pillar-box red one is made from 100% cotton and has an adorable frill detail highlighting the flattering drop waist.A multi-use makeup stickView image in fullscreenIlia multi-stick£36 at Ilia£36 at Space NKThe same logic applies to your beauty bag. Ilia’s multi-stick adds buildable colour to cheeks and lips without feeling heavy in warm weather. Its compact packaging is ideal for travelling and its stick shape makes it easy to apply on the go.Anecklace that won’t mind a dipView image in fullscreenPalma Solesi waterproof necklace£54.99 at Katie LoxtonHoliday jewellery should be effortless, joyful – and waterproof, especially if you’re dipping in and out of a pool or the sea. This gold and pastel green beaded necklace is water- and sweat-proof, and will lift an evening outfit, too.Three-in-one co-ordView image in fullscreenSightseer linen striped pant set£88 at Free PeopleA good co-ord is three outfits in one: worn together, or each piece styled separately. This ocean-blue striped linen set feels relaxed, but pair it with a sleek sandal and it could easily feel at home at dinner. With an elasticated waist and adjustable straps, it’s comfortable too.Elegant summer shortsView image in fullscreenLyrebird lace trim silky shorts£41 at AnthropologieMy summer evening staple has been this pair oflace trim shortsfrom Reformation. Paired with a white T-shirt they look subtle but dressy, thanks to the sheen of the fabric. I also love this more affordable powder-blue pair from Anthropologie. With a flattering high waist and elasticated fit, they’re comfortable without compromising on style.A beach-to-bar bagView image in fullscreenLarge mesh beach bag£30 at M&SAccessories are the easiest place to introduce personality, and a colourful bag will instantly brighten a simple outfit. I love this cobalt blueDragon Diffusion bag, but I wouldn’t necessarily want to take something so precious to the beach. Alternatively, this affordable bright blue mesh bag from Marks & Spencer is large enough for your daily essentials while adding a welcome pop of colour.Classic sunniesView image in fullscreenOversized sunglasses£42 at &Other StoriesChannel Jane Birkin and go for maximum coverage with a pair of oversizedsunglasses. This softly squared style from & Other Stories feels timeless enough to wear year after year, so look after them on holiday.Atwo-in-one hatView image in fullscreenCotton reversible bucket hat£14 at M&SA sun hat is one of the most important holiday accessories, which is why it has to be the most versatile. This reversible style from M&S gives you two looks in one, and its neutral colour palette will complement almost anything in your suitcase. In an easy canvas fabric, it will pack down to almost nothing too.A versatile silk scarfView image in fullscreenAbstract spot-print square silk scarf£65 at John LewisTied around your hair, looped through a bag, worn as a belt or even styled as a top, a silk scarf is one of the most versatile accessories there is. Best of all, it takes up little to no room in your luggage. I love this blue polka-dot print one: it’s larger than the average bandana style, making it much easier to style multiple ways. Charity shops are also brilliant hunting grounds.Explore more on these topicsFashionThe FilterBeautyAccessoriesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I work in a hospital – and didn’t know I was having a heart attack. Here’s what more women should know | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Women and men exhibit different heart attack symptoms. Knowing these lesser-known factors can help save your life
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Women and men exhibit different heart attack symptoms. Knowing these lesser-known factors can help save your life
Content: ‘The ER staff thought I might have had a heart attack and would have been on my way to another without medical intervention. When I heard the news, I was stunned.’Illustration: Yi hui Chang/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The ER staff thought I might have had a heart attack and would have been on my way to another without medical intervention. When I heard the news, I was stunned.’Illustration: Yi hui Chang/The GuardianWell actuallyI work in a hospital – and didn’t know I was having a heart attack. Here’s what more women should knowWomen and men exhibit different heart attack symptoms. Knowing these lesser-known factors can help save your lifeJulie CharnetMon 27 Jul 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew months ago at work, when I rose from my seat and walked a few steps, something felt off. There was a strange pressure in my chest and rib cage, but I ignored it, took my water bottle from the kitchen and returned to my desk.The next day it happened again. There was no pain and my breathing was fine. But whenever I stood up and took a few steps, the odd squeezing would return. I work at a hospital as a neurosurgery coordinator, and the wall was lined with posters about stroke and heart distress signs. I barely glanced at the pictures, having memorized them years ago.I stood in the hallway waiting for the sensation to pass. One of my co-workers, a nurse, saw me and asked if something was wrong. I told her I felt achy in my upper body, and that my neck and chest felt odd. She suggested I go to the ER.“You never know,” she said. I thought it was probably just a pulled muscle, but I followed her advice. I owe her my life.Deaths fromheart diseaseare the number one killer of women, according to the American Heart Association. It causes a third of deaths a year – more than all forms of cancers combined.At the ER, I mentioned the pressure in my chest area so the triage staff ran tests to check for heart trouble. However, they saw nothing abnormal on my electrocardiogram (which measures electric heart rhythm) or troponin levels (a protein blood test used to diagnose heart attacks).The emergency staff sent me home with cholesterol and blood pressure medication. The following morning, I called a cardiologist because I was still having the odd sensation. After checking my arteries with a catheter, the doctor admitted me to the hospital. They had found blockages in two of my arteries; one was in the largest coronary artery, the kind of blockage that leads to so-called “widowmaker” heart attacks.According to the physicians, it was severe enough to discuss heart bypass surgery. Fortunately, a stent was sufficient. The ER staff thought I might have had a heart attack and would have been on my way to another without medical intervention. When I heard the news, I was stunned. I worked in healthcare and was familiar with the signs of cardiac issues. How could I not know my heart was in serious trouble?It turns out that this issue is fairly common. Symptoms show up differently in women – something I am now grateful to know.What heart attack symptoms should women look out for?A heart attack is a specific event, in which the blood flow to the heart muscle is suddenly blocked. (Conversely, heart disease refers to any condition that affects the heart – a common example is coronary artery disease, a buildup of plaque in the arteries. Symptoms for heart attack and heart disease are not the same, but there is some overlap.)Symptoms of heart attacks are different for men and women, according to theAmerican Heart Association.The most common signs for men are pain in the chest, left arm, jaw, neck or back; nausea, vomiting, indigestion; and shortness of breath.For women, the list of possible symptoms is longer: chest pain or pressure in lower chest, upper abdomen, jaw, neck and upper back; nausea or vomiting; fainting and shortness of breath; indigestion or extreme fatigue. Chest pain or pressure is not always present.In addition, issues such as high blood pressure during pregnancy, menopause, hormone replacement therapy and use of birth control should be considered in evaluating overall risk.However, this list is not exhaustive. Women should be prepared to look into other areas that may not stand out as symptomatic. For instance, the heart and stomach share nerves, and many women do not know that indigestion, nausea andGI distresscan also be heart disease symptoms, said Dr Sirisha Vadali, a cardiologist at HonorHealth in Scottsdale, Arizona, specializing in women’s heart disease: “Lesser-known external factors are vital to getting an accurate diagnosis.”Vadali also said it was important to notice even small physical changes that may not seem related to the heart. I told Vadali about my unexpected diagnosis. “I hate to say it, but I’m not surprised,” she said. “I’ve spoken to many women who feel something is wrong, and don’t present the way men do. It’s difficult to explain to medical personnel that nothing really hurts, but your body is telling you there is real trouble – somewhere.”According to theBritish Heart Foundation, symptoms may come on acutely, like they did for me. Vadali cautions women to take note of any sense that their body is responding differently and consult a medical provider if concerned.“I had one young woman who couldn’t walk up a flight of stairs today, but she did two last week just fine,” she said of a patient who ended up needing prompt cardiac assistance.What tests are helpful for diagnosing heart disease?Vadali mentioned many women dismiss their own symptoms as anxiety, or just assume they are unfit.“There’s an under-appreciation of cardiovascular risks in women,” said Dr Americo Simonini, a cardiovascular specialist with Cedars-Sinai medical center in Los Angeles. Other than the usual sugar, cholesterol and blood pressure checks, what else should we be checking for?“We aggressively measure other things in men that we should be measuring in women,” said Simonini. He mentioned certain types of tests for proteins in the blood and inflammation can present a clearer picture in preventing a future incident, including:Elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, or hs-CRP, score: the level of these proteins increases with inflammation, and a high level can indicate blood vessels in the heart are narrowing (cardiovascular disease).Lipoprotein(a) elevation: a genetic test forinherited LDL (“bad”) cholesterol; high levels significantly increase risk of heart attack via plaque buildup in arteries.Apolipoprotein B elevation: measures the amount of Apo B, which carries substances in your blood that make the plaque.Coronary artery calcium score (high CAC): a high score probably means a large amount of plaque is present in arteries and the risk of a future heart attack is high.“There is a misconception that women are protected until menopause. That’s simply not true,” Simonini said. Women can develop heart disease at any age, but your riskincreasesafter your periods stop. Before menopause, your body makes more estrogen, which helps protect against heart disease. That’s also why women generally develop coronary artery disease later than men.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWomen of all ages are surprised to learn they have heart disease, said Dr Sonal Chandra of Focus Cardiology, a private practice in Chicago, Illinois.“Women are far less likely to receive imaging or other interventions. This happens even when they are showing comparable indicators and classic symptoms of heart distress,” she said. “No one should feel they have to walk away without some answers.”If patients feel their complaints are not being addressed, they can and should ask for additional diagnostic testing. The more information you have on how symptoms are evolving, the better.Physicians need to pay attention to women who notice any abnormal physical changes, rather than assume it’s temporary or simply fatigue and stress, Simonini said. Doctors should ask questions and find out why a patient is having those symptoms at that time.He acknowledged that doctors need more education about women and their disease risks. All of the experts I spoke to encourage women to advocate for themselves by doing the following:Ask your primary care doctor what kinds of cardiac testing are available to you. If bloodwork is suggested first, do it. If you have a family history of heart attacks and want to check your arteries now, discuss proteins and inflammation markers. You may need to consult a specialist for these steps.Provide as much information as possible, even if you don’t think it’s related to your current problem. It could make a difference in someone deciding on a scan or sending you to the ER. The more details you provide, the better someone can assist. For instance, if you have a stomach ache that hasn’t gone away in three days, disclose it.Keep asking about next steps. You are entitled to an answer and it’s the doctor’s job to help you find it. If your inquiries are not being taken seriously, book an appointment elsewhere. Do not give up or wait it out. Persistence can help you identify serious risks.Not every pain or ache means you have a serious health issue, nor that it is cardiac related. It’s important to remember that, outside of a sharp shooting pain above your heart, it truly could be something minor. There is also no single test that can predict your future health. Numerous variables and overlapping conditions are part of a much larger map. Experts simply encourage you to take notice of your own risk factors and monitor how you feel.Why is so little known about heart disease effects in women?Historically, large-scale research specific to female biology and genetics has not been available. In the 2010s, one heart health researchernotedthat the participants in typical cardiovascular disease clinical trials were 85% male and that female participants were predominantly postmenopausal.For example, an influential large-scaleclinical studythat began in 2011, known as the Million Veteran Program (MVP), involved mostly white, male participants from a similar age group. Participants were monitored for kidney function, blood pressure and diabetes over a span of 20 years. “They had all this data but only from a specific group,” Simonini noted. This massive pool of data informed how treatments and drugs for cardiac disease were developed – and that knowledge became the standard. The MVP has since added new data sets to include a more diverse population.If research trials were more accommodating, greater female participation would probably follow, said Chandra.“Women are often primary care givers and work full-time, and it can be a hardship for them to participate during business hours,” she said.However, the experts I spoke to agree that over the past 10 years, education about gender differences in cardiac health has been slowly improving.In 2016, the University of Pennsylvania established a dedicated women’s cardiovascular health curriculum for itscardiology fellowshipprogram. Columbia University offers program electives for medical students, residents and graduate students on cardiovascular risks unique towomen.This year at Harvard Medical School, continuing medical educationcredits(CME) are being offered for “diagnosing, managing, and treating medical conditions unique to and prevalent in women”.What should I do to monitor for heart disease?Experts stressed the importance of regular testing and checkups from your primary care provider. This can provide both of you with baseline information to compare future measurements against. Check in with them more than once a year if changes such as medications or procedures are necessary, experts say. Provide as much detail about family, environment and diet as possible. This can help your doctor design a prevention plan for the next five years or beyond. This may involve nutrition, genetic testing, imaging, medication or other lifestyle changes.“Keep asking more and more questions; we are in a profession where we can’t afford to be wrong,” Simonini said.Julie Charnet is a healthcare worker and writer in PhiladelphiaExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyHeart attackHeart diseaseWomen's healthHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The real love story behind Colin from Accounts: ‘I wouldn’t want to write with anyone else’ | Colin from Accounts | The Guardian
description: As the show takes its final bow, Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer reflect on ‘having a ball’ playing exes while being married with kids, ignoring notes from US TV executives and having ‘big old cries’ at the end
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: As the show takes its final bow, Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer reflect on ‘having a ball’ playing exes while being married with kids, ignoring notes from US TV executives and having ‘big old cries’ at the end
Content: ‘We don’t need to sell Australia to the world’ … Harriet Dyer and Patrick Brammall, the married stars and creators of Colin from Accounts, which is ending with season three.Photograph: Kenneth KwokView image in fullscreen‘We don’t need to sell Australia to the world’ … Harriet Dyer and Patrick Brammall, the married stars and creators of Colin from Accounts, which is ending with season three.Photograph: Kenneth KwokColin from AccountsInterviewThe real love story behind Colin from Accounts: ‘I wouldn’t want to write with anyone else’Sian CainAs the show takes its final bow, Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer reflect on ‘having a ball’ playing exes while being married with kids, ignoring notes from US TV executives and having ‘big old cries’ at the endMon 27 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt began, as all great romances do, with a nipple flash. WhenColin from Accounts, the little comedy that could, started airing back in 2022, the world fell in love – hard and fast. It was a surprisingly prickly Australian show about Ashley, a student doctor (Harriet Dyer), and Gordon, an older brewery owner (Patrick Brammall), who fall in love after she pops a boob at him, he hits a dog with his car, and they jointly land an astronomical vet bill and a new pet.The show shared its name with its furriest star – full name: “Colin from accounts payable, who is working on the big merger” – and it was as charming as the title suggested, winning fans across Hollywood and the world. That Brammall and Dyer were actually a couple, now married with two kids and a dog (no wheels), just made everyone love the show even more.But Colin from Accounts is now ending with its third season – which some may feel is premature, but undeniably confident. “We don’t want to flog a dead horse,” Brammall says. “It definitely feels right.”Colin from Accounts season 3 review – TV’s most charming romcom comes to a funny, emotional endRead moreAs Dyer adds: “It is not that the horse is dead yet – we don’t even want to find it is having trouble breathing.”Wrapping their show, which they both also write, has yet to fully sink in for Brammall. “I don’t think it’s hit me, honestly,” he says. “There was lots of mini moments – ‘Oh shit it’s the last time I’m gonna do this, it’s the last time I’m gonna do that.’” Dyer, meanwhile, has had three “big old cries”: “The last one was when I was in the editing suite and I just looked around at the little grey room and it came out like vomit.”Season one of Colin was a will-they-won’t-they story. Season two said well-they-have-but-should-they? Season three asks could they again? The new episodes open three years after Gordon made an excruciating marriage proposal to Ashley at a friend’s wedding: Ashley and Gordon have since split up and are dating other people, but are reunited when Gordon unwittingly makes a doctor’s appointment at Ashley’s work.View image in fullscreen‘We’re actors by trade, so we love pretendies’ … Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer in season three of Colin from Accounts.Photograph: John PlattA married couple with a hell of a lot of chemistry playing exes is fun to watch. “And it is fun to play,” says Brammall. “Obviously, we love playing the stuff where we’re falling in love, but we love having big arguments just as much. We’re actors by trade, so we love pretendies. I had a ball. I think Harri did too.”Season three has “a slight forlorn quality and an awkwardness – it’s almost like taking them back to the start”, adds Dyer. “All tension is good, I think. Yearning. It’s very easy to play that, especially with someone that you know so well.”Splitting Ashley and Gordon up just seemed like a fun, creative road to go down; the three-year time leap, meanwhile, was practical. “I’m almost 38 and Ash was 30 in the second season – we had to catch up a little bit!” Dyer laughs.The couple havepreviously said that they have one big fighteach season. What was it over this time?“Golly gosh, I think we didn’t have one,” Dyer says. “We’ve been having to get very economical with our energy.”Brammall laughs. “The last two seasons we’ve had one kid. This time we had two and it’s like, who’s got time? Who’s got the luxury of having a big fight?”“Those days are over,” Dyer adds. “Now it’s like, how do I say this in the least offensive way so we can make this butter cheese pasta and put the girls to bed?”View image in fullscreenHappier times … Gordon and Ashley in season one.Photograph: Tony Mott/BingeIt is rare that an Australian show set in Sydney would be completely devoid of the Harbour Bridge and Opera House shots the world expects. This wasn’t a conscious decision; Gordon owns a microbrewery, so Brammall and Dyer made him work in a part of Sydney populated by them: the inner west. But the result has meant international viewers have got a glimpse of a city that doesn’t feel too far from their own, bar the magpie song and gumtrees.“In episode five of this season we go to a beach, but that’s probably the first grain of sand in all the episodes of Colin. Which, yeah, as a Sydney show feels almost blasphemous,” Dyer says. “People haven’t seen that side of Sydney, which makes it interesting. Something about terraces and warehouses – it didn’t feel quintessentially Sydney, which gives it a universality.”“We don’t need to sell Sydney to the world, we don’t need to sell Australia to the world,” Brammall adds. He remembers an early attempt to market Colin as “a new Australian comedy”, to which Dyer responded: “Don’t say Australian comedy. It’s a new comedy.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Why are we so quick to brand it as Australian?” Brammall says. “How about we’re world class and we don’t have to do that? Let’s tell the story we want to tell and the Sydney of it, the Australia of it, can follow.”The stars of Colin from Accounts: ‘As I tapped Ewan McGregor’s shoulder, I knew I’d made the wrong decision’Read moreThere are enough local references in there for the home crowd – the band T-shirts, the soundtrack, the occasional “cunt” dropped by a nana. But they once did get a note from an American executive about using the word “arvo”: “They said, you should make that ‘afternoon’ so people in America know what we’re talking about. And we were like … no. It stayed in.”Part of Colin’s appeal comes from the palpable sense that every argument, every calamity, every embarrassment, has actually happened to someone in the show. A version of the poo incident in the very first episode happened to Dyer; the jibes about Gordon and Ashley’s age gap ring true too (Brammall is 50, Dyer is 37; a fan once mistook him for her father).Even Gordon hitting Colin with his car after being distracted by Ashley’s boob flash: Dyer once walked a pram into a pole after seeing a hot guy. “It wasn’tmybaby,” Dyer says, as Brammall laughs. “I wasn’t a very good babysitter. The baby was fine.”There are also the more serious moments, like Gordon’s fertility problems after surviving testicular cancer, which Brammall thinks was an unconscious link to his own infertility, caused by childhood illness. (Brammall and Dyer have two adopted daughters, Joni and Mabel.) “It’s not until you read it later that you go, ‘Oh I see that connects to something in my life,’” he says. “These little truthful thoughts or feelings or ideas or experiences can float through and generally, if it’s funny or if it feels real, then it’s in the show.”“We touch on taboo subjects that you sometimes wouldn’t dare touch. But we touch them kind of gently,” Dyer says.“And always with warmth,” Brammall adds. “We do the light and the dark thing – get people laughing and then punch them with something really heavy.”“It’s not all gold, but Pat and I are always trying to make it the best it can be,” Dyer says. (Brammall: “Oh fuck yeah.”) “We don’t think that we are authorities on anything.” (Brammall: “Oh fuck no.”) “We’re nervous today because we still caresomuch about whether people like it.”People already love Colin from Accounts, including famous fans Nick Offerman, Lena Dunham, Phoebe Waller-Bridge, Richard Curtis and Anne Hathaway; Brammall recently played the latter’s boyfriend in The Devil Wears Prada 2. From such great heights, what does success look like for Brammall and Dyer now? Dyer answers instantly: “Balance.”“Because the hours of this life are so demanding – it’s not really designed for a married couple to leave and come home at the same time when you’ve got little people looking for you,” she says. “To me, success looks like balance and finish reading my book. But we’re definitely going to work together again because I wouldn’t want to write with anybody else.”“That’s going to be an amazing life,” Brammall says.The first two episodes of Colin from Accounts season 3 are available to stream on Binge in Australia now, with new episodes streaming weekly. UK and US airdates are yet to be announced.Explore more on these topicsColin from AccountsAustralian televisionTelevisionTV comedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mayo beat 75-year-old ‘curse’ to become Gaelic football champions | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Team to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeats
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Team to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeats
Content: Fans celebrate outside Croke park stadium after Mayo beat Kerry in the 138th all-Ireland final.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAView image in fullscreenFans celebrate outside Croke park stadium after Mayo beat Kerry in the 138th all-Ireland final.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAIrelandMayo beat 75-year-old ‘curse’ to become Gaelic football championsTeam to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeatsRory CarrollIreland correspondentMon 27 Jul 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 14.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe hex is broken, dispelled, banished, and a story that bewitchedIrelandfor decades has ended in fairytale: Mayo are all-Ireland champions.Seventy-five years after a supposed curse condemned its Gaelic men’s football team toendless defeat, the county prevailed and uncorked a wave of emotion that engulfed even its rivals.The team will return to the west ofIrelandfor a euphoric homecoming on Monday evening after winning the senior football championship, a victory that thrilled Ireland and Mayo’s diaspora, including Joe Biden, Mark Carney and Noel and Liam Gallagher.View image in fullscreenMost pundits favoured Kerry to win but there were jubilant scenes when underdogs Mayo triumphed in Dublin instead.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PA“Mayo 1-20, Kerry 1-17. Chisel it on the gravestones, scribble it in the sky,” the Irish Times exulted. “Croke Park untethered, the whole place afloat for an hour on a lake of the sweetest tears that were ever cried.”Most pundits had favoured Kerry to win the 138th all-Ireland final and write another chapter of Mayo woe at Sunday’s contest at the Dublin stadium. Instead the underdogs triumphed and even some Kerry fans wept at the catharsis.View image in fullscreenMayo is the third biggest of the island of Ireland’s 32 counties but sparsely populated, with just 130,000 people.Photograph: Horizon International Images/AlamyFew seriously believed in the curse – it was said no member of the last winning team from 1951 would live to see another – but there was no doubting the drought that followed, with 11 defeats in 11 finals since 1989. A book about Mayo’s quest ​was titled House of Pain.Whenever the county made it to a final, a frisson gripped television viewers and the 82,000-strong stadium crowd: was this the day they would witness the end of the hex? On Sunday it was.“To every young boy and girl across Mayo and our diaspora across the world, never stop dreaming, stick your chest out and be proud to be from Mayo,” the team captain, Jack Coyne, declared as he held aloft the trophy named after Sam Maguire, a legendary player. “The wait is over. Sam is home.”Authorities had provisionally estimated a crowd of 40,000 would greet the team at McHale Park in the county town of Castlebar on Monday but that looks conservative, Gerry Bourke, the homecoming committee chair,told RTÉ. “After what I saw in Croke Park yesterday, I think we’ll have to revisit the plan.”Mayo, alandscape of bogs, rocks and Atlantic cliffs, is the third biggest of the island of Ireland’s 32 counties. It is sparsely populated, with just 130,000 people, but players and supporters have a reputation for fervency in the Gaelic Athletic Association, the sport’s governing body.View image in fullscreenMayo fans were delighted to put an end to 75 years of defeat, which legend had it was down to a curse.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAAccording to lore, the young victors of 1951 were on their way home to celebrate when they passed through the village of Foxford and failed to pay their respects to a funeral, prompting the enraged priest to utter the fateful words: “For as long as you all live, Mayo won’t win another all-Ireland.”View image in fullscreenLiam Gallagher, who has family ties to Mayo, was among those celebrating the win on social media.Photograph: Ireland West AirportSeven decades later, the last surviving member of that team, Paddy Prendergast,told friendshe would willingly “roll over and die” if there was any truth to the curse, but that it was a myth.“There was supposed to have been a funeral in the local church; I don’t know whether there was or not. I saw people standing around the church but we didn’t get off the truck because we couldn’t get off the bloody truck,” he told an interviewer in 2017.Researchers whoprobed church records, press cuttingsand other sources failed to find any verification of the supposed curse, which gained currency in the 1990s. The legend, however, is intact: Prendergast died in 2021, aged 95, two weeks after Mayo lost the final.Biden – who concluded a2023 presidential visit to Mayowith the rallying cry “Mayo for Sam!” – congratulated his ancestral home county. “Today, the dream becomes reality,” he posted. “You earned this victory. Enjoy every minute.”Carney, the Canadian prime minister who made his own ancestral pilgrimage to Mayo last month, echoed the joy. “The curse is broken,” he posted. The Gallagher brothers of Oasis, who also havefamily ties to Mayo, expressed pride. “Finally!! Up Mayo!!” Noel posted.Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Roster dating – is having five partners really the key to finding love? | Dating | The Guardian
description: It used be called playing the field, but now young people are claiming dating multiple people at once is intentional and growth-enhancing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It used be called playing the field, but now young people are claiming dating multiple people at once is intentional and growth-enhancing
Content: Commitment isn’t the destination.Photograph: Posed by models; Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCommitment isn’t the destination.Photograph: Posed by models; Westend61/Getty ImagesPass notesDatingRoster dating – is having five partners really the key to finding love?It used be called playing the field, but now young people are claiming dating multiple people at once is intentional and growth-enhancingMon 27 Jul 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Roster dating.Age:The term seems to be about a decade old; the practice is much older.Appearance:Hectic.What is it?It’s dating more than one person at a time.You mean what we used to call cheating?No, more like what we used to call playing the field.If it’s not new, why are we talking about it?Because gen Z have cottoned on to it.Them again.I’m afraid so.Let me guess: have they taken a messy arrangement born of indecision, insecurity and poor scheduling, and recast it as something intentional?Intentional and growth-enhancing.How so?Because roster dating is, at its core, a journey of personal discovery. “One of the biggest pros of roster dating is that you can learn so much about yourself,” one dating experttold Vice.If you ask me, these gen Zers know too much about themselves already.The important thing is to be open and honest about your intentions with everyone on your dating roster.You mean youtellthem?Not necessarily – you may simply assume that everyone on your roster also has a roster. But you shouldn’t lie.How many potential suitors make up a decent roster, then?The dating coach Sara Tick recommendskeeping it to five or fewer.Five? How am I supposed to keep track offive separate people?The idea is that they each fulfil a specific need: an exciting one, a devoted one, an artistic one, a rich one …Then how am I supposed to findfive completely different people who like me?They might not all like you – they might just have an open spot on their roster they need to fill.Let’s just call this what it really is: an inability to commit on any level.Commitment isn’t necessarily the destination with roster dating – it’s about letting go of expectations, and not wasting all your energy on a single connection.Fine, but all this presumes that dating is fun, when really it’s anxiety-ridden, soul-destroying and expensive.The last is certainly true – research indicates that theaverage cost of a gen Z datehas risen to $205 (£155).In that case, I can’t even afford a roster ofthree.Reading between the lines, you get the impression that the singles who swear by roster dating are never the ones paying.Do say:“I really think we’ve got something very special, but I have limited availability this month.”Don’t say:“Of course I’ll marry you, Frank! Sorry, I mean Fred.”Explore more on these topicsDatingPass notesRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: When it comes to predicting the future, why are TV writers better than politicians? | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: From BBC drama The Rapture on the climate crisis to Apple’s Criminal Record on the rise of the far right, culture often sees what politics fails to, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: From BBC drama The Rapture on the climate crisis to Apple’s Criminal Record on the rise of the far right, culture often sees what politics fails to, writes Zoe Williams
Content: India Amarteifio in The Rapture.Photograph: BBC/Mammoth ScreenView image in fullscreenIndia Amarteifio in The Rapture.Photograph: BBC/Mammoth ScreenOpinionClimate crisisWhen it comes to predicting the future, why are TV writers better than politicians?Zoe WilliamsFrom BBC drama The Rapture on the climate crisis to Apple’s Criminal Record on the rise of the far right, culture often sees what politics fails toMon 27 Jul 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.51 EDTShareIn the BBC’s newapocalypse drama, The Rapture, the UK is engulfed in a terrifying heatwave. I watched a preview of the programme in May, while preparing to interview the lead actor Ruth Madeley. I thought at the time: “This will be much more frightening when it chimes with the real life weather, bad luck for them that it’s not coming out for a couple of months.” But, by the time of meeting Madeley the following month, we were already in the middle of a heatwave that would lead to the highest ever recorded June temperature in the UK. The whole encounter made the show feel even more prophetic. She was in a central London hotel, air-conditioned inside, but all the door handles and surrounding street furniture – benches segmented by metal arm rests, to make life just that little bit harder for homeless people – had got way too hot. It was like playing The Floor is Lava, except instead of “floor”, “everything”. It surely can’t hit the screens at a more apposite time than this, I thought, failing to predict that by late July we’d be in heatwave number three, and France would be on fire.The Rapture review – this apocalyptic drama couldn’t be here at a better timeRead moreTheDaily Mail’sreviewer was upset that Christianity was portrayed “as a bastion of anti-science nutjobs and fundamentalists” in the show, wondering rhetorically whether the BBC would ever create such a drama about a “Muslim imam”. Peculiar thing to get upset about, I thought, since the religion is really more of a symptom of, or even a garnish to, the central atmosphere of engulfing heat. It’s like complaining that cats get a bad rap in the 1974 filmThe Towering Inferno(yes, there is a cat in it).TV puts a particular pressure on itself to describe the world it lands in, even when a show is developed at least a couple of years before. Often, the safe way to play it with surrounding factors – weather, politics, fashion – is to keep things so general that they could be any time this century. Every so often something will land that relates so tightly to current events, you forget to admire its foresight and just assume it was written yesterday. Season two ofCriminal Record (Apple TV), the police drama, which Peter Capaldi lifts so far above procedural you forget the police even have procedures, opens with a little demo outside the Ministry of Defence. It turns deadly after the far right smashes through a lackadaisical police cordon that thought it was just there to deal with a bunch of peaceniks. It felt extremely 2026, yet it was conceived before violent far-right protests were a regular news event – before the riots after thethe Southport attack, before asylum seekerhotels being set alight, before Elon Musk started talking about theinevitability of civil war in the UK. It tightly described a riven politics that had not yet arrived, the series creator and writer Paul Rutman committing himself to quite a new, distinctive and sad chapter in our civic life – unnecessarily, really, because watching Capaldi look sketchy and chase people is an evergreen delight in any context, but it paid off.The Rapture was adapted from Liz Jensen’s novel, which came out in 2009, so she must have been looking ahead to the climate crisis 20 years ago. Novels can often hit the future on the nose because they’re not trying to predict it by committee; books describing the now obvious billionaire death wish – a new kind of morbid fantasy, in which it’s not their own death they’re planning for but everyone else’s – are notable for their synchronicity. Eleanor Catton’s Birnam Wood and Naomi Alderman’s The Future came out in the same year, 2023. The ideas must have germinated at around the same time, 2020, which is surely before even the tech tycoons themselves had landed on this post-humanist outlook, and were still figuring out how to capture all the money in the world as quietly as possible.Without diminishing any of this creative perspicacity, these are things we all know; extreme weather is coming, a lot of billionaires are preparing for mass death events; politics is getting more divided because people with money are paying to cleave it. The only people not acknowledging this are politicians. They are still, in the middle of a wildfire, complaining that net zero costs too much, and squabbling about the teaspoon of crude oil left in the North Sea. The really remarkable thing is the determination of that averted gaze, denying a future that’s already arrived.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
