title: Private equity finds soft takeover targets in London – yet again | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Offer for DCC Energy leaves total of completed or agreed deals within FTSE 100 this year at five, but has Westminster noticed?
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Offer for DCC Energy leaves total of completed or agreed deals within FTSE 100 this year at five, but has Westminster noticed?
Content: DCC Energy acquired the Irish petroleum wholesale and unmanned forecourt business GreatGas in 2009.Photograph: David Creedon/AlamyView image in fullscreenDCC Energy acquired the Irish petroleum wholesale and unmanned forecourt business GreatGas in 2009.Photograph: David Creedon/AlamyNils Pratley on financeFTSEPrivate equity finds soft takeover targets in London – yet againNils PratleyOffer for DCC Energy leaves total of completed or agreed deals within FTSE 100 this year at five, but has Westminster noticed?DCC, one of FTSE 100’s biggest energy firms, agrees £5.75bn takeoverMon 27 Jul 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.49 EDTShareAnd another one goes. Dublin-basedDCC Energyis a lower-profile member of the FTSE 100, but they all count. We’re now at five completed or agreed takeovers within London’s leading index this year – and it’s still only July.The subplot at DCC was vocal opposition from a few shareholders who thought the private equity groups KKR and Energy Capital Partners, a unit of Bridgepoint, should be paying more than the£5.75bn, or £65.25 a share, at which the board has rolled over. Fidelity International and Aviva Investors were to the fore, as well as DCC’s founder.The resistance movement had good points. DCC seems to be executing, roughly on time and on budget, the eight-year strategy it adopted in 2022 to double operating profits to £830m by 2030 by slimming down to its core energy operations.The core comprises old-school petrol stations and liquid gas distribution networks across Europe, plus a growing clean energy services division that installs solar panels and suchlike. DCC, in other words, is an energy transition play with a mix of old and reliable cash earners and newer growth assets – the sort of thing the market, in theory, ought to like. About 35% of the required growth in operating profits has been achieved, and the board says it “remains confident” in the 2030 ambition.So why sell at anything less than top dollar? Neither the 24% premium on the pre-action share price, nor the 36% cited as the boost to the 12-month rolling average, scream unmissable value.View image in fullscreenDCC Energy comprises old-school petrol stations and liquid gas distribution networks across Europe, plus a growing clean energy services division.Photograph: Fotogun/AlamyFidelity International’s Alex Wright said at the start of this month he wouldn’t accept less than £70 a share and laid out his reasons: DCC’s attractive returns on capital; the scope for growth through acquisitions; pricing power in a consolidating market; share buybacks to boost earnings per share; overdone fears about the structural decline of the fossil fuel distribution business; and the potential to scale up the renewable energy activities.DCC management’s explanation for acceptance was the standard one about “a compelling and certain opportunity for DCC Energy shareholders to realise value in cash today”. Well, yes, there is always “execution risk” in any strategy. But the revealing bit was the long grumble about the difficulty of finding new investors.“The DCC Energy shareholder register has become more concentrated in recent years and the number of market participants that have engaged in the story has reduced over time,” the company said. Feedback suggested “exposure to low-volume growth end markets” – in other words, petrol stations and gas distribution – “weighs on perceived terminal value and, in turn, DCC Energy’s trading multiple”.DCC managed to tickle up the bidders in stages from £58 a share initially to £65.25 (or almost £68 if one includes an already paid dividend plus a contingent 125p that depends on a remaining technology business being sold at a good price), so one can’t say the board has not negotiated hard. The chief executive, Donal Murphy, is almost certainly correct when he predicts the majority of shareholders will vote in favour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut the basic plot here is yet another bad advert for London in terms of risk-taking and depth of capital. In short, a couple of private equity firms, via their infrastructure funds, are willing to take a far longer-term view of DCC’s prospects than public market investors (with honourable exceptions) will.The story isn’t new – most all-cash bids succeed – but a newly depressing feature is the regularity. Last week it was Segro, the warehouse landlord, falling to a bigger US rivalfor £14bn. The broker Peel Hunt calculated154 bids for UK companieswith a market value of more than £100m, equating to £165bn of stock market capitalisation, since the start of 2023. They’re not all private equity deals, of course – but London is the buyout brigade’s happiest hunting ground. In the meantime, arrivals on the London market have dried to a trickle.In a different world, the shrinking of the UK stock market, and thus soft political power on a global stage, would be causing alarm in Westminster. Sadly, the political class either haven’t noticed or aren’t bothered. They’ll regret it one day.Explore more on these topicsFTSENils Pratley on financePrivate equityMergers and acquisitionsEnergy industryStock marketscommentShareReuse this content

title: Amid the social and political panic about falling birthrates, why not ask new mothers what they think? | Lucy Jones | The Guardian
description: Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the priority is for policy that addresses women’s real concerns, says author and journalist Lucy Jones
Author: Lucy Jones
Headline: Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the priority is for policy that addresses women’s real concerns, says author and journalist Lucy Jones
Content: Mothers with young children carry an expectation to ‘do it all’: to work, manage the household and raise children.Photograph: Natalia  Lebedinskaia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMothers with young children carry an expectation to ‘do it all’: to work, manage the household and raise children.Photograph: Natalia  Lebedinskaia/Getty ImagesOpinionChildbirthAmid the social and political panic about falling birthrates, why not ask new mothers what they think?Lucy JonesNew research reveals deep anxieties. Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the priority is for policy that addresses women’s real concernsMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.30 EDTShareIt seems as though every week brings another news story on declining global birthrates. A number of political leaders have been panicking for a while, of course, instructing citizens to reproduce in tones so beguiling, who could possibly resist? JD Vance: “I want more babies”; Jacob Rees-Mogg: “We need more babies”. While in France this year, a government direct-mailing campaignurged 29-year-oldsto have a baby before it’s too late.People are busily scratching their heads and trying to work out why this is happening. The trend is described as a catastrophe for civilisation, with leaders drumming up incentives and policies in response, from medals (Russia) and a €1,000 birth bonus (Italy) to expanding access to IVF (the US, with Donald Trump crowing – and if you’re eating you may want to skip the rest of this sentence – he’ll be known as the “fertilisation president”).We hear ever-multiplying theories, from housing costs, contraception, education for women andsmartphone addictionto lower rates of hooking up,problems with car seats,global heatingand urbanisation. But something is missing in these discussions. Here’s a clue. It begins with M and it has seven letters.In all the panic about falling birthrates, the experiences of the people actually doing the births and those parenting infants – most often mothers – are strangely absent. We hear about the ruinous effect of low birthrates, but comparatively little of the difficulties mothers face, such as maternity discrimination and mental health issues. It’s as though there is something about the way we organise society that means new mothers, caregivers, are unseen.Thank goodness, then, for amajor new reportfrom the thinktank Theos – for which I wrote the foreword – which aims to make the experience of becoming a mother more visible. It is rich, fascinating and in depth, covering subjects such as mortality and tax, sleep and debt, the body and politics. While the experience of becoming a mother is obviously individual, there are recurring themes that should make us, as a society, take notice.One of the most striking findings is that many mothers feel “undervalued”. What does it mean to organise society in a way that people who are growing and raising new humans feel like this? It can’t be good. But perhaps it is convenient. While most people in the study thought that childcare was as vital to the economy as paid work, the maximum state maternity pay in the UK – from six weeks to 39 weeks after giving birth – is £6,412.56, far below the minimum wage. It is no surprise, then, that in a society where value is priced against profit mothers feel undervalued.What is it like to be a mother today? While many found childcare rewarding and enjoyable, the study also points to data showing that 48% found it stressful and 40% found it overwhelming. Perhaps this has something to do with the finding that mothers with young children carry an expectation to “do it all”: to work, manage the household and raise children. Many mothers also felt “invisible” once they had their babies. “You sort of cease to exist as a person, and you just become a mum,” said one.Another talked about people giving up their seat on the tube when she wore a badge in her pregnancy. But “it’s very rare for people to offer you a seat once you have a baby and a pram, which is funny, because I actually feel like, particularly after my C-section, I probably needed it a bit more”. This oversight should be easy to address, with a fuller rollout of priority seats on public transport for parents travelling with babies and young children, or even – as many European countries have – specific areas on trains for prams and families.What was birth and its aftermath like for the women in the study? Many described it as a time of “overwhelming exhaustion, sleep deprivation and anxiety”, with some finding postnatal visits rushed and “tick-box”, overlooking the mother, with the same at the routine six-week check. Experiences of maternal healthcare during birth and post-partum support were mixed: one woman spoke of “being handled like a piece of meat”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPeople keep asking me why I’m choosing to have a caesarean – here are my reasons | Sharon GaffkaRead moreThe study found that the interviewees were nervous or scared of sharing feelings of overwhelm after giving birth, because of the stigma attached to struggling in new motherhood. The focus on perinatal mental illness is obviously important, but it’s not the whole story. A better understanding about the dimensions of ordinary matrescence would help. The report’s recommendations also include enhancing the six-week check and improving care for new mothers in the immediate hospital stay.When we had our first child, I had never really thought about “motherhood”. I imagined my body – because I carried our kids, though of course not all mothers do – would be like a box or a flowerpot, and that when she was born I’d return to who I was, more or less. Instead, I soon realised the biological, socio-political and psychological experience of becoming a mother was a lot more complicated and intense than I’d been led to believe, from the messaging of antenatal care to the philosophy, politics and culture I had absorbed through my life.There are two intersecting problems. First, there is a lack of recognition of the heft of the experiences of pregnancy, birth and new motherhood. Second, there is a lack of social support in the perinatal period. Both are needed to improve the experience of people becoming parents.More widely, we need to understand how and why new mothers are feeling like this, what it reveals about our current value system, and how we might evolve a culture and society that is able to value birth and care, for all people. No need for any medals.Lucy Jones is a journalist and the author ofMatresenceand Losing EdenExplore more on these topicsChildbirthOpinionHealth & wellbeingMental healthHealthWomenFamilyChildrencommentShareReuse this content

title: Tariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurd | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world
Content: ‘Trump is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Trump is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpTariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurdSteven GreenhouseThe president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the worldMon 27 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.15 EDTShareWith the midterm elections less than four months away, it’s a precarious time for Donald Trump and Republicans: Trump’s war against Iran is going badly, hisapproval ratings are in the toilet, gas prices are soaring and pushing up inflation, and nation after nation is furious about Trump’s insults, bullying andugly American unilateralism.So amid all this mess, what does Trump do? He turns to his favorite economic plaything: tariffs. On Monday, Trump signed orders to slap a50% tariff on many Canadian goods, and four days later, he imposedacross-the-board 10% or 12.5% tariffson goods from more than 80 countries. Trump was no doubt thumping his chest, while millions of people overseas were dumping on him for yet another unnecessary, hostile act.Too bad for Republicans, and most Americans, though, because Trump’s fixation on tariffs will only worsen their troubles. Trump’s new tariffs will push up prices – let’s not forget that tariffs are taxes on imports, and US consumers will pay those taxes. A corollary of that: Trump’s tariffs will worsen AmericansNo 1 economic concern: affordability. In bad news for typical Americans, the Yale Budget Lab estimates that Trump’s tariffs will increase costs for the average UShousehold by $1,100 each year. The tariffs are also likely to push Trump’s approval ratings deeper into the sewer. If Trump thinks these tariffs are going to distract Americans from thinking about the Epstein files or the disastrous mess he’s made with his Iran “excursion”, he’s deluding himself. The American people aren’t going to forget those things.It’s hard to tell whether Trump’s repeated use of tariffs is a fixation or an addiction. Emperor Donald I evidently loves tariffs because he can use them to clobber other countries whenever he wants. They’re a powerful cudgel he won’t let go of. Trump imposed his new tariffs on more than 80 countries on the very day that another set of tariffs he slapped on dozens of countries was due to expire. Toparaphrase the actor Charlton Heston, I can imagine Trump saying: “I’ll give up tariffs when you take them from my cold, dead hands.”With these new tariffs, Trump is again engaged in his delusional, destructive tariff tomfoolery. They’ll push up prices, squeeze Americans’ wallets and anger other countries. Trump said his tariffs would boost US manufacturing, but the US haslost 75,000 factory jobssince he returned to office, with many executives complaining about all the herky-jerky uncertainty Trump has wrought. Assessing Trump’s effects on the economy, Atsi Sheth, the chief credit officer for Moody’s Ratings, told the New York Times :“Volatility and unpredictabilityis the new normal.”What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countriesRead moreLike so much that Trump does, his new tariffs are clearly based on pique and false premises with lots of shamelessness and absurdity thrown in. After the US supreme courtoverturned Trump’s me-against-the-whole-world tariffsin February, Trump, refusing to let go of his tariff toy, turned to other strategies. To justify his new 50% tariffs against Canada – which arepiled atopnumerous other tariffs he’s imposed on a country that was long the US’s closest ally – Trump relied on a never before usedprovision of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, a widely derided 1930 law that greatly worsened the Great Depression of a century ago. With this new tariff, placed on hockey sticks, paper, plywood, dairy products and many other Canadian goods, Trump invoked a Smoot-Hawley provision that allows retaliation against countries that engage in trade discrimination against the US.In making that case, Trump’s exhibit No 1 is something rather preposterous, or should I say rather shameless? After Trump imposed high, punitive tariffs on Canada last year, 11 of Canada’s 13 provinces and territories halted liquor imports from the US because they were so irate about those tariffs along with Trump’s outlandish and belittling statements that he wanted to make Canada the 51st state. The White Housecalled this ban on US liquor illegal discrimination, while Canadians view it as a type of traditional trade retaliation that countries engage in when another country – here the US – slaps tariffs on them, a situation made worse by the fact that Trump’s tariffs against Canada arean egregious violationof the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.Trump also insists that Canada has improperly discriminated against the US because Canada imposed a 25% tariff on select US-made cars after Trumpslapped a 25% tariffon Canadian-made cars.He is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US. That’s the logic of America’s leading stable genius, who also offered another far-fetched justification for his decision: “We’re going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke,” hetold reporterson Friday, referring to wildfire smoke that has crossed the US border.Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, isn’t happy about Trump’s painful, new 50% tariff. “We won’t back down,” he said on social media. “The fastest and only way to get US alcohol back on Ontario shelves is for the U.S. to drop its illegal tariffs on Canada.”As for the new tariffs hitting more than 80 countries, Trump, who over the years hasshown next to no concernabout worker exploitation, turned rather surprisingly to the issue of forced labor to slap on those tariffs.After the supreme court overturned his Liberation Day tariffs, Trump hit dozens of nations with a replacement tariff that would expire after 150 days. Eager to follow the boss’s wishes and impose a new tariff as soon as that one expired, Trump’s toadies uncovered a trade law provision that lets Washington punish countries that fail to take enough action against forced labor. No surprise here: Trump’s US trade representative issued a report that made the boss happy. That report found that dozens of countries, including Canada, the UK, Australia, Norway, Japan and China, plus the European Union, were not doing enough to enforce a prohibition against forced labor. That report pointed to forced labor inproducing rice in Myanmar, tobacco in Malawi, and cotton and polysilicon in China.It’s deeply perplexing that Trump is punishing some of these trading partners. Norway haspioneered lawsto crack down on forced labor in overseas supply chains, while the European Union’snew ban on goods produced with forced laborwill take effect in December 2027. Canadaalready bans imports made with forced labor, and is moving to strengthen that prohibition.If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world | Eduardo PorterRead moreIt’s not as if Trump has shown much concern before about worker exploitation or forced labor. In 1998, Trump agreed to pay$1.375m to settle a lawsuitbrought by undocumented Polish workers who said they were underpaid for their work demolishing a department store to make way for Trump Tower in New York. Sometrade experts criticize Trumpfor slamming all these longtime allies about forced labor even as he is pushing vigorously to improve ties with China, which the Biden administration found to haveserious forced labor problems in its Xinjiang region.Trump’s newfound concern about forced labor rings especially hollow considering that his administrationchopped more than $500m from the labor department’s effortsto investigate and fight against forced labor, child labor and human trafficking. “This was a completely indiscriminate meat axthat was taken to these projects, and workers will suffer,” said Thea Lee, who served as the labor department’s deputy undersecretary for international labor affairs under Biden. Bemoaning that $500m-plus in cuts, Kelly Fay Rodriguez, who was Biden’s special representative for international labor affairs, told Equal Times. “Unfortunately, it is extremely likely that child labor and forced labor practiceswill increase. We know these problems are endemic but … we’ve wiped out the resources and the prioritization for fighting them.”Imagine a world whereDonald Trumptruly cared about worker exploitation and forced labor. He would be pushing to raise the absurdly low $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage – something he has never lifted a finger to do. He would be increasing, rather than cutting, the number of safety inspectors for mines and factories. He would be pushing to strengthen – instead of repeatedly moving to weaken – the nation’s labor unions, long the most effective voice in fighting against worker exploitation. He would be pressuring China’s President Xi Jinping to stop all the forced labor in his country. But that would be a make-believe Donald Trump – he cares far more about what’s good for billionaires than what’s good for workers.Bottom line: there remains far too much forced labor in the world –more than 27 million children, women and menare in forced labor, according to the International Labor Organization. It would be great if Donald Trump sincerely seized on that issue rather than used it as an insincere pretext to clobber other nations with tariffs.Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump tariffsTariffsTrump administrationUS foreign policyCanadacommentShareReuse this content

title: Here’s why India’s cockroach protests were such a success – and why the Mamdani effect means more to come | Mukul Kesavan | The Guardian
description: The young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra Modi, says Dehli-based essayist and author Mukul Kesavan
Author: Mukul Kesavan
Headline: The young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra Modi, says Dehli-based essayist and author Mukul Kesavan
Content: Celebrations in Mumbai on 26 July after the resignation of  education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.Photograph: Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCelebrations in Mumbai on 26 July after the resignation of  education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.Photograph: Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOpinionIndiaHere’s why India’s cockroach protests were such a success – and why the Mamdani effect means more to comeMukul KesavanThe young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra ModiMon 27 Jul 2026 05.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.32 EDTShareThe rebellion in India of the young, led by theCockroach Janta party (CJP),unfolded against a backdrop of large, abstract, geometrical structures – arcs, planes, hemispheres – that together make up an observatory called Jantar Mantar, built in the early 18th century to refine almanacs and tell time. Jantar Mantar has been a byword for political protest for decades: it marks the space that the Delhi police assigns to the politically disgruntled so they can vent in a contained way. But it had never before hosted a political insurgency that started from scratch and forced the Indian state to back down in less than eight weeks.When its founder,Abhijeet Dipke, brought the CJP to Jantar Mantar, it was a social media hashtag with 20 million followers. While he was studying in Boston, Dipke took the remarks of chief justice Surya Kant, who is accused of referring to the swathes of unemployed young people and activists as “parasites” and “cockroaches”, and turned them into a here-we-come meme. When he brought the CJP home to Delhi on 6 June to make it real, people were intrigued. Given the mostly dismal fate of civil society movements during prime minister Narendra Modi’s time in office, no one anticipated the David and Goliath contest that came to a head last Saturday.Like other political tourists, I visited Jantar Mantar on 6 June out of curiosity. On that inaugural day it was modestly crowded and not that different from the dozens of demos I had attended over 50 years. The one difference was how young these so-called cockroaches were. I had seen young people mobilise against Modi’s government at close quarters before when the students ofJamia Millia Islamia, the university I taught in, came out against a pernicious citizenship bill. Their courage and idealism was defeated by a combination of police repression and organised rioting. This government’s willingness to use police brutality, vigilante violence and a pliant judiciary to snuff out protest hung over the fledgling CJP campaign like a shadow.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) celebrate the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, Mumbai, India, 26 July 2026.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPABut when I returned a month and a half later on 20 July, the scheduled day for the march to parliament, Jantar Mantar was unrecognisable. A hunger strike had raised the political temperature of the protest. The government had forcibly removed the main hunger striker,Sonam Wangchuk, from the site and detained him in a hospital. The calculation was that his absence would defuse the tension and demoralise the protesters. That didn’t happen.India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for ModiRead moreThere were tens of thousands of people crammed into the barricaded space and thousands of police officers in attendance. The government had underestimated the size of the crowd that poured in by bus, train and car from Delhi and beyond. In the afternoon the Delhi police force and its masters compounded its miscalculation by attacking this giant gathering of young people withlathis(bamboo sticks) and teargas.This tableau of brutality was shocking enough in real life, but in the hands of young digital natives, whose phone cameras were extensions of themselves, it became a gush of online content that brought the violent drama of this confrontation into every home. The callous violence of the police and the raging, mocking, laughing defiance of the young protesters played out on every mobile phone.The cockroaches won where other protesters, not unlike them, such as Jamia’s students, had lost. They won, in part, because they weren’t visibly Muslim. There were Muslims among them, but this was a protest about the corruption of competitive examinations, an issue that concerns every middle-class family inIndia. It couldn’t easily be tarred as an anti-national conspiracy in the way that the struggle for secular citizenship led by Jamia’s mainly Muslim students was. This didn’t stop India’s mostly tame mainstream media from trying, but the scandal of the medical school examination was so egregious that no one gave them a hearing.Also, this was in the heart of New Delhi, a stone’s throw from parliament. Once the government had made, from its point of view, the cardinal error of letting gen Z occupy the commanding heights of the capital, every day of the protest produced hundreds of new episodes of a national drama – a digitalMahabharat– in which the vulnerable and charismatic children of light faced off against the armed and uniformed enforcers of darkness. Bharatiya Janata party governments have sanctioned massive police violence against minorities in India’s borderlands, in Manipur, Assam and Kashmir. But this was Jantar Mantar, the sacred centre of the republic.View image in fullscreenCJP spokesperson Saurav Das (left) and founder and president Abhijeet Dipke at a demonstration at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, India, 25 July 2026.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAThe leaders of the movement, Abhijeet Dipke andSaurav Das, had set themselves up for success by demanding a difficult but doable concession: the sacking of the education minister. It was difficult because Modi had never dismissed a cabinet minister in response to political pressure; this stubbornness was central to his strongman persona. It was doable because there were precedents in the history of the republic for a minister taking responsibility for a disaster and resigning.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionModi did everything he could to wriggle out of this standoff. He even produced a comically inept Instagram video promising fast-track courts to address the corruption in the examination system. When that didn’t work, his government capitulated and Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister,departed. There was an assembly election scheduled in Uttar Pradesh next year and Modi knew that the BJP would haemorrhage political support if the Jantar Mantar impasse wasn’t resolved.The quarrel that some commentators on the left have with the CJP is that Pradhan’s dismissal was a symbolic victory but not a substantial one.Pralhad Joshi, the man who has replaced Pradhan as education minister, is not an improvement. Like Pradhan he is a member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the BJP’s far-right parent body. He publicly defended the premature release in 2022 of 11 men convicted for rape in the notoriousBilkis Bano gang-rape case.The CJP’s argument is that Pradhan was always a proxy for Modi. The point of the protest was to diminish Modi by forcing him to back down publicly. Also, it isn’t clear what a systemic victory would look like or how it would be achieved.The striking thing about the CJP’s leadership is its youth and poise. Zohran Mamdani, the youthful mayor of New York, now seems a template. He is 35. Dipke, the CJP’s Dalit leader, is 30 years old.Ashutosh Ranka, who negotiated the end of the protest with the BJP’s leadership, is about the same age. Das, the other negotiator and spokesperson, is all of 26.Neha Bora, the president of a leftwing student organisation, the All-India Students’ Association, is 25. It’s hard to know how their politics will evolve. What they have in common is eloquence, message discipline, all-round unflappability and the potential to leave a legacy. They may be an enduring problem for this government. Jantar Mantar may have just produced an echelon of homegrown Mamdanis.Mukul Kesavan is an essayist and author based in DelhiExplore more on these topicsIndiaOpinionNarendra ModiProtestSouth and central AsiacommentShareReuse this content

title: There was one thing I swore I’d never do on WhatsApp. And now I’ve gone and done it | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: Leaving your blue ticks on used to be a sign that you were trustworthy. These days it conveys a certain ‘pick me’ energy
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: Leaving your blue ticks on used to be a sign that you were trustworthy. These days it conveys a certain ‘pick me’ energy
Content: Is she busy – or is she deliberately ignoring me?Photograph: Posed by model; AlexPhotoStock/AlamyView image in fullscreenIs she busy – or is she deliberately ignoring me?Photograph: Posed by model; AlexPhotoStock/AlamyOpinionWhatsAppThere was one thing I swore I’d never do on WhatsApp. And now I’ve gone and done itPolly HudsonLeaving your blue ticks on used to be a sign that you were trustworthy. These days it conveys a certain ‘pick me’ energyMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.08 EDTShareGenuine question: am I the last person in the world who still has my blue ticks on? In the early days ofWhatsApp, if someone had gone into their privacy settings and turned them off, so you could never be sure when or evenifthis person had read your message, that told you all you needed to know. No blue ticks = red flag. Here was a slippery, sneaky individual, not to be trusted under any circumstances. As opposed to those of us who left them on – honest, noble, open books with nothing to hide. No blue ticks was an indicator that you were probably messaging a serial killer.But recently the tide has turned. Now everyone seems to have gone all mysterious and switched them off, to leave you guessing. I’m starting to feel like a desperate blue-tick loser, over-keen and needy, falling over myself to volunteer the unnecessary information that I’ve read your message, when you are far too cool to care. Blue ticks on has real “pick me” energy. It’s attention-seeking, the coloured symbol equivalent of sending a selfie of you reading the message in question, while grinning and doing a thumbs up.Feel guilty after gossiping? You’re clearly not doing it right | Polly HudsonRead moreThe only possible mitigating factor in turning your ticks off is that it instantly extinguishes the very worst aspect of WhatsApp: being stuck in blue-tick purgatory, AKA left on read. This is when the recipient has seen your message but is yet to reply. Even though, logically, you know they were just called into a meeting or run over by a bus, your mind starts to play tricks and you become convinced that they hate you.Then, as more messages arrive in their inbox, you slip down the list, out of sight and mind, into the blue-tick abyss where you will languish, your paranoia increasing exponentially by the hour. Plot twist: the ticks-off brigade were the good guys all along?Polly Hudson is a freelance writer.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Why are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers? | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists
Content: ‘Just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right does not mean that it is popular with the public.’Photograph: Inquam Photos/Eduard Vinatoru/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right does not mean that it is popular with the public.’Photograph: Inquam Photos/Eduard Vinatoru/ReutersOpinionDemocratsWhy are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers?Moira DoneganThe party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategistsMon 27 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.10 EDTShareIt’s not exactly strange thatelements of the Magaversehave embracedAndrew Tate. What’s strange is that theDemocratsdo not seem interested in holding the Trump movement to account for it.Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer who is accused by numerous women around the world andnow by British prosecutorsof rape andstrangulation, as well as assault, sex trafficking,possession ofchild abuse images and extreme pornography, and various other forms of gender violence and exploitation, was arrested in Miami last week, along with Tristan, his brother and sidekick. Or I should say, they were rearrested: the men were previously charged in Romania, where they were under house arrest until, following some conveniently timed diplomatic moves from the Trump administration, they were allowed to leave the country andresettled in the US. When asked if the Trump administration had secured their release from Romania back then, theTates’ lawyer said: “Do the math. These guys are on the plane.” Now, finally, they are awaiting extradition to the UK, where they are dual citizens.The Tate brothers have long made their living by making provocative, contemptuous statements about women online. But in June, the New Yorker’s Heidi Blake published along investigationthat centered not on what the Tates have said, but on what they’re said to have done – detailing a long and documented history of alleged sex trafficking, violence and sexual assault along with a disturbing pattern of police mismanagement, incompetence and indifference that allowed the men to go free. The Tates denied wrongdoing in that piece; their lawyer called the new British charges against them “garbage”. But if anyone thought the Tates’ misogynistic influencer career was mere bluster, the Blake investigation offered a formidable bit of counterevidence: she painted a picture of the men acting exactly the way that they talked.In a world where people take misogyny as seriously as they claim to, the Tates would long ago have been ostracized, and condemned, for their hatefully sexist rhetoric and alleged violence against women. In this world, they got rich, and ingratiated themselves to powerful figures in the Republican party.Tate is a natural fit on a Maga right that has served to unite its many different factions – from Christian conservatives to Silicon Valley eugenicists, to beer-chugging barstool denizens, conspiracy mongers, and the male hosts of multi-hour podcasts – around a foundation of male supremacy. Contempt for women is the uniting force on the American right, more uniform across the competing styles within the movement even than the hatred of immigration or devotion to the prerogatives of capital. Donald Trump cemented the presidency, after all, when he was revealed to have bragged about “grab[bing]” women “by the pussy” and still maintained his base of support. In the decade that followed, his domineering, narcissistic, vulgar style of masculinity, and the alternately belittling and hateful treatment of women that accompanies it, have come to be seen on the right as a feature, not a bug. Other men within the Maga movement now imitate Trump’s style of misogyny with a gleeful competitiveness; the coalition welcomes men who collect harems of women to breed their children, those who have been multiply accused of sexual abuse and those whodecry our right to vote. Andrew Tate, in this milieu, is not an exception. He is the rule.But just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right – in which sex is seen to elevate men’s status at women’s expense, in which women’s aspirations to education, skilled work, dignity, public participation, or even mere decency are mocked; and in which men’s mistreatment of women is the key way for them to gain the esteem of other men – does not mean that it is popular with the public. Tate’s version of vulgar, avowed, preening misogyny has a constituency of Republican politicians and unlikable teenage boys; it does not have a constituency among the majority of the American public.Why areDemocratsnot making the Tates into symbols of Maga’s hateful and bizarre cultural project, of Trump’s personal alleged affinity for sexual misconduct, or of the antisocial, anti-democratic and anti-equality stances of the Maga movement?Rape, after all, might be the most quintessentially anti-democracy act: a violent refusal of equality in the most intimate terms. One could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that built from anti-rape principles into pro-democracy ones; less ambitiously, one could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that merely drew a link between Trump’s pathetic narcissism and that of the sleazeball Tates and their manosphere ilk. It seems like an easy win.That the Democratic party is not taking it shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists, and how anathema even the most basic and remedial feminist claims are now understood to be by those same forces. Because one explanation for why the Democrats are not taking advantage of the Tates’ links to Trump is as simple as it is dark: they do not want to alienate the Tates’ base of manosphere content consumers.It is by now a cliche to say that Democrats arelosing men, a demographic reality that is treated as a much greater emergency than the GOP’s parallel loss of women. Sects within the Democratic consultant class have made the recruitment of manly men candidates into their singular mission. Following the 2024 election, major party players fundraised a massive$20mfor a “Speaking with American Men” project, meant to lure men back to the party; the California governor,Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 presidential candidate, has forged his own podcast project, in which he has taken to embracing some rightwing cultural positions on things like trans rights. The party is running white male candidates who saycartoonish thingslike it’s OK “to be a manly man” – as if anyone was confused.It is this desperate and frantic effort to re-masculinize the party at any cost that led to the recruitment ofGraham Platner, the ex-marine who dropped out of the Maine Senate race earlier this month after being accused of rape (he has denied the allegations). Major players in the Democratic party did the right thing in that case, calling on Platner to drop out en masse. But many of them still believe in the strategy that elevated him in the first place: that of prizing men over women, of coveting men’s votes and men’s support as somehow more legitimate, more valuable, than women’s.In this sense, there is another reason that some in the Democratic party won’t seize upon the Tate issue: even if they don’t condone his alleged violence, on his most fundamental principle – that men are better and more important than women are – they may not entirely disagree.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionWomenGenderAndrew TateUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Europe’s wildfires: politics must catch up with the new reality | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: At a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritised
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: At a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritised
Content: A pyrocumulonimbus, a giant cloud created by a large wildfire, seen in the Fontainebleau forest region of France.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APView image in fullscreenA pyrocumulonimbus, a giant cloud created by a large wildfire, seen in the Fontainebleau forest region of France.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APOpinionWildfiresThe Guardian view on Europe’s wildfires: politics must catch up with the new realityEditorialAt a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritisedMon 27 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.43 EDTShareAnew and ominous word has entered the vocabulary of firefighters struggling to cope with the vast wildfire sweeping through south-west France. Apyrocumulonimbusis a fire-generated thunderstorm that can whip up winds in unpredictable ways, making the containment of a blaze and assessment of its likely course far more difficult. A known phenomenon in North America and Australia, firefighters believe France is suffering its first in the Bordeaux region, as the country endures the consequences of the third major heatwave of the summer and prepares for a fourth.The direstatisticsof the ongoing fires in France and Spain tell a story of deepening devastation and human misery. A far greater expanse of French land has already been burnt this year, compared with the 30,000 hectares during the whole of 2025, while 220,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the Gironde. In Spain, the environment ministry has calculated that over 170,000 hectares have been affected, compared with 29,000 last year. Over 100,000 people have been forced to flee.View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez greeting emergency service workers.Photograph: Eva Manez/ReutersAs climate scientists long warned would be the case, Europe’s wildfires are worsening in intensity, scale and duration as the planet heats up. When the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez,attributedthe current crisis to the effects of the climate emergency, he was stating the obvious. But to his great credit, Mr Sánchez has been among the few leaders toarguethat the European Union’s green transition should be accelerated accordingly. Whether on funding adaptation efforts, or driving the macro changes needed to slow the rate of global heating, far too many others appear happy to fiddle while the continent burns.In June, for example, with spectacularly badtiming, Emmanuel Macron’s government sought savings by announcing steep cuts to a Green Fund designed to help local authorities address climate and environmental challenges. Across Europe more generally, amid persistent low growth and the fallout from Donald Trump’s war on Iran, a false dichotomy is increasingly being drawn between green ambition and competitiveness. This month, underpressurefrom countries such as Giorgia Meloni’s Italy, the European Commission unveiled proposals toweakenthe EU’s emissions trading system, its flagship climate policy. If adopted, heavy industry would receive free polluting permits for longer and at lower cost.Calls for the dilution of green measures are generally accompanied by the assertion that Europe needs to take a more pragmatic approach, at a time of geopolitical uncertainty and aggressive economic competition. The argument is wrong twice over: the faster the EU moves towards net zero, the better it will consolidate Europe’s position in the global markets of the future. More fundamentally, as the appalling impact of this summer’s wildfires vividly illustrates, the notion that climate measures are a kind of optional add-on, appropriate only when times are good, is wildly at odds with the developing reality.As a fourth heatwave hits Europe, temperatures in south-west France are predicted to hit 40C on Wednesday. According to a recentstudy, if the warming rate of the last decade continues, the 1.5C limit set by the Paris agreement will be redundant by 2030. Yet, far from seeking to catch up with the pace of change, too many governments and leaders are seeking to put their foot on the policy brake. That is not realism; it is a dereliction of duty.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on ancient DNA: a female shaman exposes our flawed assumptions about the past | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Thanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly know
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Thanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly know
Content: We Go Way Back, an exhibition exploring how ancient DNA is revealing new insights into human evolution, migration, culture and disease, is at the Francis Crick Institute in London.Photograph: Martin Stacey/Easy Animal StudioView image in fullscreenWe Go Way Back, an exhibition exploring how ancient DNA is revealing new insights into human evolution, migration, culture and disease, is at the Francis Crick Institute in London.Photograph: Martin Stacey/Easy Animal StudioOpinionArchaeologyThe Guardian view on ancient DNA: a female shaman exposes our flawed assumptions about the pastEditorialThanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly knowMon 27 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 19.34 EDTShareArchaeologists believe the Upton Lovell Shaman, who lived in what is now Wiltshire 4,000 years ago, was an important religious leader and metalworker because of the artefacts and tools buried with the body. Until very recently it was also believed, on considerably slimmer evidence, that this shaman was a man: it was simply assumedthat someone of such status must be male, and the view was barely questioned over the years. Now ancient DNA analysis performed at the Francis Crick Institutehas revealedthat the body, held by the Wiltshire Museum, is in fact a woman.That should cause a stir in bronze-age studies. But it is also yet another example of how many of our assumptions about human history have been upended by the rise of ancient DNA analysis over the past two decades. Others include the revelation that there were (frequent) liaisons between humans and Neanderthals just 50,000 years ago, a reconstruction suggesting that thefirst modern Britonshad “dark to black” skin, and the closing of longstanding mysteries such as what really killed two members of Italy’s powerful Medici family in the 16th century (probably malaria, not murder as was often believed). Every time we widen our keyhole view of the past even slightly, we are confronted by how many of our seemingly grounded assumptions are, in fact, wrong.These insights have emerged because the technology to extract and read DNA from ancient, poorly preserved samples has improved exponentially since around 2010. DNA analysis hardly provides a total picture of the past, but it has been useful for mapping migrations, sexual relations and family structures, as well as tracking plagues and diseases. For instance, it has told us that groups of ancient humans moved around and intermixed with each other far more often than previously thought, allowing us to imagine a more dynamic, less lonely ancient world.It also suggests that the replacement of one group with another, such as evidence of thenear-total disappearanceof the Stonehenge-building Neolithic Britons, just a few centuries after the arrival of the Bell Beaker people around 2400BC, was relatively common. But it cannot answer why or how that replacement took place. These are big questions that will keep scientists, anthropologists and archaeologists busy for decades.Alongside a deeper and richer view of the past, we should take a lesson from the constant stream of debunking and myth-busting emerging from this research. The politics behind assuming a shaman is male are obvious, but last year a studytook on more subtle biasesby proving that famous plaster casts of citizens of Pompeii long believed to show a mother and child locked in a final embrace were in fact two people who were not related, and the adult was male. The authors note that there was no published evidence suggesting the sex or family relations of these bodies, but both scholars and the public found the romantic (and very modern) interpretation irresistible.We will probably always try to see something of ourselves in our ancestors. But the past is more interesting when we consider it on its own, often bracingly foreign, terms. DNA evidence will not conveniently overturn every one of our biased judgments about the ancient world, but each case does make it easier to recognise how readily it happens, and to be humble about how little we really understand.Explore more on these topicsArchaeologyOpinionMalariaeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: How Andy Burnham can make his devolution agenda work | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Letters: Rabbi Jeff Newman, David Williams and Tom Carr respond to an editorial on the new prime minister’s plans to decentralise power
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Rabbi Jeff Newman, David Williams and Tom Carr respond to an editorial on the new prime minister’s plans to decentralise power
Content: Andy Burnham officially opens No 10 North at Heron House in Manchester on 24 July, along with Louise Haigh, minister for the Cabinet Office, and John Healey, chancellor of the exchequer.Photograph: James Speakman/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham officially opens No 10 North at Heron House in Manchester on 24 July, along with Louise Haigh, minister for the Cabinet Office, and John Healey, chancellor of the exchequer.Photograph: James Speakman/ReutersDevolutionLettersHow Andy Burnham can make his devolution agenda workRabbi Jeff Newman,David WilliamsandTom Carrrespond to an editorial on the new prime minister’s plans to decentralise powerMon 27 Jul 2026 12.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.17 EDTShareYour editorial (22 July) rightly identifies the structural paradox at the heart of Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda – that it takes a confident assertion of central power to give real power away. But one institutional mechanism that goes some way to resolving this paradox operationally deserves mention: the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (Nista), which has sat jointly between the Treasury and the Cabinet Office since April 2025.Inherited from Keir Starmer’s government, Nista (with about 250 civil servants) merges what were the National Infrastructure Commission and the Infrastructure and Projects Authority into a single body reporting simultaneously to both departments. Under Starmer, the Cabinet Office side of that dual accountability was relatively weak. Under Louise Haigh’s newOffice of the Prime Minister and Cabinet– explicitly endorsed by the Institute for Government as implementing long-called-for structural reforms – that balance may shift.Nista becomes, potentially, the operational expression of the relationship between Haigh andJohn Healey, the new chancellor, that your editorial identifies as central to whether Burnham’s ambitions survive contact with Treasury orthodoxy.Whether it works will depend significantly on Healey. Your editorial frames him as “not a big beast of the species likely to build a power base to rival Mr Burnham”, which may be accurate. But it understates the more interesting question of his formation. Before entering parliament, Healey spent years in disability rights and trade union work – at Mind and the Trades Union Congress, where he helped design the national minimum wage.That pre-parliamentary biography suggests a chancellor whose instincts may align more naturally with the “preventive state” agenda than his Brown-era Treasury service implies. His predecessor Denis Healey’s capitulation to Treasury orthodoxy in 1976 shaped British politics for 50 years – the stakes of getting this relationship right are that high.The paradox that your editorial identifies is real. Nista, under a genuinely strengthened Cabinet Office, is at least an attempt to resolve it institutionally rather than just rhetorically.Rabbi Jeff NewmanFinchley, LondonAndy Burnham’s determination to make regional devolution a reality rather than a catchphrase (remember the “northern powerhouse”?) is laudable and potentially gamechanging, but it depends so much on the ability, altruism, efficiency and drive of the regional mayors and civic leaders whose job it will be to deliver it. How many of them have the capability that Andy Burnham has shown in Manchester?I suspect the truth is that we don’t really know. How many of us even know the names of these people, never mind what their particular strengths and proclivities are? And if that is true of those in our own region, how much more so of those we entrust to deliver in their part of the country, within the context of the national interest? Who are they, what is their motivation and what got them into the positions they occupy?If Burnham’s policy is to be carried out properly, our expectations of these representatives have now become much wider. They are potentially champions of us all. I for one would be interested in a Guardian profile of these key regional ambassadors.Having been in regional development in a past role myself, I have seen both good and bad, and I recognise how crucial these roles can, and must, be if they are to be the engineers of growth for us all.David WilliamsHexham, NorthumberlandIt is certainly refreshing to hear that our new prime minister is trying to decentralise our London-centric government by opening a No 10 North inManchester. However, reading his comments, it appears that he identifies Manchester as “the north”. He must realise that the north of England is much more than just the Manchester conurbation, and that replacing a single-centre approach with a double-centre one will not in itself achieve his aims of improving every postcode in the country.Tom CarrNewcastle upon TyneHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Councils can lead on housing improvements | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Stephen Battersby on the lessons this Labour government can learn from the 1970s
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Stephen Battersby on the lessons this Labour government can learn from the 1970s
Content: ‘A new approach is required, but we can also learn from the renewal approaches of the 1970s.’Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘A new approach is required, but we can also learn from the renewal approaches of the 1970s.’Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverExtreme heatLettersCouncils can lead on housing improvementsDr Stephen Battersbyon the lessons this Labour government can learn from the 1970sMon 27 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.18 EDTShareYour editorial quoting Sam Johnson-Schlee saying that our ability to trust that our homes will keep us safe is under threat is not news to environmental health officers working in housing (The Guardian view on Britain’s uninhabitable homes: as temperatures rise, a new approach is needed, 23 July). Every day they are faced with homes that contain threats to the health and safety of occupiers – from excess heat or cold, or damp and mould. For many years there has been a lack of resources, including environmental health staff to inspect homes or the political will to tackle the problems on the scale needed.You are right to suggest that a new approach is required, but we can also learn from the 1970s, when local authorities would take the lead on collective action to improve housing. So councils should be the place to look to get things moving. This will require funding, not only to help homeowners but also to ensure that councils have sufficient staff with the right skills.After the 1981 English House Condition Survey, which showed the high rate of disrepair in the housing stock, the government introduced generous repair grants, and contributed £1bn through subsidies. The decision to discontinue funding for the private sector housing renewal programme, which had been reduced to £376m in 2009‑10, was a result of austerity. Perhaps Andy Burnham and Angela Rayner need to revisit the past to learn what can be done.Dr Stephen BattersbyEnvironmental health and housing consultant (retired)Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Content: A still from The Odyssey by Christopher Nolan.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreenA still from The Odyssey by Christopher Nolan.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesBrief lettersThe OdysseyLettersMy thrilling Odyssey on BBC SoundsSimon Armitage’s Odyssey | Preventing lobbying | Surviving obituaries | Cream cracker lunch | DIY decisionMon 27 Jul 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.17 EDTShareRe Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, Charlotte Higgins urges us to watch the film, but also read the poem – “you won’t regret it” (25 July). I bypassed the verse and went straight to Simon Armitage’s stunning four-hour radio adaptation of Homer from 2004, now on BBC Sounds, which helped, thrillingly, to clarify much of what remained a bit murky in the movie.Quentin FalkLittle Marlow, BuckinghamshireRe your article on lobbying the government (Besieged by lobbyists, will UK ministers protect our ecosystems? No, they’ll chicken out, 23 July), the NHS trust I worked for had a policy that prevented doctors from meeting drug representatives without a pharmacist present. This ensured doctors’ prescriptions were based on good evidence rather than drug firms’ promotions. Perhaps it’s time for a similar system to be put in place when MPs meet lobbyists.Stephen CarterCullompton, DevonAs a dedicated reader of the obituaries, I notice that the deceased regularly succumb to a “short illness”. title: No, Centrica, customers don’t prefer bots to humans | Centrica | The Guardian
description: Letters: Charles MacKinnon disagrees with the British Gas owner’s justification for cutting 1,300 jobs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Charles MacKinnon disagrees with the British Gas owner’s justification for cutting 1,300 jobs
Content: ‘We are being gaslit by large companies, including banks, that have gradually withdrawn face-to-face access to customer service.’Photograph: Charles Taylor/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘We are being gaslit by large companies, including banks, that have gradually withdrawn face-to-face access to customer service.’Photograph: Charles Taylor/AlamyCentricaLettersNo, Centrica, customers don’t prefer bots to humansCharles MacKinnondisagrees with the British Gas owner’s justification for cutting 1,300 jobsMon 27 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.18 EDTShareAccording to Centrica’s boss, Chris O’Shea, most people using British Gas prefer to talk to a chatbot rather than a person (Customers prefer AI chatbots, says British Gas owner as 1,300 call centre and back office jobs axed, 23 July).He says that 90% of his customers prefer to use digital channels than speak to a person in the first instance, and that the number of customer calls has fallen by 20%. Well, this is hardly surprising, given the difficulty of getting through to a real person. Finding a telephone number to do so is a challenge in itself, and then there are all the layers of numbers and deflections to encourage use of the digital channels while you are kept on hold at your own cost before you can get to an employee.We are being gaslit by large companies, including banks, that have gradually withdrawn face-to-face access to customer service, which is more expensive, but more efficient from a customer’s viewpoint. First we saw the emergence of contact centres taking phone calls, and then digital channels of access to a human, and now it is digital access to a bot.The cost saving goes to the company and the cost is exported to customers in the time and effort they have to spend having a text message “conversation” with a robot. Clearly for these large firms, company human time is precious, while customer human time is not.This is not about improving the quality of service or adding value to the customer experience. It is simply naked cost reduction using available technology, and removing the expense of employing people from the balance sheet. Customer preference has nothing to do with it.Charles MacKinnonGlasgowHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: ‘It’s human first, then athlete’: Ramsay-Peaty happy with second bronze in new reality | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Adam Ramsay-Peaty said: ‘It’s human first, then athlete, which is a fair price to pay,’ while Scotland’s Archie Goodburn was racing despite his brain cancer diagnosis
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Adam Ramsay-Peaty said: ‘It’s human first, then athlete, which is a fair price to pay,’ while Scotland’s Archie Goodburn was racing despite his brain cancer diagnosis
Content: South Africa’s Michael Houlie (left), Sam Williamson of Australia (centre) and Adam Ramsay-Peaty of England after the 50m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSouth Africa’s Michael Houlie (left), Sam Williamson of Australia (centre) and Adam Ramsay-Peaty of England after the 50m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026‘It’s human first, then athlete’: Ramsay-Peaty happy with second bronze in new realityFormer Olympic champion admits ‘superpower’ waningScotland’s Archie Goodburn in final despite brain cancerSean Ingleat the Tollcross Swimming CentreMon 27 Jul 2026 16.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly after Adam Ramsay-Peaty had battled desperately to snatch another bronze medal at theseCommonwealth Games, it was put to him that he was no longer a winning machine.Once upon a time, Britain’s greatest swimmer might have bristled. Instead he nodded – before pointing out that, at 31, he was now winning in an altogether different way.English part-time sprinter bursts with ‘national pride’ and slams Games no-showsRead more“That period of time where I was undefeated for eight years, whatever it was, it was athlete first, then human,” Ramsay-Peaty said. “Now it’s human first, then athlete, which is a very fair price to pay.”He was then asked whether he could get his superpower back. “My superpower looks very different now. I think juggling babies with milk and having a toddler around is, I guess, a different superpower when that time comes. But as a professional athlete, I’m still committed. I’ve still got that mentality. We just had to approach it very differently because I’ve been that person who wins all the time, and it costs you pretty much everything, and I won’t say it’s worth it now.”Ramsay-Peaty was smiling as he spoke. And he was also smiling after a 50-metre breaststroke final in which he needed a dramatic finish to even get on the podium. He alsowon bronze in the 100m breaststrokeat the weekend.View image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty in the men’s 50m breaststroke.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianNormally Ramsay-Peaty’s best part of his race is the first 30m. At his best, he has already established clear blue water by then. Not this time. He was fighting the water, and his opponents, and it needed a late surge to take him into bronze in 26.94sec – just 0.01 clear of Chris Smith of South Africa. That time was 0.99sec off Ramsay‑Peaty’s world record – and well behind Australia’s Sam Williamson who took gold in 26.50, adding to his 100m breaststroke triumph, with South African Michael Houlie winning silver in 26.77.But while Ramsay-Peaty may be more zen these days, he admits that he is still frustrated with his recent performances. “We weren’t good enough, and we have to look at why because the data in training, the data this whole season, has been tracking on an upward trend, and I can’t really put my finger on it where I’ve just lost that power per stroke,” he said.“I’m not going to lie, it’s very frustrating. Something is not clicking. But it is my first championship since Paris to get two bronzes. You know, we’ve still got relays to go. I’d say that’s success. I’m not going to be too hard on myself, not any more. Let’s keep it in perspective.”That refreshing attitude came to mind as Scotland’s Archie Goodburn received the biggest roar of the night in the same race despite finishing tied last. And no wonder, given the 25‑year‑old was competing here having been diagnosed with terminal brain cancer two years ago.View image in fullscreenArchie Goodburn received a diagnosis of terminal brain cancer two years ago.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA“The reception was monumental,” said Goodburn, who was strikingly positive afterwards. “I tried to prepare myself for it. But that was the next level.”Doctors have diagnosed oligodendrogliomas, which accounts for roughly 3% of all primary brain tumours, and means he may have only a decade to live. But Goodburn has made it his mission to raise as much awareness as possible about the condition.“Every athlete talks about tough times, but there’s been some really tough times,” he said. “And the shoes I was in, or the position I was in this time last year, it was a dark spot.“So looking back on where I am now 12 months later, and everything we’ve managed to achieve over the year, thanks to the support of my friends, family and the University of Edinburgh. I can’t say a big enough thank you. And long may that continue.”Last year, Goodburn started using Vorasidenib – a breakthrough new treatment designed to slow the spread of cancer. That has delayed the prospect of chemotherapy. But there are plenty of tough times ahead.When asked how he remained positive, he was powerful and direct. “I advocate because I believe that my own advocacy can make a difference to my own life. And the best way I can do that is to be positive about the situation and positive for change.“But I also advocate for the future Archies. I swim for future Archies that want to succeed on an international level. But also young patients and people with brain cancer under the age of 40.“Brain cancer is the biggest killer of all cancers for people under the age of 40 in the UK. And I do believe that our advocacy groups are making a difference to that. That we’ll hopefully see over the next few years.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Adam Ramsay-PeatySwimmingCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: English part-time sprinter bursts with ‘national pride’ and slams Games no-shows | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: No one grabbed the opportunity offered by late absentees harder than Elliot Jones, a part-time athlete whose day job is working for Uefa
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: No one grabbed the opportunity offered by late absentees harder than Elliot Jones, a part-time athlete whose day job is working for Uefa
Content: Elliot Jones of England after winning his heat in the 100m at the Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenElliot Jones of England after winning his heat in the 100m at the Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PACommonwealth Games 2026English part-time sprinter bursts with ‘national pride’ and slams Games no-showsElliot Jones grabs golden ticket offered by withdrawalsWelsh sprinter Azu: ‘I would never disrespect the flag’Sean Ingleat Scotstoun StadiumMon 27 Jul 2026 12.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt took Elliot Jones, an unheralded English 100m sprinter making his major international debut at the grand age of 28, to cut through the noise. Asked about all the no-shows at theseCommonwealth Games, he began to shake his head, almost in disbelief.“The national pride I have is so, so high,” Jones said. “I personally don’t understand why athletes wouldn’t want to come and represent their country, regardless of timetables. I’m going to take every international call I can get.”Gabriel Langton feared he had let England down after horror fall at Commonwealth GamesRead moreFor those not counting, nine Team England athletes have withdrawn during the past week, including the former world champions Katarina Johnson-Thompson and Dina Asher‑Smith. Most have not given a reason why. The poster girl of these Games, Scotland’sEilish McColgan, also withdrew on Saturdayafter failing to recover from injury in time.Yet those absentees have created a potential real-life golden ticket for others. And no one grabbed it harder on Monday than Jones, a part‑time athlete whose day job is working for Uefa on matchday operations in the Champions League and the Europa League.On Thursday night, he received a phone call from the England team’s sprints manager to ask whether he fancied running in the 100m after Louie Hinchliffe pulled out. “Let me think about that,” Jones replied, before shouting: “Yes!”“I had to get the Glasgow bus at nine the next morning, quickly pack and restructure my training plan but it’s fine, we’re always ready,” Jones said. “It was supposed to take us six hours but it took us seven with the traffic.”And having got here, Jones was in no mood to mess about in his first major championship as he ran 10.07sec to qualify third overall for the semi-finals on Tuesday.It was heartening to hear – especially given that several Olympic and world champions are missing, including Keely Hodgkinson, Letsile Tebogo and Julien Alfred, the women’s 100m champion in Paris whose poster is outside the Scotstounhill train station.View image in fullscreenA poster at Scotstounhill railway station showing Julien Alfred, one of the high-profile absentees.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianA similar message was delivered by the Wales athlete Jeremiah Azu, the world indoor 60m champion last year, after he had scooted through his 100m heat in 10.10. Asked why he had decided to go to Glasgow, he pointed to the word Cymru on his vest. “Because of this,” Azu said. “To put this vest on is such a privilege and an honour, and I would never put that opportunity to the side. I would never disrespect the flag like that.”Despite the absence of the 100m world champion Oblique Seville, a strong men’s field still includes athletes such as Nigeria’s Kanyinsola Ajayi, who ran 9.84 to win the London Diamond League meeting ahead of Seville just over a week ago.On the women’s side, though, the story is very different. Six of the top 10 100m times in 2026 have also been run by Commonwealth athletes – none of whom are actually running the event in Glasgow. However, England’s Imani-Lara Lansiquot, who has two 4x100m Olympic medals to her name, said she was delighted to be at the “Friendly Games”.Lansiquot said: “I think this competition is a great springboard for athletes. And it’s a great springboard for us as a country, in a time where it feels very divided. You walk around our hotel, the energy is buzzing. Everyone has that sense of togetherness, and that’s what I love about this competition.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCompetitors start in a heat of the men’s 100m at the Scotstoun Stadium.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThat mood was reflected in a surprisingly strong crowd of 7,500 on the opening morning, despite temperatures in the low teens. As Billy Connolly once joked: “There are two seasons in Scotland, June and Winter.” Yet on the track and off, it soon warmed up.And they cheered everyone on, including stragglers such as Tye Leo‑Stroud of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha, who ran a season’s best 11.85 in the men’s 100m – nearly two seconds behind. “It was cold – I didn’t expect it,” Leo‑Stroud said. “Where I am from is very hot, both during day and at night. I pulled my hamstring a couple of years ago. It’s a bit tight.”There will be lots of good races in the days ahead, especially in the men’s mile when the new world record-holder, Josh Kerr, faces off against his compatriot Jake Wightman and the brilliant new Australian star, Cam Myers. The women’s 800m, meanwhile, is also a tantalising rematch between Kenya’s Lilian Odira and England’s Georgia Hunter Bell, who finished first and second at the world championships.View image in fullscreenEdna Ng’Andula of Zambia shows off her sharp nail extensions in a 100m heat.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAt the end of the first session on Monday the EnglandAthleticsteam leader, Scott Grace, defended those who had pulled out, saying that some had preferred to focus on the European championships in Birmingham in two weeks’ time. “Because when you’re a world-class athlete, putting your body through three rounds here, three rounds there, is hard,” Grace said.True. But in a marketplace where track and field is fighting for every eyeball it can get, the lack of sustained star power during a home Games matters.Euan Crumley, the editorial director of Athletics Weekly, said: “On my train to Scotstounhill, I heard a lot of spectators asking which athletes would actually be here. Some are – like Amy Hunt. But not all the names they mentioned will be, sadly.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026AthleticsCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jon McConnell chasing Commonwealth Games treasure after rejecting Love Island | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Before these Commonwealth Games, Northern Irish boxer Jon McConnell made headlines for turning down the 13th season of Love Island
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Before these Commonwealth Games, Northern Irish boxer Jon McConnell made headlines for turning down the 13th season of Love Island
Content: Jon McConnell is enjoying the limelight at the Commonwealth Games despite turning down Love Island.Photograph: François Nel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon McConnell is enjoying the limelight at the Commonwealth Games despite turning down Love Island.Photograph: François Nel/Getty ImagesCommonwealth Games 2026Jon McConnell chasing Commonwealth Games treasure after rejecting Love IslandNorthern Irish boxer one victory away from a medalTryagain Morning Ndevelo inspired by his nameYara El-Shabouryat SEC Centre, GlasgowMon 27 Jul 2026 18.15 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore theseCommonwealth Games, Jon McConnell made headlines for turning down the 13th season of Love Island. Now the Northern Irishman is one win away from a medal after defeating India’s Sumit Sumit to reach the 70kg quarter-finals in Glasgow.“I didn’t expect [the attention] at all,” he said. “Someone sent me the interview [about Love Island auditions] and I was a wee bit shocked. I didn’t even know I said half of it. It was after a sparring session and with the adrenaline I was just saying different stuff.“Now I am just going along with it a bit; the lads were winding me up. But boxing comes first.
