Skills pay the bills.”English part-time sprinter bursts with ‘national pride’ and slams Games no-showsRead moreThe 23-year-old had to dig deep against Sumit to secure a 4-1 victory after finding himself down early before producing a strong finish. “I came from behind; from two rounds down basically,” said McConnell, who had a point deducted. “I am proud of myself.”Having arrived in Glasgow on Tuesday, McConnell said the days leading up to his opening contest had tested his patience. “It was a long wait to be honest with you. It was really long. It has been a week. Every day felt the same: it was wake up, training, rest. It was getting a bit monotonous. This here is what I live for.”Earlier, Namibia’s Tryagain Morning Ndevelo also booked his place in the quarter-finals. Named after the lesson his mother instilled in him growing up, he has carried that philosophy into the ring, producing a unanimous points victory over Bangladesh’s Md Ruhin Reza in the men’s 60kg competition.After receiving a walkover in the opening round when Trinidad and Tobago’s Anthony Joseph failed to make the call time, Ndevelo finally got the opportunity he had been craving to compete. On Sunday, Ndevelo had completed his ring walk through the smoke before discovering he was the only boxer inside the ropes. Joseph never answered the call to the ring, leaving the Namibian warming up alone before the opening bell sounded with just one fighter present.View image in fullscreenTryagain Morning Ndevelo is through to the quarter-finals of the men’s 60kg competition.Photograph: François Nel/Getty ImagesFor a boxer chasing a breakthrough at his third Commonwealth Games, it was hardly ideal preparation. “Today was nice,” he said after his fight against Reza. “I’m glad that I got to go into the ring. Got to face somebody. I can see my level.“A lot of hard work has gone into this. So at least I finally got a chance to practise what I have been learning. I was thinking: ‘Am I really fine?’ and ‘Am I ready?’ because I didn’t get a taste. At least now I know. I don’t feel tired. I have an extra level I can get to. I was excited to have him [Reza] at least show up.”Now, in Glasgow, he has the opportunity to take the next step, with his remarkable first name becoming one of the stories of these Games. “My mother is my whole world,” he said. “[Growing up], whenever I missed training or I was feeling down, I would be told: ‘You don’t have to miss training. Just show up. Even if you are not good, just show up.’ She has always been behind me and that itself is the definition of my name.“Every day you wake up in the morning and you have the chance to do what you didn’t do yesterday. That is why my middle name is Morning. Tuesday, Wednesday, whenever I fight again, I have the chance to better what I did here today. That’s all from her, for giving me this name. Every time I feel low, I get up and try again.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026BoxingCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mind the ever-growing gap: the Premier League keeps spending big | Premier League | The Guardian
description: English clubs have spent more on players this summer than the other four major European leagues combined
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: English clubs have spent more on players this summer than the other four major European leagues combined
Content: Bradley Barcola could be the next expensive import to move to the Premier League.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenBradley Barcola could be the next expensive import to move to the Premier League.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyPremier LeagueMind the ever-growing gap: the Premier League keeps spending bigEnglish clubs have spent more on players this summer than the other four major European leagues combinedAndrew BeasleyMon 27 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe financial power of thePremier Leagueis unmatched. The teams in England’s top division have collectively invested more than £1.4bn in new players already this summer (through disclosed fees alone), around £303m more than the 76 clubs from the Bundesliga, La Liga, Ligue 1 and Serie A combined.These figures are the gross spend, so take no account of players sold to help balance the books. Factoring this in only increases the divide. The clubs of Ligue 1 and the Bundesliga are £203.4m and £72.2m in credit from their transfer dealings respectively. While La Liga (£163.1m) and Serie A (£124.1m) have spent more than they have earned, they are an ocean adrift of the Premier League’s net spend of £523.6m.None of this is new; it has been the trend for many years. The worrying aspect for teams across the continent is that the gap between the Premier League and the rest may grow wider before the summer is out.Chart showing net transfer spend in Europe’s big five leagues in summer 2026Despite their enormous outlay, top-flight English teams have spent about £230m less than Premier League clubs of 2025-26 had at this point last year. But only 25 deals were completed by the end of 1 July (which is when new contracts usually start, explaining why pre-arranged moves are often finalised then). It’s roughly half as many as the 47 that occurred by that date last summer. The expanded World Cup will probably have delayed some deals, creating a potential backlog of transfer spending that will soon hit the books.Assessing clubs individually highlights why most might continue spending. Aston Villa, Brighton and Tottenham have already spent more in gross terms than in the entirety of the summer 2025 transfer window. Unai Emery has a net £109.6m burning a hole in his pocket following business which includes the departures of Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans. Brighton will need a larger squad as they have a Conference League campaign on the horizon while Tottenham are hoping to improve upon consecutive 17th-place finishes. Their trading may not be complete even though they’ve already outspent their efforts from last summer, with Spurs’ net spend of £149.7m the highest in Europe’s big five leagues.Chart showing net transfer spend by Premier League clubs in summer 2025 and summer 2026Chelsea also have a higher net spend than last year, even before their reportedly agreed deal for Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix goes through. Even if that transfer is not completed, would you bet against BlueCo throwing more money around, especially with a new manager to back?Danny Welbeck is the latest to emergeon the Stamford Bridge radar. Either way, Chelsea have already invested more in new talent than they had on this day last year. The same is true for Everton, Fulham, Manchester City and Newcastle, all of whom may have further incomings in the pipeline, too.There are other clubs with work to do. The three promoted teams have only spent £8m more between them than Sunderland alone had at this point in 2025. Régis Le Bris added a total of 18 new players to his squad last summer, with fellow promoted sides Burnley (15) and Leeds (11) also hitting double figures for incomings. By these standards, Ipswich (with seven new players), Hull (four) and Coventry (three) must recruit further.At the opposite end of the Premier League scale, Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have collectively spent two-thirds of a billion less on new talent than they did last summer.The latest rumour millgossip says the champions may make a move for Vinícius Júnior. If not the Brazilian then perhaps Bradley Barcola, though Liverpool are also said to be pursuing the Paris Saint-Germain winger. Neither player will be remotely cheap. United are believed to be targeting Ollie Watkins – he wouldn’t cost Vinícius or Barcola money, but neither would Villa sell to a rival at a reduced fee.The Premier League also has clubs who have yet to make an outlay. It is unlikely Crystal Palace, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland end the summer without spending a transfer fee as is now the case. It would be remiss of Palace and Sunderland not to invest when they are in European competition this season. As for Forest, like Chelsea they have had an insatiable thirst for player turnover in recent times. With Elliot Anderson having left for an enormous fee, replacements will surely arrive soon.It is remarkable to think the Premier League may not be halfway through its summer outlay when £1.4bn has already been used for recruitment. The top-flight English clubs collectively spent £3.1bn on players last summer, with over £600m in the final week of dealing alone. That figure may be blown away by the time the transfer window closes on 3 September.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTransfer windowfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: John Stones set for Inter move after shining for England at World Cup | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: The England defender John Stones is poised to complete a free transfer to Inter after leaving Manchester City
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The England defender John Stones is poised to complete a free transfer to Inter after leaving Manchester City
Content: John Stones started the World Cup quarter-final and semi-final for England.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenJohn Stones started the World Cup quarter-final and semi-final for England.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PATransfer windowJohn Stones set for Inter move after shining for England at World CupDefender left Manchester City on free transfer‘I still feel I have so much to give to a club’Jamie JacksonMon 27 Jul 2026 17.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInter are closing in on signing John Stones as a free transfer after the 32-year-old defender leftManchester Cityin June.Inter and their rival Italian club Juventus were interested in Stones before the World Cup and theNerazzurriare now in pole position to recruit him following his impressive form in England’s run to the semi-finals.Manchester City hope Rodri will sign new deal as Real Madrid weigh up offerRead moreStones made 13 appearances for City last season before being injured in December. Yet after being out for two months and staying injury-free, he was selected only five more times by City’s then manager Pep Guardiola.At the World Cup, Stones started the opening game for Thomas Tuchel’s team against Croatia, was an unused substitute against Ghana and Panama, made substitute appearances in the knockout wins against the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mexico, before starting the quarter-final victory against Norway and the 2-1 semi-final defeat against Argentina.Towards the end of last season Stones spoke of his continuing ambition to play at the top level. “I still feel I have so much to give a club and I feel in a good moment physically,” he said. “There is a lot for me still to fight for in my career and a new challenge will be exciting. I’m keeping an open mind. I can take what I have learned here and maybe pass it on.”While Inter are confident of signing Stones, the deal could yet collapse should a requisite Premier League club express an interest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsenal’s William Saliba is out for an extended period with a back injury, meaning a defender is needed for cover in Mikel Arteta’s squad. Chelsea under Xabi Alonso are expected to play with three centre-backs so are in the market to sign at least one. Neither Arsenal nor Chelsea, though, are yet to make a move for Stones.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowJohn StonesInternazionaleManchester CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Untouchable and a world apart: cycling world reacts to Pogacar’s fifth Tour win | Tour de France 2026 | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar has quickly drawn level with the Tour de France greats and Paul Seixas, the young home hope, is keen to acknowledge the Slovene’s dominance
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tadej Pogacar has quickly drawn level with the Tour de France greats and Paul Seixas, the young home hope, is keen to acknowledge the Slovene’s dominance
Content: Tadej Pogacar (left) and Isaac del Toro, wearing the best young rider's white jersey, helped UAE Emirates XRG to win €832,750.Photograph: Mosa’ab Elshamy/APView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar (left) and Isaac del Toro, wearing the best young rider's white jersey, helped UAE Emirates XRG to win €832,750.Photograph: Mosa’ab Elshamy/APTour de France 2026Untouchable and a world apart: cycling world reacts to Pogacar’s fifth Tour winSlovene has quickly drawn level with the greatsPaul Seixas acknowledges Pogacar’s dominanceJeremy Whittlein ParisMon 27 Jul 2026 08.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar woke up in Paris on Monday as the fastest and the youngest cyclist to win five Tours de France. The 27-year-old Slovene tookhis fifth overall victoryon the Champs Élysées on Sunday evening in a thrilling final stage won by Mathieu van der Poel.Pogacar is level with Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin and he is expected to continue racing in pursuit of a record-breaking sixth win.Tadej Pogacar’s ability to win unopposed stands champion out among Tour legends | William FotheringhamRead more“When it’s not fun any more, that’s when he will stop,” his mother, Marjeta, said. Asked how long her son might continue at his current level, she replied: “Maybe 10 years – I don’t know, we’ll see.”The French media were, broadly, supportive of Pogacar’s success, with L’Équipe lauding his membership of the “club of five”, while Le Figarodescribed him as “untouchable, implacable and unbending”.Pogacar’s CV is indeed untouchable. His record of victories is arguably more complete than Merckx’s, with only Paris-Roubaix and the Vuelta a España, which starts in Monaco on 22 August, still to be won.The stats reveal just how dominant a Tour champion he has been. Over the 16,911km he has ridden during his five wins, he spent almost 9,500km in the yellow jersey. Given he took the lead inhis first Tour win, in 2020, on the penultimate day, that is extraordinary.Pogacar was the youngest of the five‑time winners to take the title and achieved his successes in just under 404 hours of racing; it took Anquetil almost 613. Pogacar’s average speed, 41.99kmh, was faster than any other five-time winner and he has won more mountain stages. These figures reflect changes in technology, equipment and athlete ability, allied to shorter stages, increased rest days and the diminishing number of time trials in the Tour.While Pogacar and his team thrived, with Isaac del Toro joining his team leader on the Paris podium by finishing third, others plumbed the depths. Their dominant UAE Emirates XRG team won €832,750 (about £712,000) in prize money, while the Picnic PostNL team won €12,770.French cyclists had a mixed experience. For only the third time there were no home stage wins, but three French riders – Paul Seixas, Lenny Martinez and Jordan Jegat – finished in the top 10.Seixas represents the future for the home nation but the 19‑year‑old rider, who began the Tour recovering from a crash in June and nursing a cold, was disappointed to finish fourth in the general classification. “I’d hoped to make the podium in Paris as there wasn’t much between me and Del Toro,” he said. “But between myself and Pogacar, it’s a world apart.“But it’s motivating and inspiring. It will make me work harder. I’ve a concrete vision of what I need to do, to get closer to my dream of winning the Tour.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPaul Seixas impressed with his maturity during the Tour but he was still disappointed by his fourth place.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPAPogacar is expected to confirm that he will start the Vuelta, while the future plans of his longstanding rival Jonas Vingegaard,who crashed out of the Touron the day he was visited by doping control at 2am, remain unclear.The nocturnal doping controlssubjected to both ridersby the International Testing Agency provoked intense speculation, although no results have been made known.However, Le Figaro,while acknowledging Pogacar’s achievement, captured the climate that still surrounds any serial winner, saying that credibility for the Tour and for Pogacar is a “challenge greater than any record”.Explore more on these topicsTour de France 2026Tour de FranceTadej PogacarCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: McLaren’s team principal hails ‘great trajectory’ of Lando Norris after win | Lando Norris | The Guardian
description: Andrea Stella, the McLaren’s team principal, has said Lando Norris is ‘more in control of his emotions’ after the world champion won his first race of season in Hungary
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Andrea Stella, the McLaren’s team principal, has said Lando Norris is ‘more in control of his emotions’ after the world champion won his first race of season in Hungary
Content: Lando Norris exploited the improvements of his McLaren to win the Hungarian Grand Prix.Photograph: Márton Mónus/ReutersView image in fullscreenLando Norris exploited the improvements of his McLaren to win the Hungarian Grand Prix.Photograph: Márton Mónus/ReutersLando NorrisMcLaren’s team principal hails ‘great trajectory’ of Lando Norris after win‘He’s more in control of his emotions,’ says Andrea StellaWorld champion won his first race of season in HungaryGiles Richardsin BudapestMon 27 Jul 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLando Norris is at the peak of his powers afterhis win at the Hungarian Grand Prixdemonstrated the world champion has a stronger psychological approach to driving, according to the McLaren team principal, Andrea Stella.Norris took his team’s first win of the season on Sunday with a commanding drive at the Hungaroring after Mercedes dominance for much of the campaign. The Briton has always maintained his team would come back into contention and duly did so, beating the Red Bull of Max Verstappen into second and the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli into third.‘Pretty bad’: Lewis Hamilton hits out at Ferrari after dropping points in F1 title raceRead moreMcLaren brought more upgrades to Hungary, which proved effective on a track that is dominated by relentless cornering, but Stella pointedly noted how much Norris had developed since takinghis first title last year. “He hasn’t really had the machinery to show it so far, but he showed it today,” he said. “Lando is much more confident. He’s much more aware of his tools he has in his driving, how to deploy these tools. He’s also more in control of his emotions.”Norris had been very quick in the race, despite dropping a place to hisMcLarenteammate, Oscar Piastri, on the opening corners. Having regained the lead, Stella admired how well Norris had handled the situation. “When he was behind Oscar, he said a couple of times that he had pace in hand, but he didn’t get frustrated. The fact he wasn’t overly frustrated then allowed him to use the pace at the right time and lead him to the victory. We’ve seen a great trajectory of development for Lando.”George Russell, who is now trailing his Mercedes teammate, the championship leader Antonelli, by 59 points, finished in seventh place after a technical problem on the grid left him with a slow start. He dropped to 20th before rallying back to seventh, but after a series of problems with his car this season he has all but lost patience with the repeated problems that had cost him so many points.“I’m past the point of disappointment now, because if I’m continuing to be disappointed with everything that goes on, I’ll just be disappointed every day of the week,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s just unbelievable, the list of things that’ve happened this season. It does feel like it is happening substantially more to me than others and hopefully it swings around. I don’t wish any bad luck on anyone, but I’ve never had a season like this in my whole career, let alone my F1 career.”Explore more on these topicsLando NorrisMcLarenFormula OneFormula One 2026Motor sportGeorge RussellMercedes GPnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jockey Club staff cull leaves Derby feeling flat with Ascot and Goodwood riding high | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Jim Allen’s drive, enthusiasm and focus will be a big loss to the five-year Epsom project to revive the Derby
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Jim Allen’s drive, enthusiasm and focus will be a big loss to the five-year Epsom project to revive the Derby
Content: The five-day Glorious Goodwood festival will have some major renewed rivalries.Photograph: Kieran Cleeves/PA Media Assignments/PAView image in fullscreenThe five-day Glorious Goodwood festival will have some major renewed rivalries.Photograph: Kieran Cleeves/PA Media Assignments/PATalking HorsesHorse racingJockey Club staff cull leaves Derby feeling flat with Ascot and Goodwood riding highJim Allen’s drive, enthusiasm and focus will be a big loss to the five-year Epsom project to revive the ClassicGreg WoodMon 27 Jul 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe King George card at Ascot on Saturday was an day that showcased Flat racing at its best and the sense of optimism at the end of the afternoon was only enhanced by the prospect of five days atGlorious Goodwoodthis week.Scandinavia and Trawlerman will reprise their Ascot Gold Cup rivalry in Tuesday’s Goodwood Cup. The big three of Bow Echo, Gstaad and Opera Ballo have been declared for Wednesday’s £1.5m Sussex Stakes. Diamond Necklace, the French Oaks winner, is lined up for the Nassau Stakes on Thursday while on the final day the fierce punting challenge of the Stewards’ Cup, one of the biggest betting races of the summer, lurks on the Saturday card.King George glory days are back and Ascot has Europe’s top racing prize in sightRead moreRacing rarely proceeds seamlessly from one highlight to another, however, and news emerged last week that Jockey Club Racecourses, the biggest commercial operator in British racing, is to lose up to 30 staff after a restructuring overseen by Jim Mullen, the former boss of Reach, who joined the Jockey Club as chief executive in June 2025.For the moment at least, the redundancy process remains voluntary, but 30 jobs is nearly 5% of a 650-strong workforce, not all of whom are being offered the chance to leave, so some compulsory redundancies may yet be required. The most surprising departure so far is Jim Allen, the general manager at Epsom since October 2024, who is an originator as well as the public face ofthe track’s five-year planto revive the status and popularity of the Derby.Allen, who opted for voluntary redundancy in preference to applying for a newly created role overseeing a “London Hub” of tracks that includes Epsom,told the Racing Post on Sundayhe is “sure [the five-year plan] will stay”, though “it will be tweaked and improved as there’s still a way to go and it was never going to happen in one year”.View image in fullscreenEpsom has a five-year plan to attract 100,000 to the two-day Derby meeting.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersFor Allen, the Derby project was not just a professional commitment. He had a deep personal investment in the scheme having grown up near the course and started his career in racing as a work-rider on the downs. His rich and varied path through the sport has included senior roles in racecourse management and a spell as a trainer in the United States. He may now return to a more hands-on role as a trainer or syndicate manager.“It’s all very amicable,” he told the Post, “and I’m hoping I’ll be back at next year’s Derby festival with some sort of runner.”Amicable though it may be, Allen’s drive, enthusiasm and focus will be a big loss to the Derby project, which has the ultimate aim of returning to a 100,000 attendance for the two days of Epsom’s Classic meeting.It is not a loss that can be easily quantified on a balance sheet, and Mullen – who oversaw a 25% cut in headcount during his six-year tenure at Reach – has targeted cost savings to arrest a decline in JCR’s profitability.Mullen signed an exclusive £100m, 20-year deal in March with the hospitality company Levy with the aim of improving the raceday experience for spectators, but JCR’s recently filed accounts for 2025 reflect the extent to which the business’s costs – including the wage bill and increased national insurance obligations – have been rising faster than revenue.“With that in mind,” a Jockey Club spokesperson said on Monday, “we have been working over the past six months on a plan to ensure we have an organisation able to maximise the potential of investing the £100m … realised earlier this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Our aim is to give our racecourse teams more autonomy when it comes to commercial decision-making and ownership of the customer experience at their venues. It is also about us creating a more successful and sustainable business that can play a larger role in supporting, investing in and growing the sport while promoting racing and the thoroughbred.”Quick GuideGreg Wood's Tuesday tipsShowBeverley1.35 Perfidia 2.10 Talking In Kode 2.45 Dorothea Hope 3.20 Apulia Bay 3.55 Norcross Brow 4.30 Jojo RabbitGoodwood1.50 Noble Horizon 2.25 Undiscovered 3.00 Qirat 3.35 Scandinavia 4.10 Spring Is Sprung (nap) 4.45 Final Objective 5.20 Annastarzy (nb) 5.55 MachadadorpYarmouth2.35 Educator 3.10 Mithaaly 3.45 Luminous Warrior 4.20 Divot 4.55 Charency 5.25 MethgalFfos Las6.00 Dream On Kent 6.30 Distinct Spirit 7.00 Knightmare 7.30 Summerson 8.00 Pureis King 8.30 LegendsofthelandWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.JCR remains the biggest commercial entity in the sport and is unlikely to surrender that status any time soon. A round of job cuts, though, is a sharp contrast to the mood at tracks such as Ascot, Goodwood and York, where the Ebor meeting will take centre stage next month.What is also unclear – because the accounts do not single out individuals tracks’ profit-and-loss figures – is the extent to which JCR’s profits depend on the major National Hunt festivals at Cheltenham and Aintree in March. That only Cheltenham has been left as a stand-alone entity in the restructuring probably tells its own story.It is an odd turn of racing history that has led the Jockey Club, which is so firmly rooted in Newmarket and Flat racing, become increasingly reliant on the runaway success of Cheltenham and its festival meeting over the past two or three decades.The five-year scheme to revive the Derby was, and remains, a way to bring Flat racing – which, unlike jumping, has a global audience – at least a little more back into the JCR mix. There are still plenty of very capable people at the operation’s HQ, but losing Jim Allen’s passion for the project feels like a setback it could well do without.Explore more on these topicsHorse racingTalking HorsesHorse racing tipsGlorious GoodwoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It felt like being in a disaster movie’: uncertainty after evacuation from France’s Gironde wildfire | France | The Guardian
description: Residents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blaze
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Residents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blaze
Content: Evacuees at the exhibition centre in Bordeaux.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersView image in fullscreenEvacuees at the exhibition centre in Bordeaux.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersFrance‘It felt like being in a disaster movie’: uncertainty after evacuation from France’s Gironde wildfireResidents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blazeAngelique Chrisafisin BordeauxMon 27 Jul 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSitting in their suburban apartment in Mérignac on the outskirts of Bordeaux, Krishma, an interpreter, and her husband, Nassir, first felt a sense of dread when a strange black cloud turned the sky dark in the middle of the day. Then a bitter burning smell filled the air outside.“The sky changed colour. It seemed like a cloud but it was smoke covering the sun – it wasn’t a natural phenomenon. It didn’t seem real,” said Nassir, an English literature graduate from Kabul who has been living inFrancefor seven years. “We couldn’t breathe easily, you could feel it in your lungs.”The acrid smell, which at first seemed like burning rubber then unmistakably like wood smoke, was blowing on the wind from themassive wildfire in Girondein south-western France. The blaze has torn through 42,000 hectares, an area four times the size of Paris, causing one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war. The government said on Monday that although the fire had stopped growing, it was still blazing and a new heatwave this week could make it harder to fight.Nassir and Krishma had slept at the exhibition centre for three nights and did not know when they would be allowed home.Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The GuardianAs authorities carried out one of the biggest evacuations in modern French history, Krishma and Nassir were among 220,000 people ordered to flee their homes in Gironde. Many people were evacuated from wooded areas directly hit by fire, where at least 240 homes were destroyed. But in an unprecedented move, tens of thousands more were ordered by police to evacuate from more built-up, urban streets as the fire reached 9 miles (15km) from the outer edge of Bordeaux’s vast suburban area.Krishma and Nassir had to evacuate their suburban street at midnight on Friday. With their two children aged 10 and eight, they quickly packed toothbrushes, toys, one change of clothes and personal documents into their car. On Monday afternoon, they were sitting on camp beds among hundreds of people sheltering in a hangar at Bordeaux’s exhibition centre. They had slept there for three nights and did not know when they would be allowed home. The fire had not reached their residential area, but with the French government warning that the blaze was “extremely intense and unpredictable”, authorities would not yet allow a return, they said.View image in fullscreenA woman and her dog at the emergency shelter.Photograph: Caroline Blumberg/APThe couple’s main feeling was great sadness to see the Gironde forest destroyed. Krishma said: “When we were in Afghanistan there were lots of explosions, suicide attacks, but that was related to around 30 years of war. When we came here, we never thought there would be a situation like this. It brought us back to the bad memories from our past.”What is a ‘fire cloud’, and how have they worsened wildfires in Europe?Read moreAcross the vast hangar, Yves, who used to work on road maintenance in Bordeaux, was sitting with his 13-year-old mastiff dog, Ichka. Yves had fled his suburban house and garden in Le Haillan outside Bordeaux with his dog’s bed under one arm and had carefully laid it out next to his camp bed. He had been ordered to evacuate in the early hours of Saturday morning.11:13Race against time to contain wildfires in France and Spain - The Latest“We had to leave because of the smoke,” he said. His wife, an administrator who did not want to be named, said she still felt shaken. “It was terrifying – you would look up at the sky and it was completely orange, even after nightfall. It was bizarre. The fire was causing that, and it really made you anxious. I feel quite a lot of anger that all this forest has burned and been lost. Seeing all that is beautiful in nature just go up in smoke is extremely painful and sad.”View image in fullscreenA firefighter watches the flames of a forest fire  in Saint-Jean-d'Illac near Bordeaux.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesOthers who had fled slept in their cars. Loïc, 66, a widower who worked in the metals and glass industries before becoming a decorator, had to leave his house in Saint-Jean-d’Illac outside Bordeaux. “I had been watching this strange fog in the sky. It was a darkness almost like an eclipse,” he said. “There was a kind of ochre mist as light from the sun was diffused through falling ash. So much ash was falling that my car was turned completely grey.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA wildfire in Saint-Jean d’Illac, in the Gironde region.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersAt 1am on Saturday, Loïc was woken by banging on the door from his neighbour, a fire officer, saying he had to leave immediately. He grabbed only his wallet and car keys and ran to the car, leaving his mobile phone behind. There were so many people on the road and heading to the evacuation centre that he decided to stop elsewhere and get a bit of sleep in his car.When he woke on Saturday, listening to the news on the car radio, he knew he could not go home and headed instead for central Bordeaux, thinking the cinema would be a safe and comfortable place. “I watched the two-part Charles de Gaulle epic – the wrong way round, with the second film first, but I knew the story already – then I watched The Odyssey. Then I went back to sleep in my car.”The next day, he visited the graveyard where his wife was buried. On Monday morning, he arrived at the Bordeaux evacuation centre to get information on what to do next. He felt deeply saddened by the loss of the forest. “My generation grew up really attached to nature,” he said.View image in fullscreenA firefighter helps to battle the wildfires.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersFlorence, a former teaching assistant in a primary school, sat on a camp bed with her two cats in their travelling cases after having to evacuate Le Haillan outside Bordeaux. “I was distraught,” she said. “I’m asthmatic, I put tape around the windows of my apartment but I could still smell the smoke which was seeping in under my front door, so I put down wet rags. The sky was orange and grey, and there was soot everywhere.”She said having to suddenly evacuate knowing a fire was raging in Gironde felt like something out of a war. “It felt like being in a disaster movie,” she said. “I’ve always really loved disaster movies – but now I feel like I’ve actually been in one, so I don’t ever want to watch a disaster movie again.”View image in fullscreenFire rages in Saint-Jean-d’Illac, some 30km from Bordeaux.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsFranceWildfiresEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Home Office blocking evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Refugee family reunions in limbo, despite Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of war-torn territory
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Refugee family reunions in limbo, despite Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of war-torn territory
Content: A child looks through a covering made from blankets at a tent camp sheltering displaced Palestinians in Khan Younis last week.Photograph: Ramadan Abed/ReutersView image in fullscreenA child looks through a covering made from blankets at a tent camp sheltering displaced Palestinians in Khan Younis last week.Photograph: Ramadan Abed/ReutersImmigration and asylumHome Office blocking evacuation of dozens of women and children from GazaRefugee family reunions in limbo, despite Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of war-torn territoryDiane TaylorMon 27 Jul 2026 07.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHome Officeis blocking the evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza, despite the Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of the war-torn region.Last September, the Home Office announced it was suspending refugee family reunion applications and that new, more restrictive rules would be announced in the spring. So far there has been no announcement and the process remains suspended.Applications made before the announcement continue to be processed. However, families inGazawho applied to reunite with an immediate family member before the suspension have been blocked from joining loved ones in the UK.The Home Office and the Foreign Office are involved in evacuations from Gaza. At the moment families who have a right to leave are evacuated via Jordan. However, the Home Office is not providing the required onward travel assurance (OTA) and is using legal challenges to block these families coming to the UK, sometimes deploying several senior barristers to a single case.The Home Office says biometrics are obtained before families travel to Jordan, even though the visa centre in Gaza has been closed since October 2023. Other European countries such as Belgium, France, Italy and Ireland are facilitating such evacuations and the Foreign Office has said it is willing to evacuate the families.Lawyers for the families stranded in life-threatening conditions in Gaza say the Home Office appears to be taking a harsher line with Palestinian families than with refugees from other countries hoping to reunite with loved ones in the UK. They say that in some cases the Home Office has stated that the family members, including small children, pose a security risk because they come from a “territory where terrorists operate”, even though some of the refugees in the UK were granted leave to remain on the basis of having been persecuted by Hamas in Gaza.The Guardian has previously reported on the case ofBassem Abudagga, a PhD student who has been separated from his family. Although the Foreign Office has agreed to help with evacuating his family, the Home Office has said they will have to wait until December before officials make a decision about whether to grant an OTA.In a communication with Abudagga’s lawyers on 15 July 2026 in response to descriptions of insanitary conditions, infested tents and frequent bombings, the Home Office said: “While this is acknowledged the conditions your clients face in Gaza alone are not considered to amount to compelling circumstances under the [relevant] guidance.”In another case, a Palestinian refugee in the UK is separated from his wife, their three children – aged nine, 12, 14 – and his 17-year-old nephew who they adopted after the teenager was orphaned by the war.He said:“My family are in constant danger and I worry about them every minute of every day. The UK government promised to help my family but has now gone back on that promise.“They say my family could be dangerous because there are terrorists operating in Gaza. I don’t understand how a mother and her children can be considered a security threat. The Foreign Office has offered to evacuate my family, so why is the Home Office doing everything in its power to stop it?”Sarah Crowe, a solicitor at the law firm Leigh Day representing some of the families trapped in the Palestinian territory and hoping to reunite with immediate family in Britain, said: “The UK government has abandoned vulnerable families in Gaza after promising to assist them. The Home Office is blocking family reunification when theForeign, Commonwealth and Development Officeis ready and willing to evacuate them.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “Under our reforms to create a fairer asylum system, family reunion will no longer be automatic. Those seeking to bring family members to the UK will need to meet stricter criteria.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumGazaHome OfficeRefugeesForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeIsrael-Gaza warPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Machine could make more donated lungs suitable for transplant | NHS | The Guardian
description: Nice backs wider use of system that keeps organs alive outside the body, to help improve low transplantation rates
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Nice backs wider use of system that keeps organs alive outside the body, to help improve low transplantation rates
Content: It is hoped the machine will enable more donated organs, including lungs, remain viable until surgery.Photograph: NHS Blood and Transplant/PAView image in fullscreenIt is hoped the machine will enable more donated organs, including lungs, remain viable until surgery.Photograph: NHS Blood and Transplant/PANHSMachine could make more donated lungs suitable for transplantNice backs wider use of system that keeps organs alive outside the body, to help improve low transplantation ratesAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentMon 27 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA machine that keeps organs alive outside the body could save four in every five donated lungs that currently go to waste in England and Wales.The UK hasone of the poorest lung transplantation ratesin the world. The latest figures from NHS Blood and Transplant show that 170 patients in the UK, including six children, are waiting for new lungs.Most adults wait a year for a transplant and some wait two years or more. Up to a fifth of adults awaiting an urgent transplant die within a year of joining the transplant list, before a suitable lung is found. But only 23% of all donated lungs are used, with donated lungs sometimes declined not only because of organ quality but due to staffing and theatre capacity issues.Draft guidance from the National Institute forHealthand Care Excellence (Nice) recommends that the XVIVO perfusion system be used in the NHS for a four-year period to assess its effectiveness and value for money. Nice estimates that the machine could help rescue four in five donated lungs that are currently unused, by helping them remain viable for transplantation, which could unlock hundreds of organs for transplants.The machine warms donated lungs to body temperature and pumps a fluid through them that mimics blood plasma, while also ventilating them to mimic normal breathing. This allows transplant teams to monitor how the lungs are functioning, treat infection, drain excess fluid and reinflate collapsed areas.While the machine has been trialled at three adult transplant centres, until now Nice had not endorsed the technique in all transplant centres or approved its use in paediatric cases. Nice says the draft guidance aims to ensure all transplant centres can benefit from the technology, regardless of their size or location.Dr Anastasia Chalkidou, the healthtech programme director at Nice, said the machine should allow more lungs to remain available for transplantation that otherwise would be discarded.“Every donated lung is a precious gift, and right now too many of them never reach a patient who needs them,” she said. “This technology has the potential to change that, giving transplant teams the time and information they need to make the most of organs that would otherwise go unused.”Chalkidou said the move reflected wider efforts to improve access “so that where a patient is treated no longer determines whether they can benefit from a transplant”.Jonathan Blades, the head of policy at Asthma + Lung UK, said: “Lung transplant rates in the UK remain lower than in many other developed countries, while respiratory health outcomes remain the worst in Europe. Renewed political and research focus is needed to transform lung health in the UK, and this new technology marks an important step towards that ambition.“We look forward to seeing the results of this trial, which could give more people with serious lung conditions more precious time with their loved ones. It could also reduce the number of donated lungs that currently go to waste if they are unsuitable for transplantation.”​Prof Andrew Fisher​, a member of the British Transplantation Society​ and a consultant transplant physician at Newcastle upon Tyne hospitals NHS​ foundation trust, said: “It​’s important that robust evidence is generated that shows exactly how much impact the use of this device has on lung transplant activity and supports timely access to transplant for patients desperately waiting for a suitable organ.”Explore more on these topicsNHSOrgan donationHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa president Gianni Infantino called to appear before Congress over Trump ties | World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Democrat Jamie Raskin pushes Fifa to release records of contact with Trump, administration and family business
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: Democrat Jamie Raskin pushes Fifa to release records of contact with Trump, administration and family business
Content: Donald Trump joins Fifa president Gianni Infantino on the field for the trophy presentation at the World Cup final.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenDonald Trump joins Fifa president Gianni Infantino on the field for the trophy presentation at the World Cup final.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto/AllstarWorld Cup 2026Fifa president Gianni Infantino called to appear before Congress over Trump tiesDemocrat Jamie Raskin pushes Fifa to release records of contact with Trump, administration and family businessElla BrockwayMon 27 Jul 2026 16.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, has launched an investigation into Fifa presidentGianni Infantino, seeking documents that would detail the ties between soccer’s governing body and Donald Trump and his administration.In a Sunday letter, Raskin wrote to Infantino and called forFifato provide any documents and communications related to gifts, payments or benefits provided to Trump and his associates, as well as the visitor logs for Fifa’s office space in Trump Tower, which it acquired last year. The committee also requested that Infantino sit for a transcribed interview.Infantino’s relationship with Trump came under scrutiny in the lead-up to this summer’s World Cup. In December, at the World Cup draw in Washington, Trump was awardeda newly created “Fifa peace prize”at the Kennedy Center, where renovations were allegedly “rushed” on theadministration’s ordersto prepare for the event. Fifaopenedits office in Trump Tower in midtown Manhattan last July.Fifa president Gianni Infantino accuses critics of spreading hate at World CupRead moreSuch scrutiny intensified during theWorld Cup. Trump made several calls to Infantino to lobby for a review of US striker Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before the Americans’ last-16 match against Belgium. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team and drew the ire of other teams and associations from around the world.Alongside the leaders of Canada and Mexico, TrumpjoinedInfantino for the World Cup trophy presentation after Spain beat Argentina in the final. The pair, who watched the final together in a glassed-in section of luxury seats, were met with boos from the New York New Jersey Stadium crowd when they took the field.Raskin’s letter references the Department of Justice’s decision to “dismiss the indictments” of defendants in US government investigations into corruption in global soccer, including the 2015 prosecution of more than 20 high-level Fifa officials and sports-marketing executives.“[Y]our election as Fifa president was supposed to mark a red-card break from a decades-long culture of corruption and scandals that dressed down world soccer’s reputation,” Raskin wrote to Infantino in the letter. “Instead, at the start of your tenure, you dismantled Fifa’s ethical guardrails and disabled the organization’s ethics committee by pushing out most of its members. This lack of transparency and oversight has since paved the way for you to ingratiate yourself with the Trump administration via tactics that a New York University law professor and one of your former ethics committeemen described as ‘legal bribery’.”The letter also addresses Fifa’s World Cup ticketing policy, which is already the subject ofinvestigationsby several attorneys general in the United States. The use of dynamic pricing drew much criticism during the tournament, leading to massive surges and pricing out many fans from attending games.“The most recent quid pro quo that Fifa and President Trump orchestrated is not a victimless crime. It hurts Americans. Fifa has taken its newfound favored status in the Trump administration as a sign that it may rip off its consumers, most notably, by employing illegal price-gouging and fraudulent sales tactics for the World Cup,” Raskin said in the letter.The letter gives a deadline of 9 August to provide the requested documents and schedule the interview. Raskin does not have the power to compel Infantino to appear, given that Democrats do not hold the majority in the House, unless he garners Republican support.Fifa’s interactions with the US government did not end with this summer’s World Cup. The US is expected to be the primary host of the Women’s World Cup in 2031, and the success of this year’s tournament has led many to speculate thatthe 2038 men’s World Cupcould be hosted by the US. Fifa has been approached for comment.Earlier on Monday, Infantinoused a 15-part messageon Instagram to denounce his critics, accusing them of spreading hate and false narratives. He touted the World Cup as a success.More than 200 Fifa members haveendorsedInfantino ahead of the presidential election in March, but some associations have stood in opposition. The Norwegian football federation isplanningto submit a formal complaint to Fifa ethics investigations over Trump’s role in the reversal of Balogun’s ban.Explore more on these topicsWorld Cup 2026World CupUS sportsGianni InfantinoFifaDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hull funeral director broke families’ trust on ‘almost industrial scale’, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Robert Bush, owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, left bodies ‘rotting away’, family members say
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Robert Bush, owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, left bodies ‘rotting away’, family members say
Content: Robert Bush appeared at Hull crown court on Monday for a five-day sentencing hearing.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenRobert Bush appeared at Hull crown court on Monday for a five-day sentencing hearing.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAUK newsHull funeral director broke families’ trust on ‘almost industrial scale’, court hearsRobert Bush, owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, left bodies ‘rotting away’, family members sayPriya BharadiaMon 27 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fraudulent funeral director broke the trust of families on an “almost industrial scale” as their loved ones’ bodies were left “rotting away”, a court has heard.Robert Bush, owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, appeared at Hull crown court on Monday for a five-day sentencing hearing. He previously pleaded guilty to 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing lawful and decent burial.Several family members read out their victim impact statements to the court, recounting nightmares and PTSD from Bush’s offending, with some breaking down in tears and struggling to speak.On his way into court, Bush, 48, from Otley, West Yorkshire, told reporters he was sorry to the families affected.Several family members recalled Bush “smiling” as he handed them the wrong ashes, while their loved ones remained secretly uncremated. When Jayne Rimmington came to collect the ashes of her 86-year-old mother, Shirley Wright, in October 2023, she was surprised by how heavy they were. Bush claimed this was due to her “bone density”.The body of Wright was recovered on the Legacy premises five months after her death. “I trusted him,” said Rimmington. “He stood there smiling, handed me the box, when she was still laying there, rotting away. It’s a purely evil thing to do.”Vicky Mitchell received the ashes of her father, Colin Wainman, in a navy blue box inside a Hobbycraft bag, with Bush apologising at the time for not having any gift bags at hand. The 69-year-old’s body was recovered on 8 March 2024, 198 days after his death.“My opinion is he is a charlatan,” Mitchell told the court. “A gravedigger from the 1800s. He didn’t care.”Prosecutor Chris Paxton KC said Bush “operated within the heart of the community for around 14 years, entrusted by hundreds of bereaved families in their time of need”. However, Bush “breached that trust on an almost industrial scale in a myriad of ways”.In a search of the Legacy premises in March 2024, Humberside police found many bodies left uncovered and in varying states of decomposition, stored on racks on both sides of the room. One naked body still lay on a stretcher on the floor. Flowers, rings, teddy bears and cards with messages, intended to be placed with loved ones, had been swept under the floor.The removal of bodies took two days and several officers, including a disaster identification team. Bodies had to be identified by dental records, DNA examination or fingerprints.Police also uncovered the remains of an 18-week stillborn boy, identified as Sunny Beverley-Conlin, on the floor of the premises, inside what appeared to be a police evidence bag. His mother, Jasmine Beverley, believed he had been given a funeral and cremated.Rea Burton, granddaughter of David Burton, attended the Legacy funeral home to collect his ashes in December 2023. Bush asked Burton what the family intended to do with the ashes, to which Burton replied they would be put in necklace charms for the family and her uncle would put some into the ink for a tattoo. Bush told her this was a “brilliant idea”.“In reality, Rob had deceived us,” said Burton. “He had abandoned and hidden our loved one for months and had given us a stranger’s ashes with a smile on his face.”After the funeral service of 94-year-old Norman Bridger, his daughter, Karen King, placed what she believed to be her father’s ashes into lockets worn by her and her mother. “I now feel violated [that] I had some unknown person’s ashes so close to me,” King said.To thank him for his work on the funeral, King had also given Bush a bottle of port. “The smile on his face as he accepted it will always haunt me,” she told the court.David Gorbutt visited Bush to collect what he believed were the ashes of his wife, Susan, in September 2023. He was handed a paper bag containing a small cardboard box with her name. When Gorbutt told Bush he “hope[d] they’re the right ones”, Bush replied: “Yes, they are definitely the right ones.”Gorbutt scattered the ashes at the same site as her son’s in a local country park, as per Susan’s wishes. Her body was recovered at the Legacy premises six months after her death.In his statement, Gorbutt said he felt guilty for being “unable to fulfil my wife’s last request, that I deal with her death quickly” as she wanted, recalling that “Susan would say: ‘You know I do not like the cold.’”Like many families, Gorbutt also called for stronger regulation of the funeral industry. “It is hard to believe a person needs more permits to sell burgers than to deal with the dead,” he said.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: PM urged to uphold climate pledges made as mayor and ban new North Sea oil drilling | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Experts who helped Burnham draw up Manchester carbon neutral pledge say backtracking would send wrong message amid wildfires and heatwaves
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Experts who helped Burnham draw up Manchester carbon neutral pledge say backtracking would send wrong message amid wildfires and heatwaves
Content: An oil rig in the North Sea. Andy Burnham’s government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow new drilling at the Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfields.Photograph: Rick Wood Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn oil rig in the North Sea. Andy Burnham’s government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow new drilling at the Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfields.Photograph: Rick Wood Photography/AlamyGreenhouse gas emissionsPM urged to uphold climate pledges made as mayor and ban new North Sea oil drillingExperts who helped Burnham draw up Manchester carbon neutral pledge say backtracking would send wrong message amid wildfires and heatwavesSandra LavilleMon 27 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeading climate scientists who created Greater Manchester’s carbon neutral by 2038 commitment are urging Andy Burnham to unequivocally reject new drilling in the North Sea.Ina letterto the prime minister they said he, as mayor of Greater Manchester, had unveiled one of the UK’s mostambitious local climate programmesthat tackled housing, green growth and public transport.Reports over the weekend continued to suggest Burnham was set to give the green light to controversial new drilling in the North Sea by approving theJackdawand Rosebank oilfields, which were given approval under the Conservatives but put on hold by legal action. The ruling in court said a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact was required to take into account the effect on the climate of burning any fossil fuels extracted.Prof Kevin Anderson and scientists from the Tyndall Centre at the School of Engineering at the University ofManchester, who wrote the open letter to the prime minister, said it was “with considerable concern” that they had read reports suggesting his government intended to approve the further development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields.To do so would send a signal around the world that the UK was backtracking on its international climate commitments, they said.Burnham risks Labour backlash if he reverses ban on new oil and gas drillingRead moreIf the reports were accurate that he intended to give the go ahead to drilling at Jackdaw and Rosebank, the scientists wrote, “they represent a profound departure from the principles you promoted as Mayor of Greater Manchester”.Labour made a manifesto promise that no new oil and gas licences would be issued, but Jackdaw and Rosebank were already in the system at the time of the last general election. A consultation on Jackdaw will finish on 8 August.With extreme heat and wildfires acrossthe UKand Europe this summer, the academics said the evidence showed global emissions must be cut by 8% every year if the world was to meet the upper limit of a maximum of 2C of heating in the Paris climate agreement.Anderson and his colleagues urged Burnham to adhere to commitments he made when announcing the Greater Manchester carbon neutral by 2038 policy.They undertook the carbon budget analysis that underpinned the target championed by Burnham in 2024, when he said Greater Manchester could be front and centre of the green industrial revolution.At the time Burnham said he needed greater powers than those of a mayor to deliver the pace of change required to tackle the climate crisis.Now he has those powers, the scientists who helped him create the carbon neutral plan in Manchester said he must not abandon unequivocal scientific evidence in the face of short-term political pressure.“The scientific evidence has only strengthened since those earlier commitments were made,” the letter said.“Global temperatures have already risen to the lower limit of the Paris Agreement’s temperature range (1.5°C). Extreme weather events are becoming increasingly evident across the UK, most vividly the widespread moorland fires driving air quality to unsafe levels in Greater Manchester.”Remaining global carbon budgets, which give policymakers headroom for action, continue to shrink rapidly. If governments are to respect even the weaker 2C interpretation of the Paris Agreement, global carbon dioxide emissions must now fall by almost 8% every year, starting immediately, they said.“Against that backdrop, approving the further development of oil and gasfields cannot be reconciled with the UK’s repeated commitment to honour its international climate obligations,” the letter said.Anderson and his colleagues said any approval of new drilling would send the wrong signal to the rest of the world.“It would suggest that, on climate change, the UK is prepared to step back from obligations it has repeatedly urged other nations to uphold.”The letter urged Burnham to show the same commitment to evidence and political courage that characterised his leadership in Greater Manchester in response to pressure to open up new drilling in the North Sea.“Future generations will not judge governments by the ingenuity with which they justified expanding fossil fuel production,” the scientists wrote. “They will judge whether, when faced with unequivocal scientific evidence and clear international commitments, they had the courage and compassion to act in a manner consistent with the obligations they had freely entered into.”Explore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsFossil fuelsOil and gas companiesClimate crisisManchesterLabourGreater ManchesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Bill Oddie, naturalist and broadcaster, dies aged 85 | Bill Oddie | The Guardian
description: Coming to fame in The Goodies, Oddie was later known for his wildlife expertise and presented BBC Springwatch
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Coming to fame in The Goodies, Oddie was later known for his wildlife expertise and presented BBC Springwatch
Content: Oddie established himself as an authority on wildlife after first coming to prominence in comic roles.Photograph: Laura LewisView image in fullscreenOddie established himself as an authority on wildlife after first coming to prominence in comic roles.Photograph: Laura LewisBill OddieBill Oddie, naturalist and broadcaster, dies aged 85Coming to fame in The Goodies, Oddie was later known for his wildlife expertise and presented BBC SpringwatchBill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBCBill Oddie – a life in picturesHannah J DaviesMon 27 Jul 2026 06.32 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 05.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe writer, comedian and conservationistBill Oddiehas died aged 85. Having come to prominence with the comedy group The Goodies, Oddie later established himself as an authority on wildlife, presenting television series including the BBC’s Springwatch and Autumnwatch.Oddie’s agent paid tribute to his “intelligence and wit”. In a statement, David Foster said: “It is with deep sadness that I announce the passing of Bill Oddie, the country’s best-loved birder. Bill was a multitalented celebrity – wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued.Bill Oddie – a life in picturesRead more“Instead he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment. He taught us the wonder of it. He protested, lobbied and campaigned for it. He led the way and people of all ages and backgrounds responded to his call. And such a massive contribution to conservation will never be forgotten.“As Bill’s agent I witnessed close-hand his intelligence and wit. He was my friend and it was an honour and a privilege to represent him for so many years. I will miss him terribly. My thoughts and love are with Bill’s wife, Laura, and his daughters Bonnie, Kate and Rosie, who have asked not to be contacted at this sad time. Please respect their wishes.”View image in fullscreenOddie with his fellow Goodies, Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden.Photograph: BBC/Sportsphoto/AllstarOddie was born in Rochdale in Lancashire, and grew up in Birmingham, later studying at Cambridge University. It was at Cambridge that he met Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden, with whom he would form the sketch group The Goodies. After various TV projects, Oddie appeared alongside Brooke-Taylor and Garden in the TV show The Goodies for 10 years from 1970 to 1980. The show was revived by ITV for a 1981 Christmas special and a six-part series that aired in 1982.As well as creating and performing comic musical numbers with The Goodies, including The Funky Gibbon and Black Pudding Bertha (The Queen of Northern Soul), Oddie’s music projects included a role in the English National Opera production of The Mikado in the late 1980s.An avid birder, Oddie made forays into natural history television in the 1970s and 1980s, going on to present wildlife series for the BBC and publishing several books on conservation.Oddie had depression and bipolar disorder. In 2015,he told the Guardianthat he had “inherited the same genetic flaw” as his mother, who was diagnosed with schizophrenia but may have also had bipolar disorder.In September 2020, Oddie said on X that he had been “very ill most of this summer. Lithium toxicity. Almost fatal! I am still here but very confused about most things! But then aren’t many of us. IT fuddles my brain. Confusion. Will I return? I Really dunno. I do hope so. Please wish me luck. XX.” Lithium is prescribed as a mood stabiliser.Bill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBCRead moreHe said in 2014 that he still felt a lingering sadness that his days on Springwatch had been cut short, and he rarely watched the programme.“I very much miss it, but when I do see it, it brings back many happy memories and I like to think I contributed to its success,” he said.“It’s still so well loved and helps encourage people to enjoy the natural world. That’s all to the good because I fear so many people wear earphones for their phones and music players that increasingly they miss out on everyday joys like birdsong.“My plea to people would be to ‘go naked’ occasionally – take off those earpieces so you hear nature and, of course, birdsong. You may not realise how precious it is until it’s gone.”The RSPCA’s chief executive, Jo Rowland, said: “Everyone at the RSPCA is deeply saddened by the loss of our former vice-president Bill Oddie OBE.“While his comedy, music and, of course, work with The Goodies delighted so many, his tireless commitment to British wildlife will define so much of his extraordinary life.“Bill was an exceptional and steadfast champion for the natural world, whose passion for birds and wildlife was truly infectious.“He campaigned tirelessly alongside his many friends at the RSPCA, including taking the fight to governments against plans to cull badgers.“I know many of our wildlife rescuers were inspired into animal welfare by Bill’s groundbreaking broadcasting work and incredible knowledge of British birds, which brought the wonders of nature into millions of homes across the country.”She said “nature has lost one of its best friends, fiercest champions and most iconic defenders”.Oddie is survived by his wife, Laura, and three daughters – Rosie, from his marriage to Laura, and Kate and Bonnie from his first marriage to the jazz musician Jean Hart.Explore more on these topicsBill OddieTelevisionWildlifeTV comedyComedynewsShareReuse this content

title: Jodrell Bank Observatory facing closure after major funder cuts support | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Scientists say decision is blow to UK astronomy as deep space observatory is home to world-leading facilities
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Scientists say decision is blow to UK astronomy as deep space observatory is home to world-leading facilities
Content: Jodrell Bank is home to a world-leading network of radio telescopes and hosts the Grade I-listed Lovell telescope.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJodrell Bank is home to a world-leading network of radio telescopes and hosts the Grade I-listed Lovell telescope.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAstronomyJodrell Bank Observatory facing closure after major funder cuts supportScientists say decision is blow to UK astronomy as deep space observatory is home to world-leading facilitiesIan SampleScience editorMon 27 Jul 2026 11.39 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 08.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJodrell Bank Observatory, the hub of a world-leading network of radio telescopes, is facing closure after government funding for the facility was slashed.The deep space observatory includes the Grade I-listedLovell telescopeand is prized by astronomers who study galaxies, black holes, star formation, planets beyond the solar system and the afterglow of the big bang.The observatory’s funder, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), said on Monday it would withdraw funding for the e-Merlin network, the UK’s national radio astronomy facility at Jodrell Bank, when the current agreement ends in March 2028.Scientists said the decision was a blow to UK astronomy, with observations at Jodrell Bank due to end completely unless other funding is found. “Jodrell has been delivering spectacular discovery science for decades,” said Prof Catherine Heymans, Scotland’s astronomer royal. “To see this world-leading facility cut is just devastating.”Further deep cuts were announced for dozens of facilities, instruments and projects, which are expected to result in about 800 job losses. Brian Cox, the TV scientist and professor at the University of Manchester, said he was stunned that the funder had pressed ahead with cuts and not worked with the new government to avoid them.View image in fullscreenProf Brian Cox said he was astonished the UKRI was ploughing ahead with the decision.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/Alamy“These devastating and irreversible cuts are a legacy from a series of hasty and ill-considered decisions taken by UKRI, overseen by a government department that no longer exists,” Cox said. “I am astonished that UKRI are still ploughing ahead, and not working with the [Andy] Burnham government to find a solution.”The UKRI has an annual budget of nearly £10bn, but the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), which it funds, needs to makesubstantial savingsafter cost overruns as a result of soaring electricity and staff costs at UK facilities and high foreign exchange rates for international collaborations, such as the Cern nuclear research laboratory near Geneva.Prof Simon Garrington, an associate director of the Jodrell Bank Observatory, said staff were shocked by the decision. “Withdrawing the funding from e-Merlin effectively pulls the rug out from under Jodrell Bank,” he said. The move threatens 28 jobs at the observatory and will affect nearly 3,000 researchers who work with the facility.Garrington intends to challenge the decision but hopes that new uses for the telescope in tracking satellites and space debris might draw in some alternative funding.Jodrell Bank was among dozens of facilities, instruments and projects hit by the cuts on Monday. There will be a 20% cut to UK participation in theRubin Observatoryin Chile, which only began work last month to capture the largest astronomical movie of all time. Another telescope, the Next-Generation Transit Survey, which is searching for solar systems similar to the Earth’s, received a 45% cut.TheRoyal Astronomical Societypresident, Prof Jim Wild, said: “At a time when technological innovation is crucial to our country’s prospects, discarding unique, globally significant observatories threatens both our scientific future and the inspiration of future generations of astronomers.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn further cuts, funding for future instruments on the Extremely Large Telescope in Chile, which is searching for life elsewhere, has been completely cut. The UK will also withdraw from theEvent Horizon Telescopethat allowed astronomers to image the black hole at the heart of the Milky Way.Sue Ferns at the Prospect trade union, said: “Jodrell Bank is not just an iconic site in UK science in the north-west of England, it is a facility that underpins our world leading research capabilities. Closing it would be a tragedy that undermines the mission for the UK to be a science superpower …“This is just the tip of the iceberg of a programme of cuts that is set to devastate UK public sector science and cost many scientists their jobs. The new government, with its focus on regional growth, must reconsider before irreparable harm is done.A spokesperson for the STFC said the body had “undertaken a rigorous prioritisation process to focus investment on the areas that will deliver the greatest long-term scientific capability, impact and value for the UK”.They added that the decision to withdraw funding from e-Merlin was “the result of a comprehensive, evidence-based prioritisation process. As part of this, STFC is focusing investment on the areas that will deliver the greatest long-term scientific capability and value, including the next generation of world-leading radio astronomy facilities.”Explore more on these topicsAstronomySpaceScience policynewsShareReuse this content

title: GB News pundit Matthew Torbitt pleads guilty to fraud while Labour aide | UK news | The Guardian
description: Torbitt admits to two counts of fraud by false representation in relation to his parliamentary expenses
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Torbitt admits to two counts of fraud by false representation in relation to his parliamentary expenses
Content: Matthew Torbitt was granted unconditional bail and will be sentenced later this year.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenMatthew Torbitt was granted unconditional bail and will be sentenced later this year.Photograph: BBCUK newsGB News pundit Matthew Torbitt pleads guilty to fraud while Labour aideTorbitt admits to two counts of fraud by false representation in relation to his parliamentary expensesGeraldine McKelvieMon 27 Jul 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAGB Newspundit has admitted fraud in relation to his parliamentary expenses when he was a Labour aide.Matthew Torbitt, a prominent political commentator who once described himself as “Britain’s favourite lefty”, pleaded guilty to two counts of fraud by false representation at a hearing at Thames magistrates court on Monday.During a brief appearance the 35-year-old, dressed in a navy blue suit and an orange tie, spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth, address and guilty plea. The offences occurred between 2022 and 2024, when Torbitt was working for Christian Wakeford, the MP for Bury South.The court heard that Torbitt, who claims to champion “positive social change”, obtained free rail tickets and accommodation for trips that did not relate to parliamentary business.Maisha Mannan, prosecuting, said the rail tickets were booked between 23 August 2022 and 29 September 2024 via the parliamentary travel system. She said on 2 October 2024 Torbitt submitted a separate claim for reimbursement of travel and accommodation expenses.The court heard that the claims totalled more than £6,000, according to an early estimate by the Crown Prosecution Service. Their exact worth will be determined when Torbitt is sentenced. Expenses filed by MPs’ staff are funded by the taxpayer.The Guardian revealed last monththat the Metropolitan police began an investigation into Torbitt in April last year after receiving a report that a parliamentary staffer had made “unauthorised purchases” through a travel booking system. He was charged on 9 June.The district judge Navneet Sher granted Torbitt unconditional bail and told him he would be sentenced at Snaresbrook crown court later this year.Torbitt rose to prominence by sharing his experiences of rough sleeping in his native Manchester as a teenager. As well as appearing frequently as a panellist on GB News, he has also been on the BBC’s Newsnight, Sky News, TalkTV and a range of podcasts.His introduction to Westminster came when he was “invited to shadow” Andy Burnham in 2014, according to his LinkedIn profile. At the time, the now prime minister was serving as shadow health secretary.Torbitt said the internship had been arranged after he impressed Burnham when filming for a documentary. He went on to work as a caseworker for variousLabourMPs between 2018 and 2024. He no longer works in parliament.Torbitt remains a supporter of Burnham, although he has no official role in his team. Last year, he became a senior fellow at the Centre for Social Justice and an ambassador for Alcohol Change UK.Explore more on these topicsUK newsGB NewsLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I knew what he had done to those boys’: murderer to stay in jail after journalist’s fight for justice | UK news | The Guardian
description: Gibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990s
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Gibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990s
Content: Grimson has been found guilty of a string of sexual offences. He had been nearing release after being jailed in 2001 for two murders.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenGrimson has been found guilty of a string of sexual offences. He had been nearing release after being jailed in 2001 for two murders.Photograph: PAUK news‘I knew what he had done to those boys’: murderer to stay in jail after journalist’s fight for justiceGibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990sSteven MorrisMon 27 Jul 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRos Astengo, a journalist based in Gibraltar who usually focuses on politics and social issues, had qualms when she began investigating the case of the suspected serial killer Allan Grimson as he neared release from prison after serving more than 20 years.She worried that she might reopen the scars of survivors of Grimson – but also that she could be putting herself in the “crosshairs” of a dangerous man who had sexually assaulted and battered two young men to death in the late 1990s when he was a Royal Navy petty officer.“But the public interest overrode it,” Astengo said. “It would have been so easy for me to have just done nothing. But I thought to myself, how would I feel if as soon as they let him out he reoffended and harmed another young man.
