My motive was to keep the public safe.”Because of Astengo’s work,four men came forward to report sexual assaults by Grimsoncarried out on them in the same era as the two murders.On Monday, a jury at Winchester crown court found Grimson guilty of 13 sexual offences relating to the men, which may mean he remains in prison for years to come.Judge Dugdale told Grimson he was an extremely dangerous man in the 1990s and asked for reports to be prepared to help him understand if he still posed a serious risk.The judge also asked for victim personal statements to be taken from the men. He thanked the jury for hearing a “very unusual case” and invited them to return to court when he sentenced Grimson in November.View image in fullscreenRos Astengo: ‘For me, it was about justice and to prevent a serial offender from being released.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“The men were incredibly brave to come to court, bring all this back into their lives,” Astengo said.Grimson was jailed for life in 2001 and told he would serve at least 22 years in prison for sexually abusing and murdering Nicholas Wright, 18, and Sion Jenkins, 20, in Portsmouth, both of whom had served in the navy. The sentencing judge described him as a“serial killer in nature if not by number”.At the time, Grimson also admitted in police interviews sexual offences or contact with another four men – three young sailors and a teenage boy. He said he had thought of killing two of them but the Crown Prosecution Service did not pursue the allegations because he was going to serve a long jail term for the murders anyway.While in prison Grimson was on best behaviour in the hope that he would be released after serving his 22 years and in November 2020the Parole Boardrecommended he be moved to an open prison to prepare him for freedom.At this time, Astengo was covering the search for the body of another sailor, Simon Parkes, who vanished in Gibraltar in 1986. Grimson was in the British overseas territory at the time. He has long been a suspect but denies involvement.View image in fullscreenSimon Parkes vanished in Gibraltar in 1986.Photograph: PANo remains were found and Astengo said she was deeply moved when Parkes’s elderly parents, Margaret and David, from south-west England,described itas their last chance to get justice. “It was a very lonely journey for them.” She promised themshe would write a bookabout their son’s case to keep his memory alive.She began her research and was disturbed to find he had made admissions over the four boys and young men but no action had been taken.“I was astonished that he was never charged over them,” Astengo said. She was alarmed that Grimson seemed close to being released. “I knew what he had done to those boys. That really worried me. How could he be fully rehabilitated? I was worried he would go back into the community thinking he’s gotten away with it. I realised I was putting myself in the crosshairs of a killer but I thought something needed to be done.”Astengo tracked down one of the four and travelled to the UK to speak to him. “I found a very angry man who was still hurt, angry and upset that he had never seen justice. He started talking about the fact that he was older now and a parent. He understands today what he didn’t back then – that was that he was groomed.”Astengo told the man he could file a fresh complaint about Grimson. “I said to him, think very carefully about what you’re doing because you are going to open a can of worms for yourself.”The man went ahead and spoke to police. Initially no action was taken so Astengo contacted thechild sexual abuse review panel, which examines allegations of non-recent child sexual offences.Nicholas Wright.Photograph: PAIt agreed that the case was worth re-examining. Detectives interviewed the man and tracked down the three others. In February 2025, Grimson was charged over the attacks on the four.The month-long trial highlighted how far the justice system had come in dealing with sexual crimes.In the late 1990s and early 2000s it was not uncommon for serious sexual allegations not to be pursued if a defendant faced a long jail sentence for even more serious crimes. Now it is considered the state’s duty to do so.View image in fullscreenSion Jenkins.Photograph: PAIt is also a reminder that until the turn of the century, gay people were not allowed to serve openly in the armed forces, meaning some of those assaulted by Grimson were keen not to talk about what had happened back then because they feared dismissal.In court, Grimson’s legal team tried to argue that it was unfair for him to be charged with offences that the authorities had not pursued a quarter of a century ago. They made it clearhe felt he was being prosecuted now as a tactic for keeping him in prison, to “stymie” his parole.His legal team also criticised Astengo, suggesting she had been motivated by making money from her book, which is due to come out next year.John Price KC, prosecuting, urged the jury to ignore “conspiracy theories” about Astengo’s involvement and said good was achieved by energetic journalists.Astengo said it was not about money. Every time she travelled to the UK she has had to pay her own way, take leave – and could make very little, if anything, from her book. She said: “The defence tried to paint me as somebody who has exerted undue influence all because I’m writing a book. For me, it was about justice and to prevent a serial offender from being released.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsGibraltarRape and sexual assaultCrimeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years ago | Chile | The Guardian
description: Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile
Author: John Bartlett
Headline: Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile
Content: Víctor Jara was arrested and killed by soldiers in the coup that brought the rightwing dictator Augusto Pinochet to power in Chile in 1973.Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/APView image in fullscreenVíctor Jara was arrested and killed by soldiers in the coup that brought the rightwing dictator Augusto Pinochet to power in Chile in 1973.Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/APChilePinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years agoNelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in ChileJohn Bartlettin SantiagoMon 27 Jul 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singerVíctor Jara, the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice.Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man.Chilean police announced on Saturday that Haase Mazzei had been arrested in Puyehue, in the rural south of the country, with a judge ordering his immediate imprisonment.The Víctor Jara Foundation, set up by his widow, the British dancer and activist Joan Jara, said in statement: “We learned that retired Colonel Nelson Haase Mazzei, who had been a fugitive from justice since 2023, was found and imprisoned. We welcome this news.“However, it is important for us to emphasize that, half a century after the murders of Víctor Jara and Littré Quiroga, it is difficult to see this as this justice.”Jara, a singer and leftwing activist, was arrested in Santiago, the capital of Chile, on 11 September 1973, the day afterGen Augusto Pinochet’s bloody US-backed coupto depose the socialist president, Salvador Allende.View image in fullscreenVíctor Jara’s widow, Joan, who died in 2023, was a British dancer and activist who set up a foundation in her late husband’s name.Photograph: Roberto Candia/APJara was held along with thousands of others at a small covered stadium in central Santiago. Four days later, he was murdered in the changing rooms alongside Allende’s national director of prisons, Littré Quiroga.Haase Mazzei’s arrest is likely to be the final act in the long quest for justice on behalf of Jara, one of the most recognisable victims of the Pinochet dictatorship, which killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people and detained and tortured tens of thousands during 17 years of repressive rule.At the stadium, Jara was tortured and humiliated by officers who played Russian roulette with him before breaking his hands, shattering his skull, and riddling him with automatic gunfire.His body was found dumped near the main cemetery in Santiago with 44 bullet wounds and 56 broken bones. He was 40 years old. The body of Quiroga, who had been shot 23 times, was found at the same time.After evading justice for nearly half a century, seven retired soldiers were found guilty of the murder and sentenced in absentia to varying jail terms in August 2023. Haase Mazzei received a 25-year sentence.He claimed for years that he was not at the stadium, since renamed Estadio Víctor Jara, but sworn testimony placed him at the scene.Haase Mazzei joined the Chilean army’s notorious Tejas Verde brigade in 1972, and was later part of Pinochet’s secret police, the Dirección Nacional de Inteligencia (Dina), where he worked closely with its leader, Manuel Contreras, a renowned regime loyalist who was sentenced to more than 500 years’ jail time for crimes against humanity before his death in 2015.View image in fullscreenPedro Barrientos being deported from the US to Chile in 2023.Photograph: Policia de Investigaciones de Chile/ReutersSentenced alongside Haase Mazzei was 86-year-old Hernán Chacón. When police arrived to arrest him at his home in a wealthy district of Santiago in 2023, he asked officers for a moment to take his medication, before slipping off into a side room and taking his own life.Another Tejas Verde officer sentenced for the killing was Pedro Barrientos, who left Chile for the US in 1989 and wasdeported back in December 2023, more than a decade after his extradition was first sought.One former soldier testified that Barrientos had the habit of brandishing his pistol and declaring: “I killed Víctor Jara with this!”Barrientos was eventually arrested in the US after a routine traffic stop, and lost his US citizenship not because of his crimes, but on the grounds that he had failed to disclose his military background in his application.Jara’s widow died at the age of 96, just weeks before Barrientos was returned to Chile to face justice.Haase Mazzei’s defence has already requested his transfer from a prison in the southern city of Osorno to Punta Peuco, a well-appointed jail north of Santiago, built to house the human rights criminals of the Pinochet era.Explore more on these topicsChileAugusto PinochetAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gunther von Hagens, creator of Body Worlds and plastination, dies aged 81 | Science | The Guardian
description: Controversial anatomist’s body ‘will definitely be plastinated’ in line with his wishes, a spokesperson said
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Controversial anatomist’s body ‘will definitely be plastinated’ in line with his wishes, a spokesperson said
Content: Gunther von Hagens with a plastinated human body, displayed as part of a touring Body Worlds exhibition in 2007.Photograph: LM Otero/APView image in fullscreenGunther von Hagens with a plastinated human body, displayed as part of a touring Body Worlds exhibition in 2007.Photograph: LM Otero/APScienceGunther von Hagens, creator of Body Worlds and plastination, dies aged 81Controversial anatomist’s body ‘will definitely be plastinated’ in line with his wishes, a spokesperson saidPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorMon 27 Jul 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 14.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGunther von Hagens, who developed a technique for permanently preserving human bodies in rigid states and toured the world with his controversial Body Worlds exhibition, has moved closer to fulfilling a long-held wish to be sliced up and displayed in a museum after dying aged 81.“It is with deep sadness that the family and the Institute for Plastination announce the passing of Dr Gunther von Hagens, inventor of plastination and creator of the Body Worlds exhibitions,” the German anatomist’s institute said in a statement on Monday.Von Hagens, who was diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2008, died in a hospital in Heidelberg on 24 July, a day after suffering a cerebral haemorrhage.He frequently said he wanted his own body to be preserved after his death, though he wavered on his preferred mode of presentation.“I could envisagemy plastinated body standing in a welcoming pose at the entrance of an exhibition, or rendered into slices and distributed across various sites,” he wrote in the Guardian in 2018.On Monday, a spokesperson for the Plastinarium – a museum von Hagens founded in Guben,Germany, in 2006 – said the anatomist’s body “will definitely be plastinated, as this was always a long-held wish of his”, though where it would be put on display had not been determined.View image in fullscreenA plastinated body posed as if playing chess, on show in 2001.Photograph: Jockel Finck/APVon Hagens was born Gunther Gerhard Liebchen in January 1945 in Skalmierzyce, Poland, then under German occupation and named Alt-Skalden. He grew up in socialist East Germany and took part in protests against the violent Soviet suppression of the Prague Spring in 1968. The following year, he was imprisoned after trying to flee into the west.In 1970, West Germany paid 40,000 deutschmarks for him to be released to its care as a political prisoner. In the west, he met and married his first wife, Cornelia von Hagens, adopting her surname and its connotations of nobility.Von Hagens came up with his technique for preserving bodies in 1977, while working as a research scientist at the University of Heidelberg’s institute of pathology and anatomy. “Looking at specimens embedded in plastic – the most advanced preservation technique then available – I wondered why the plastic was poured around bodies rather than into them,” he wrote in the Guardian.Plastination involves extracting bodily fluids and soluble fat from a dead body and replacing them with resins, silicon rubbers and epoxies. The technique lends a high degree of rigidity to the tissue, enabling bodies to be displayed in upright, lifelike poses.From 1995, von Hagens’ plastinated bodies were displayed in travelling exhibitions. Some were sliced up to reveal internal organs, while others were posed playing chess, doing physical exercise or having sex. Called Body Worlds, the displays became a global phenomenon, attracting more than 50 million visitors globally.Von Hagens curated the shows in tandem with his second wife, Angelina Whalley, and said they were driven by a desire to “democratise anatomy” and shatter taboos around death.But many critics felt the exhibitions deliberately tried to titillate audiences with exhibits such as a series of foetal specimens at various stages of gestation.View image in fullscreenVon Hagens with his wife and co-curator, Angelina Whalley, at the opening of a Body Worlds exhibition in London in 2018.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe anatomist insisted the bodies displayed in the shows belonged to people who had authorised the use of their bodies after their deaths for educational benefit, though the use of infant and animal bodies raised difficult moral questions.In 2004 German news magazine Der Spiegel published documents appearing to show that von Hagens’ plastination facility in Dalian, northern China, had purchased “ownerless bodies” from police, some of which had been executed and bore bullet holes. After the expose was published, he reportedly instructed his employees not to accept executed bodies anymore.Von Hagens’ fedora-and-leather-vest wearing public persona – “a cross between evil scientist and the television cliche of ghoulish murder-scene pathologist”,according to one review– may not have helped dispel questions about his motives.After Parkinson’s disease left him with reduced motor skills and limited speech, von Hagens transferred organisational and financial duties to his wife and son, Rurik.“Sometimes, at this stage of my life and illness, I wish I could suspend my convictions and embrace the idea of a divinity and an afterlife,” he wrote in 2018. “But I don’t think there is a continuum beyond death. Every deceased body I have seen has shown me the absence of the soul. I don’t believe anything is left of us after we die.”Explore more on these topicsScienceAnatomy and physiologyExhibitionsGermanyDeath and dyingMuseumsParkinson's diseasenewsShareReuse this content

title: British YouTuber Yung Filly describes night he met fan in Australian nightclub before allegedly raping her  | Western Australia | The Guardian
description: Performer on trial on six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Performer on trial on six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consent
Content: Andrés Felipe Valencia Barrientos, the British YouTuber and rapper known as Yung Filly, is on trial over rape allegations.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPView image in fullscreenAndrés Felipe Valencia Barrientos, the British YouTuber and rapper known as Yung Filly, is on trial over rape allegations.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPWestern AustraliaBritish YouTuber Yung Filly describes night he met fan in Australian nightclub before allegedly raping herPerformer on trial on six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consentAustralian Associated PressMon 27 Jul 2026 04.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 05.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British YouTuber and musician accused of violently raping a fan after a gig never asked his alleged victim if she wanted sex, a court has been told.Rapper Yung Filly, whose real name is Andrés Felipe Valencia Barrientos, is fighting six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consent in a Perth hotel room in September 2024.The 30-year-old also denies impeding the woman’s breathing by applying pressure to her neck, and three counts of assault occasioning bodily harm.His trial on Monday heard the performer met the woman at a nightclub called Bar1 after his performance.“I fancied her and we got chatting,” Barrientos told the West Australian district court.“The vibes were good, and she had a really good energy about her.”The entertainer said he asked the woman if she wanted to come back to his hotel room while the pair were chatting in the VIP area of the nightclub. He said they later left in a minivan with his entourage and drove to the Intercontinental hotel in Perth’s CBD and the pair had consensual sex.“The sex was great,” he said from the witness box.Asked to describe the sex by his barrister, the rapper said there was “Grunting and moaning in a good way”.He denied choking and slapping the woman, as has been alleged in the court. But he agreed he did bite her numerous times.“In England we would call it a love bite. My mouth on her skin; it involves sucking [and] my teeth were involved to some extent.”The jury has been shown images of the woman’s alleged injuries after the alleged assault. These include photos of deep bruising and bite marks on the woman’s face and neck.Under cross-examination by prosecutor Danielle Clarke, Barrientos said he wasn’t surprised the woman came back to his hotel.“I could just tell she was into me,” he said.He agreed that when he asked her to leave with him, he didn’t mention having sex, but he believed they would do so. He said he initially grabbed the woman’s hand as they were leaving the nightclub about 3.30am, but let go.“I quickly realised I didn’t want to be seen on socials,” he said.The woman previously told the court Barrientos put his hands down her pants and touched her breast while they were in the club.But the rapper denied the acts.“It didn’t happen,” he said.“I recall putting my hand on her waist.”The entertainer also denied giving the woman tequila shots, contradicting the alleged victim’s evidence. He said these were handed around by the bar manager.CCTV of the pair leaving the venue in Perth’s northern suburbs was played to the court. It showed Barrientos and other people getting into a white minivan and the woman following a short time later.She paused at the door of the van before stepping in.“All I remember is me leaving in front of her … and before I know it she was in the vehicle,” Barrientos said under questioning from his barrister.The rapper didn’t recall whether the pair chatted during the drive to the hotel.CCTV from the hotel showed him striding ahead of his entourage and the woman after they left the van. The group was then shown entering a lift.“The vibes were good; we walked through the concierge and got into the lift … and I went into my room with [the woman],” Barrientos said.The rapper agreed the woman’s phone was taken from her, as she alleged.“It is standard practice for someone in the limelight to protect privacy,” he said.The trial continues.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse is available from the following organisations. In Australia, support is available atFull Stop Australia(1800 385 578). In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsWestern AustralianewsShareReuse this content

title: Fauci expressed disillusionment with ‘rambling, crazy’ Trump in journal | Anthony Fauci | The Guardian
description: Former top US health official wrote about challenging interactions with publicity-fixated Trump during Covid
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: Former top US health official wrote about challenging interactions with publicity-fixated Trump during Covid
Content: Dr Anthony Fauci looks on as Donald Trump speak to reporters following a meeting of the coronavirus taskforce at the White House on 7 April 2020.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDr Anthony Fauci looks on as Donald Trump speak to reporters following a meeting of the coronavirus taskforce at the White House on 7 April 2020.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesAnthony FauciFauci expressed disillusionment with ‘rambling, crazy’ Trump in journalFormer top US health official wrote about challenging interactions with publicity-fixated Trump during CovidMartin PengellyMon 27 Jul 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiary entriesreleasedby a Republican senator in an attempt to damage Anthony Fauci also show the former top US government science adviser’s growing disillusionment with Donald Trump in the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic, branding the president “rambling”, “crazy”, “desperate”, “bumbling”, “incompetent”, “an idiot”, “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”.From the earliest days of the crisis six years ago, Fauci noted in his journal challenging interactions with the publicity-fixated Trump. On 27 February 2020, amid the first stirrings of public alarm, he wrote of a surprise late-night call, in which the US president “wanted to chat about the coronavirus situation in general”.For “about 20-25 minutes”, Fauciwrote, he “encouraged [Trump] not to underplay the seriousness of the situation since if it turns out bad, it would look like he is covering up. I even spoke to him from a political standpoint that his chances for re-election might be more damaged if he downplayed the potential spread of virus in the USA than if he said we may face serious problems and even if the Stock Market goes down further, he was at least honest and the country would respect him for it.“I thought that he heard what I said, but the next day, he again underplayed it.”By 14 March, in the thick of the first Covid shutdowns, Fauci is bemoaning Trump’s fixation on “the fluff of ratings and publicity. And so he wants us to do 2 press conferences/day – one in AM and one in PM … We now will have no time to do work.”‘A true embarrassment’On 22 May, Fauci wrote that Trump is “getting out of control in pushing to open up the country and get the economy back before election day. He is desparate [sic]. This is all about re-election.”That proved correct. In October 2020, Fauci wrote: “As the [presidential] election nears, the cases increase and surges are inevitable as we enter cooler weather. Trump is on the campaign trail spewing nonsense. He is really out of control. A true embarrassment.”By March 2021, having watched Trump attempt to retain power despite electoral defeat in a way that reminds him “historically of Hitler”, Fauci writes: “He is truly an obnoxious adolescent.”View image in fullscreenAnthony Fauci and Donald Trump participate in the daily coronavirus taskforce briefing at the White House on 22 April 2020.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesFauci’sdiary entriesread as raw source material for reporting on the pandemic and its politics. He admitted to being a source himself, and worried about being suspected as a leaker, but wrote in late May 2020: “Had long conversation on ‘background’ with [Washington Post reporter] Bob Woodward who is writing a book on the early response to Covid in the USA. I provided him with some history of our response in early January and into February. Will tlak [sic] more with him tomorow [sic].”Thereleaseof Fauci’s diaries was orchestrated by Rand Paul, the Republican senator from Kentucky, who has long voiced skepticism about the Covid-19 response Fauci led, accusing him of needlessly shutting down the country while covering the supposed truth that the virus was human-made, and that US-funded research contributed to its creation. Fauci has consistently said the virus originated in animal-to-human transmission, the generally accepted theory.The two men have clashed before. At a hearing in January 2022, for example, FaucitoldPaul his attacks put him in danger, “kindl[ing] the crazies out there and I have threats upon my life, harassment of my family and my children with obscene phone calls because people are lying about me”. Fauci also charged: “You are making a catastrophic epidemic for your political gain.”Paul and Fauci will square off again on Wednesday, at a hearing for which Fauci, 85, wascompelledto appear. Paul has said he will “make sure Fauci answers for his dangerous decisions and the consequences they had for millions”.In the rightwing press,coverageof the Fauci diaries has focused on his notes about his rise to global fame amid the Covid response, particularly about meeting celebrities or appearing on TV and in the press. The singer Joan Baez and actors Julia Roberts and Sean Penn are among names prominently noted.Fauci does seem to have been proud of his newfound celebrity. On 13 July 2020, his relationship with Trump rapidly souring, he turned to his diary.“Major, Major show of support for me for multiple and varied sectors,” he writes. “Most peo[p]le expressing outrage that the trump administration woud [sic] be so bumbling and incompetent to try to discredit the most credible scientist in the world.”Explore more on these topicsAnthony FauciCoronavirusDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsInfectious diseasesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil prices fall as US pauses strikes on Iran over strait of Hormuz | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fall
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Brent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fall
Content: The US has suspended its bombing campaign around the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/APView image in fullscreenThe US has suspended its bombing campaign around the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/APOilOil prices fall as US pauses strikes on Iran over strait of HormuzBrent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fallJasper JollyMon 27 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 04.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOil prices have dropped sharply as traders bet that a pause in US attacks on Iran could prevent an escalation in the conflict that would further restrict global supply.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, initially fell 9% to below $88 a barrel on Monday after climbing to $100 last week, when the Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea.An attempted recovery later in the day was halted by comments from Donald Trump that the US was having “good talks” with Iran, pushing Brent back down about 8%.The retreat from the short-lived return to more than $100 a barrel came as the US and Iran paused hostilities after 13 days of fighting, amid Trump’s comments suggesting that talks to end the conflict had resumed.US pauses Iran attacks after Trump advised to halt bombingRead moreIran said it hadstopped “retaliatory” attacksafter two nights without American missiles, after the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, told journalists on Sunday that Trump had decided to pause the attacks to allow more time for diplomacy. Separate reports claimed that US military officials had told Trump that the bombing campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness and warned of dwindling stocks of munitions.The comments raised hopes that a renewed focus on diplomatic solutions could de-escalate the regional conflict, which since the end of February has disrupted flows of oil and gas from Gulf states via the strait of Hormuz, and in recent weeks has interrupted vesselsleaving the Red Sea via the Bab al-Mandabstrait, too.However, the brief reprieve from rising oil prices was met with scepticism by some market observers. “We’ve been here multiple times since March,” said Ole Hvalbye, an analyst at SEB Research. “And each rally on a leak has faded as substance failed to materialise.”John Evans, an analyst at PVM, said he expected oil prices would only be able to fall further if there was a meaningful decline in demand, “not questionable mini-ceasefires”.He said: “The market seems to be forever seeking good news from an arena that really is not providing any. A stay of military strikes might seem an improvement, but it does not come with any guarantees that oil will soon flow from the area.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnalysts at Deutsche Bank led by Jim Reid said the 10% increase in Brent crude prices last week had “added to fears that the global economy was facing a prolonged inflation shock, and that the Fed might need to hike rates more aggressively in response”.The expectation of higher inflation caused by rising global energy costs has put pressure on central banks to raise interest rates. In recent weeks that has pushed up sovereign bond yields, which move inversely to prices. However, the oil price drop on Monday prompted yields to fall. The yield on UK 10-year government debt dropped below 5%, down 0.05 percentage points during the day. The rate-sensitive two-year yield fell 0.06 percentage points to 4.35%.Higher oil prices could harm Trump politically, with many members of the Republican party nervous of the effects of inflation on their prospects at midterm elections in November. Some Federal Reserve policymakers may feel the need to raise interest rates to try to counteract price increases, a move that could slow the US economy – despite Trump’s wish for lower rates.Explore more on these topicsOilEnergy industryCommoditiesInterest ratesStrait of HormuzEconomicsGlobal economynewsShareReuse this content

title: Boss of startup hacked by rogue OpenAI agent urges ‘radical transparency’ in investigation | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Artificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face CEO
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Artificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face CEO
Content: Hugging Face’s boss said the attack by the OpenAI agent deserved an ‘unprecedented response’.Photograph: Andre M Chang/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHugging Face’s boss said the attack by the OpenAI agent deserved an ‘unprecedented response’.Photograph: Andre M Chang/Zuma Press/ShutterstockOpenAIBoss of startup hacked by rogue OpenAI agent urges ‘radical transparency’ in investigationArtificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face CEODan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 27 Jul 2026 08.15 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 08.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of the startup hacked by an OpenAI agent has called for the investigation intothe incidentto show “radical transparency”.Clément Delangue, the chief executive of Hugging Face, said the “unprecedented” attack on his business required a similar response.Writing on X afterOpenAIrevealed that its technology had gone rogue during a cybersecurity test, Delangue also called on the company to provide $100m (£75m) worth of computing power to help build defences against such attacks.Be skeptical of OpenAI’s rogue hacker agent story | John ThickstunRead more“The first autonomous agent cyber-attack is an unprecedented event. It deserves an unprecedented response!” he wrote.OpenAI revealed on Wednesday last week that Hugging Face had been hacked by an agent – an AI tool that can carry out a series of tasks autonomously – powered by a combination of its latest publicly available model,GPT-5.6 Sol, and an even more capable model that was yet to be released. This occurred during a test of the models’ hacking abilities, which included deploying them in a supposedly safe “sandbox” – an enclosed digital laboratory – with lower safety guardrails.Once they had gained the open internet access needed to exit the sandbox, the models targeted Hugging Face, according to OpenAI, because they “inferred” that the startup had the information needed to “cheat the evaluation”. Hugging Face first reported the hack on 16 July and at the time was not aware OpenAI had inadvertently carried out the attack.Delangue, whose company provides a database of AI models to developers, called for a fully transparent review of the incident, which has led to expressions of concern over safety standards at OpenAI and within frontier AI labs.Writing that he had asked for “radical transparency” from OpenAI, Delangue said: “Let’s release the traces from the ‘rogue’ agents so the entire research community can study what happened.” Calling for extra funding from OpenAI to build protection against AI, he added: “Let’s commit $100M in compute from OAI to help the Hugging Face community build powerful cyber defenses with the best open and closed models.”Reuters reported last week that the agent spent days hacking Hugging Face without OpenAI noticing. It also reported an OpenAI agent had left notes for future versions of itself should it require tips on breaking free from internal constraints, although Reuters was unable to verify whether that incident was related to the Hugging Face agent. Time magazine reported that agent-related safety incidents had been “happening for a while”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said Delangue’s call should be heeded. “It’s too easy to ‘blame’ the AI as having gone rogue whereas this is all about how OpenAI were running the tool. What is required is that OpenAI give full details of their setup and how that failed,” he said.OpenAI was approached for comment and referred the Guardian to its initial statement last week in which it said it was investigating an “unprecedented security incident” with Hugging Face.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)HackingInternetTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: AstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’ | AstraZeneca | The Guardian
description: Europe and US risk being outpaced on innovation, as happened in the car industry, warns Pascal Soriot
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Europe and US risk being outpaced on innovation, as happened in the car industry, warns Pascal Soriot
Content: Pascal Soriot is AstraZeneca’s chief executive and the highest-paid leader of a FTSE 100 company.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/ReutersView image in fullscreenPascal Soriot is AstraZeneca’s chief executive and the highest-paid leader of a FTSE 100 company.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/ReutersAstraZenecaAstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’Europe and US risk being outpaced on innovation, as happened in the car industry, warns Pascal SoriotJasper JollyMon 27 Jul 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstraZeneca must operate at “Chinese speed” to ensure it does not suffer the fate of the western automotive industry by losing out to more innovative rivals, the drug company’s boss has said.The FTSE 100 company is watching the rise of China’s pharmaceutical industry closely and collaborating to take drugs to global markets, but its chief executive, Pascal Soriot, said the US and European pharmaceutical sectors must focus on increasing the speed of innovation.“We have to make sure we don’t fall behind,” Soriot said. “What we are learning ourselves is we have to move much faster. We always talk about Chinese speed in our company, and we want to operate in Chinese speed.”AstraZeneca said on Monday it was confident of hitting its growth targets for 2030, when itexpects to make $80bn (£60bn) in annual sales, up from $59bn last year. The British company, headquartered in Cambridge, reported revenues of £30.7bn in the first half of 2026, a 6% increase on the same period a year earlier at constant exchange rates.Soriot, thehighest-paid FTSE 100 chief executive, said the pipeline of new drugs from the company was “unmatched”, putting it on course to hit the growth targets in 2030 and beyond despite the surprise failure of Wainua, one of its major heart disease drug prospects, in clinical trials earlier this month.“We have to accept to fail some of the time,” Soriot said. “Biology is biology.”AstraZeneca makes surprise U-turn with £300m pharma investment in UKRead moreDespite confidence in growth prospects, French-born Soriot acknowledged that dominant pharmaceutical companies in Europe and the US needed to be aware of the potential challenge from Chinese competitors.He cited the automotive industry as an example, where western companies had predominantly focused on making cars with petrol engines, leaving the way clear for Chinese companiesto dominate electric car sales.“Chinese companies were focused completely on electric vehicles and batteries and those kinds of technologies,” Soriot said, adding that Chinese pharmaceutical companies were investing heavily in equivalent novel technologies such as antibody drug conjugates, which deliver chemotherapy agents directly to cancer cells, and cell therapy, in which live cells are injected into the body to help fight diseases.Sorit also played down the risk to jobsposed by AI, which he said could increase the speed of drug development, particularly in the design of trial protocols.He said he believed AI tools would help improve productivity in the pharma industry, allowing for economic growth rather than meaning fewer people would be needed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This story about AI killing jobs is a bit of a fake story,” Soriot said. “I can tell you it makes me faster and smarter,” he added, of his experience interacting with AI tools.Soriot said that AstraZeneca would engage with the UK government under its new leader, Andy Burnham, to seek clarity on adeal with the USthat could result in the NHS paying billions of pounds more for medicines.He said it was too early to say whether the change in leadership would have any effect on the deal – struck under pressure from Donald Trump, who threatened to impose heavy tariffs on UK drug exports to the US – which analysis has suggested could lead to229,000 excess deaths in England.“We need to understand their priorities and where the priorities are,” Soriot said. “You have to establish your priorities and then fund them.”Explore more on these topicsAstraZenecaPharmaceuticals industryDrugsEuropenewsShareReuse this title: DCC, one of FTSE 100’s biggest energy firms, agrees £5.75bn takeover | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: KKR and Energy Capital Partners poised to buy firm despite misgivings from founder and biggest shareholders
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: KKR and Energy Capital Partners poised to buy firm despite misgivings from founder and biggest shareholders
Content: The LPG supplier Flogas is a wholly-owned subsidiary of DCC Energy.Photograph: Justin Kase/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe LPG supplier Flogas is a wholly-owned subsidiary of DCC Energy.Photograph: Justin Kase/AlamyEnergy industryDCC, one of FTSE 100’s biggest energy firms, agrees £5.75bn takeoverKKR and Energy Capital Partners poised to buy firm despite misgivings from founder and biggest shareholdersNils Pratley: Private equity finds soft takeover targets in London – yet againJillian AmbroseMon 27 Jul 2026 07.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the biggest energy businesses listed on the London Stock Exchange has agreed a controversial £5.7bn takeover by private equity, adding to the growing exodus of companies from the UK market.The US private equity groups KKR and Energy Capital Partners are poised to buy DCC Energy after the company’s board recommended the offer despite misgivings from its founder and biggest shareholders.The proposed takeover of the Dublin-based company follows recent agreements to take a host of UK businesses private, including Mitie, Tate & Lyle and the William Hill owner, Evoke. The budget airline easyJet is subject to a possible £5.7bn offer.Oil prices fall as US pauses strikes on Iran over strait of HormuzRead moreThe potential blow to the LSE has already attracted criticism from DCC’s founder, Jim Flavin, who is one of the company’s biggest shareholders, and the pension companies Aviva and Fidelity, which also hold significant stakes in the company.Flavin said he was “astounded” by the board’s backing for the deal, which he believes undervalues the off-grid energy services supplier after its updated strategy in 2022 set out an aim to double its operating profits to £830m by 2030.“Why would the board go along with such a charade? I regard this price as totally inadequate,” Flavin said.The board gave its approval to the private equity consortium’s offer to pay £65.25 a share in cash for DCC, which supplies liquid gas and fuels in Europe and the US, after the bidders also agreed to add a £1.25 per share sweetener on the condition that the ongoing sale of DCC’s technology arm, Nexora, reached a certain price.The cash offer was 36% higher than the company’s average share price over the three-month period before the takeover talks became public. But it has failed to win over shareholders.Matt Bennison, the head of UK active equities at Aviva Investors, said last week that the takeover would “represent a bad outcome for shareholders” and Aviva would not support the deal if the board chose to recommend it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This ‘increased’ offer, a very modest increase to that, is unsurprisingly not enough. We firmly believe that [it] is not in the interest of our clients to sell the business at this level,” Bennison said.DCC’s board said the offer “represents a compelling and certain opportunity” for the company’s shareholders to “realise value in cash today”.DCC shares edged up just under 1% to £63.40.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryFTSEStock marketsPrivate equityMergers and acquisitionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It reminded me of James Bond’: Guardian readers on The Odyssey | The Odyssey | The Guardian
description: The Odyssey is the summer’s biggest film: an adaptation of an almost 3,000 year old poem that everyone is talking about. So what was our readers’ verdict?
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: The Odyssey is the summer’s biggest film: an adaptation of an almost 3,000 year old poem that everyone is talking about. So what was our readers’ verdict?
Content: ‘My 14-year-old son and I loved it. For different reasons’ … The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘My 14-year-old son and I loved it. For different reasons’ … The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesThe Odyssey‘It reminded me of James Bond’: Guardian readers on The OdysseyThe Odyssey is the summer’s biggest film: an adaptation of an almost 3,000 year old poem that everyone is talking about. So what was our readers’ verdict?Guardian readers,Alfie PackhamandRosie Peters-McDonaldMon 27 Jul 2026 08.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Not as profound as it wanted to be’As expected fromChristopher Nolan, The Odyssey is an immense technical achievement: vast in scale, beautifully shot and carried by an absorbing soundscape, particularly impressive on the Imax screen. I did enjoy it, but it did not resonate with me emotionally as some of Nolan’s other films have. For a film reaching for something deep and mythic, I’m not sure it felt quite as profound as it wanted to be. I also wasn’t wholly convinced by the casting. There were so many big names that at times I found myself seeing the actors more than the characters. Matt Damon, especially in the island scenes, reminded me of his early Bourne performances when the character had lost his memory. Charlize Theron felt underused, Jon Bernthal seemed to bring his familiar swagger, and Tom Holland did not fully convince me in the more conflicted moments. Samantha Morton, however, was excellent, as she always is.Samiul Kamal-Uddin, 49,London,UKSex, beds and grisly executions: what Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey changed, invented – and left outRead more‘A poignant and painful story’I expected controversy, but what I found was a poignant and painful story of a man who has to reckon with all the death and destruction he was personally responsible for. If Nolan had remained a fundamentalist, we wouldn’t have had such a beautiful, moving story of redemption and healing.Carmen,StLouis, US‘A very American version’Here in Greece, the release of Nolan’sThe Odysseywas much anticipated for all the bad reasons. The uproar from some conservative parts of our society around the casting of a Black actor for the role of Helen was really concerning. I however was eager to watch it because I was curious to see how Nolan adapted such a difficult work. In our country, we teach The Odyssey in schools as a separate course in the first year of middle school, so every Greek has spent a long time reading parts of The Odyssey and writing analysis of its characters and events. Personally, I don’t remember a lot – it’s been 10 years – but I have the general picture. When I saw the movie, it was pretty much as I expected. A good movie, with a solid screenplay, with very good actors, made by a great director with a huge budget. But I couldn’t help but feel that it was a very American version with little connection to Homer’s creation. I don’t mind that some parts of the story were cut or changed, because that’s the point of an adaptation. However, the movie didn’t capture (or didn’t care to capture) the core of Odysseus’s character – that he was very bad as well as very good.Victoria Panagiotaki, 23, Athens, Greece‘Gutted both the main character and the story’I read a lot of reviews right before the film came out:Peter Bradshaw’s, Danny Leigh’s, Kyle Smith’s. Most were over-the-top glowing. Then I saw the film. I was disappointed, to say the least. I felt Christopher Nolan, whose work I generally revere, gutted both the main character and the story, turning Odysseus into a modern-age, two-dimensional good guy. Like the world couldn’t handle the more-than-occasionally ruthless, determined schemer he was. As an example, in the poem the fight with the suitors was anything but a fair one; it was very much a slaughter. I’m very familiar with the story, having read Robert Fitzgerald’s translation at least a dozen times in my life; this is part of the problem. Maybe the film is great for those not intimately familiar with the story, which is fair, I suppose, but that’s not me.John Grgurich, 60, Maryland, USView image in fullscreen‘He could have made Penelope more of a matriarch’ … Mia Goth as Melantho and Anne Hathaway as Penelope in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures‘Reminded me of James Bond’Odysseus’s character update reminded me of the way James Bond has been recently updated for a modern audience. He used to be a lovable rogue; now he is a thoughtful, conflicted man who uses violence reluctantly. Tom Holland was actually excellent as Telemachus and showed us a more nuanced version of masculinity. It is clear that Nolan’s whole take on the poem is that it’s about the bronze age collapse. There’s a number of references to the “sea peoples” and Odysseus even says something like “our age of bronze is collapsing” towards the end of the film. Being as he is interested in historical interpretations, Nolan might have interpreted the scene of Odysseus coming back as being about our shift from matriarchal societies to patriarchal ones. This is something Margaret Atwood does in her novel The Penelopiad. He could have made Penelope more of a matriarch rather than someone who sits at a loom for 20 years. I loved Anne Hathaway’s performance but the act of waiting for a man for 20 years is so antiquated it took me out of it a bit.April McCarthy, 38, London,UKThe Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilersRead more‘Filming in occupied lands doesn’t sit right’I feel it could have been more campy, as Greek mythology is wont to do. More importantly, though, for part of the film theypaid an occupying nation to film in Western Sahara, which doesn’t sit well with me. We see the suffering that lingers from the ignorance of dominion over others and the denial of freedom everywhere in our lives and in other nations. In a time of rising fascism, it’s incumbent for creative people to acknowledge that power incongruence. Christopher Nolan could have shot those scenes anywhere but he chose to do them on occupied lands.Alexander, Chicago, US‘If more movies were like this, I’d go to the cinema more often’Yesterday, my 14-year-old son and I went to see the movie. We both loved it, though perhaps for different reasons. To be perfectly honest, I was looking to have an outing with my son by going to see a movie that I thought I could manage to sit through. I was expecting gruesome battles and a little downtime but what we got was alternating thoughtful dialogue and action-filled scenes. Frankly, if more movies were like The Odyssey, I would pay for tickets to go to the cinema more often. Though I hadn’t expected to, I watched this movie as a parable of our times: a questioning of armed conflict and the need to see common humanity in others, however far they may be from wherever one calls home.Emily Hardouin-Cox, 42,Dijon, France‘Played like a thriller’Christopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer's epic | Charlotte HigginsRead moreRather than leaning into the usual action or fantasy cliches, it played more like a thriller, which I really enjoyed. There were several moments where I genuinely felt the suspense, and I thought it was a strong interpretation of Homer’s story without relying on constant spectacle. My only real criticism was the use of American accents throughout the film. It pulled me out of the experience at times, especially when characters used modern phrases like “Dad!”, which felt out of place in the setting. I’d also love to see more films like this cast actors from the cultures they’re portraying. Greece has an incredible acting community, and it would be refreshing to see more native talent in major productions rather than relying almost exclusively on Hollywood stars. That said, the cast all delivered excellent performances.Kristian, 41, Brisbane, Australia‘I had to put earplugs in’I saw it in Imax, which I hated. Fifteen minutes in I had to put foam earplugs in to abate the skull-crushing loudness. After that, I could actually hear the dialogue. The film has moments of greatness and grandeur, but a lot of flat spots. I understand the repeated scenes with Calypso are used to build the narrative, but there is no chemistry between Matt Damon and Charlize Theron. The film really comes alive in the last 30 minutes or so, especially as Odysseus recalls the sack of Troy and comes to self-understanding of his responsibility and shame for the impending collapse. I was welling up at this point, so the film must have been effective!Alan, 58, Edinburgh,UKView image in fullscreen‘I had to put earplugs in to abate the skull-crushing loudness’ … Matt Damon as Odysseus in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures‘It made me want to go back to the original text’I agree with Emily Hauser’snuanced verdict. As someone who knows Homer’s epic in its original form (I studied Ancient Greek), I found it hard to stomach many of the liberties taken with the story. As pointed outby Emily Wilson, the Phaeacians don’t even appear in the film, which is a shame. Why Circe, the powerful and beautiful sorceress Odysseus happily stays with for a while as well as sleeps with, has been turned into a rather weird witch is also a mystery to me. Athena, the mighty goddess who drives the action, helps and counsels Odysseus, even fights alongside him, is sidelined and depicted as quite a fragile being. Eumaios, the loyal swineherd, has been turned blind and cannot fight with Odysseus. The suitors in the original are not armed and none of them survives; Penelope does not immediately rush into her husband’s arms but puts him to the test once more; Odysseus is not exiled but peace is restored by Athena … There are many other deviations from the story, but these are some of the most striking. Homer’s epic has its own magic and still speaks to modern readers in a way no film adaptation can. It felt quite hollow, but it made me want to go back to the original text and enjoy the amazing stories in it.Christina, 46, Regensburg, GermanyChastity, nodding and enormous pores: will women also love Nolan’s Odyssey?Read more‘Nolan is beginning to feel formulaic’It had the feeling of a theme park ride at a movie studio, stopping at one set piece after another for thrills with little connective tissue in between. Even some of the stops were not what they could have been because little dramatic context was provided – for example, the Sirens and the giants. It’s the one film that made me feel Nolan is beginning to feel formulaic. The soundscape was remarkably similar to Dunkirk, with familiar dynamics and sounds to crank up the tension. I found it very hard to suspend my disbelief with the American accent. Sorry! Greek mythology feels too classical for that and I felt it would have been better served in RP, a la Gladiator.Nick Hughes, 50,Lancashire,UK‘A proper summertime blockbuster’A great, epic, mythical sea adventure. It has the stature and heft of a proper summertime blockbuster. I loved many of the choices. The fights were awesome, the sea vast and powerful. The script is very clever in its pacing, but ditching the lyricism in favour of more straightforward modern dialogue occasionally felt clunky. The drawbacks are typical of a Nolan movie: the palette is desaturated, the interiors stark, and the dialogue barely audible over random booming. Nolan just does not seem very materialistically imaginative – that’s why it’s weird he created such an amazing fantasy movie.Patrick, Seattle, USExplore more on these topicsThe OdysseyChristopher NolanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s so much magic!’: how we made Harry Potter and the Cursed Child  | Harry Potter and the Cursed Child | The Guardian
description: ‘The ripple of energy and anticipation from the audience was almost visual. It was like opening a new Star Wars film – I didn’t hear a phone go off once’
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: ‘The ripple of energy and anticipation from the audience was almost visual. It was like opening a new Star Wars film – I didn’t hear a phone go off once’
Content: ‘Bringing something new to audiences’ … the final battle scene in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at the Palace theatre in London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreen‘Bringing something new to audiences’ … the final battle scene in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at the Palace theatre in London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanHow we madeHarry Potter and the Cursed Child‘There’s so much magic!’: how we made Harry Potter and the Cursed Child‘The ripple of energy and anticipation from the audience was almost visual. It was like opening a new Star Wars film – I didn’t hear a phone go off once’Interviews byImogen TildenMon 27 Jul 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamie Parker, played Harry PotterMy initial response when I was asked if I was interested in the role was confusion – I felt a bit long in the tooth to play a teenager. I had read the firstHarry Potterbook and seen a few of the movies, but was just past the right age when it was all kicking off. I didn’t know that there was the coda in the final book that places the action 19 years later, and that’s where the play would be picking up from.I’m happy to admit now that I thought the show was a terrible idea. But a lot of hit showsareterrible ideas on paper. And I’m used to eating my own words – which began the moment I saw the team involved – producers Sonia Friedman and Colin Callender, and so many of the other creatives I would have taken a contract blind just to work with them, not leastJack Thorne. I thought, if this is as close as I get to being in This Is England, I’ll do it.Of course, once I took the role, I had Stephen Fry’s readings of the books on a loop. By the time I got through the rehearsals, the year in London, and then the year in New York when it went to Broadway, I had listened to the entire series seven times and was a bit of a Potterhead.View image in fullscreen‘By the end I was a Potterhead’ … Jamie Parker as Harry with Noma Dumezweni as Hermione and Paul Thornley as Ron.Photograph: Manuel Harlan/PR Company HandoutThe two parts of the play are the story of the next generation coming up, and of chickens coming home to roost, but it wasn’t a one-man show and the pressure felt shared. Everything you do ends up being a crucible for your own neuroses that you pestle and mortar into some kind of grit that you use as part of making the theatre piece. Like Harry, I was barely 12 when I also got on a train and went to a boarding school in Scotland. I also had round glasses!double quotation markMy wand helicoptered downstage right. I launched myself after it with half my torso off the stage in the auditoriumI’m always looking for things that challenge me, and I had never done anything like this with all the magic. I thought, I hope I can learn how to do that … I don’t know, but let’s find out! Playing various musical instruments helped – there’s a musicality built into the rhythm of the illusions. But, as anyone in my life will tell you, I can’t walk through a doorway without banging the back of my hand against the latch – my spatial awareness is dreadful. That I went through all those tight entrances and exits, and around all those bits of heavy moving machinery at speed, in the dark, without ever doing myself or anyone else serious mischief is a miracle.There were occasional moments when things didn’t go as planned. One night in the duel scene with Alex Price (Draco), I gesticulated and my wand caught on part of my clothing. It skittered out of my hand, and helicoptered downstage right. Without thinking I launched myself after it and blindly reached into the dark with half my torso off the stage in the auditorium. Somehow I caught it. Alex just went, “Yes!” – like he was watching the cricket!During the first preview, the ripple of energy and anticipation that went through the theatre was almost visual. It was put to us that this was like opening the new Star Wars film but in one cinema worldwide – we had audiences coming from Australia to the Philippines to Canada. But, outside of the big commercial opening aspect, there was a real sense of this place being a precious, even dare I say, sacred space. Audiences were in their seats 10 minutes before the start and I didn’t hear a phone go off once. I’ve never known attentiveness in an audience like it.Jamie Harrison,illusionsdesignerI got into magic as a child and for a while made a living out of it, but later, studying acting at drama school, I was told by some of the lecturers that it was vaudevillian and that I should hide it from my CV. I set up my own theatre company, Vox Motus, and began introducing illusion into our shows without really knowing what I was doing, but it was a safe environment to explore new things.When I got the first draft, I couldn’t sleep for three nights thinking, “What have I done? This is so full on. There’s so much magic!”There were moments that Jack had written into the script – ”and they vanish” or “a spell happens here” – and it was up to me to decide what to do. Then there were other points where we knew exactly that it had to be a Patronus charm, or the Polyjuice potion that turns one character into another.View image in fullscreenShadows and light … Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.Photograph: Manuel HarlanPeople often think that magic and illusion are off-the-shelf. They say, “Who invented that?” But I’ve always tried to draw on the work of brilliant illusionists of the past, while reworking them so that we’re bringing something new to audiences.Audiences particularly love the phone box and the entry to the Ministry of Magic by dialling “MAGIC”. That almost didn’t happen at all. John [Tiffany, the director] was trying to give the show its own identity and make it distinct from the films. He said, “I don’t want to a big red phone box on stage … can we think of a different way of doing it?” Christine Jones, the designer, and I looked over old photographs of King’s Cross and we spotted an emergency telephone on a wall in one of those small booths.I made it out of cardboard and bits and pieces in fabric, and we started to re-create a famous trick called the mascot moth that a magician called David Devant created 120 years ago – a person comes on stage with big moth wings on, folds them around himself and vanishes. It was terrible to begin with but we developed it and brought in clever makers to make different iterations. We got it working and it looked fantastic – I was really proud. Then we did the first preview in front of a test audience of Harry Potter superfans. And one of the main bits of feedback was: “You can’t do the Ministry of Magic without a phone box!” So Sonia and John said, “We know we said we didn’t want a phone box, but we need one by this time next week!”I’m not going to reveal any of our secrets. Absolutely not! I can say that people often think there are trapdoors being used in sequences where there aren’t. The show uses shadows and light in ingenious and incredibly precise new ways. It might look very organic and handmade, but there is an absolute wodge of technology involved and a huge crew. There are a lot of computers – it looks like a spaceship.View image in fullscreen‘There’s a wodge of technology involved’ … Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, at London’s Palace theatre.Photograph: Manuel HarlanThe Expelliarmus spell (where a wand jumps from one person’s hand into another’s) is a highly skilled effect that the performers have to start practising on day one – there’s a real knack to getting it right. There are now probably hundreds of actors who have toiled away and have an insight into what life could be like to be a magician. That was the first thing that I had to showJK Rowling. She was really interested to see that and the Time Turner when she came to one of the early workshops. We set up a presentation, but none of the performers were confident enough to do it yet. So John said, “You’re going to have to perform it.” I was more nervous than the flipping actors! I demonstrated it and she went, “Oh! Do that again!” You know you’ve got somebody if they ask to see it again. I was thrilled. I wanted to say no, a magician never repeats his tricks, but it was JK Rowling, so, yes, we did do it again.The original two-part production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child celebrates its 10th anniversary on 30 July and is at the Palace theatre, London until 20 September; theone part production opens on 9 October.Explore more on these topicsHarry Potter and the Cursed ChildHow we madeHarry PotterTheatreJK RowlingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The plane movie I’ll watch anytime’: why Up in the Air is my feelgood movie | Up In The Air | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers’ most pleasurable comfort films is a journey through US airports with George Clooney
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our series of writers’ most pleasurable comfort films is a journey through US airports with George Clooney
Content: George Clooney in Up in the Air,Photograph: Dale Robinette/APView image in fullscreenGeorge Clooney in Up in the Air,Photograph: Dale Robinette/APMy feelgood movieUp In The Air‘The plane movie I’ll watch anytime’: why Up in the Air is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers’ most pleasurable comfort films is a journey through US airports with George ClooneyJoe EllisonMon 27 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirports have always been my happy place. From shiny citadels jutting out of the desert to shoddier European hubs located 120 miles outside the city they’re designated to serve; I love them all. With so many stories to be told, all those connections and people colliding, it’s a first-class seat to life itself. Which should go some way to explaining why I hold such a deep admiration for 2009’s comedy-dramaUp in the Air.‘Justice, morality and triumph’: why Matilda is my feelgood movieRead moreDirected by Jason Reitman and based on the book of the same name by Walter Kirn, it stars an Oscar-nominatedGeorge Clooneyas Ryan Bingham, a US corporate downsizer who spends 322 days a year flying state to state doing the job cowardly employers prefer to outsource, leaving him with “43 miserable days at home”. That is until graduate Natalie Keener (Anna Kendrick) enters the firm with a cost-saving idea of firing people by video call, and hits the road with her older colleague, who is suddenly forced to grapple with the future of his own industry while re-evaluating his nomadic lifestyle.Clooney’s hatchet man is closing in on 10m frequent flier miles – a feat he gleefully reveals has been achieved by fewer people than have set foot on the moon – and has managed to get air travel down to an exact science: flexing his airline Concierge Key like Patrick Bateman might a business card, and rolling his (perfectly sized) suitcase through the minefield of departures with panache, this is a traveller who stacks security trays withconviction. It’s infectious to watch, truly.In my early 20s (around the time of the film’s release) I would often travel to far-flung places on somebody else’s dime, preferring lonely barstools, a buzzy career and fleeting relationships abroad over any real adult responsibility that lay back home in London’s tricky rental market. Though I was two decades younger than its central character, Up in the Air connected with me in such a way that I would watch the movie near religiously during those trips, screening it on any device possible for that extra hit of wanderlust. It remains the plane movie I’ll watch anytime, anywhere.What keeps me coming back to this movie isn’t some inner desire to travel – it’s the heart. For all his commitment issues, Bingham is pretty empathetic when he’s on the clock. Fortune 500’s answer to Freddy Krueger at least does his best to connect with the staffers he’s letting go, cutting the bullshit when necessary and reminding Kendrick’s eager bee that in this line of work they’re meeting people on the worst day of their lives. Firing people from thousands of miles away, he tells her, is morally wrong on every level (this from a guy she accuses of living in “a cocoon of self-banishment”, no less) but most of all it lacks a real duty of care – and as we hurtle ever closer towards workplaces being ruled by big AI, I find this message more prescient than ever.Another plotline that yanks at the heartstrings is Bingham’s romance with a similarly well-travelled businesswoman, played by Vera Farmiga. Kindred spirits? Not quite. Late in the movie, he makes a surprise dash to her home only to realise that their love story has been about as transactional as room service when he sees signs of a husband and kids through the door frame. Clooney’s wide-eyed expression as he backs away into the snowy Chicago night never fails to floor me.And there is a happy ending – just not for the reasons you might think. By far the biggest masterstroke of this movie is Reitman’s decision to cast real people who had recently been fired, instructing them to talk to the camera crew as they would their ex-employer, providing an unfiltered snapshot of the casualties on the frontline of a recession. The director found these talking heads by pretending to cast for a documentary – and it really shows, feeling part-HBO doc and part-episode of NBC’s The Office as real faces (and tears) are intermingled alongside stellar performances from the likes of JK Simmons and Zach Galifianakis, as employees who bite the dust.Throughout the runtime these genuine voices turn from collective anger to dumbfoundment and even optimism, reminding us just how unbreakable the human spirit can be. In fact, by the movie’s finale you’ll find it so uplifting that you may have the urge to put a tray table up.Up in the Air is available on Kanopy or Hoopla, to rent digitally in the US, on YouTube, to rent digitally in the UK and to rent digitally in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsUp In The AirMy feelgood movieGeorge ClooneyAnna KendrickComedy filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Phantom Pain of Rojava review – Kurdish veterans of the war against IS tell story of courage and survival | Movies | The Guardian
description: Maryam Ebrahimi’s documentary about a home for survivors of the war in northern Syria is tender, gentle and incredibly moving
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Maryam Ebrahimi’s documentary about a home for survivors of the war in northern Syria is tender, gentle and incredibly moving
Content: ‘Wounded for democracy’ … The Phantom Pain of Rojava.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreen‘Wounded for democracy’ … The Phantom Pain of Rojava.Photograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewThe Phantom Pain of Rojava review – Kurdish veterans of the war against IS tell story of courage and survivalMaryam Ebrahimi’s documentary about a home for survivors of the war in northern Syria is tender, gentle and incredibly movingCath ClarkeMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpeaking over footage filmed at the funeral of a female army commander, documentary-maker Maryam Ebrahimi notes that it’s the first time she has seen women carrying a coffin in the Middle East. As they move through crowd of mourners, she adds: “Their sisterhood amazes me.” Ebrahimi is talking about the women of Rojava, the Kurdish-led autonomous socialist region in northernSyria. At the cemetery, the women dig the soil with their bare hands; it is a tradition in Rojava, a final act of solidarity with their fallen sister.Ebrahimi’s tender, gentle film is about a home for injured army veterans in Rojava; most are survivors of the war againstIslamic State(IS). The house is mixed genders; one of the men living there is Fadakhar, who has had both his legs amputated and is haunted at night by phantom itches and pains. Mostly, though, Ebrahimi’s gaze is drawn to the female veterans, who made headlines a decade ago for their courage on the battlefield. We learn that women started leaving their villages to fight IS in 2011 – though in truth a little more background about the history of Kurdish all-female battalions might have been helpful.The commander in charge of the house is an Iranian Kurd called Sorkhin, whose gentleness and warmth seem at odds with her reputation; she is famous in Rojava for saving Yazidi women and girls held as slaves by IS. Sorkhin says her mission has always been the same: “Everything I have done is for women … I want women to live as human beings.” Like many commanders she lives in a constant state of hyper-vigilance, a target for drones sent by Turkey to assassinate Kurdish military leaders. Another resident in the house is Zarin, an expert sniper who served under Sorkhin, and was shot in the head. Zarin’s brain injury has mostly robbed her of speech but she tells the camera, beaming: “I was wounded for democracy.” Incredibly moving.The Phantom Pain of Rojava is at Bertha DocHouse, London from 31 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsSyriaKurdsIslamic StatereviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the amazing story of the first animal to poo | Television | The Guardian
description: Chris Packham gets to the bottom of things in the fantastic Evolution. Plus, has reality TV found its next big star? Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Chris Packham gets to the bottom of things in the fantastic Evolution. Plus, has reality TV found its next big star? Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: The real bat man … Chris Packham in the new episode of Evolution.Photograph: CREDIT LINE:BBC Studios/Seb BlachView image in fullscreenThe real bat man … Chris Packham in the new episode of Evolution.Photograph: CREDIT LINE:BBC Studios/Seb BlachTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the amazing story of the first animal to pooChris Packham gets to the bottom of things in the fantastic Evolution. Plus, has reality TV found its next big star? Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Ali Catterall,Priya Elan,Jack Seale,Hannah J DaviesandGraeme VirtueMon 27 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvolution9pm, BBC TwoWhich animal was the first to poo? Chris Packham’s belting biology lesson continues with the story of the bat – and the origins of its insatiable hunger are in the urbilaterian, an animal that floated about in the waters of the Ediacaran period, about 570m years ago. Food entered and exited through one hole … until a vital mutation: “The anus was a breakthrough!”Hollie RichardsonThe Ghettos & the Holocaust11.50am, PBS America“Today, the Jewish ghetto was officially created,” wrote Warsaw resident 15-year-old Miriam Wattenberg in her journal in November 1940. “Where is the Moses who can free us from this oppression?” Historians, archive footage and unearthed diary extracts found in metal boxes bring the terrible era and conditions to life in this poignant documentary.Ali Catterall24 Hours in A&E9pm, Channel 4A 23-year-old woman is rushed to Queen’s Medical Centre after falling off a horse, which then rolled on top of her. Meanwhile, a five-year-old boy is brought into A&E after badly cutting his hand at school, and doctors urgently need to determine if a man in his 20s is having a stroke.Priya ElanHouse of the Dragon9pm, Sky Atlantic“The patient hunter gets the kill,” says suave antagonist Ormund Hightower (James Norton), as the reign of Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D’Arcy) fractures and frays. As attacks from within and without threaten to take the queen’s throne from her, Daemon (Matt Smith) wants to quite literally fight fire with a lot more fire.Jack SealeSecret Lives of Gypsy Wives10pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenTrewley Precious Temple in The Secret Lives of Gypsy Wives.Photograph: Jude Edginton/Jude Edgington/Channel 4/OptomenBehind the very 00s title, this new reality series is surprisingly wholesome and boasts a bona fide, Gemma Collins-esque star in Traveller influencer Trewley Precious Temple. This week, Trewley unveils a beauty collab, the perfect project for someone who, says her manager, “came out of the womb in lashes”.Hannah J DaviesSecrets of the Celebrity Sex Tapes12.05am, Channel 4When Love & Hip Hop: Atlanta reality TV star Mimi Faust featured in a 2014 sex tape, it triggered a media frenzy in the US (not least because of an unintentional bit of slapstick involving a shower rail).
