title: A Dairy Story review – giving cows and calves a happier life through progressive farming | Movies | The Guardian
description: Filled with shots of emerald pastures and gambolling animals, this documentary shows that challenging accepted practices can benefit animals and the environment
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Filled with shots of emerald pastures and gambolling animals, this documentary shows that challenging accepted practices can benefit animals and the environment
Content: Mum’s the word… at Rainton Farm calves stay with their mothers for five or six months.Photograph: A Dairy Story.View image in fullscreenMum’s the word… at Rainton Farm calves stay with their mothers for five or six months.Photograph: A Dairy Story.MoviesReviewA Dairy Story review – giving cows and calves a happier life through progressive farmingFilled with shots of emerald pastures and gambolling animals, this documentary shows that challenging accepted practices can benefit animals and the environmentPhil HoadMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnew addition to the ranks ofneo-rural cinemathat is getting its hands dirty with the realities of the modern countryside, this mellow Scottish documentary lauds the emerging practice of cow-and-calf farming. It focuses on Rainton Farm in Dumfries and Galloway where, instead of the dairy-industry norm of separating calves from their mothers a few hours after birth, owners David and Wilma Finlay allow them to stay together until the youngsters are five or six months old. Having run a fully fledged organic operation since the 1990s, the Finlays have progressive form; Rainton is thought to be the first European site where cow-and-calf has been attempted at commercial scale.This shakeup breaks dairy-farming orthodoxy, which refuses to waste lucrative milk on calves. Not only are neighbouring farmers sceptical, the cows initially are too: in the 2012 pilot, the animals were stressed out by the sudden change of routine when they were confronted with needy offspring that they had expected to disappear. Milk yields dropped, but rebounded to a 25% increase in subsequent trials, as the mums settled down and extra suckling stimulated production. An even greater revelation are the damaging routines imposed on dairy farmers by old-style methods: a stressed-out factory milking schedule that, ringfenced by intensive veterinary and crop fertilisation, has ecological repercussions in the fields.Ian Findlay’s film, filled with drone shots of emerald pastures and gambolling calves, makes a handsome case that change is possible. The animal sentience considerations that spurred the Finlays to change their ways crystallise even further – with more time to acknowledge their needs, each animal’s individual personality becomes undeniable. Staunchly proselytising as well as slightly repetitive, this manifesto film glosses over a few details: fine ones, such as the economics at the farm, which David Finlay admits are a work in progress; and the real nitty-gritty, including the fact that the milk of human kindness has its limits at a beef-producing outlet such as Rainton. All the same, this is a quiet, steadfast challenge to the industrial-agricultural complex – as well an uplifting epitaph to Wilma Finlay, who died last year of lung cancer.A Dairy Story is at Norwich Cinema City on 30 July,then tours.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsFarmingAnimalsScotlandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The No 1 Ladies Detective Agency creator makes the world happier: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Author Alexander McCall Smith’s new series is an attempt to use short fiction to make listeners feel better about the world. Plus, what happened when two London gangsters decided to make a film?
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Author Alexander McCall Smith’s new series is an attempt to use short fiction to make listeners feel better about the world. Plus, what happened when two London gangsters decided to make a film?
Content: ‘Cover a whole sweep of history’ … Alexander McCall Smith.Photograph: Simone Padovani/Awakening/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Cover a whole sweep of history’ … Alexander McCall Smith.Photograph: Simone Padovani/Awakening/Getty ImagesBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioThe No 1 Ladies Detective Agency creator makes the world happier: best podcasts of the weekAuthor Alexander McCall Smith’s new series is an attempt to use short fiction to make listeners feel better about the world. Plus, what happened when two London gangsters decided to make a film?Hannah J Davies.Alexi DugginsandHollie RichardsonMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekThe Positive Distraction PodcastWhile he is best known for his No 1 Ladies’ Detective Agency novels, Alexander McCall Smith has something of a soft spot for short stories, which can “cover a whole sweep of history in a couple of paragraphs”. Hisnew seriesfeatures a selection of short original works that he hopes will make listeners feel better about the state of the world, beginning with a pleasingly twee tale inspired by a friend’s miniature helicopter landing pad.Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyShadow World: Breakin’ the CycleIn the early 00s, two of London’s most ruthless criminals decided to escape gangsterdom by creating a movie about their lives. Thisslick showfeatures one of them, plus the film’s editor, telling the tale of how they ended up getting S Club 7’s Bradley involved – before the creators’ background threw the production into chaos.Alexi DugginsBBC Sounds, episodes weeklyYou’ve Got BrailleView image in fullscreenAlison Steadman.Photograph: Joe Maher/Getty ImagesComedy producer Reece Finnegan and writer Jack Bernhardt have written this four-partseriesfor Hat Trick and the RNIB, about an “idiot” twentysomething who also happens to be blind. While light and sitcomy, it beautifully tackles the issues that Paddy (Finnegan) faces as a result of his disability. Alison Steadman, Steve Pemberton and Chloe Petts also star.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyCome CloserIt’s hard not to be compelled by host “Aries goddess extraordinary, keeper of dark stories” Rae Review – check out her horns on theYouTube version. She tells one of history’s grimmest tales in each episode, starting with Lorena Bobbitt, who chopped off her husband’s penis.Hollie RichardsonWidely available, episodes weeklyThe Gaza Chef“How do you investigate a questionable death when you can’t go to the place it happened?” So asks thispodcastabout Mahmud, a chef who ran a Gaza soup kitchen but was killed by a projectile from the sky. It’s a grippingly told listen from Yassin Musharbash; he sets up the story by explaining the relationship he developed with Mahmud – who sent him voice messages explaining life in Gaza.ADWidely available, episodes weeklyWhat have you been listening to this week? title: Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason review – a witty story of infatuation set in the literary world | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A sad, heartbroken woman becomes obsessed with a famous writer in a continuously humorous and touching story from the Sorrow and Bliss author
Author: Sam Leith
Headline: A sad, heartbroken woman becomes obsessed with a famous writer in a continuously humorous and touching story from the Sorrow and Bliss author
Content: ‘A Bridget-Jones-meets-Pirandello caper’: Meg Mason’s new novel Sophie, Standing There is out now in Australia.Composite: Guardian design/HarperCollinsView image in fullscreen‘A Bridget-Jones-meets-Pirandello caper’: Meg Mason’s new novel Sophie, Standing There is out now in Australia.Composite: Guardian design/HarperCollinsAustralian book reviewsFictionReviewSophie, Standing There by Meg Mason review – a witty story of infatuation set in the literary worldA sad, heartbroken woman becomes obsessed with a famous writer in a continuously humorous and touching story from the Sorrow and Bliss authorSupported byAbout this contentSam LeithMon 27 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist.No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos of real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising.Sophie lurks in the wings of her own life, too. She likes her job but she has much to be sad about. Not long ago, her husband brought their relationship to an end with oafish callousness (she was in the shower; he didn’t bother to take his earbuds out while he delivered the news), and with it her hope of becoming a mother. Now her beloved books are in storage in the garage of her old house and she’s living alone in a dingy rental flat owned by her husband: “The water in Sophie’s glass tasted like pipes. She felt very tired … The coffee table was actually a cable spool with ‘12 AWG’ spray-painted on the drum.”I Made This Just For You by Chris Ames review – absurd satirical takes on the bleak absurdity of modern lifeRead moreMason’s prose is wan and witty, handling the admixture of pathos and bathos well; and her sinuous sentences capture the wavering movements of thought with less fuss and more laughs than, say, Virginia Woolf. As a bookish person, and one inhabiting a lightly metafictional narrative, Sophie is glumly aware of her literary analogues. There’s “a lot of sad girl fiction” on her Kindle. “Eleanor Oliphant,” she reflects. “That was the worst. Even though it was extremely well written and Sophie had recommended it to about 10 people when it first came out, in this moment, she wished she’d never heard of it and couldn’t recall the cheese scones and those cappuccinos Eleanor always ordered, the saddest of all the coffees.”Mason is brilliant, too, at describing the small but intense joys of everyday life – getting your scalp massaged at the hairdresser, for instance, or owning one really nicely designed pair of trousers. She’s likewise good at life’s routine humiliations and inanities, such as bumping into your ex with a leaky bottle of coconut water in your handbag, or asking a favour from someone whose text messages you have been ignoring, or realising how much it’s going to cost to take an Uber back from Ikea.The engine of the plot is a parasocial relationship but an old-fashioned one: Sophie becomes obsessed with a famous writer. (The writer is just “the author” for the first part of the book but then, perhaps finding the conceit unwieldy, Mason gives her a name, Lilac Dunne.) Sophie rereads her books, talks to an imaginary version of Lilac, and spends hours scrolling images of her and listening to her on podcasts. Then fantasy and reality collide when, to Sophie’s terror, Lilac is booked to appear after Elizabeth Strout drops out of an event.An infatuation with the idea of Lilac, with her public persona and her authorial voice, is complicated by a first glancing and then apparently deepening encounter with the real thing. Lilac takes Sophie up, a little, and Sophie is flattered and flustered. She thinks of herself as a nobody but Lilac seems not to. And then … well, no spoilers.If there’s a fault to be identified in this continuously witty and touching narrative, it’s in the person of Lilac. As a writer she appears to be unstuffy, poised, wise and at ease in the world; Sophie isn’t the only one to fall for her. When we encounter Lilac in person, she’s harder and more ruthless than her public persona but no less impenetrable, with none of the psychological complexity or vulnerability displayed elsewhere. She’s moredeus ex machinain Sophie’s story than fully realised character.But perhaps that’s by design. In this Bridget-Jones-meets-Pirandello caper, Mason is nothing if not knowing. As she writes in one of the closing chapters, opening a little postmodernmise en abyme: “If someone wrote a novel about Sophie, which they wouldn’t, but if they did, it could end there.” It doesn’t.Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason is out now in Australia (HarperCollins) and will be published in the UK on 27 August (Bloomsbury)Explore more on these topicsFictionAustralian book reviewsAustralian booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot review – Anne Enright celebrates a landmark feminist novel | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Half a century on, this tale of a woman who abandons her children in search of her self remains thrillingly original
Author: Anne Enright
Headline: Half a century on, this tale of a woman who abandons her children in search of her self remains thrillingly original
Content: ‘Joan Barfoot understands the inside-out logic of maternal obligation.’Photograph: eyevine/Chloë Ellingson/The Observer/eyevineView image in fullscreen‘Joan Barfoot understands the inside-out logic of maternal obligation.’Photograph: eyevine/Chloë Ellingson/The Observer/eyevineBook of the dayFictionReviewGaining Ground by Joan Barfoot review – Anne Enright celebrates a landmark feminist novelHalf a century on, this tale of a woman who abandons her children in search of her self remains thrillingly originalAnne EnrightMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 05.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a growing literature of maternal flight: novels about women who leave not just their husbands but also the children they have made. In the real world, men are the more frequent deserters; the connection of the father to family life is seen as contingent, while motherhood is revered as an intrinsic state. This means that women who “un-mother” themselves are doing something impossible: the connection between a woman and her child is not just emotional, but also creational. Joan Barfoot understands the inside-out nature of the logic involved in maternal obligation: “she created these other people and their need for her,” says Abra, the abandoning mother of Gaining Ground, “and now she must fulfil them.”Abra neglects to fulfil her children or their needs. The novel is rigorously and meditatively about the business of separation, which is also the business of becoming a single and undivided self.Gaining Ground came out in Canada in 1978, under the title Abra, before it was published in the UK under the current title by the Women’s Press in 1980. This was around the time Barfoot’s fellow Canadian Alice Munro began to write her adulterous, runaway women, whose instinct for freedom chimed so well with the feminism of the day. Abra is not sprung from domesticity by her desire for another man, however, nor does she return to her children, as Leda inElena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughterdoes, after years spent regaining what she had lost. Abra is closer to the protagonist in Cathy Sweeney’s recentBreakdown, who has no single answer to the question of why she left her former life: In Japan, Sweeney writes, “So many people disappear that there is a word for them –johatsu. It translates as evaporated people.”These novels cannot fully resist the question of whether the bolting mother is a monster or a victim of societal expectation. Gaining Ground was written before any of them and, already, Barfoot was wise enough to refuse the terms of the debate: Abra never questions the morality of becoming her true self.The novel begins with the arrival of a young woman at Abra’s cabin in the woods, nine years after she drove away from her old life. Abra feels her presence as a pressure, an expectation, but can barely remember who the girl is, or who she herself used to be. Then, a moment of recognition – it is her 18-year-old daughter, Katie: “I know her now, and it locks me to her.”double quotation markBarfoot was wise enough to refuse the terms of the debate: Abra never questions the morality of becoming her true selfKatie’s arrival tips Abra into a recollection of her lovely, ordered home in Toronto; her marriage, in which there would sometimes be “late movies and making love on the couch and popcorn”; and her two children. Her first baby, a son, provoked a fierce sense of attachment: “I didn’t even want to talk about him, although he so completely occupied my mind, because I felt somehow that talking about him took him a distance away, made him separate, gave a piece of him to someone else.” Her second child seemed less of a miracle: “she was a baby, beautiful, and she was mine and Stephen’s and we had created her, but it seemed natural now”.The story may be about maternal ambivalence, depression, the loss of meaning, but it always revolves around ideas of truth and pretence. Abra’s life does not feel “real”. Barfoot delivers about 16 different kinds of dissociation without going over her own footprints or saying the same thing twice. The build to Abra’s departure has a cumulative, relentless modernist effect, but she manages to keep it human, or within the human, and we are fully convinced, when Abra sees the cabin for the first time, that this is her “home”.She has brought no clocks and no mirror, and is at pains to avoid talking to other people. On her first day of digging a vegetable garden her hair proves bothersome and so she lops it off, blind. Abra works to grow food, gather wood and keep herself alive through the long Canadian winter. She thinks only about what is in front of her. The descriptions of work, the natural world and the changing seasons recall the self-reliance of Annie Dillard or Thoreau, who write in a transcendent spiritual tradition. Abra’s revelation is not about God’s infinite majesty, however, but about a kind of unbecoming. She wants to make a life in which she can slowly lose “my name, my memory, the labels I’d used, and so my sense of all words”, to arrive at a place of joy.When Katie arrives from a world where “there are motives and angers everywhere”, Abra tries to share what she has discovered about “blankness”. She considers the way she once saw her husband and wonders, “Did I make him up?” The answer is that she invented everyone: “I simplified them. And then I reacted to what I had made up, behaved as if what I had invented was real.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is hard to find an ending for a book that is trying to be about nothing, so it is considerably to her credit that Barfoot manages an affecting, dramatic conclusion to Katie’s visit. Gaining Ground is a wonderful slow burn of a book and Barfoot’s originality and control remain exciting, nearly half a century on. It is great to see this reissue put the novel at the centre of things, where it belongs.Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot is published by Faber (£9.99). title: What If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypse | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answers
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answers
Content: Eleanor Drage, senior research fellow at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.Photograph: Apple Photos Clean UpView image in fullscreenEleanor Drage, senior research fellow at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.Photograph: Apple Photos Clean UpScience and nature booksReviewWhat If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypseThe academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answersSophie McBainMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe AI ethicist Eleanor Drage believes that to thrive alongside artificial intelligence, humans need to recognise AI’s “humanity”. She means that while we often speak of AI as though it were some mystical, formless thing, it is the product of hours of human labour, in silicon and quartz mines, microchip factories and data labelling centres. If citizens want to wrest power from the tech companies that are building AI, it helps to understand clearly what they are selling us. This also means seeing through the marketing and hype: “the cloud”, that nebulous, distant place where your photos are stored, is just someone else’s computer; an AI “hallucination” is a system error or data labelling mistake; intelligence is a very broad – and potentially misleading – term.The story in Silicon Valley is that AI will either save us, ushering in a new era of prosperity and human longevity, or it will wipe us all out. Drage argues, convincingly, that big tech cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises while it continues to chase profit and power above all else, and while it serves the interests of a narrow few. Meanwhile, the cultural obsession with the AI-induced apocalypse conveniently redirects attention from the practical conversations we could be having about how to make AI safer – by ensuring citizens have more power over how their information is used, and how AI models are trained and regulated, for example. Tech titans’ apocalyptic visions also create the false impression that AI safety is more important than climate change, geopolitical tensions and inequality, three problems that are already causing a huge amount of suffering and that, if addressed, would reduce many AI-linked risks too.Drage, an assistant research professor at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, has conducted research that debunks AI-powered recruitment processes, and exposes the dangers of incorporating AI into law enforcement. Many of her criticisms of big tech will be familiar: that AI algorithms perpetuate and entrench pre-existing biases; that for all their bland, generic promises to be “transparent” and “accountable”, tech giants have become too big to care about ethics; that a handful of executives have amassed far too much power; and that the rollout of AI is happening without our consent and without consideration for planetary health. But her writing has intellectual heft, and her philosophical explorations of, for example, how we define intelligence and why this matters, are very interesting.Occasionally, however, Drage’s arguments seem rushed and become sloppy. “It’s merely an illusion that the labour force is disappearing: work is simply shifting, from artists to data labellers and from marketeers to engineers,” she writes at one point. But it’s not clear that artists and “marketeers” will become redundant in the coming AI era. It’s also not as though the data labellers working for poverty wages in Kenya would have been artists 10 years ago. Equally, given the importance she rightly places on promoting diversity in AI, it’s disappointing that she dismisses unconscious bias as “merely another way of taking the perspective of the perpetrator rather than the recipient of harm”, as though intention is completely irrelevant. She writes that people are ready for “less placid” conversations about equality, I’d add that these conversations also demand accuracy and nuance.The book’s title suggests Drage wants to offer an alternative vision of what AI could be. She gives a few examples of the kind of ethical, community-based AI projects she thinks should be replacing top-down big tech products, and many of them are strangely underwhelming. They include an app called Mumkin designed to facilitate difficult conversations about female genital mutilation (FGM) in India, and Kuini, an AI chatbot built to help Māori women quit smoking. In both instances I found myself wondering what value AI brings to these endeavours – particularly given all that Drage has discussed about its environmental impact and exploitative supply chains. Is an app more effective than training community members to act as counsellors, or funding support groups and peer support workers?Drage describes a toolkit she co-designed to help AI companies act ethically and comply with EU regulations as a “cornerstone of utopianism”, because it shifts the focus on to how AI is built and made. In her view, utopia is not a destination but the “process of working together to develop a fairer world”. Maybe it would be unfair to expect too specific a utopian vision, but I’d nonetheless be interested to know how AI, specifically, can help us build a better future. She does not mention the things that many of AI’s biggest critics nonetheless welcome, such as its potential to improve drug discovery and disease detection. What if we got AI right, this book asks. After reading it, I can’t say I really know.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Haex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventure | Games | The Guardian
description: The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes
Content: Growing fascination … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsView image in fullscreenGrowing fascination … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsSummer games previewsGamesHaex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventureThe debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyesLewis GordonMon 27 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wilds of the sub-Arctic north: towering pine trees, flashes of psychedelic-yellow lichen, and a sun that never wholly sets during the summer months. This land is gorgeous, yes, but also unforgiving, yet in Haex (pronounced “hex”) you have an unusual tool at your disposal to make it a little more hospitable: a cube that fits snugly in the palm of your hand out of which grows a plant. You plant this so-called Seed in the earth and – voilà – the world around you transforms: new vegetation and topography but also narrative threads to follow, and, naturally, enemies. Wield these small-but-mighty kernels of change at your own peril.“Your adventure and your world is player-shaped,” says Haex’s creative director Tobias Nyman. He explains that everyone starts a campaign with a unique, procedurally generated world. Each Seed then contains further procedural data that causes it to terraform before your eyes. “You change the world as you go,” he says. “It becomes even more unique.”The singularity of each game world is crucial for keeping not just you but other players on their toes. That’s another of Haex’s wrinkles: it is an online co-operative game, meaning your friends may join you on this ever-transforming survivalist adventure.View image in fullscreenRoom for more … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsTeaming up, you play as a group of research scientists sent to investigate an anomaly in the rugged Scandinavian landscape. You come across odd, shapeshifting objects and beasts: for example, an ash-grey humanoid creature with spikes protruding from its face that would make even Pinhead from Hellraiser wince; also, a sentient wall so supermassive that it scrapes the clouds. There is a further layer to these spatial and, perhaps, alien mysteries: an unknown language of arcane sigils that must be decoded.Nyman talks effusively of influences: sci-fi movies such asAnnihilationandArrival(as is clear from the trailer); the weird fiction thrillers of author Jeff VanderMeer, too. Unexpectedly, the creative director cites the niche music genre known ascosmic black metalas a touchstone. “There is the wild, grim, frostbitten north, an extraterrestrial entity and a thing that traverses the mist,” says Nyman, hinting at a shared emotional effect between his beloved music genre and the game: a mingling of dread and awe, and of seeking transcendence in nature.Nyman co-founded Haex’s studio Dead Astronauts (anothernod to VanderMeer), in 2024, having previously worked at Ubisoft Massive, where he helped make recent open-world blockbusters,Avatar: Frontiers of PandoraandStar Wars Outlaws. Yet where those titles’ settings are gorgeous and gigantic (“monumental,” stresses Nyman), they are also somewhat static. By contrast, Haex’s game world is more dynamic, and it is being made by just 12 developers. The theory is that its morphing, geo-engineered space should foster more fluid, interesting experiences, despite Haex’s focus on somewhat familiar-feeling shooting and survival mechanics.Taking the leap to independence has also enabled Nyman to make a game that is more personal to him. As a youngster, he split his time between Stockholm and the far north of Sweden. He recalls looking up at the night sky blanketed with constellations as his father explained Einstein’s theory of relativity. Another memory: gazing out at an expansive crop of cloudberries – a “field of gold,” says Nyman, by virtue of the small fruit’s colour. What has stuck with him most, however, is the region’s silence – a silence so great that it was “almost screaming at me”, he says. That feels like an apt summation of Haex’s aims: an experience that is miraculous and malicious; a setting that is beautiful yet can feel as if it is bearing down on you with cruel intensity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaex is due for release onPCin 2027.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Glitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the Backrooms | Games | The Guardian
description: The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
Content: Interior landscape … the 2022 game Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeView image in fullscreenInterior landscape … the 2022 game Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeGamesGlitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the BackroomsThe horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spacesAlex SpencerMon 27 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future$262mA24movie sensation.“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in theBackrooms,” the post begins. For the uninitiated, “noclip” refers to a game mode in which collision with solid objects is disabled, allowing players to move freely through walls and floors. Think of Chiwetel Ejiofor’s character in the film, finding a permeable wall in the basement of his furniture store and passing through to the world on the other side.Backrooms review – Kane Parsons’ icily disturbing horror rewrites the genre rulebookRead moreIn games, noclip is intended for use by developers testing out their creations – but for decades now, players have been finding ways to access it themselves and reach hidden places they were never intended to see. It’s a phenomenon that Studio Chyr creative director William Chyr is intimately familiar with, both as a maker of games and as a player.View image in fullscreenChiwetel Ejiofor in a scene from Backrooms the film.Photograph: A24/AP“Going behind the scenes, noclipping, and seeing the logic of the space, it’s like this Wizard of Oz moment of pulling open the curtain,” Chyr says. He remembers an early encounter with this inBatman: Arkham City:“There was this glitch that allowed you, if you kept spamming one of the grenades, to keep going higher and higher.” From there, the caped crusader could soar outside the level, into sections of Gotham that were only ever intended as a backdrop. “The streets had these cars that moved, but it was just a flat texture.”Watching Backrooms, Chyr was also reminded of a similar bug in the notoriously jankySkyrim, where holding a wooden plate provided a quick way of noclipping out of the world. Looking at it from the outside in, players discovered that many of the game’s “tables” were in fact just bookcases embedded deep in the ground – just like the memorable Backrooms shot of a room in which the furniture is clipping through the floor. All these things that, in video games, the player is never meant to see.The feel ofKane Parsons’ filmis actually closer to these experiences than any of the many “official” Backrooms games that have popped up. The open-source nature of this mythos (as well as 4chan and Reddit, there are sprawling fan wikis cataloguing and expanding the lore) means that it’s possible to release your own game set in the Backrooms, using the name and iconography, in a way you couldn’t with another horror movie.View image in fullscreenPlaces you weren’t meant to see … Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeThe most high-profile of these games, Escape the Backrooms, was first available in early-access form in August 2022, just months after Parsons’ first video. It offers a perfectly faithful recreation of the Backrooms aesthetic, from the yellow hallways to the yellow hazmat suits worn by agents of Async, the mysterious organisation only introduced towards the end of the film but a mainstay of the online incarnations. But all this is just wallpaper applied over the blueprint of a multiplayer survival horror game.At its best, Backrooms taps into a sense of a place being “off”, in a way that’s unsettling but hard to pin down. It’s a delicate sensation, easily shattered (as it is in the film, I’d argue) by the presence of killer monsters. Even more so by the sight of another player in their gas mask and reindeer onesie, bunny-hopping through the hallways ahead.Thankfully, there’s another stripe of Backrooms-inspired games offering nothing more than a self-guided tour through environments with a growing sense of weirdness and the constant suggestion of a threat lurking out of view.View image in fullscreenEndless halls… Hotel Infinity.Photograph: Studio ChyrPools and Dreamcore both shine a spotlight on Poolrooms, an infinite swimming-baths dimensionfirst glimpsed in one of Parsons’s videosand codified by the fandom asLevel 37of the Backrooms, with a similarly alien approach to architecture. In Dreamcore, it’s just one of a selection pack of realms to explore. You’ll also explore a “dead mall” and the looping corridors of a hotel: both abandoned and seemingly endless, like the spaces explored in the film, but with less of an obvious supernatural edge.These malls and hotels are prime examples of a larger online taste for liminal spaces from which Backrooms is just one offshoot.“These spaces always feel like they’re past their prime,” says Chyr. “It’s clear there was human activity here, at one point, but no longer.” His 2025 game Hotel Infinity is steeped in all these ideas, to the extent that at one point Hotel Liminal was considered as a title, Chyr says. “But I thought that was just too on the nose!”Set in the lifeless corridors of a hotel seemingly designed by MC Escher, it’s a VR game that uses some clever spatial trickery to fold its endless halls into a 2x2m square of your living-room floor. One particular sequence late in Backrooms made me think of Chyr’s game – he confirms that he thought the same thing. “I was like, damn, I wish we’d done that!” he laughs.View image in fullscreenImpossible architecture …  Exit 8.Photograph: Kotake CreateHotel Infinity is primarily focused on the impossible architecture of these places, something it shares withExit 8(also adapted into a film this year), a Japanese-made game that traps you in an infinitely looping section of a Tokyo metro station. The other side of the liminal coin is the sensation summoned by that original 4chan image: the eeriness of an empty place that no longer has any obvious function, or perhaps never did.One game exploring this aspect is Interior Worlds, a “liminal photography” game in which you explore such spaces armed only with an SLR camera. The game’s developer, who goes by the moniker Sodaraptor, remembers first encountering the concept of liminal spaces “back in 2020, when the original Backrooms post on 4chan started going viral.”It was an emotion they’d felt in such places but never previously had a name for. “A strange liminal discomfort”, Sodaraptor says, mixed with pangs of “anemoia”: nostalgia for an era that predates your own experience.View image in fullscreenShelf discovery … Interior Worlds.Photograph: Raptorsoft GamesSo it’s only fitting that the phenomenon’s virtual inspirations are now, in video game terms, as ancient as all those dead malls.The aforementioned Arkham City and Skyrim both came out in 2011. The same year, Valve released Portal 2, the mind-bending first-person puzzler which Parsons has repeatedly cited as his biggest influence. The director even made a couple of Portal fan-videos;the last onewas uploaded to his YouTube channel in 2021, just months before the first Backrooms clip.It is probably inevitable that the aesthetics of these 15-year-old games would just now be beginning to seep through into the cinematic mainstream. Parsons was a young child when Portal 2 came out, and it’s only natural that he – and the generation of film-makers just now coming of age – would make things informed by the dark rooms they got lost in as kids.A Minecraft Movie may already exist (unfortunately) but what will be much more interesting are the films and other artworks shaped by the experience of playing Minecraft at a formative age. Those dark caverns, the endless mines, the sounds of the zombies, the threat of the creepers – once those strange experiences have sunk into internet lore, who knows what will emerge and where it will take us.Explore more on these topicsGamesIndie gamesBackroomsSkyrimfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Womad festival review – ​hugely welcome return of joyous planet-spanning music fest | Womad | The Guardian
description: ​In a new home after a year off, there’s a thread of fierce political anger running alongside the spirited musical performances – including standout sets from Barrington Levy and Daniela Mercury
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ​In a new home after a year off, there’s a thread of fierce political anger running alongside the spirited musical performances – including standout sets from Barrington Levy and Daniela Mercury
Content: ‘Love is better, no war’ … Oumou Sangaré headlines at Womad festival.Photograph: C Brandon/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘Love is better, no war’ … Oumou Sangaré headlines at Womad festival.Photograph: C Brandon/RedfernsWomadReviewWomad festival review – ​hugely welcome return of joyous planet-spanning music festNeston Park, Wiltshire​In a new home after a year off, there’s a thread of fierce political anger running alongside the spirited musical performances – including standout sets from Barrington Levy and Daniela MercuryPanashe NyadunduMon 27 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtWomad, opening at new home Neston Park after a year off in 2025, the boundary between spectator and performer dissolves entirely: you bump into headliners in the loo queue, spot them wandering the site with their kids, or sit in on an intimate panel discussion with them hours after their main-stage set. Phone signal is practically nonexistent at the new site, forcing a crowd reliant on group chats into analogue meet-ups; the new arboretum layout holds a cosier, village-like setup than before, complete with a mercifully shorter trek from all camping areas. You can start the morning at your own speed: pounding through a west African djembe workshop, joining “laughing yoga”, or relaxing in a wood-fired tub while distant basslines echo through the trees.Musical highlights often happen when artists go off-script.Reggaelegend Barrington Levy provides Friday’s standout moment by rejecting strict act times, turning to the side of the stage to deliver a blunt ultimatum: “Mr Promoter, don’t invite me to your festival and tell me to get off the stage. I’m fucking playing as long as I like.” The crowd back him and he stays, launching back into Black Roses and Here I Come, his star power locking in a crowd of nodding, fist-pumping seniors, families, and kids getting a proper musical education.View image in fullscreenA fierce political charge … Daniela Mercury.Photograph: Samir Hussein/WireImageGreentea Peng closes Friday with a sultry set, backed by an all-female brass section who sound remarkably tight despite having rehearsed only the night before. For sheer stagecraft, though, Brazilian singer Daniela Mercury dominates. Against visuals of favelas and Indigenous tribes raising awareness for conservation, her set is a fierce political charge, and she calls out for democracy before signing off with Michael Jackson’s They Don’t Care About Us.That political edge runs straight through the weekend. The festival’s talks stage directly confronts political instability and the rise of rightwing populism; Green Party leader Zack Polanski draws a packed tent as he details arms sales and a call for rent controls while The Lincoln Project’s unbarred Rick Wilson dismantles the mechanics of Maga.View image in fullscreen‘Don’t invite me to your festival and tell me to get off the stage’ … Barrington Levy.Photograph: Samir Hussein/WireImageAcross the music stages, that message takes the form of a shared plea for peace and solidarity. At Taste the World, Freshlyground cook a chicken and peanut curry while sharing memories of performing Waka Waka at the 2010 World Cup. The Garifuna Collective bring ancestral grooves from Belize, reminding the crowd that after four songs, “we’re not strangers any more, we’re family.” On Sunday, Oumou Sangaré commands the main stage with simple messages of unity: “Love is better, no war”, before teasing women to stay away from handsome, fast-talking playboys on Kamelemba.Hidden gems are found by wandering into smaller tents, where artists hold crowds in cult-like fixation. At the Sunflower tent, 83-year-old Aboriginal Australian elder Kankawa Nagarra delivers spellbinding desert blues and gospel; on the Village Stage, Sabine McCalla’s vocals feel entirely detached from time, howling mid-song like her dog to an unblinking audience.View image in fullscreenSpellbinding desert blues and gospel … Kankawa Nagarra.Photograph: C Brandon/RedfernsMinor structural snags remain, such as the low stages at workshops, which mean anyone past the sixth row has to blindly mirror the person ahead of them during dance and yoga classes – but flailing limbs aside, it’s accepted as part of the fun.The festival’s longevity is anchored in its community, from stallholders like Marina at Ghana Goods (22 years and counting) to adults who first arrived in prams, now carting their own kids about. Japanese outfit Seppuku Pistols sum up the festival’s chaotic energy, determination and passion: one band member breaks their ankle mid-show but doesn’t realise and adrenaline keeps them going, with a similarly unaware crowd chanting “one more tune!” for two solid minutes after they’ve finished.Explore more on these topicsWomadFestivalsMusic festivalsPop and rockReggaelive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rienzi review – Wagner’s early opera makes its Bayreuth debut as a frenzied contemporary election drama  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Alexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production swaps 14th-century Rome for an abstract near future in an over-busy staging . Jennifer Holloway’s Adriano is a standout in a strong cast
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Alexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production swaps 14th-century Rome for an abstract near future in an over-busy staging . Jennifer Holloway’s Adriano is a standout in a strong cast
Content: Too much happening … Rienzi at Bayreuth festival.Photograph: Enrico NawrathView image in fullscreenToo much happening … Rienzi at Bayreuth festival.Photograph: Enrico NawrathOperaReviewRienzi review – Wagner’s early opera makes its Bayreuth debut as a frenzied contemporary election dramaBayreuth festival theatre, BayreuthAlexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production swaps 14th-century Rome for an abstract near future in an over-busy staging . Jennifer Holloway’s Adriano is a standout in a strong castFlora WillsonMon 27 Jul 2026 08.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 08.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was Adolf Hitler’s favourite opera – and thus vital to a historical chapter that Germany’sBayreuth festivallong preferred to avoid. But Rienzi has finally arrived atWagner’s symbolic HQ, opening the 150th anniversary season as an exception to the festival’s rigid canon of his 10 “mature” works.Rienzi’s problems are unavoidable. Since the complete handwritten score was given to Hitler and subsequently disappeared, no authentic version of Wagner’s longest opera exists. Aesthetically, Rienzi shares the vast scale of French grand opera but sounds broadly Italian. Flashes of chromatic ambition hint at a Wagnerian language to come. Yet there are endless repetitions and the sense of an epic both overcompressed and underpowered.Bayreuth’s acoustic worked its magic, lending even four-square passages a diffuse luminosity. But this performance’s sporadic momentum was down to conductorNathalie Stutzmann, who found moments of pure chamber-music tenderness, majestic poise and vast surges of bass amid the military marches and rousing choral outbursts.View image in fullscreenAbstract near-future … Rienzi at Bayreuth festival.Photograph: Enrico NawrathInAlexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production, 14th-century Rome becomes an abstract near-future (smartphone-like devices for all, screens everywhere, dystopian concrete) that also references recent political events in the US and beyond. One political faction brandishes placards screaming “lock him up” and “bringing Rome back”; Rienzi’s supporters insist they’re “stronger together”. Events onstage are filmed and projected, labelled “live from theCapitol”. Rienzi’s narrative becomes an election drama incorporating psychosis and incest. Bayreuth itself gets a cameo in the act two ballet, a madcap compilation of Wagner’s operas directed by a child dressed as the composer. At one point, Bible verses spool across the stage. We see numerous video clips of pigeons. There is, in short, too much happening.Leading the cast,Andreas Schagerwas characteristically high-wattage in the title role, his clarion tenor thrilling if unvaried, his gentleness in act four a rare instance of poignancy.Andreas Bauer KanabasandMichael Nagywere persuasive as his political rivals Colonna and Orsini whileGabriela Scherergleamed as his sister Irene. Best of all wasJennifer Holloway’s Adriano – now a soft-butch lesbian rather than Wagner’s trouser role – whose desperation and torn loyalties remained sympathetic, her singing searing, as catastrophe raged around her.Rienzi continues at the Bayreuth festival until 26 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaRichard WagnerClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: CBSO/Yamada review – Poulenc and Adams pairing is stylish, witty and thrilling | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lucas and Arthur Jussen brought fun and energy to Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos, and John Adams’ Harmonium was monumental and moving in the City of Birmingham Orchestra and Chorus’ Prom under their chief conductor Kazuki Yamada
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Lucas and Arthur Jussen brought fun and energy to Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos, and John Adams’ Harmonium was monumental and moving in the City of Birmingham Orchestra and Chorus’ Prom under their chief conductor Kazuki Yamada
Content: Lucid and urbane … Kazuki Yamada and the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenLucid and urbane … Kazuki Yamada and the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewCBSO/Yamada review – Poulenc and Adams pairing is stylish, witty and thrillingRoyal Albert Hall, LondonLucas and Arthur Jussen brought fun and energy to Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos, and John Adams’ Harmonium was monumental and moving in the City of Birmingham Orchestra and Chorus’ Prom under their chief conductor Kazuki YamadaAlexandra CoghlanMon 27 Jul 2026 07.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 07.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican minimalism can punch and thrill, hypnotise and slow your pulse, but how often does it make you laugh? What a brilliant idea, then, from Kazuki Yamada and theCity of Birmingham Symphony Orchestrato pair John Adams’ formative 1980 epic Harmonium – a sonic wrestle with love and death and desire – with music by the wittiest, slipperiest, most self-puncturing composer in the business, an artist who will break your heart with the cheekiest of grins: Francis Poulenc.It’s entirely typical that Poulenc can’t even bring himself to call a symphony a symphony. Any delusions of grandeur are seen off at the pass by diminutising his 1948 “Sinfonietta”, which duly unfolds in a series of impeccably shaded and textured dances, marches and melodies that thumb their nose at anything so dutiful as development.Lucid and urbane, Yamada’s Poulenc was impeccable – a crisp musical suit, an Hermès pocket-square of whimsy just visible in silky woodwind solos and harp, always undercut by clean architectural lines. When the music has this many punchlines you have to play it absolutely straight; all the more essential, because there was a riotous coda to come in the form of Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos.View image in fullscreenFingers flying as one … the Jussen brothers.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouDutch duo theJussen brothers(who’ve been playing this since they were teenage prodigies) bounded on for their Proms debut in matching suits and flung themselves at this naughty musical satire – whose target is modernism as much as a Mozart piano concerto – with irrepressible rhythmic energy. Two heads nodded vigorously from either side of the stage, fingers flying absolutely as one: enormously stylish fun.A performance of Harmonium at home in Birmingham a few weeks ago lacked choral welly, but with the CBSO Chorus now bolstered by the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs we had the rippling textural canvas the Adams demands for this quasi-choral-concerto – voices treated as pulsing points of light inNegative Love; as an explosive, ululating jangle inWild Nights. Central movementBecause I could not stop for Deathwas the only sticking point, sagging where it should have held us rapt. But to demand electricity here is rather like asking for more pace in mile 22 of a marathon – a quibble in a frankly monumental achievement.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicCity of Birmingham Symphony OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance Again | Boy George | The Guardian
description: Culture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attack
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Culture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attack
Content: Boy George performs on stage in Hamburg this month.Photograph: Tristar Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBoy George performs on stage in Hamburg this month.Photograph: Tristar Media/Getty ImagesBoy George‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance AgainCulture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attackBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 27 Jul 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoy George has released a new song entitled We Will Dance Again, which voices support for Israel’s military action in Palestine.Posted on X and Instagram with the Hebrew title עוד נרקוד alongside its English translation, the song features a pop-reggae backing. The opening lyrics are: “You say genocide, I say war / When you’re attacked, that’s what the army’s for / Does it get ugly? You bet it does / When I know you wanna kill every last one of us.”Boy George cites theattack by Hamas at the Nova music festival in October 2023, saying the civilians killed there were “murder[ed] … for the crime of dancing”. A total of 344 civilians and 34 security personnel were killed and 44 people were taken hostage.The overall Palestinian death toll since the war started ismore than 73,000.The title phrase We Will Dance Again, repeated for the song’s chorus, has been used by Israelis to express hope and solidarity in the wake of the 7 October attack, and was used as the title of an acclaimed documentary about it.Elsewhere in the chorus, Boy George asserts: “There will be no war / But if you’re ever confused / I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human.”He also criticises the pro-Palestinian movement, including musicians who have condemned Israel: “You condemn the Jews, with selective memory / Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet feels so weak.” Musicians who have supportedPalestineinclude Stormzy, Damon Albarn, Clairo and Brian Eno, the latter of whom conceived an all-star charity single, Lullaby, which vied for Christmas No 1 in 2025.Boy George, who is not Jewish, has recently voiced support for Jewish communities. In an interview with the Telegraph, when discussing his admiration for Jewish peers in the 1980s during his time fronting Culture Club, he said: “Over the years it’s been a really personal thing. It doesn’t mean that I don’t have compassion for Palestinians, it doesn’t mean that I agree with what’s going on in Israel, but I am always going to defend the people that I love. I have a lot of Jewish friends and there would never be a situation where I’d turn my back on them.”He also voiced his support after theknife attack in Golders Green in April which left two Jewish men injured, saying: “We need to make our Jewish community know we support them.”His new song marks an intensification of his support for Israel, having said earlier in the year that he didn’t have an opinion on the country.View image in fullscreenBoy George with San Marino contestant Senhit at the Eurovision song contest in Vienna in May.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APSpeaking ahead of an appearance with San Marino for their Eurovision song contest entry (which didn’t reach the contest’s final), he was questioned about the boycott of Eurovision from countries opposing Israel’s inclusion in the contest. “I have many Jewish friends, whom I’ve known since I was 15 or 16 years old,” he replied. “Are people asking me, as someone with principles, to turn my back on my Jewish friends? That is not going to happen – it will never happen. From the beginning of my career, I wore the Star of David … I feel very connected to the Jewish people. I’m not necessarily connected to Israel. I don’t really have an opinion on that. But the mission of music is to unite people.”His characterisation of Israel’s action against Palestine as a legitimate military response rather than genocide runs counter to aUnited Nations inquiry, which stated in 2025 that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel’s foreign ministry called the report “distorted and false”. Last month, anotherindependent UN inquiryfound that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by targeting children. That report was dubbed a “libellous sham” by Israel.Boy George was one of the most flamboyant and recognisable pop stars of the 1980s, with Culture Club scoring four UK Top 10 albums including 1983’s chart-topping Colour By Numbers. Hit singles include Do You Really Want to Hurt Me? and Karma Chameleon, which were both hugely successful in the US as well as UK, and have endured as staples on oldies radio.The band also had a hit with an anti-war track, The War Song, which reached UK No 2 in 1984 and featured the chorus: “War is stupid and people are stupid / And love means nothing in some strange quarters.”Last month, Boy George launched a new company called Artist Included, which will use AI to allow artists to create new versions of earlier songs which resemble the originals, as a way of wresting back control of master recordings. It launched with a new version of Karma Chameleon, which Boy George recorded then de-aged. “When I heard it, I was absolutely gobsmacked,” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “It sounds like another take from that original session.”Explore more on these topicsBoy GeorgePop and rockIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Charli xcx portrait added to National Portrait Gallery collection | Charli xcx | The Guardian
description: Pop star is celebrated as ‘one of the defining cultural figures of her generation’ by gallery, which acquires Brat-era portrait by Harley Weir
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Pop star is celebrated as ‘one of the defining cultural figures of her generation’ by gallery, which acquires Brat-era portrait by Harley Weir
Content: Harley Weir’s 2024 portrait of Charli xcx.Photograph: Harley Weir/PAView image in fullscreenHarley Weir’s 2024 portrait of Charli xcx.Photograph: Harley Weir/PACharli xcxCharli xcx portrait added to National Portrait Gallery collectionPop star is celebrated as ‘one of the defining cultural figures of her generation’ by gallery, which acquires Brat-era portrait by Harley WeirBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 27 Jul 2026 06.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA portrait of Charli xcx has been added to the National Portrait Gallery’s collection, in the week that she hopes for a No 1 chart position for her new album Music, Fashion, Film.The photograph by Harley Weir was taken in 2023 and became one of the key images associated with Charli’s Brat era: the 2024 album that became a pop cultural phenomenon for its candour and debauchery.Brandei Estes, the National Portrait Gallery’s senior curator of photographs, said the gallery was “delighted” with the acquisition. Charli is “one of the defining cultural figures of her generation”, she said, and Weir “has developed a distinctive photographic language that combines intimacy with a powerful sense of presence”.The photo is exhibited in the gallery’s History Makers Now space, and its acquisition was funded by a gift from the Bukhman Foundation.Charli’s album Music, Fashion, Film has been a critical and commercial success since its release on Friday, with the Guardian describing her as “our most consistently bracing pop star” ina five-star review. It could become her fourth UK No 1 and second this year, after her soundtrack to Wuthering Heights topped the chart in February. It is at No 1 in the midweek chart ahead of new releases by Snow Patrol, Shania Twain and the Strokes.Over the weekend she released three additional songs not included on Music, Fashion, Film, described as B-sides of the album tracks, and titled I Keep on Thinking Bout You Every Single Day and Night, Playboy Bunny and If You Take Away the Music Then What Has She Got? “I felt adamant I wouldn’t put them on streaming because it sort of felt counterintuitive to the whole ethos of those songs, but I know you all really wanted them so I’ve begrudgingly put them on iTunes lol,” she said on Instagram.Charli xcx: Music, Fashion, Film review – slippery search into selfhood that hits just as hard as BratRead moreOne song from the album, Camera, documents Charli’s recent forays into film acting: she has recently appeared in the Polish arthouse drama Erupcja, the fantastical 100 Nights of Hero, and opposite Anya Taylor-Joy and Chris Evans in Sacrifice, plus she starred as herself in the mockumentary The Moment.She’ll next be seen in Gregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex, comedy thriller The Gallerest, and the remake of 1978 horror movie Faces of Death. She is starring in and producing the untitled next film by Takashi Miike, the Japanese director of Audition and Ichi the Killer.Her next major live shows are headlining the Reading and Leeds festival, before a North American tour in September and October.Explore more on these topicsCharli xcxPop and rockNational Portrait GalleryPhotographynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ronnie Le Drew, puppeteer behind Zippy and David Bowie’s goblins, dies aged 78 | Puppetry | The Guardian
description: Canadian-born British operator, president of the British Puppet Guild, died after a ‘short illness’
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: Canadian-born British operator, president of the British Puppet Guild, died after a ‘short illness’
Content: Zippy and Ronnie Le Drew on The Big Breakfast TV show in 2022.Photograph: Tom Dymond/Channel 4/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZippy and Ronnie Le Drew on The Big Breakfast TV show in 2022.Photograph: Tom Dymond/Channel 4/ShutterstockPuppetryRonnie Le Drew, puppeteer behind Zippy and David Bowie’s goblins, dies aged 78Canadian-born British operator, president of the British Puppet Guild, died after a ‘short illness’Martin BelamMon 27 Jul 2026 13.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRonnie Le Drew, best known for operating the puppet Zippy on the classic children’s television programme Rainbow, has died aged 78 after a short illness. The news was confirmed by the British Puppet Guild, of which Le Drew was president.The Canadian-born British puppeteer was also known for working on 1986’s Labyrinth alongside David Bowie as well as 1986’s Little Shop of Horrors and various Muppet movies including in 1992’s The Muppet Christmas Carol. He worked on various iterations of Sooty, alongside Harry and Matthew Corbett, usually as Sweep, Sooty’s sidekick.He trained at London’s award-winning puppet theatre the Little Angel Theatre, with which he enjoyed a long association, eventually teaching there. He also co-founded the London School ofPuppetrywith his partner Caroline Astell-Burt.In the statement announcing his death, the British Puppet Guild said: “We are saddened to announce the death of our president and friend Ronnie Le Drew, following a short illness. Ronnie has been our president for 10 years, possibly the most active and supportive president we have ever had or will have. Attending nearly every event whether it be online or in person, often performing when asked and always willing to chat, tell stories and entertain in whatever way he could.”Le Drew’s son, John, wrote via his father’s social media channels: “We’re devastated to announce that dad passed away this morning, after a brief illness. We’re all grieving and sorry for our loss of such a sweet beautiful man.”The puppet duo of Zippy and George were initially voiced by Roy Skelton, who also voiced Doctor Who’s Daleks between 1967 and 1988.He died in 2011, aged 79, and contributed to the enduring popularity of brash mouthy know-it-all orange Zippy, and the rather more shy and retiring pink hippopotamus George.The programme launched in 1972 and was made by ThamesTelevisioncontinuously until 1992, with David Cook as the original presenter, and Geoffrey Hayes taking over in 1974. A revival by Tetra Films from 1994 to 1997 featured Le Drew also performing as the voice of Zippy, as well as operating the puppet.Rainbow was conceived as a British equivalent of Sesame Street, with a bunch of friends exploring different educational topics together – often via the medium of conflict between Zippy, George or Bungle the bear, which Hayes,who died in 2018, would reconcile.Ronnie Le Drew talking about his career on YouTube.Le Drew was working until recently, having just appeared on YouTube channelMy 70s TV Childhood, talking about his career and the job as Zippy, which he described as “a six-week contract that lasted 20 years”.Explore more on these topicsPuppetryTelevisionChildren's TVCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Morris the staffie – the shameless thief who stole an entire roast chicken | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Abandoned as a puppy, he pinched everything from birthday cake to raw potatoes. Beneath the comic greed was a much-loved companion who kept us laughing for 12 years
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Abandoned as a puppy, he pinched everything from birthday cake to raw potatoes. Beneath the comic greed was a much-loved companion who kept us laughing for 12 years
Content: Hilariously selfish … Morris the staffie.Photograph: Kate RiordanView image in fullscreenHilariously selfish … Morris the staffie.Photograph: Kate RiordanThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Morris the staffie – the shameless thief who stole an entire roast chickenAbandoned at the age of two, he pinched everything from birthday cake to raw potatoes. Beneath the comic greed was a much-loved companion who kept us laughing for 12 yearsKate RiordanMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe adopted Morris after he’d been abandoned in a park at the age of two. The shelter named him Kai but it didn’t suit him. An old soul (read: curmudgeon) who tried to pull us into old-school boozers, and who demanded routine and treated walks as a favour to us, Morris was perfect.Incorrigibly lazy and happiest on the sofa, preferably on top of us, his only real motivation was food. Perhaps he knew hunger in that park, and vowed never to meet it again. Among the countless petty thefts from unattended plates were some truly audacious schemes. There was the sandwich stolen right out of a stranger’s hand. The birthday cake polished off, tinfoil and all, before its intended recipient tasted a single bite. The multiple raw baking potatoes eaten, this last crime caught on video or we’d never have believed it.His Brink’s-Mat moment came after a 12-person barbecue. Under cover of darkness, he ate the bones of 24 chicken drumsticks and a large rack of ribs, and paid for it with a three-day sentence at the animal hospital, where successive X-rays showed the agonising progression through his digestive system of 100 needle-sharp bone shards. Luckily, he didn’t seem to be in too much pain.View image in fullscreenIncorrigibly lazy … author Kate Riordan’s staffie, Morris, in 2013.Photograph: Kate RiordanHe survived and learned nothing: a couple of years later he dispensed with a roast chicken so thoroughly that we wondered if it had even existed. The meat had obviously gone, but so had the entire carcass. The metal platter it had been resting on was clean and shining. The foil had somehow been replaced neatly on top of the platter. Forensic examination of the scene showed only a slightly misaligned chair – used for clambering up – and a single smear of grease.Even when grey streaked his fur and he lost his hearing, we avoided talking about the end. This small staffie contained multitudes, and it was impossible to imagine life without him and his warmth, his groans, his hilariously selfish ways. Perhaps we’d assumed he’d go out in a blaze of feasting glory but, when he developed dementia, the terrible responsibility of deciding when to say goodbye fell to us.On his last day, like all those before it, he ate like there was no tomorrow. Of course, he didn’t know there wouldn’t be. If he had, I think he would have been satisfied with his haul, which included posh sausages, Marmite toast and his unlikely favourite, satsumas. “Where’s Morris?” we always used to say, meaning, “Oh god, what’s he stealing now?” Now it’s taken on new meaning: the disbelief that he’s gone and won’t ever be back. But we still have the stories. We’re still so much richer for the 12 years our funny little Morris gave us.The Last Time I Saw Her Alive by Kate Riordan is out 30 July and is published by Penguin (£16.99).
