title: Screamers welcome: Chicago scream club lets people ‘give in and let go’ | Chicago | The Guardian
description: Chicagoans come together for cathartic and communal screaming experience as activity gains traction across US
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: Chicagoans come together for cathartic and communal screaming experience as activity gains traction across US
Content: Emanuel and Elena from the Chicago Scream Club.Photograph: Mariya ArtBelkaView image in fullscreenEmanuel and Elena from the Chicago Scream Club.Photograph: Mariya ArtBelkaChicagoScreamers welcome: Chicago scream club lets people ‘give in and let go’Chicagoans come together for cathartic and communal screaming experience as activity gains traction across USAdam GabbattMon 27 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 08.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople strolling along North Avenue Beach, a sandy strip on Lake Michigan, in the Lincoln Park neighborhood ofChicago, are apt to see something unusual on Sunday evenings.That’s because Chicago’s“Scream Club”meets there every week during the city’s warmer months, bringing together a community of up to 300 people who like to scream out over the water – and it’s an activity that seems to be spreading across the US.Founded last year by couple Emanuel Hernandez and Elena Soboleva, the Chicago Scream Club has become a popular resource for anyone looking to release stress or, in at least one case, celebrate getting married. Videos online of people standing in line, each shrieking into the lake, proves that it’s a popular group activity.“I think a lot of people think screaming is silly by themselves. So then, when they have permission from other people, screaming with them, I think it just gives them confidence to be able to do it,” said Hernandez, who works as a breathwork practitioner, a men’s coach and a fitness coach.The screaming, videos of which went viral online this week, started after Hernandez and Soboleva found themselves arguing. Hernandez had moved to Chicago to be with Soboleva, leaving behind a career as an actor and crossfit coach. The pair were having issues settling into their new routine, Hernandez said.“One day we were walking by the lake, and I said: ‘Do you want to just go scream into the lake? And she said: ‘You know, yes, but, like, what if people were around?’” Hernandez, 41, recalled.“And I go: ‘I’ll just ask them if they want to join us.’ And so that’s what we did. We found a pier that goes out into the water far enough so that if somebody was around they wouldn’t be able to hear us, but there were people there. So we just asked them: ‘Hey, look, we’re about to scream into the lake. If you’d like to join us, you’re more than welcome.’”Hernandez, 41, said those people responded, “Hell yeah” – and joined the couple in screaming.“That’s when Elena and I were like: “Wow, that was really cool! And I think that we should probably do something with it.’”They created a poster inviting people to come and scream with them, and slowly more and more people started showing up weekly. The pair said that by the sixth week, more than 300 people were showing up. Since then, Hernandez and Soboleva have expanded the club, with screaming events held in cities including Austin, Phoenix, and Washington DC. There’s even anonline Scream Club website– although this is not associated with Hernandez and Soboleva’s club – where people can “scream with others across the internet”.“Everyone has a very different reason [for coming]. Some do come because they need to release that stress and those anxieties, and the buildup of emotions, but there are some people who come to celebrate. Two weeks ago we had a new bride come with her girlfriends to scream and celebrate her wedding in this really unique form,” said Soboleva, a branding consultant for women-owned businesses who moved to the US from Russia in 2011.“We’ve seen people of all ages, people of all nationalities, all different walks of life coming over. There are people who cry, there are people who break down, you know it’s just all this pent-up stuff that they’ve they’ve been holding on to for so long.”The pair guide attenders through the screaming session. They hand each person “a piece of biodegradable paper”, Soboleva, 36, said, where people are encouraged to write down “what they want to let go of”, or what their intention is. They then throw the paper into the water and scream.Soboleva said there is no need for specialist clothing or equipment. “Just feel comfortable,” she said. Hernandez advised that individuals scream quietly at the beginning, before building to their loudest scream.“The biggest tip I would just tell people is just: don’t be afraid. It’s: just give in and let go. It’s such a taboo thing to think about screaming, so when we give people that permission to do it, it’s just like just: show up,” he said.“That’s the most important thing. You’re not only showing up for yourself, but you’re showing up to the people in your life who love you and want to see you doing well.”Explore more on these topicsChicagonewsShareReuse this content

title: Quick and easy summer salad: Georgina Hayden’s grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah recipe | Salad | The Guardian
description: Sweetness and spice abound in this refreshing summer salad
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: Sweetness and spice abound in this refreshing summer salad
Content: Georgina Hayden's grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah salad.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden's grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah salad.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.Quick and easySaladQuick and easy summer salad: Georgina Hayden’s grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah recipeSweetness and spice abound in this refreshing summer saladGeorgina HaydenMon 27 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the weather is glorious, I have very little desire to do any “proper cooking”. Turning the grill on for about 15 minutes is the maximum amount of heat I want to subject my home to, which is why, in the summer months, I eat this sort of salad on repeat: stone fruit with golden slices of halloumi is my favourite pairing. Add a little freshness with some sweetness and spice, and it is a glorious thing. You could even spoon it on to slices of toasted ciabatta for an open sandwich or elegant crostini.Grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah saladWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIf you make your own dukkah, amazing; otherwise, you can pick up some pretty good mixes from most supermarkets these days. It really works here, and feel free to add more, if you like.Prep10 minCook25 minServes43 peachesSea salt andblack pepperExtra-virgin olive oil90g rocket½ bunchmint,leaves picked and torn1 tsp dijonmustardJuice of1 lemon225g block of halloumi,cut into 1cm-thick slices1 tbsp runny honey2 tbsp dukkah1 green chilli, halved and finely sliced – pith and seeds removed first, if you want less heatHeat the grill to high. Halve and stone the peaches, then cut each half in half again. Arrange the peach quarters in a small to medium roasting tray, so they don’t have too much space between them, and season generously. Drizzle with olive oil, toss to coat, then grill for about eight minutes, until the edges of the peach wedges are a little charred and gnarly.Meanwhile, put the rocket and mint leaves in a large bowl.When the peaches are done, transfer them to a platter, and reserve all the juices in the tray. Mix the mustard into the sweet peach juices, then whisk in the lemon juice and two tablespoons of olive oil. Taste and tweak the seasoning, then pour this dressing over the rocket.Lay the halloumi slices in the now empty peach tray and pop them under the grill for five minutes, turning once halfway so the cheese goes slightly golden all over.Meanwhile, toss the dressing through the rocket and mint, then place on the grilled peach platter, dotting the fruit on top and around the leaves. As soon as the halloumi is ready, drape the slices over the top of the salad, finish with a drizzle of honey, sprinkle on the dukkah and sliced green chilli and serve right away.Explore more on these topicsSaladQuick and easySummer food and drinkFoodFruitCheeseHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Vegan pho and Thai fishless cakes: Richard Makin’s southeast Asian-style tofu recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Fragrant, punchy vegan dishes that can be kept in the kept in the fridge or freezer for an easy midweek dinner
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fragrant, punchy vegan dishes that can be kept in the kept in the fridge or freezer for an easy midweek dinner
Content: Richard Makin's pho now or pho later.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenRichard Makin's pho now or pho later.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.FoodVegan pho and Thai fishless cakes: Richard Makin’s southeast Asian-style tofu recipesFragrant, punchy vegan dishes that can be kept in the kept in the fridge or freezer for an easy midweek dinnerRichard MakinMon 27 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether you love it or loathe it, tofu is one of the most versatile ingredients in any kitchen. For me, it’s the saviour of stressful dinner times, because it cooks in minutes, absorbs flavour like no other and packs a real nutritional punch. Here, it plays two very different roles: crisped until golden in a fragrant, spice-infused Vietnamese-style pho, and mashed to give body and bite to bold, punchy Thai-ish fishless cakes.Pho now or pho later (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThe best bit about pho, IMO, is the broth; unfortunately, it’s also the most time-consuming part. But don’t fret, I’ve streamlined the process for you. Once made, the broth can sit in the fridge for up to a week, ready to be reheated and poured over noodles and vegetables at a moment’s notice. And, because it’s full of spices and aromatics, it’ll taste even better with time.Prep10 minCook30 minServes21 tsp vegetable oil200g extra-firm tofu, drained and cubed2 shallots, peeled and roughly chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly crushed with the flat of a knife2½cm piece fresh ginger, roughly sliced2 star anise4cloves2 tsp coriander seeds2 green cardamom pods1 cinnamon stick½ tsp chilli flakes½ tsp fennel seeds1½ litres vegetable stock150g long-stem broccoli, ends trimmed170g flat rice noodles1 tbsp soy sauce1 tbsp brown sugar1 tsp fine sea salt2 tbsp white rice vinegarTo serve1 shallot, peeled and finely chopped1 red chilli, stalk, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely chopped1 smallcarrot, peeled and julienned or gratedFresh coriander, mint and basil2 lime wedgesPut the vegetable oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat, then fry the tofu for five minutes, turning often, until browned all over. Lift it out of the pan, stir the shallots, garlic, ginger and spices into the hot oil left in the pan and cook, stirring, for two minutes, until fragrant. Pour in the stock, bring to a boil over a medium heat, then leave to bubble for 10 minutes.Put the broccoli in a steamer basket (or sieve) and place it over the top of the simmering pot. Turn down the heat to a simmer, cover the pan with a lid and steam the broccoli for five minutes, until tender. Take out the broccoli and set aside.Strain the stock to remove the spices and aromatics, then return the clear broth to the pan and put it on a medium heat. Add the rice noodles and cook for five minutes, or until tender.Divide the noodles between two deep bowls, and top them both with half the steamed broccoli and fried tofu. Stir the soy sauce, brown sugar, sea salt and rice vinegar into the hot broth, then take it off the heat.If serving straight away, pour the seasoned broth over the noodles, broccoli and tofu in each bowl; if serving later, leave the broth to cool to room temperature, then transfer to an airtight container. Cover the noodle bowls (or transfer to a heat-proof jar) and keep in the fridge for up to a week.When ready to serve, bring the broth back to a boil, then pour it over the noodles. Garnish with chopped shallot, red chilli, julienned carrot, fresh herbs and a lime wedge.Red curry fishless cakes with peanut slawWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenThis recipe is for my mum. She went vegan not long after I did, back in 2017, and although she doesn’t say as much explicitly, Iknowthat she misses seafood. She also loves Thai food, so these fishless cakes are a win–win. They’re gently spiced and super fragrant, with a light, flaky texture; they’re also freezable and, because they’re dinky, they don’t need to be defrosted before frying.Prep15 minCook20 minServes2For the fishless cakes1400gtin hearts of palm, drained and roughly chopped150g medium-firm tofu, drained2 spring onions, trimmed and finely chopped1 tbsp vegan red curry paste1 tsp ginger paste, or 1 tsp grated fresh ginger1 garlic clove, peeled and minced1 tsp brown sugarFinely grated zest of ½ lime1 small bunchcoriander, leaves and tender stems chopped3 tbsp plain flour, plus extra for dusting1 tbsp vegetable oilLime wedges, to serveFor the peanut slaw50g shredded red cabbage50g shredded white cabbage1 small carrot, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks50g cooked edamame beans1 spring onion, trimmed and finely chopped40g salted peanuts, roughly chopped1 tbsp agave syrup1 tbsp rice vinegar, or lime juice1 tbsp olive oil1 tbsp soy sauce1 tbsp smooth peanut butter2 tsp sriracha1tsp ginger pasteWrap the chopped hearts of palm and the tofu in a clean kitchen towel and wring out as much moisture as possible. The tofu will get mushed up, but not to worry: that’s what you want.Put the hearts of palm and tofu in a large bowl, add the spring onions, curry paste, ginger, garlic, brown sugar, lime zest, coriander and flour, then mix thoroughly with your hands until well combined.Form the mixture into six patties and dust the outsides with the extra flour. If you’re making the fishless cakes in advance, put the patties on a small baking sheet and freeze until solid. Transfer them to an airtight container or zip-lock bag, and freeze for up two months.To cook, put a large frying pan on a medium heat, add the vegetable oil, then fry the patties for five to eight minutes on each side, until lightly browned (if cooking from frozen, you’ll need to add a few minutes to the cooking time ).While the fishless cakes are cooking, in a large bowl mix the two cabbages, carrot matchsticks, edamame, spring onion and chopped peanuts. In a small bowl, whisk the agave syrup, rice vinegar, olive oil, soy sauce, peanut butter, sriracha and ginger paste, pour half of this dressing over the slaw and toss to coat.Serve the fishless cakes with the peanut slaw on the side, with lime wedges alongside and the remaining dressing for dipping.These recipes are edited extracts from Stress-Free Dinners: Over 90 Quick and Delicious Everyday Vegan Recipes, by Richard Makin, published by Bloomsbury at £22. To order a copy for £19.80, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodTofuSnacksStarterVietnamese food and drinkThai food and drinkMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: I risk losing my livelihood because Nissan failed to repair my car | Motoring | The Guardian
description: I’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicle
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: I’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicle
Content: Delays in getting spares to repair a dual-controlled Nissan threatened a driving instructor’s livelihood.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyView image in fullscreenDelays in getting spares to repair a dual-controlled Nissan threatened a driving instructor’s livelihood.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyConsumer championsMotoringI risk losing my livelihood because Nissan failed to repair my carI’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicleAnna TimsMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy livelihood as a self-employed driving instructor is under threat owing to Nissan’s failure to repair my leased dual-control car.It has been off the road awaiting a spare part for three months, and I’ve now been told it will take at least a further month to arrive.In order to continue working I have had to hire a dual-control vehicle at a cost of more than £2,500 so far, while also continuing to pay PCP finance of about £1,500 on a car I can’t use.I have had to borrow more than £1,000 from relatives to extend the hire of the dual-control vehicle. After that, I will have no remaining funds to renew the hire, and will have to stop teaching and lose my customers and my income.CW,EastbourneYou contacted me in mid-March when the latest estimated repair date had been postponed for the third time, until the end of April. Since your hire contract was due for renewal on 15 April, and you had no money left to extend it, time was of the essence.There was no sense of urgency at Nissan, however. You complained that it had continuously kept you in the dark about timescales and reimbursements, and I had to repeatedly chase it for information.Meanwhile, you were forking out £490 a month in PCP payments and a monthly hire fee of £952.I managed to get the company to agree to reimburse you for the hire car costs up to the (as yet unspecified) repair date, but agreeing and paying are different things. Days passed, no money came.Two weeks after I waded in, Nissan told me the spare part had been sourced and the repair was planned for 15 April, the day your car hire contract ended.Your reimbursement for the hire, it said, should be paid within 10 days. This meant it would not be with you in time to pay to renew the car hire if the repair was delayed again.When I pointed this out, the company said it would fund any further hire contracts directly, then refused to put the promise in writing. In the event, your car was repaired in the nick of time.Next began the battle for compensation. You calculated that, apart from the hire charges, the delays and uncertainty had cost you nearly £900 in lost earnings and other expenses.Nissan’s response was to offer you two years of free servicing, then it ignored your protest that you had already paid in advance for a service plan and that you were due to replace the car in 12 months.Back I went to Nissan, and this month it apologised for ignoring you and agreed to pay you compensation, the value of which you have agreed not to disclose.It says: “We are sympathetic to the customer’s experience, which fell below the high standards Nissan and its dealer partners strive to deliver.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. title: Is it true that … sit-ups are the best exercise for abs? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: The classic routine doesn’t isolate your stomach muscles as much as you might think, but here are five that will
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: The classic routine doesn’t isolate your stomach muscles as much as you might think, but here are five that will
Content: Illustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianIs it true that …Health & wellbeingIs it true that … sit-ups are the best exercise for abs?The classic gym routine doesn’t isolate your stomach muscles as much as you might think, but here are five that willKate LloydMon 27 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf someone in a film or TV show wants a six-pack, chances are they’ll drop to the floor and start doing sit-ups. According to Dr Lee Brown, senior lecturer in strength and conditioning at the University of East London, that’s more Hollywood than science.“It’s embedded in the archaic practices of boxing coaches and therefore everyone seems to follow it,” he says. “But they’re far from the best exercise for training your core.”A sit-up involves lying on your back with your knees bent, then lifting your torso towards your thighs and lowering it again. While the abdominal muscles certainly are involved, Brown says much of the movement is driven by the hip flexors, particularly a deep muscle called the psoas major, meaning the exercise doesn’t isolate the abs as effectively as many people think.double quotation markIf you’re doing too many sit-ups, it can cause problems with the lower backIs it true that … it’s harder for women to build muscle than men?Read moreIt can also lead to injury. “If you’re doing too many sit-ups, it can cause problems with the lower back,” Brown says. “Overworking the hip flexors can make them hypertonic [stiff and tight]. Your torso leans forward because you have overly toned and tight hip flexors, creating an imbalance and a dumping ground for sheering forces in your lower back.”Brown recommends moves such as planks, side planks, farmer’s carries (walking while holding a heavy weight in each hand), suitcase carries (walking with a weight in one hand to challenge stability) and bird dogs (lifting the opposite arm and leg from all fours). Pilates and yoga can also help build core strength.“I worked with a sprinter who’d had a back injury and had been doing sit-ups for ever,” Brown says. “I asked him how long he could hold a plank for. He said less than 30 seconds. Six weeks later, he could hold one for seven minutes and his back pain had gone.”Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingIs it true that …featuresShareReuse this content

title: In search of Valencia’s ‘white gold’: my hunt for the perfect horchatería | Valencia holidays | The Guardian
description: Horchata, the revered creamy drink made from tiger nuts, is still served in grand Valencian parlours – always accompanied by sugar-glazed pastries
Author: Gordon Cole-Schmidt
Headline: Horchata, the revered creamy drink made from tiger nuts, is still served in grand Valencian parlours – always accompanied by sugar-glazed pastries
Content: A glass of horchata and a sweet farton at Horchatería de Santa Catalina in Valencia.All photographs: Mirja VogelView image in fullscreenA glass of horchata and a sweet farton at Horchatería de Santa Catalina in Valencia.All photographs: Mirja VogelValencia holidaysIn search of Valencia’s ‘white gold’: my hunt for the perfect horchateríaHorchata, the revered creamy drink made from tiger nuts, is still served in grand Valencian parlours – always accompanied by sugar-glazed pastriesGordon Cole-SchmidtMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a glimpse of an old couple sharing a tender moment in the bustlinghorchateríathat drew me into one of Valencia’s most storied culinary traditions. As he sipped his milkyhorchata de chufaand a white crescent moon appeared on his coiffed moustache, they shared a soft laugh and she dabbed it away from his upper lip.“There’s no fixed time to drink horchata,” the lady said. “As long we have at least one every day.”In Valencia, this refreshing, creamy, non-alcoholic drink is so beloved it is nicknamed “white gold”, and grand parlours dedicated to making it are still going strong in the city’s most sought-after locations. These often historic, traditional places are calledhorchaterías(ororxateriasin Valencian) and there are dozens dotted around the region.Production is authorised in 16 towns in the Valencia region, with the quaint town of Alboraya (Alboraia in Valencian), about 45 minutes’ walk from Valencia old town, acknowledged as its birthplace and global capital. Here, buried in the low-lying, fertile fields around the town, you’ll find the drink’s principal ingredient: thechufa.Chufas, known as tiger nuts in English, have been cultivated in Valencia for more than 1,000 years. They look like wooden raisins but taste nutty and slightly sweet when eaten raw. Tiger nuts are not actually nuts, but tubers of a grass-like plant from the sedge family. Valencia’s agricultural zone north of the city produces 5.3m to 8m kilograms of dried tiger nuts a year. Most of the harvesting takes place in spring to ensure ample supply for the balmy summer months.View image in fullscreen‘The horchata is darker, creamier and richer than most’ … a table at Horchatería De Santa Catalina in Valencia.To turn the wrinkly tubers into horchata, chufas are cleaned, soaked and crushed, then mixed with water. Nowadays, cinnamon, lemon or orange zest and sugar are added to boost the flavour.Alboraya is also the birthplace of horchata’s companion: thefarton, a long, cigar-shaped pastry glazed with sugar, created in the 1960s by the Polo family to dip in and mop up every last drop of horchata from the bottom of the glass. Some stay loyal to its humble predecessor,rosquilletas(breadsticks), which are less absorbent but an intriguingly salty, anise-flavoured counterpart to horchata’s sweetness nonetheless.Leaving Alboraya with a bellyful of the indulgent combination, I weighed the task of finding the perfect horchatería. It felt wrong to split up horchata from its farton, so I would consider both. Horchaterías tend to offer three versions of horchata:líquida(liquid),granizada(semi-frozen slush) ormixta(a blend of liquid and slush). It would be the traditional classic líquida for me.In Valencia, there are hundreds of places serving horchata and fartons, but I wanted tradition and old-world charm – places that exist only to make horchata, not as an afterthought to spiced lattes or ice-cream. After sifting out the cafes, coffeehouses and ice-cream parlours, a handwritten list on a single sheet of A4 remained.Horchatería FabiánView image in fullscreenIt’s early evening in the old town, and the narrow shopping alley leading to my first stop, family-runHorchatería Fabián, is filled with tourists and an after-work crowd. Past bustling taverns and restaurant terraces, I glimpse its entrance and the date it was founded: 1975. Sounds promising, but something is missing. Where are the customers?Although the place is empty, the staff are distracted and cold. The horchata they unwillingly produce is over-sweet, almost artificial tasting, and the farton is parched and crumbles on to the plate. Horchata seeps into its pores nicely when I dip it into the glass, but the overriding sensation is a numbing sweetness.I slink out of the unwelcoming room, back on to the busy street and into a local tavern, fearing my high expectations for this jaunt are misplaced.Horchata €3, 4/10Farton €1, 3/10Horchatería DanielView image in fullscreenThe next day, I spy the queue spilling out of the glass-panelled room atHorchatería Daniel. This is arguably the most well-known horchatería company in Valencia, founded in 1949 and still a family business, with three locations in Valencia.I visit all three. The original, and the largest, is in Alboraya, decked with wooden tables and a constant flow of regulars. In its basement, production of horchata and fartons begins at 5am for here and its other locations – one in the famous Mercado de Colón and the third in a grand parlour in the centre of the old town, near to Plaza de la Reina.That’s where I wait now, warmed by the evening sun, before I’m shuffled into a grand, airy room and handed a glass from a cluttered tray.I can barely hear myself think over the noise of chatter and glasses clinking. The horchata is creamy and only moderately sweet. Together with the traditional farton, it’s easy to see why this is still one of the most popular horchaterías in town. Giddy, I order its newest farton creation – coated in a layer of chocolate, raspberries and crushed pistachios. Its dry interior and disjointed melange of flavours bring me back down to earth. Stick with the old favourites here and you can’t go wrong.Horchata €1.95, 6.5/10Farton85 cents, 6/10Horchatería SantabárbaraView image in fullscreenSouth from the old town the streets widen out into sun-filled, palm-lined avenues leading to the suburb of Montolivet, where neighbourhood favouriteHorchatería Santabárbarahas been in situ for four years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost tables are busy, but this does not deter the manager, Rafa, from skipping between them to pat regulars on the back and run through each step of horchata production with wide-eyed tourists. By the time he reaches our table, my glass – which is refreshing but a little too sweet – is empty.“Try this,” Rafa commands, passing me a new glass. “This is the original horchata, no sugar, no nothing. Just chufa and water.” It’s a revelation. The overburdening sugary aftertaste is gone, and what’s left is a clean, refreshing natural drink that sings above the mediocrity of the sweetened version. Pair it with its spongy, glazed farton and you’ll want to join the sea of smiling regulars coming back for more.Horchata €2.50, 7/10Farton80 cents, 6.5/10Horchatería de Santa CatalinaView image in fullscreenIn the shadow of the stunning 17th-century baroque bell tower of the Santa Catalina Church in the old town,Horchatería de Santa Catalinais the grandest of them all.A tight entrance decorated with ceramic tiles from Manises opens into a grand dining room packed with marble tables. A curved wooden staircase leads into an equally beautiful room upstairs – both are heaving when I arrive in the evening.A chilled white glass and a longer farton dusted with icing sugar arrive on the table. Like the locals around me, I don’t hesitate. The farton melts in my mouth, while the horchata is darker, creamier and richer than most. It is a delightful combination. The place itself is a class act in one of the city’s most beautiful neighbourhoods.Horchata €4, 8/10Farton €1.55, 6.5/10Horchatería Mari ToñiView image in fullscreenNorth of the river in residential La Saïdia is another neighbourhood favourite, Horchatería Mari Toñi. It’s just a few minutes from artsy Benimaclet and on the way to Alboraya, if you’re leaving from the old town.Opening at 6.15am, it’s the first place in town to get a horchata and stays busy until it closes 15 hours later. Fartons are freshly made each morning and initially they look dry. The sugar glazing seems to wilt rather than crack. But the first bite proves looks aren’t everything – they are light and fluffy, perfectly porous to the creamy horchata produced in this charming, authentic location.Horchata €3, 6/10Farton80 cents, 7.5/10On the move? The takeaway alternativeView image in fullscreenHorchatería Mon Orxata.In more than 20 visits to different Valencian horchaterías, I watched as horchata was decanted into unbranded buckets and large flasks, conducted away from the main floor. In Alboraya, at bothHorchatería PanachandHorchatería El Sariers, at least 10 litres of horchata were transported out by three families in under 10 minutes.In the city, two standout takeaway alternatives emerged. Across most central plazas in Valencia,Món Orxatais bringing back a lost 400-year-old tradition of selling unpasteurised horchata from street carts. Its horchata is clean, crisp and one of the most refreshing on the hottest of days.Pair it with the orange-infused farton, made with fermented dough by award-winning Valencia-born pastry chef Migue Señorís atGelática Ice Conceptnear the coast, and enjoy both during a sunset walk along the city’s beach.Món Orxata horchata €3.30, 7/10Gelática Ice Concept farton €1.90, 8.5/10Explore more on these topicsValencia holidaysFood and drinkSpain holidaysEurope holidaysSpanish food and drinkMilkFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A job that changed me: My year as a ‘gopher’ taught me that all errand runners are holy | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: The work was simple: deliver letters, notices of assessment and other important legal documents, by bicycle. The locations, I came to realise, were varied and inconvenient
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The work was simple: deliver letters, notices of assessment and other important legal documents, by bicycle. The locations, I came to realise, were varied and inconvenient
Content: ‘“Gopher.” As in, go for it. Fetch things? Surely my entire life as an only daughter of immigrants had prepared me for this.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘“Gopher.” As in, go for it. Fetch things? Surely my entire life as an only daughter of immigrants had prepared me for this.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesA job that changed meAustralian lifestyleA job that changed me: My year as a ‘gopher’ taught me that all errand runners are holyThe work was simple: deliver letters, notices of assessment and other important legal documents, by bicycle. The locations, I came to realise, were varied and inconvenientRead more inthis series hereFarz EdrakiMon 27 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgopher is a small, solitary rodent with large front teeth native to North and Central America. It’s also the name of the job some workplaces give to errand runners (though it’s more usually spelled gofer).When I was a 21-year-old law student in Canberra, I was in desperate need of casual work. I came across an ad pinned to one of the corkboards outside the library. Bleary-eyed after another all-nighter to finish an assignment, I took down the number of the law firm.The title itself wasn’t off-putting: “Gopher.” As in,go for it. Fetch things? Surely my entire life as an only daughter of immigrants had prepared me for this. It also seemed like a great way to ride my bike in business hours. Besides, looking at my dwindling bank balance, I didn’t have much choice.When I turned up to work on my first day in black pants and a crisp ironed shirt, I immediately felt overdressed. The law firm receptionist wore shorts and a jumper proclaiming, I KISSED A VAMPIRE AND ILIKEDIT. Well, I liked her. She pointed to a stack of papers marked “gopher’s in-tray”.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe job, she explained, was simple: deliver letters, notices of assessment and other important legal documents. The locations, I came to realise, were varied and inconvenient.Some days, I precariously balanced packages on handlebars on my way to the courts. Others, I’d find myself weaving through foot traffic to get to the bank before they closed at their unreasonably early hour. The kind man at the revenue office came to know me by name. Presumably because I was the only out-of-breath twentysomething in a magpie-proof helmet in the waiting area.About a week into my tenure, I noticed a new inscription on the sheet on the top of the in-tray. It was a file addressed to “G.O.D.”“God? What’s that?” I asked the receptionist.“No,G.O.D. Gopher. On. Duty.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA job that changed me: At the one-hour photo lab, customers were determined to immortalise their genitals on 35mmRead moreOn my bike, valiantly carrying stacks of papers or packages, I did feel – briefly – like the G.O.D. of my email signature. If I didn’t deliver these letters, then very serious legal cases could not continue. Vulnerable clients were relying on me.Or that’s what I kept telling myself. In truth, when you’re an errand runner people don’t tend to take you seriously. Once the delivery is done, lawyers forget your name. Worse still, they call you by your extended title: “Tuesday Gopher.” While I was sometimes asked to cover reception, my duties never really expanded. Although on one occasion, a paralegal standing by the fax machine did ask me to scratch her back.A career adviser at university told me people in their latter years of law school usually want paralegal positions. But in the end, my time there would be my only job in a law firm. After graduating, I did not go on to practise. Instead, I got a job in a far more stable and financially lucrative industry: media.Still, that year where I was G.O.D. taught me more than the five with my head buried in books about torts and litigation. It taught me to appreciate every errand runner, every delivery driver, every courier I’ve met since.Delivery isn’t easy, whether you’re working for a law firm or a postie or someone on a motorbike bringing an ice-cream to a share house at two in the morning. I can look back and smile at my time running errands. But for many with more precarious work or visa conditions, it’s not a source of comedic reflection. It’s a daily reality. One that brings many, often disguised, challenges.In some places, workers with two legs and two wheels are being replaced with robots. But in the year of our lord 2026, physical objects and paper and the people who deliver them still matter.One person’s gopher is the world’s G.O.D. – someone who we all rely on.Explore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleA job that changed meCyclingAustralian lawfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A new start after 60: stuck in a hospital bed, I decided to retire. Now I’m a tap dancer | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Stephen Walsh was such a workaholic that none of his colleagues would believe he’d ever leave. But then he learned to dance and he’s now part of a dazzling tap troupe
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: Stephen Walsh was such a workaholic that none of his colleagues would believe he’d ever leave. But then he learned to dance and he’s now part of a dazzling tap troupe
Content: Stephen Walsh as part of Pat’s Happy Tappers at Great Alne Park retirement Village in Worcestershire.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStephen Walsh as part of Pat’s Happy Tappers at Great Alne Park retirement Village in Worcestershire.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianA new start after 60Life and styleA new start after 60: stuck in a hospital bed, I decided to retire. Now I’m a tap dancerStephen Walsh was such a workaholic that none of his colleagues would believe he’d ever leave. But then he learned to dance and he’s now part of a dazzling tap troupePaula CocozzaMon 27 Jul 2026 01.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen he was 57, Stephen Walsh found himself in hospital with a stomach bleed from an ulcer. As he lay in bed recovering, he thought about his future. “‘You always had this vague idea that you’d retire early,’” he told himself at the time. “‘Well, I’m going to do it.’”Discharged from hospital, he gave his business partners three years’ notice. They had worked together at the General Electric Company, and after it was broken up in 1999, they launched their own training and consultancy business specialising in how to improve companies’ efficiency and outcomes.But his partners didn’t believe Walsh. “You’ll never retire,” they said. He had been a workaholic most of his life. After three years, he kept his word. He told his remaining business partner (the other had died): “I’m not doing the retirement thing where I come back for 20 days a year to get some pocket money. This is really and truly it. Only invite me back for the Christmas parties.” (He attends every year.)That was nine years ago. At first, Walsh did “all those projects around the house” that he’d ignored for 20 years. But after a while, “every day was like Groundhog Day … I thought: ‘What do I do now?’”Always one to analyse a process, he considered the prospect of ageing – he wanted to stay young as long as possible, and be supported in his later years – and moved into a retirement community, Great Alne Park in Warwickshire, run by Inspired Villages. A new world opened up. He gave talks to fellow residents on astronomy, became active in the film club – and learned to tap dance. “Retirement once had that end-of-your-life feel,” he says. “Now you’re not hanging up your boots. In this case, I was getting new ones – with taps on them.”Many people “wait till it’s too late” to move, Walsh says, but he was 62 when he did it.“There were only 25 people here. Now there are 200. I’ve seen it grow. I’ve become part of that community.”Walsh grew up in Leigh, Greater Manchester. His dad drove a lorry for the National Coal Board; his mother worked in the textile industry. “Everybody around us was working class. Everyone in the row of houses knew each other. There was closeness with your neighbours.”View image in fullscreenWalsh with fellow tappers at Great Anne Park.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianHe used to play on the slag heap behind his house, rode bicycles too fast down hills, climbed trees – and on Sunday afternoons watched musicals on TV with his sisters.“I loved watching the dancing,” he says. But he was no Billy Elliott. “I couldn’t dance at all. Trying to learn the waltz, after three steps, I’d get lost … I’ve always had a mental block. I thought of myself as not a very good dancer.”After he moved into Great Alne Park, a fellow resident and former dance teacher started a tap club. Walsh went along to give moral support. He was 67.“I thought: ‘Why don’t I overcome my mental block and keep trying?’” Soon, he was working on his shim-shams and flaps, and buying his first pair of tap shoes. When they arrived, he immediately tried them out on his kitchen tiles. “We don’t want to break people,” he says. “There’s always one foot on the floor. No big jumps.”The troupe – Pat’s Happy Tappers, named after the class teacher and fellow resident – put on shows, and have taken part in a flash mob in Stratford-on-Avon. “Before you knew it, a whole group of us were dancing.”Tapping in front of an audience is “exciting and scary”, Walsh says. He is currently learning Anything Goes from the Cole Porter musical to perform for fellow residents. “We danced it [in rehearsal] and at the end we burst out laughing. It was pretty faultless. There’s that buzz of it coming together. When we’re coordinated, we hear it. It’s not a clatter – we’re tapping in time.”Tap is a replacement for work. “I have a sense of purpose. I feel valued. I have a sense of belonging. And I’m having fun.”In some ways, the retirement community reminds him of the one he took for granted growing up, and which he lost when he moved away to university. “It’s about finding common interests and helping each other when we need help, and supporting each other through loneliness.” As a boy, he enjoyed the benefits of a longstanding community. Now, he says, he is helping to create one.Tell us: has your life taken a new direction after the age of 60?Explore more on these topicsLife and styleA new start after 60Older peopleRetirement planningRetirement ageHobbiesDancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Honor Magic V6 review: sleek foldable phone lacking a bit of polish | Android | The Guardian
description: Super-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by software
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Super-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by software
Content: Slim, light and long-lasting, the Magic V6 goes the distance while fitting a tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSlim, light and long-lasting, the Magic V6 goes the distance while fitting a tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianAndroidReviewHonor Magic V6 review: sleek foldable phone lacking a bit of polishSuper-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by softwareSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Honor’s svelteAndroidphone-tablet has been given a glow-up for its sixth version, offering a great alternative to Samsung for a fancy foldable with a red suede-like back framed in gold.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Magic V6 continues the Chinese challenger brand’s strategy of taking a razor-thin device and slapping a giant circular lump on the back to fit in top-class cameras, something others often forgo. It costs a not inconsiderable £1,500 (€1,700/A$2,999) but only until August when the price jumps to a cool £2,000 (€2,300) – a solid £300 more than last year’s model as the cost ofRAMageddon continues to bite, even at the very top end of the market.Other than a new red-backed version, the Magic V6 is almost indistinguishable from the greatV5 from last year. It is one of the thinnest and lightest foldable tablets on the market, has a great fingerprint scanner in the power button and has a proper IP68 water resistance rating matching the best slab phones, making it easy to use as a daily driver. When closed it handles just like a regular flagship Android phone with a great, crisp and smooth OLED display.View image in fullscreenThe red fabric back adds texture and grip to the Magic V6, offering something a bit different from standard glass or metal.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOnce opened, the internal screen is one of the best available, ready for all your media-watching or multitasking needs. But the crease down the middle that allows the screen to fold is slightly more noticeable than some rivals and the integrated screen film is a fingerprint magnet, so it will need cleaning regularly to make the best of it.SpecificationsMain screen:7.95in (403ppi) 120Hz OLED flexible displayCover screen:6.52in (406ppi) 120Hz OLEDProcessor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5RAM:16GBStorage:512GBOperating system:MagicOS 10 (Android 16)Camera:50MP + 50MP ultrawide + 64MP 3x tele; 2x 20MP selfieConnectivity:5G, dual sim + esim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, GNSSWater resistance:IP68/69(1.5 metres for 30 minutes)Dimensions folded:156.7 x 74.5 x 8.75-9mmDimensions unfolded:156.7 x 145.6 x 4.0-4.1mmWeight:219-224gTwo-day battery lifeView image in fullscreenA full charge takes 59 minutes using a standard 100W USB-C charger (not included) hitting 50% in 25 minutes.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Magic V6 has Qualcomm’s top Android chip for 2026, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, making it one of the best performers on the market, rivalling top slab phones such as theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.However, by default the Magic V6 uses a “balanced” battery mode, which significantly inhibits the phone’s top performance. It isn’t noticeable in day-to-day messaging and browsing but it was in games and other high-intensity tasks. Switching the phone to its “performance” battery mode significantly improved things at the expense of heat and battery life.The Honor has a very large battery compared with most foldable phone rivals, which helps it last almost two full days between charges while actively using a mixture of the screens for more than eight hours for general browsing, messaging, work and media consumption. Playing games drains the battery a bit faster but the Magic V6 should outlast even the heaviest of usage days.MagicOS 10 software still needs workView image in fullscreenUp to three apps can be used in split-screen, including the ability to push one mostly off the screen for maximising useful space.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe phone runs Honor’s version of last year’s Android 16,MagicOS 10, which means it isn’t as up to date as some rivals runningAndroid 17. Honor will provide seven years of Android version and security updates for devices sold within Europe.MagicOS has improved since last year. It looks quite nice, has plenty of customisation options and tools for making the most of the folding screen, including the excellent ability to split-screen three apps beyond the bounds of the physical display,which was introduced last year.Various AI tools are strewn throughout the operating system, including Google’s Gemini, which you can set to open in split-screen next to whatever app you are using at the time by quickly flexing the tablet. Many of the tools work as shortcuts for performing tasks such as saving screenshots, editing photos and changing settings on your phone.The “AI button” is meant to launch actions such as turning on the torch or opening an AI tool by double-tapping, though not depressing, the power button, but it doesn’t work. There are various other parts of the operating system that are unpolished. A bug prevents Google’s Chrome browser from opening in split-screen. Apps that are out of date are described as having a “low version” by Honor’s App Market, which also insists on trying to update apps installed from Google Play, bringing the two app stores into conflict. The Honor lacks the ability to have a different home screen layout for the inside and outside screens, and messaging apps such as WhatsApp routinely insist on opening as small floating windows if you tap a message notification, even on the outside screen.These little niggles could be overlooked on a significantly cheaper phone, but not on a £1,500-£2,000 device. You can and should expect better.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app is easy to use and has most of the tools you would want. You can shoot with the Magic V6 open or closed.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe enormous circular bump on the back houses three cameras, with a 20MP selfie camera in each of the two screens for a total of five cameras.The cameras have changed little since last year’s V5 and perform very similarly. The main 50MP camera shoots great photos at 12MP as standard with good detail and range with its cropped 2x zoom, though it can notably suffer frommoiréon stripped textures. The 50MP ultra wide camera has been improved since the V5, solving some of thedistortion problems. The 64MP 3x telephoto is the best of the bunch, capturing excellent detail, even with its 2x crop zoom for an effective 6x magnification. Its digital zoom remains good to 30x before becoming obviously blown up.Low light photography is pretty good across all the lenses, while the camera app has tons of features, including many AI tools and a good manual mode for more creative photography. The Magic V6 shoots decent video up to 4K at 60 frames a second and can be used in various partly folded orientations.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe Magic V6 is easy to use like a regular medium-sized slab phone when closed.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery will maintainat least 80% capacity after 1,200 full-charge cycles. The phone is generally repairable and Honorpublishes pricing for spare parts, including £609 for an internal screen and £152 for the external screen, plus labour and shipping. Honor offers a free screen repair (Care+) for 24 months if bought before 2 August.The device contains limited recycled materials, which Honor breaks down in the phone’senvironmental impact report. The company offerstrade-inandrefurbished products.PriceThe Honor Magic V6 has an introductory price of£1,499.99(€1,699.90/A$2,999), which will increase to £1,999.99 (€2,299.90) from August 2026 in some regions.For comparison, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs£1,899and theGoogle Pixel 10 Pro Foldcosts£1,749.VerdictThe Magic V6 is another very attractive book-style foldable from Honor, but it fails to move things on from last year in an increasingly competitive category.It has really great battery life, matching some of the best slab phones. The outside screen is great, while the inside screen is good but has a more visible crease than some recent rivals. The Magic V6 feels particularly good when used as a phone, while the massive bump fits in some great cameras and means it doesn’t rock around on a table like some others.But it is the software that continues to let Honor down. It just isn’t as up to date or polished as it needs to be on a device this expensive.As good as the Magic V6 is, it lacks a compelling reason to buy it over more complete rivals from Samsung, Google and others.Pros:slim, light, just like a normal phone when closed, great performance, very long battery life, good internal screen, decent camera, good fingerprint scanner, IP68/9 water and dust resistance rating.Cons:very expensive, software not as refined as needed, more fragile than a regular device, costly to repair, not much of an upgrade on previous model.View image in fullscreenThe Magic V6 is about as thin and svelte as a regular flagship Android phone, complete with huge camera cluster on the back.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsAndroidTablet computersMobile phonesSmartphonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Impossible things are possible’: the murals celebrating lives beyond homelessness | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: St Mungo’s project aims to challenge stereotypes by narrating stories of people supported out of rough sleeping
Author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
Headline: St Mungo’s project aims to challenge stereotypes by narrating stories of people supported out of rough sleeping
Content: Lee, one of the St Mungo’s case studies and a former rough sleeper, at his dedicated mural in Bethnal Green, London.Photograph: St MungoView image in fullscreenLee, one of the St Mungo’s case studies and a former rough sleeper, at his dedicated mural in Bethnal Green, London.Photograph: St MungoHomelessness‘Impossible things are possible’: the murals celebrating lives beyond homelessnessSt Mungo’s project aims to challenge stereotypes by narrating stories of people supported out of rough sleepingRosie Peters-McDonaldMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his days of rough sleeping, Lee, 54, recalls the nights that were so cold it hurt. Having lived in North America for several years – including a year spent sleeping rough in Canada – he returned home toLondonfor mental health support, hoping the NHS would be able to help. Instead, he ended up homeless.On his first night on the streets of London, a St Mungo’s outreach worker came across him. He was taken to A&E to await help in the warm and, in the middle of the night, he got a call. “I’m outside,” a St Mungo’s team member told him. Knowing that help was there, he says, was when things started to change.Lee now volunteers for St Mungo’s and runs creative writing classes. On Tuesday, a mural, commissioned by the charity, went on display in Bethnal Green. It brings his story to life in a series of graffiti-style words and motifs. Musical notes, a shamrock and a key feature alongside words such as “see me” and “creativity”. The focal point of the mural is three huge words: Lee was here.It is one of three murals installed across east London,Readingand Bristol, all of which spotlight former rough sleepers – Lee, Tamika, Ray and Lawretta – in the places where St Mungo’s supported them out of homelessness. Each integrates a QR code that allows passersby to listen to the narrated stories of those featured.View image in fullscreen‘This is a really beautiful way to get the message out there’: Luke Embden next to the mural dedicated to Ray.Photograph: Richard Dawson/PA“I wanted to give these case studies a voice,” the mural artist, Luke Embden, says. “A lot of people don’t know where to turn and this is a really beautiful way to get the message out there.” Embden met Lee in Bethnal Green after finishing the mural and recalls how touched he was at seeing his life recreated through art.View image in fullscreenThe murals contain QR codes that link to narrated stories of the people featured.Photograph: Richard Dawson/PAIn the UK, rough sleeping numbers have risen to 4,793,the highest on record. The charity says 77% of the people it helped off the streets last year were not seen to have returned to rough sleeping. The project aims to push back on stereotypes and misconceptions about rough sleepers, focusing on their personalities and journeys instead of their hardships.Emma Haddad, the chief executive of St Mungo’s, says she wants the murals to encourage people not to ignore homelessness: “They’re asking people to stop and look and listen,” she says. “Recovery is possible, hope is possible, and support plays a fundamental role in that.”Haddad argues that raising awareness through campaigns such as this one is especially important in the summer, when the UK’s increasingly frequent heatwaves exacerbate the “life-threatening” dangers of living on the streets.The crisis was thrust into the national consciousness last Monday, when Andy Burnham used his first address as prime ministerto promise to end rough sleeping. According to the new government, an additional £340m will be put towards the policy. The timing of the announcement could not have been more apt for St Mungo’s, which launched the installations the next morning.“He could have talked about anything, but he chose rough sleeping,” said Haddad. “He gets it, and he knows that it’s an absolute scandal.”Lee says he feels the problem of homelessness is in good hands given the prime minister’s record as mayor of Greater Manchester. In 2020, he vowed to end rough sleeping in the city and, under his leadership, the number dropped from 268 in 2017 to 90 in 2021. In 2025, however,the Manchester Mill reportedrough sleeping had increased again, to 197.View image in fullscreenThe mural dedicated to Tamika in Reading.Photograph: Richard Dawson/PA“Completely eliminating rough sleeping seems like a massive and impossible task but, as people, we should set ourselves these kinds of goals,” says Lee.“Impossible things are possible. How we treat the weakest, the most vulnerable members of our society, people who are literally overlooked, does demonstrate who we are at our heart as a people.”The installations can be found on Bethnal Green Road, London (until 30 July),Stokes Croft, Bristol(until 27 July) andKing Street, Reading(until 29 July).Explore more on these topicsHomelessnessPovertyCommunitiesLondonBristolReadingSocial exclusionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Ukraine and Sudan to Gaza: why have hospitals become a target of war? | Global development | The Guardian
description: International law states only military sites can be targeted during conflicts, but this is routinely being ignored
Author: Liz Cookman
Headline: International law states only military sites can be targeted during conflicts, but this is routinely being ignored
Content: Ambulance in Kherson hit by Russian drone. Both passengers survived with injuries.Rights and freedomGlobal developmentFrom Ukraine and Sudan to Gaza: why have hospitals become a target of war?International law states only military sites can be targeted during conflicts, but this is routinely being ignoredSupported byAbout this contentLiz CookmanMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwice every day, Liubov Martynenko leaves the underground maternity ward where she works in Kherson and travels by ambulance to collect meals from another hospital in the Ukrainian city’s “red zone”, close to the Dnipro River and the Russian forces on the other side.On 4 June , just before midday, the vehicle entered the grounds of Luchansky city clinical hospital as usual, but Martynenko, who also works as a midwife, heard a strange sound in the air. “It’s flying!” the driver screamed, as she realised there was a drone nearby.“It was so close, just a couple of metres away, a flying box with a black eye,” she told the Guardian this week.The driver reversed sharply and it shot towards them, crashing into the side of the ambulance and exploding. Confused by the impact of the blast, Martynenko ran into a nearby clinic shouting that the driver had been killed. Both survived, however, receiving treatment for minor shrapnel wounds and concussion.Have attacks on hospitals become a weapon of war? - videoThe vehicle, a donation from Italy, was clearly marked “ambulanza” and with a red cross on the roof – the internationally recognised legal symbol of protection and neutrality. Martynenko was wearing a red flak jacket, often worn by frontline medical workers to identify them.“If it weren’t for the driver’s quick reactions, the drone would have hit the front of the vehicle and we probably would have died,” she says. “The Russian operators attacked precisely on the hospital grounds – and it’s not the first time it has been hit, either.”The incident is part of a growing pattern of attacks on medical workers and health infrastructure in conflict zones. From Sudan to Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Afghanistan, such incidents have more than doubled globally since 2021.Fuelled by the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and Israel’s war in Gaza in 2023, figures peaked in 2024 but have remained at a historic high, withmore than 2,500documented incidents last year across 33 countries, according to the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition.Bar chart showing countries with most attacks on healthcare personnel, with Palestine, Lebanon and Ukraine far ahead of Sudan in fourth placeSince Israel began a new offensive in Lebanon in March, there have been 247 incidents affecting healthcare and 148 health workers killed in the country, despite repeated ceasefires, according toSafeguarding Health In Conflict. Three hospitals were hit insouthern Lebanon in just one weeklast month, with medical workers making up most of the 150 wounded.Under international law, hospitals, healthcare workers and wounded people are afforded special protection. It was a founding principle of the first Geneva convention in 1864 and was reaffirmed 10 years ago when the UN security council adopted a resolutioncondemning such attacks.In practice, however, those protections are steadily being eroded. Healthcare attacks have become so common that state actors are now regarded as routinely using them as a weapon of war by some experts.“If you can’t even protect hospitals, the first line of humanitarian protections, then it will lead to the breakdown of all international law,” says Rohini Haar, an emergency doctor who lectures on human rights at the University of California, Berkeley. “I believe we are seeing that.”Last year, the Guardianvisited three frontline maternity hospitalsin Kharkiv, Sloviansk and Kherson – the ward where Martynenko works – where women were forced to give birth in basements as drones circled overhead and explosions boomed nearby.For the last few years, the vast majority of attacks have been carried out by state actors, which increasingly invoke “dual-use” claims to justify the assaults. Two of the worst offenders, Russia and Israel, argue that hospitals are used for military purposes, yet disclose little evidence publicly to back their claims.Lawyers say the “dual-use” loophole does not legitimise these attacks, however, because international law requires that a target be verified as a military objective, that any harm is proportionate, and that advance evacuation warnings are given.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, there has never been a standalone conviction for a healthcare attack in international courts. They have only appeared as part of broader war crimes charges, such as those brought against the Bosnian Serb commanders Stanislav Galić and Dragomir Milošević over thesiege of Sarajevo.It fits a wider pattern of a lack of enforcement for war crimes, allowing states and armed groups to act with near impunity.The nature of warfare has changed too. Drones and long-range airstrikes are pounding cities and changing the idea of a defined battlefield, with military targets redefined as anything that might help to sustain the capability of a force.Map showing countries with most attacks on healthcare facilities, with Palestine and Ukraine far outnumbering other countriesThe cost of these attacks is devastating for civilian populations. A cascade of preventable deaths often follow because of the lack of emergency care and disruptions to routine care, and because people stop visiting hospitals out of fear. It leads to unassisted childbirths, surges in preventable sickness and outbreaks of disease as vaccinations are halted.The fallout can last for decades, medical experts warn, especially when trained staff are killed.‘Russia is targeting us deliberately’: how attacks on maternity hospitals fuelled a birth-rate crisis in UkraineRead moreLiz Harding, a humanitarian representative at Médecins Sans Frontières, says: “Humanitarians and hospitals now almost have to justify why we shouldn’t be targeted rather than those launching the attacks having to explain themselves.”After two weeks off, Martynenko is back at work, collecting meals from Luchansky for the patients on the maternity ward twice a day, but always in fear. CCTV footage of the attack appears to show the ambulance was struck little more than a metre away from the crater left by a previous explosion.“I am scared to go to work after the attack, especially when I hear any kind of buzzing noise,” she says. “I have to do my job though.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRights and freedomUkraineEuropeGlobal healthHuman rights (Law)Human rights (Global development)Drones (military)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger  | Global development | The Guardian
description: Government move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutrition
Author: Samuel Okiror
Headline: Government move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutrition
Content: Food distribution under way at Potome primary school, Lodiko, watched by Sam Engola, Uganda’s minister for disaster preparedness.Photograph: Prime minister's office, UgandaView image in fullscreenFood distribution under way at Potome primary school, Lodiko, watched by Sam Engola, Uganda’s minister for disaster preparedness.Photograph: Prime minister's office, UgandaAid cutsGlobal developmentUganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hungerGovernment move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutritionSupported byAbout this contentSamuel OkirorMon 27 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUganda has launchedemergency food relief distributionafterat least 19 deathsfrom hunger were reported in an area of prolonged drought in the east of the country.A crisis has been building in the Karamoja region ofUgandaas crops have failed without the season’s expected rains, leaving the region’s 1.5 million people facing acute food shortages and rising malnutrition.TheFamine Early Warning Systems Network(Fews Net), a global mapping network designed to raise the alert on food security, reported the situation haddeteriorated to a crisisacross Karamoja.In the first large-scale operation of its kind organised by the Ugandan government after the funding void left by aid cuts, authorities announced plans to distribute 9,400 tonnes of relief food over the next two months. The supplies were procured using a 45bn-shilling (£9m) emergency funding allocation, approved by parliament.Sam Engola, minister for disaster preparedness and refugees, launched the aid distribution efforts at a primary school in Lodiko sub-county in Kaabong district on Wednesday.“The president does not want to hear of anyone in Karamoja dying of hunger. I am here to supervise the distribution of this food to the end. I will ensure that everyone receives food. No one will be left behind,” Engola said.View image in fullscreenSam Engola, with the labour minister, Davinia Esther Anyakun, and minister for Karamoja affairs, John Baptist Lokii, at a school in Lodiki.Photograph: Prime minister's office, UgandaKaramoja is experiencing its most severe dry spell in years. Farmers have lost crops since the last meaningful rainfall was recorded in April – the beginning of the planting season.Angelina Nakiru, a 21-year-old mother of two in Rupa, about 5 miles from Moroto town in Karamoja, said she was struggling to feed her children after all her crops failed. Now she goes early each morning to join other women at a small-scale grinding mill where machines are used to crush rock into powder to wash out gold-bearing ore. The pay is meagre.“The work is dusty and exhausting, but it is the only way I can earn money to buy a cup of maize and beans to feed the children,” Nakiru said.“If I don’t, the children will sleep hungry. Other days when I fail to get the meagre income from the mill, we go to bed on empty stomachs,” she said.“The situation is terrible. People are starving and dying due to hunger. The government must come to the rescue of the people.”Health facilities report treating hundreds of children for severe malnutrition. Anutrition reportpublished in June found nearly half of the population in Karamoja’s Kaabong and Kotido districts in a crisis situation.Experts attribute the region’s recurring food insecurity and vulnerability to climate crisis shocks, environmental degradation such as deforestation and overgrazing, as well as poverty and low agricultural productivity.In 2022, a devastating hunger crisis claimedmore than 2,200 lives, according to figures from Uganda’s human rights commission body.While emergency food aid is expected to provide short-term relief, the government said it remained committed to implementing long-term remedial measures with the recently approved Karamoja regional development plan, which is intended to strengthen communities’ resilience to drought.John Baptist Lokii, minister for Karamoja, said: “The government will provide drought-resistant, disease-resistant and early-maturing seeds ahead of the next planting season.”Agnes Kirabo, executive directorof Uganda’sFood Rights Alliance (FRA), said the government was taking the lead on distribution as a necessity as much as a policy choice as the landscape of humanitarian aid had changed dramatically.Following significant funding cuts, most notably from USAID, which previously had an annual budget of about $42.8bn (£32.bn), agencies such as the World Food Programme (WFP) have been forced to drastically scale back their aid.In Uganda, the WFP has phased out food assistance for 63% of the refugee population, cutting off more than 1 million people from aid, and reducing rations to just 663,000 recipients.View image in fullscreenKaramoja residents collecting food at the distribution centre.Photograph: PM's office, Uganda“This transition should not be viewed solely as a reaction to aid cuts, but also as a positive shift towards nationally owned, sustainable development. Government leadership is a constructive move, provided it is part of a long-term strategy to establish durable national systems,” said Kirabo.“Emergency food distribution is a life-saving measure, not a permanent solution. To break this cycle, we must address the root causes of food insecurity through structural reforms.”The FRA, Kirabo said, wanted access to food to be made a fundamental human right and the government to turn its attention to water infrastructure and climate resilience. “Karamoja possesses adequate rainfall and water routes to achieve food self-sufficiency, but requires the political will to strategically invest in water infrastructure for production,” she said.“Ultimately, the Karamoja hunger crisis is a governance crisis. The government’s leadership in this emergency is welcome, but it must be matched by the political will to implement the systemic changes required to permanently protect the people of Karamoja and Uganda from predictable, preventable hunger.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentAid cutsUgandaHungerAfricaYoweri MuseveniDroughtWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Pinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years ago | Chile | The Guardian
description: Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile
Author: John Bartlett
Headline: Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile
Content: Víctor Jara was arrested and killed by soldiers in the coup that brought the rightwing dictator Augusto Pinochet to power in Chile in 1973.Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/APView image in fullscreenVíctor Jara was arrested and killed by soldiers in the coup that brought the rightwing dictator Augusto Pinochet to power in Chile in 1973.Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/APChilePinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years agoNelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in ChileJohn Bartlettin SantiagoMon 27 Jul 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singerVíctor Jara, the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice.Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man.Chilean police announced on Saturday that Haase Mazzei had been arrested in Puyehue, in the rural south of the country, with a judge ordering his immediate imprisonment.The Víctor Jara Foundation, set up by his widow, the British dancer and activist Joan Jara, said in statement: “We learned that retired Colonel Nelson Haase Mazzei, who had been a fugitive from justice since 2023, was found and imprisoned. We welcome this news.“However, it is important for us to emphasize that, half a century after the murders of Víctor Jara and Littré Quiroga, it is difficult to see this as this justice.”Jara, a singer and leftwing activist, was arrested in Santiago, the capital of Chile, on 11 September 1973, the day afterGen Augusto Pinochet’s bloody US-backed coupto depose the socialist president, Salvador Allende.View image in fullscreenVíctor Jara’s widow, Joan, who died in 2023, was a British dancer and activist who set up a foundation in her late husband’s name.Photograph: Roberto Candia/APJara was held along with thousands of others at a small covered stadium in central Santiago. Four days later, he was murdered in the changing rooms alongside Allende’s national director of prisons, Littré Quiroga.Haase Mazzei’s arrest is likely to be the final act in the long quest for justice on behalf of Jara, one of the most recognisable victims of the Pinochet dictatorship, which killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people and detained and tortured tens of thousands during 17 years of repressive rule.At the stadium, Jara was tortured and humiliated by officers who played Russian roulette with him before breaking his hands, shattering his skull, and riddling him with automatic gunfire.His body was found dumped near the main cemetery in Santiago with 44 bullet wounds and 56 broken bones. He was 40 years old. The body of Quiroga, who had been shot 23 times, was found at the same time.After evading justice for nearly half a century, seven retired soldiers were found guilty of the murder and sentenced in absentia to varying jail terms in August 2023. Haase Mazzei received a 25-year sentence.He claimed for years that he was not at the stadium, since renamed Estadio Víctor Jara, but sworn testimony placed him at the scene.Haase Mazzei joined the Chilean army’s notorious Tejas Verde brigade in 1972, and was later part of Pinochet’s secret police, the Dirección Nacional de Inteligencia (Dina), where he worked closely with its leader, Manuel Contreras, a renowned regime loyalist who was sentenced to more than 500 years’ jail time for crimes against humanity before his death in 2015.View image in fullscreenPedro Barrientos being deported from the US to Chile in 2023.Photograph: Policia de Investigaciones de Chile/ReutersSentenced alongside Haase Mazzei was 86-year-old Hernán Chacón. When police arrived to arrest him at his home in a wealthy district of Santiago in 2023, he asked officers for a moment to take his medication, before slipping off into a side room and taking his own life.Another Tejas Verde officer sentenced for the killing was Pedro Barrientos, who left Chile for the US in 1989 and wasdeported back in December 2023, more than a decade after his extradition was first sought.One former soldier testified that Barrientos had the habit of brandishing his pistol and declaring: “I killed Víctor Jara with this!”Barrientos was eventually arrested in the US after a routine traffic stop, and lost his US citizenship not because of his crimes, but on the grounds that he had failed to disclose his military background in his application.Jara’s widow died at the age of 96, just weeks before Barrientos was returned to Chile to face justice.Haase Mazzei’s defence has already requested his transfer from a prison in the southern city of Osorno to Punta Peuco, a well-appointed jail north of Santiago, built to house the human rights criminals of the Pinochet era.Explore more on these topicsChileAugusto PinochetAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shots fired near US consulate in Canada for second time in four months  | Toronto | The Guardian
description: No one was injured and no suspects have been identified in connection to shooting near Toronto compound, police say
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: No one was injured and no suspects have been identified in connection to shooting near Toronto compound, police say
