Content: Police work the scene of an early morning shooting outside the US consulate in Toronto on 27 July 2026.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice work the scene of an early morning shooting outside the US consulate in Toronto on 27 July 2026.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockTorontoShots fired near US consulate in Canada for second time in four monthsNo one was injured and no suspects have been identified in connection to shooting near Toronto compound, police sayAgence France-Press in MontrealMon 27 Jul 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShots were fired near the US consulate inTorontoearly on Monday but no one was injured in the second shooting near the diplomatic compound in four months.“Officers heard a firearm being discharged in the area,” and “a white sedan was seen fleeing the scene”, Toronto police said on X.The area was cordoned off and shell casings were found. No one was injured and no suspects have been identified, police said.The US consulate thanked the police for their response to Monday’s shooting.Toronto police link dozens of shootings to ‘multilayered’ gun-for-hire networkRead moreOn 10 March,two men fired shots at the consulate in what police described as a “national security incident”,prompting beefed-up protection for the US and Israeli diplomatic buildings in the Canadian city, as war gripped the Middle East.Two men, aged 18 and 19, were arrested in June as part of the investigation into that shooting. Police said the men were recruited to carry out violent acts but did not provide further details.Police also said they were investigating shootings with a recurring and similar modus operandi, such as the shooting at a Toronto synagogue on 2 March.More details soon …Explore more on these topicsTorontoCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Off-duty police officer detains man who attacked three women with knives in Paris | Paris | The Guardian
description: Two women severely wounded before bystanders intervened in incident near Porte de Clichy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two women severely wounded before bystanders intervened in incident near Porte de Clichy
Content: Investigators at the site of the incident near Porte de Clichy in Paris.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenInvestigators at the site of the incident near Porte de Clichy in Paris.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersParisOff-duty police officer detains man who attacked three women with knives in ParisTwo women severely wounded before bystanders intervened in incident near Porte de ClichyReuters in ParisMon 27 Jul 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 07.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man attacked three women with knives in Paris before bystanders pinned him to the ground and an off-duty police officer detained him, the French interior ⁠minister, Laurent Nuñez, has said.The man attacked the three women, aged 19, 24 and 36, with ⁠two kitchen knives, severely wounding two of them, near Porte de Clichy on Monday, Nuñez said.A video shared on Snapchat ​and verified by Reuters showed a man ‌with long black ‌hair and wearing a cream tracksuit wielding one big knife in each hand and ‌attempting to attack and stab a young woman. It was unclear if the woman was injured.Mohamed-Ali Bouhadjar, 26, who filmed the video and posted it on Snapchat, told Reuters: “When I saw him stab a woman in the back, I started shouting: ‘Come on, let’s stop him.’ Several people stepped in.“One person threw a suitcase ‌at him. He dropped the knives. At that moment I grabbed him, swept his legs out from under him, and we pinned him ​to the ground.”Another part of the video shows the same man in a tracksuit lying on the ground immobilised by bystanders, while the two knives are seen lying nearby on a pedestrian crossing.“It is Allah who commanded me,” the man ⁠lying on the floor says in the video.Nuñez said the man was detained ​by an off-duty police officer. “I ​pay tribute to him, it ​was a courageous act,” he added.Nuñez said earlier that the motive for the attack was unknown and police could ​not verify the ​identity of the attacker, whose declarations were “incoherent” while he was being arrested.The French national anti-terrorist prosecutor’s office said it was considering whether to open an investigation.Explore more on these topicsParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It felt like being in a disaster movie’: uncertainty after evacuation from France’s Gironde wildfire | France | The Guardian
description: Residents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blaze
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Residents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blaze
Content: Evacuees at the exhibition centre in Bordeaux.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersView image in fullscreenEvacuees at the exhibition centre in Bordeaux.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersFrance‘It felt like being in a disaster movie’: uncertainty after evacuation from France’s Gironde wildfireResidents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blazeAngelique Chrisafisin BordeauxMon 27 Jul 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSitting in their suburban apartment in Mérignac on the outskirts of Bordeaux, Krishma, an interpreter, and her husband, Nassir, first felt a sense of dread when a strange black cloud turned the sky dark in the middle of the day. Then a bitter burning smell filled the air outside.“The sky changed colour. It seemed like a cloud but it was smoke covering the sun – it wasn’t a natural phenomenon. It didn’t seem real,” said Nassir, an English literature graduate from Kabul who has been living inFrancefor seven years. “We couldn’t breathe easily, you could feel it in your lungs.”The acrid smell, which at first seemed like burning rubber then unmistakably like wood smoke, was blowing on the wind from themassive wildfire in Girondein south-western France. The blaze has torn through 42,000 hectares, an area four times the size of Paris, causing one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war. The government said on Monday that although the fire had stopped growing, it was still blazing and a new heatwave this week could make it harder to fight.Nassir and Krishma had slept at the exhibition centre for three nights and did not know when they would be allowed home.Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The GuardianAs authorities carried out one of the biggest evacuations in modern French history, Krishma and Nassir were among 220,000 people ordered to flee their homes in Gironde. Many people were evacuated from wooded areas directly hit by fire, where at least 240 homes were destroyed. But in an unprecedented move, tens of thousands more were ordered by police to evacuate from more built-up, urban streets as the fire reached 9 miles (15km) from the outer edge of Bordeaux’s vast suburban area.Krishma and Nassir had to evacuate their suburban street at midnight on Friday. With their two children aged 10 and eight, they quickly packed toothbrushes, toys, one change of clothes and personal documents into their car. On Monday afternoon, they were sitting on camp beds among hundreds of people sheltering in a hangar at Bordeaux’s exhibition centre. They had slept there for three nights and did not know when they would be allowed home. The fire had not reached their residential area, but with the French government warning that the blaze was “extremely intense and unpredictable”, authorities would not yet allow a return, they said.View image in fullscreenA woman and her dog at the emergency shelter.Photograph: Caroline Blumberg/APThe couple’s main feeling was great sadness to see the Gironde forest destroyed. Krishma said: “When we were in Afghanistan there were lots of explosions, suicide attacks, but that was related to around 30 years of war. When we came here, we never thought there would be a situation like this. It brought us back to the bad memories from our past.”What is a ‘fire cloud’, and how have they worsened wildfires in Europe?Read moreAcross the vast hangar, Yves, who used to work on road maintenance in Bordeaux, was sitting with his 13-year-old mastiff dog, Ichka. Yves had fled his suburban house and garden in Le Haillan outside Bordeaux with his dog’s bed under one arm and had carefully laid it out next to his camp bed. He had been ordered to evacuate in the early hours of Saturday morning.11:13Race against time to contain wildfires in France and Spain - The Latest“We had to leave because of the smoke,” he said. His wife, an administrator who did not want to be named, said she still felt shaken. “It was terrifying – you would look up at the sky and it was completely orange, even after nightfall. It was bizarre. The fire was causing that, and it really made you anxious. I feel quite a lot of anger that all this forest has burned and been lost. Seeing all that is beautiful in nature just go up in smoke is extremely painful and sad.”View image in fullscreenA firefighter watches the flames of a forest fire  in Saint-Jean-d'Illac near Bordeaux.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesOthers who had fled slept in their cars. Loïc, 66, a widower who worked in the metals and glass industries before becoming a decorator, had to leave his house in Saint-Jean-d’Illac outside Bordeaux. “I had been watching this strange fog in the sky. It was a darkness almost like an eclipse,” he said. “There was a kind of ochre mist as light from the sun was diffused through falling ash. So much ash was falling that my car was turned completely grey.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA wildfire in Saint-Jean d’Illac, in the Gironde region.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersAt 1am on Saturday, Loïc was woken by banging on the door from his neighbour, a fire officer, saying he had to leave immediately. He grabbed only his wallet and car keys and ran to the car, leaving his mobile phone behind. There were so many people on the road and heading to the evacuation centre that he decided to stop elsewhere and get a bit of sleep in his car.When he woke on Saturday, listening to the news on the car radio, he knew he could not go home and headed instead for central Bordeaux, thinking the cinema would be a safe and comfortable place. “I watched the two-part Charles de Gaulle epic – the wrong way round, with the second film first, but I knew the story already – then I watched The Odyssey. Then I went back to sleep in my car.”The next day, he visited the graveyard where his wife was buried. On Monday morning, he arrived at the Bordeaux evacuation centre to get information on what to do next. He felt deeply saddened by the loss of the forest. “My generation grew up really attached to nature,” he said.View image in fullscreenA firefighter helps to battle the wildfires.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersFlorence, a former teaching assistant in a primary school, sat on a camp bed with her two cats in their travelling cases after having to evacuate Le Haillan outside Bordeaux. “I was distraught,” she said. “I’m asthmatic, I put tape around the windows of my apartment but I could still smell the smoke which was seeping in under my front door, so I put down wet rags. The sky was orange and grey, and there was soot everywhere.”She said having to suddenly evacuate knowing a fire was raging in Gironde felt like something out of a war. “It felt like being in a disaster movie,” she said. “I’ve always really loved disaster movies – but now I feel like I’ve actually been in one, so I don’t ever want to watch a disaster movie again.”View image in fullscreenFire rages in Saint-Jean-d’Illac, some 30km from Bordeaux.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsFranceWildfiresEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I knew what he had done to those boys’: murderer to stay in jail after journalist’s fight for justice | UK news | The Guardian
description: Gibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990s
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Gibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990s
Content: Grimson has been found guilty of a string of sexual offences. He had been nearing release after being jailed in 2001 for two murders.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenGrimson has been found guilty of a string of sexual offences. He had been nearing release after being jailed in 2001 for two murders.Photograph: PAUK news‘I knew what he had done to those boys’: murderer to stay in jail after journalist’s fight for justiceGibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990sSteven MorrisMon 27 Jul 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRos Astengo, a journalist based in Gibraltar who usually focuses on politics and social issues, had qualms when she began investigating the case of the suspected serial killer Allan Grimson as he neared release from prison after serving more than 20 years.She worried that she might reopen the scars of survivors of Grimson – but also that she could be putting herself in the “crosshairs” of a dangerous man who had sexually assaulted and battered two young men to death in the late 1990s when he was a Royal Navy petty officer.“But the public interest overrode it,” Astengo said. “It would have been so easy for me to have just done nothing. But I thought to myself, how would I feel if as soon as they let him out he reoffended and harmed another young man. My motive was to keep the public safe.”Because of Astengo’s work,four men came forward to report sexual assaults by Grimsoncarried out on them in the same era as the two murders.On Monday, a jury at Winchester crown court found Grimson guilty of 13 sexual offences relating to the men, which may mean he remains in prison for years to come.Judge Dugdale told Grimson he was an extremely dangerous man in the 1990s and asked for reports to be prepared to help him understand if he still posed a serious risk.The judge also asked for victim personal statements to be taken from the men. He thanked the jury for hearing a “very unusual case” and invited them to return to court when he sentenced Grimson in November.View image in fullscreenRos Astengo: ‘For me, it was about justice and to prevent a serial offender from being released.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“The men were incredibly brave to come to court, bring all this back into their lives,” Astengo said.Grimson was jailed for life in 2001 and told he would serve at least 22 years in prison for sexually abusing and murdering Nicholas Wright, 18, and Sion Jenkins, 20, in Portsmouth, both of whom had served in the navy. The sentencing judge described him as a“serial killer in nature if not by number”.At the time, Grimson also admitted in police interviews sexual offences or contact with another four men – three young sailors and a teenage boy. He said he had thought of killing two of them but the Crown Prosecution Service did not pursue the allegations because he was going to serve a long jail term for the murders anyway.While in prison Grimson was on best behaviour in the hope that he would be released after serving his 22 years and in November 2020the Parole Boardrecommended he be moved to an open prison to prepare him for freedom.At this time, Astengo was covering the search for the body of another sailor, Simon Parkes, who vanished in Gibraltar in 1986. Grimson was in the British overseas territory at the time. He has long been a suspect but denies involvement.View image in fullscreenSimon Parkes vanished in Gibraltar in 1986.Photograph: PANo remains were found and Astengo said she was deeply moved when Parkes’s elderly parents, Margaret and David, from south-west England,described itas their last chance to get justice. “It was a very lonely journey for them.” She promised themshe would write a bookabout their son’s case to keep his memory alive.She began her research and was disturbed to find he had made admissions over the four boys and young men but no action had been taken.“I was astonished that he was never charged over them,” Astengo said. She was alarmed that Grimson seemed close to being released. “I knew what he had done to those boys. That really worried me. How could he be fully rehabilitated? I was worried he would go back into the community thinking he’s gotten away with it. I realised I was putting myself in the crosshairs of a killer but I thought something needed to be done.”Astengo tracked down one of the four and travelled to the UK to speak to him. “I found a very angry man who was still hurt, angry and upset that he had never seen justice. He started talking about the fact that he was older now and a parent. He understands today what he didn’t back then – that was that he was groomed.”Astengo told the man he could file a fresh complaint about Grimson. “I said to him, think very carefully about what you’re doing because you are going to open a can of worms for yourself.”The man went ahead and spoke to police. Initially no action was taken so Astengo contacted thechild sexual abuse review panel, which examines allegations of non-recent child sexual offences.Nicholas Wright.Photograph: PAIt agreed that the case was worth re-examining. Detectives interviewed the man and tracked down the three others. In February 2025, Grimson was charged over the attacks on the four.The month-long trial highlighted how far the justice system had come in dealing with sexual crimes.In the late 1990s and early 2000s it was not uncommon for serious sexual allegations not to be pursued if a defendant faced a long jail sentence for even more serious crimes. Now it is considered the state’s duty to do so.View image in fullscreenSion Jenkins.Photograph: PAIt is also a reminder that until the turn of the century, gay people were not allowed to serve openly in the armed forces, meaning some of those assaulted by Grimson were keen not to talk about what had happened back then because they feared dismissal.In court, Grimson’s legal team tried to argue that it was unfair for him to be charged with offences that the authorities had not pursued a quarter of a century ago. They made it clearhe felt he was being prosecuted now as a tactic for keeping him in prison, to “stymie” his parole.His legal team also criticised Astengo, suggesting she had been motivated by making money from her book, which is due to come out next year.John Price KC, prosecuting, urged the jury to ignore “conspiracy theories” about Astengo’s involvement and said good was achieved by energetic journalists.Astengo said it was not about money. Every time she travelled to the UK she has had to pay her own way, take leave – and could make very little, if anything, from her book. She said: “The defence tried to paint me as somebody who has exerted undue influence all because I’m writing a book. For me, it was about justice and to prevent a serial offender from being released.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsGibraltarRape and sexual assaultCrimeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mayo beat 75-year-old ‘curse’ to become Gaelic football champions | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Team to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeats
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Team to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeats
Content: Fans celebrate outside Croke park stadium after Mayo beat Kerry in the 138th all-Ireland final.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAView image in fullscreenFans celebrate outside Croke park stadium after Mayo beat Kerry in the 138th all-Ireland final.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAIrelandMayo beat 75-year-old ‘curse’ to become Gaelic football championsTeam to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeatsRory CarrollIreland correspondentMon 27 Jul 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 14.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe hex is broken, dispelled, banished, and a story that bewitchedIrelandfor decades has ended in fairytale: Mayo are all-Ireland champions.Seventy-five years after a supposed curse condemned its Gaelic men’s football team toendless defeat, the county prevailed and uncorked a wave of emotion that engulfed even its rivals.The team will return to the west ofIrelandfor a euphoric homecoming on Monday evening after winning the senior football championship, a victory that thrilled Ireland and Mayo’s diaspora, including Joe Biden, Mark Carney and Noel and Liam Gallagher.View image in fullscreenMost pundits favoured Kerry to win but there were jubilant scenes when underdogs Mayo triumphed in Dublin instead.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PA“Mayo 1-20, Kerry 1-17. Chisel it on the gravestones, scribble it in the sky,” the Irish Times exulted. “Croke Park untethered, the whole place afloat for an hour on a lake of the sweetest tears that were ever cried.”Most pundits had favoured Kerry to win the 138th all-Ireland final and write another chapter of Mayo woe at Sunday’s contest at the Dublin stadium. Instead the underdogs triumphed and even some Kerry fans wept at the catharsis.View image in fullscreenMayo is the third biggest of the island of Ireland’s 32 counties but sparsely populated, with just 130,000 people.Photograph: Horizon International Images/AlamyFew seriously believed in the curse – it was said no member of the last winning team from 1951 would live to see another – but there was no doubting the drought that followed, with 11 defeats in 11 finals since 1989. A book about Mayo’s quest ​was titled House of Pain.Whenever the county made it to a final, a frisson gripped television viewers and the 82,000-strong stadium crowd: was this the day they would witness the end of the hex? On Sunday it was.“To every young boy and girl across Mayo and our diaspora across the world, never stop dreaming, stick your chest out and be proud to be from Mayo,” the team captain, Jack Coyne, declared as he held aloft the trophy named after Sam Maguire, a legendary player. “The wait is over. Sam is home.”Authorities had provisionally estimated a crowd of 40,000 would greet the team at McHale Park in the county town of Castlebar on Monday but that looks conservative, Gerry Bourke, the homecoming committee chair,told RTÉ. “After what I saw in Croke Park yesterday, I think we’ll have to revisit the plan.”Mayo, alandscape of bogs, rocks and Atlantic cliffs, is the third biggest of the island of Ireland’s 32 counties. It is sparsely populated, with just 130,000 people, but players and supporters have a reputation for fervency in the Gaelic Athletic Association, the sport’s governing body.View image in fullscreenMayo fans were delighted to put an end to 75 years of defeat, which legend had it was down to a curse.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAAccording to lore, the young victors of 1951 were on their way home to celebrate when they passed through the village of Foxford and failed to pay their respects to a funeral, prompting the enraged priest to utter the fateful words: “For as long as you all live, Mayo won’t win another all-Ireland.”View image in fullscreenLiam Gallagher, who has family ties to Mayo, was among those celebrating the win on social media.Photograph: Ireland West AirportSeven decades later, the last surviving member of that team, Paddy Prendergast,told friendshe would willingly “roll over and die” if there was any truth to the curse, but that it was a myth.“There was supposed to have been a funeral in the local church; I don’t know whether there was or not. I saw people standing around the church but we didn’t get off the truck because we couldn’t get off the bloody truck,” he told an interviewer in 2017.Researchers whoprobed church records, press cuttingsand other sources failed to find any verification of the supposed curse, which gained currency in the 1990s. The legend, however, is intact: Prendergast died in 2021, aged 95, two weeks after Mayo lost the final.Biden – who concluded a2023 presidential visit to Mayowith the rallying cry “Mayo for Sam!” – congratulated his ancestral home county. “Today, the dream becomes reality,” he posted. “You earned this victory. Enjoy every minute.”Carney, the Canadian prime minister who made his own ancestral pilgrimage to Mayo last month, echoed the joy. “The curse is broken,” he posted. The Gallagher brothers of Oasis, who also havefamily ties to Mayo, expressed pride. “Finally!! Up Mayo!!” Noel posted.Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump warns of return to ‘strong military action’ if Iran diplomacy fails | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Washington and Tehran issue conflicting messages over the status of talks to end Middle East crisis
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Washington and Tehran issue conflicting messages over the status of talks to end Middle East crisis
Content: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/ISNA/ReutersView image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/ISNA/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranTrump warns of return to ‘strong military action’ if Iran diplomacy failsWashington and Tehran issue conflicting messages over the status of talks to end Middle East crisisPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 27 Jul 2026 18.14 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has once again warned that the US will return to “strong military action” againstIranif diplomatic efforts do not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East.“We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.”He reiterated the line to reporters later the same day on Air Force One. “They want to meet, and we’re meeting. Without what we did, they wouldn’t even be talking to us … They would not have requested the meeting if we were doing poorly. The only reason they want to meet is because we’ve been hitting them very hard.”He doubled down at a rally in Michigan soon after. “You ⁠can’t bribe them. ​You’ve ‌got ‌to beat them, ‌and we’ll beat the hell out of them. But we’ll ‌see how it turns out,” ​he said . “Right now, ⁠there are very ​friendly negotiations going ​on.”Earlier, Tehran said there were no direct talks with the US to end the conflict, which began in late February with a wave of US-Israeli strikes and has rocked the region and the global economy.“Mediators may convey messages from the American side to us regarding current developments in the region. But at present we are not engaged in any negotiations with the United States,” said the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei.View image in fullscreenPresident Donald Trump said diplomatic efforts did not have much time to succeed.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APThe diplomatic back and forth came asOmanand Iran drew closer to an agreement in principle on the future management of the strait of Hormuz, but remained unable to resolve Tehran’s demand that all ships passing through the strategic waterway must pay some type of transit fee or toll to a consortium led by the two countries.Oman and Iran met for technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday that may hold the key to preventing a further round of fighting.US pauses Iran attacks after Trump advised to halt bombingRead morePerceived progress in the talks – backed by China, Qatar and Pakistan – was understood to have fed into the US decision to pause its attacks on Iran after nearly two weeks.Senior US officials are also reported to havewarned Trump over dwindling US munitions stockpilesand the impact of Iranian reprisals on US bases in the region, including Kuwait and Jordan.The top US military commander in the Middle East, Adm Brad Cooper, reportedly recommendedstopping the bombing campaignaround the strait because it had reached the limit of its effectiveness.The US attacks have been described by Washington as a response to repeated Iranian breaches of the memorandum of understanding signed in June, including by trying to prevent commercial shipping from transiting the strait through a southern route overseen by the US.Iran argues the southern route breaks the ceasefire agreement, which it insists left the country in sole charge of how the strait was reopened.A diplomat said: “The aim of the Tehran talks is to marry the Iran and Oman proposals so what emerges is clearly compliant with the law of the sea, and internationally acceptable.”At a Tehran press conference, Baqaei denied that the pause in US fighting amounted to an informal ceasefire.Oman has been trying since May to persuade Tehran that any plan for charging fees in the strait must be voluntary, to comply with the law of the sea. It has proposed a model similar to that which governs the strait of Malacca: countries that use it voluntarily contribute to a fund that provides for environmental and safety services to shipping.Oman argues that a similar entity could be set up in the strait of Hormuz with the agreement of the UN and the International Maritime Organization. The IMO secretary general, Arsenio Dominguez, has told the Guardian that the Malacca strait model is worth considering for the strait of Hormuz.View image in fullscreenThe top US military commander in the Middle East, Adm Brad Cooper, reportedly recommended stopping the bombing campaign because it had reached the limit of its effectiveness.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAIran’s department of environment has drafted its own plan, under which “the annual passage of over 50,000 ships and oil tankers through the strait of Hormuz and their role in polluting the Persian Gulf” must be compensated for. Under the plan, Iran would be able to collect “fees” from passing vessels proportional to the type of ship, cargo volume, navigation history and history of pollution.The comparison between the straits of Malacca and Hormuz is imperfect since fewer ships see ports in the Malacca strait as a destination point. But the Iranian media appear increasingly drawn to the Malacca model. The Khabaronline news agency argued such an agreement would be “a win-win situation for Iran”.Baqaei described the talks with Oman as useful and constructive but said they had nothing to do with the US. “The goal is for Iran and Oman, as two coastal states, to develop mechanisms to ensure safe shipping in the strait of Hormuz, while respecting the sovereign rights of the two coastal states and also preserving Iran’s security and national interests,” he said.Oman is in a tight spot since it knows the US is opposed to the introduction of tolls, but it may accept a very clearly delineated system of fees for specific services.The talks come as the US continues to encourage commercial shipping to test the strength of the Iranian blockade of the strait.Iranian officials reported that six vessels with their navigation systems switched off attempted to pass through the southern route of the strait on Sunday. One of them was fired upon and the others were turned back to the Persian Gulf. The US has reimposed a blockade of Iranian oil exports and ended a sanctions waiver on its oil exports.The United Nations Office for Project Services said on Monday that transits through the strait of Hormuz had fallen to an average of approximately five ships a day over the past week, compared with nearly 130 a day before the war.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranOmanStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance Again | Boy George | The Guardian
description: Culture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attack
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Culture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attack
Content: Boy George performs on stage in Hamburg this month.Photograph: Tristar Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBoy George performs on stage in Hamburg this month.Photograph: Tristar Media/Getty ImagesBoy George‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance AgainCulture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attackBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 27 Jul 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoy George has released a new song entitled We Will Dance Again, which voices support for Israel’s military action in Palestine.Posted on X and Instagram with the Hebrew title עוד נרקוד alongside its English translation, the song features a pop-reggae backing. The opening lyrics are: “You say genocide, I say war / When you’re attacked, that’s what the army’s for / Does it get ugly? You bet it does / When I know you wanna kill every last one of us.”Boy George cites theattack by Hamas at the Nova music festival in October 2023, saying the civilians killed there were “murder[ed] … for the crime of dancing”. A total of 344 civilians and 34 security personnel were killed and 44 people were taken hostage.The overall Palestinian death toll since the war started ismore than 73,000.The title phrase We Will Dance Again, repeated for the song’s chorus, has been used by Israelis to express hope and solidarity in the wake of the 7 October attack, and was used as the title of an acclaimed documentary about it.Elsewhere in the chorus, Boy George asserts: “There will be no war / But if you’re ever confused / I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human.”He also criticises the pro-Palestinian movement, including musicians who have condemned Israel: “You condemn the Jews, with selective memory / Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet feels so weak.” Musicians who have supportedPalestineinclude Stormzy, Damon Albarn, Clairo and Brian Eno, the latter of whom conceived an all-star charity single, Lullaby, which vied for Christmas No 1 in 2025.Boy George, who is not Jewish, has recently voiced support for Jewish communities. In an interview with the Telegraph, when discussing his admiration for Jewish peers in the 1980s during his time fronting Culture Club, he said: “Over the years it’s been a really personal thing. It doesn’t mean that I don’t have compassion for Palestinians, it doesn’t mean that I agree with what’s going on in Israel, but I am always going to defend the people that I love. I have a lot of Jewish friends and there would never be a situation where I’d turn my back on them.”He also voiced his support after theknife attack in Golders Green in April which left two Jewish men injured, saying: “We need to make our Jewish community know we support them.”His new song marks an intensification of his support for Israel, having said earlier in the year that he didn’t have an opinion on the country.View image in fullscreenBoy George with San Marino contestant Senhit at the Eurovision song contest in Vienna in May.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APSpeaking ahead of an appearance with San Marino for their Eurovision song contest entry (which didn’t reach the contest’s final), he was questioned about the boycott of Eurovision from countries opposing Israel’s inclusion in the contest. “I have many Jewish friends, whom I’ve known since I was 15 or 16 years old,” he replied. “Are people asking me, as someone with principles, to turn my back on my Jewish friends? That is not going to happen – it will never happen. From the beginning of my career, I wore the Star of David … I feel very connected to the Jewish people. I’m not necessarily connected to Israel. I don’t really have an opinion on that. But the mission of music is to unite people.”His characterisation of Israel’s action against Palestine as a legitimate military response rather than genocide runs counter to aUnited Nations inquiry, which stated in 2025 that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel’s foreign ministry called the report “distorted and false”. Last month, anotherindependent UN inquiryfound that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by targeting children. That report was dubbed a “libellous sham” by Israel.Boy George was one of the most flamboyant and recognisable pop stars of the 1980s, with Culture Club scoring four UK Top 10 albums including 1983’s chart-topping Colour By Numbers. Hit singles include Do You Really Want to Hurt Me? and Karma Chameleon, which were both hugely successful in the US as well as UK, and have endured as staples on oldies radio.The band also had a hit with an anti-war track, The War Song, which reached UK No 2 in 1984 and featured the chorus: “War is stupid and people are stupid / And love means nothing in some strange quarters.”Last month, Boy George launched a new company called Artist Included, which will use AI to allow artists to create new versions of earlier songs which resemble the originals, as a way of wresting back control of master recordings. It launched with a new version of Karma Chameleon, which Boy George recorded then de-aged. “When I heard it, I was absolutely gobsmacked,” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “It sounds like another take from that original session.”Explore more on these topicsBoy GeorgePop and rockIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Home Office blocking evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Refugee family reunions in limbo, despite Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of war-torn territory
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Refugee family reunions in limbo, despite Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of war-torn territory
Content: A child looks through a covering made from blankets at a tent camp sheltering displaced Palestinians in Khan Younis last week.Photograph: Ramadan Abed/ReutersView image in fullscreenA child looks through a covering made from blankets at a tent camp sheltering displaced Palestinians in Khan Younis last week.Photograph: Ramadan Abed/ReutersImmigration and asylumHome Office blocking evacuation of dozens of women and children from GazaRefugee family reunions in limbo, despite Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of war-torn territoryDiane TaylorMon 27 Jul 2026 07.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHome Officeis blocking the evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza, despite the Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of the war-torn region.Last September, the Home Office announced it was suspending refugee family reunion applications and that new, more restrictive rules would be announced in the spring. So far there has been no announcement and the process remains suspended.Applications made before the announcement continue to be processed. However, families inGazawho applied to reunite with an immediate family member before the suspension have been blocked from joining loved ones in the UK.The Home Office and the Foreign Office are involved in evacuations from Gaza. At the moment families who have a right to leave are evacuated via Jordan. However, the Home Office is not providing the required onward travel assurance (OTA) and is using legal challenges to block these families coming to the UK, sometimes deploying several senior barristers to a single case.The Home Office says biometrics are obtained before families travel to Jordan, even though the visa centre in Gaza has been closed since October 2023. Other European countries such as Belgium, France, Italy and Ireland are facilitating such evacuations and the Foreign Office has said it is willing to evacuate the families.Lawyers for the families stranded in life-threatening conditions in Gaza say the Home Office appears to be taking a harsher line with Palestinian families than with refugees from other countries hoping to reunite with loved ones in the UK. They say that in some cases the Home Office has stated that the family members, including small children, pose a security risk because they come from a “territory where terrorists operate”, even though some of the refugees in the UK were granted leave to remain on the basis of having been persecuted by Hamas in Gaza.The Guardian has previously reported on the case ofBassem Abudagga, a PhD student who has been separated from his family. Although the Foreign Office has agreed to help with evacuating his family, the Home Office has said they will have to wait until December before officials make a decision about whether to grant an OTA.In a communication with Abudagga’s lawyers on 15 July 2026 in response to descriptions of insanitary conditions, infested tents and frequent bombings, the Home Office said: “While this is acknowledged the conditions your clients face in Gaza alone are not considered to amount to compelling circumstances under the [relevant] guidance.”In another case, a Palestinian refugee in the UK is separated from his wife, their three children – aged nine, 12, 14 – and his 17-year-old nephew who they adopted after the teenager was orphaned by the war.He said:“My family are in constant danger and I worry about them every minute of every day. The UK government promised to help my family but has now gone back on that promise.“They say my family could be dangerous because there are terrorists operating in Gaza. I don’t understand how a mother and her children can be considered a security threat. The Foreign Office has offered to evacuate my family, so why is the Home Office doing everything in its power to stop it?”Sarah Crowe, a solicitor at the law firm Leigh Day representing some of the families trapped in the Palestinian territory and hoping to reunite with immediate family in Britain, said: “The UK government has abandoned vulnerable families in Gaza after promising to assist them. The Home Office is blocking family reunification when theForeign, Commonwealth and Development Officeis ready and willing to evacuate them.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “Under our reforms to create a fairer asylum system, family reunion will no longer be automatic. Those seeking to bring family members to the UK will need to meet stricter criteria.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumGazaHome OfficeRefugeesForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeIsrael-Gaza warPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: US pauses Iran attacks after Trump advised to halt bombing | Iran | The Guardian
description: Top military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitions
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Top military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitions
Content: US naval forces carry out an operation as part of their blockade on Iranian ports and ships.Photograph: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS naval forces carry out an operation as part of their blockade on Iranian ports and ships.Photograph: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP/Getty ImagesIranUS pauses Iran attacks after Trump advised to halt bombingTop military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitionsAndrew Rothin JerusalemMon 27 Jul 2026 02.33 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has paused strikes on Iran for a third night as top military officials advisedDonald Trumpto halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war.Oil prices fell on Monday as markets responded to the pause in combat.Trump is said to be weighing up diplomatic and military options in the nearly five-month-old conflict, withBenjamin Netanyahuexpected to visit the White House on Tuesday. The Israeli prime minister is a vocal critic of Washington’s negotiations with Iranian leaders and has pressed for the US to continue its strikes against Iran.Netanyahu is under considerable political pressure to show that his military campaigns againstIranand Hezbollah in Lebanon have yielded results before elections scheduled for October.Tehran said on Sunday it would pause what it called “retaliatory” attacks against US allies in the region. “These [US] attacks continued until two nights ago, but over the past two nights the Americans have stopped their attacks,” said the army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia. “Our strategy has essentially been retaliatory, we have also halted our retaliatory operations.”‘Shameful’: Pentagon accused of cover-up over US military casualties in Iran warRead moreSenior officials in the Trump administration are reported to have told the president about dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region.Axios reported on Sunday that Adm Bradley Cooper, the top US military commander in the region, had told Trump the US military campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness.The message was said to affect Trump’s decision to hold strikes on Iran for the first time in nearly two weeks. Cooper told Trump the US had nearly exhausted the list of targets that it had developed to attack in Iran, and without a return to major combat operations there was little point in continuing the bombing campaign, the news website reported.Asked on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press whether Trump was ruling out additional strikes in Iran, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz said: “I wouldn’t go that far at all. The president is keeping all options on the table.”The lull in fighting, which began on Friday evening, follows nearly two weeks of strikes against Iran and the collapse of a ceasefire brokered by Trump. Washington blamed Iran for strikes on US forces and allies in the region and its closure of the strait of Hormuz, a conduit for an estimated 20% of the world’s oil and gas.Senior diplomats from Iran and Oman were said to be holding negotiations on Sunday on reopening the vital waterway and an official in Tehran confirmed colleagues had been in touch with US negotiators to prevent a return to war. Iran has demanded payment and control over which ships pass through the strait.“Mediators are working and trying to prevent tension from escalating,” the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, told a press conference on Sunday.But an Iranian army spokesperson signalled defiance, saying the US had no clear strategy and was “experiencing strategic decision-making fatigue”.Graph showing how fighting has stopped ships transiting HormuzThe US vice-president,JD Vance, and Dan Caine, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff, warned Trump of the risks of a renewed military campaign against Iran at an Oval Office meeting on Friday, according to media outlets. The president then ordered the military to call off new strikes, which he had warned could “knock out everything they have”.“We’re talking to [the Iranians] right now,” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think they’re getting more and more serious as the days go by. We’re locked and loaded and ready to go, but we’re talking to them.”At a White House Correspondents’ Association dinner that evening he said he did not think Iran was ready to make a deal but he was ready to listen.View image in fullscreenIsraeli army units stage a raid near Nablus in the occupied West Bank after the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israelis when armed settlers entered a village.Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/ReutersCaine warned Trump about dwindling munitions stockpiles, which include Patriot missile interceptors and offensive weapons like Tomahawk cruise missiles. Vance campaigned on his opposition to US military interventions in the Middle East and has grown more vocal in his opposition to the war in Iran.Netanyahu’s office announced on Sunday that he would convene a meeting of his security cabinet before leaving for Washington on Monday. He played a crucial role in lobbying Trump to launch joint strikes against Iran in February and has said that US negotiators must take a strong line on Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programme. US negotiators have instead prioritised opening the strait of Hormuz.Netanyahu will travel to Washington amid some of the worst violence this year in the West Bank, where his military is launching an “extensive” operation after the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israelis when armed settlers entered a Palestinian village on Thursday.The US and the UK under its new prime minister, Andy Burnham, are discussing plans for a high-level meeting in London this week to discuss the potential for a coalition to protect ships in the strait of Hormuz and de-mine the waterway. The discussions will be an early test for Burnham’s administration. The Labour government has so far refused to allow Washington to use a British airbase for offensive operations against Iran.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpUS foreign policyIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Monday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s government | India | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable
Author: Hettie O'Brien
Headline: In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable
Content: Narendra Modi has never been challenged so publicly and so widely.Photograph: Altaf Hussain/ReutersView image in fullscreenNarendra Modi has never been challenged so publicly and so widely.Photograph: Altaf Hussain/ReutersFirst Edition newsletterIndiaMonday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s governmentIn today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchableHettie O'BrienMon 27 Jul 2026 01.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 01.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. As flames engulfed parts of France and Spain this weekend, in India, the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was trying to put out a very different kind of fire. Thousands of people arrived in Delhi on Saturday to demand the resignation of his education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. Whenhe stepped downin the early afternoon, the protests turned into a triumphant block party.But the Cockroach protests that haveswept through India this summerare about much more than a single minister. They have humiliated Modi and undermined the indomitable power of his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) that has ruled India for the past 12 years. They’re also a lesson in using humour to political advantage.Modi likes to present himself as aninfallible messiah, but young people have mocked the prime minister online and in the streets, calling him a “56-inch monkey” (a reference to Modi boasting about his ample 56-inch chest), and parodied his social media addresses. “Hating Modi is cool on the internet now, after years of criminalising dissent,” one told a reporter.Now the protesters have secured a victory, will their calls for revolution continue? For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondentHannah Ellis-Petersen, who has been reporting on the “Cockroaches” inDelhi, about what their anger stems from and what it means for the BJP. That’s after a roundup of the biggest stories of the weekend.Weekend roundupWild fires| Authorities in Francebattled to contain a huge wildfirenear Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency.Germany| A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attackhas been shot dead by police, German officials have said.Iran| The US haspaused strikes on Iranfor a second night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war.UK politics| Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas developmentat the heart of UK international relationsby taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank.UK news| Five Palestine Action activistsface being sentenced as terroristsfor breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire.In depth: ‘What if all cockroaches come together?’View image in fullscreenThe Cockroach Janta party has tasted victory and might widen the scope of the changes they seek.Photograph: Indranil Aditya/ReutersIt started asa sardonic joke. On 16 May, Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student at Boston University, posted on X: “What if all cockroaches come together?” It was a tongue-in-cheek response to India’s chief justice, who had called unemployed young Indians “cockroaches”. Online, thousands of people responded to Dipke’s message. Realising he had tapped into something big, Dipke flew to Delhi on 6 June and went to Jantar Mantar, its famous protest ground.The protests drew young people from across the country, and the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) – a play on the BJP’s name – created a website listing their demands, including reform of India’s education system.Indiahas a young population who are better educated than ever before, but it has proven a weak point for the BJP, with the country’s universities crumbling and its economy failing to provide jobs for many graduates. Millions of young people spend years prepping for gruelling public exams in the hope of securing a decent job, and their parents go into debt or sell their land to fund these studies.To make matters worse, these exam papers are routinely leaked and sold to the highest bidder. “Anyone rich enough can buy the answers,” Hannah tells me. This is devastating for millions of young people, forcing them to retake tests for which they’ve already studied. After a medical entrance exam was leaked in May, at least 12 students took their own lives; some left notes behind saying they could not bear the thought of resitting the test. The leaks are a potent symbol of institutional corruption, inflaming the anger that young people feel towards a political system that is failing them.Thief, thiefSonam Wangchuk, an engineer and education reformer from Ladakh, joined the protest on 28 June and declared he would go on indefinite hunger strike until the education minister resigned. “The idea of a hunger strike has a particularly powerful resonance in India,” says Hannah. “Gandhi put his life on the line several times with his hunger strikes for independence.”Delhi police forcibly removed Wangchuk from Jantar Mantar on 18 July and took him to hospital, supposedly for the sake of his health. Footage of his hospital stay went viral, and the Cockroach party called for a march on parliament. On Monday, tens of thousands of people started to fill Delhi’s streets. “In my whole time covering India, I’ve never seen so many people turning out,” Hannah says. The mood was jubilant, but by the afternoon, things had turned violent as the police began firing teargas and using batons on the protesters.Despite that, many of the protesters stayed put, and Hannah went back to Jantar Mantar in the following days. “It wastheplace to be in India,” she says. “There were people camping out, delivery guys bringing pizza and biryani, people cooking food. It had become about more than just the education minister resigning. More, even than education.”The protesters’ very public displays of contempt – graffiti of Modi’s name under the image of a urinating dog; people stamping on a poster of his face and chanting“thief, thief”– would have seemed unimaginable just two weeks ago. “People were just revelling in the opportunity to speak their mind,” Rahul Bhatia, a writer and author of The New India, who attended the protests on Saturday, tells me. “It was delightful. It made people think: things are possible.”Modi lost control of the narrativePradhan’s resignation is a major victory for the Cockroach protesters. He is a Modi loyalist and former organiser for the RSS, the Hindu supremacist group closely affiliated with the BJP (for more on its sinister ideology, it’s worth reading this fascinating2020 pieceby Samanth Subramanian). “It creates a crack in the BJP’s armour,” Hannah says. Modi has projected an image of total authority, but this is one of the first instances where he has bent to popular will. He demands unflinching loyalty from his ministers. Theymay now be questioning whether their positions are quite as secure as they thought.India has taken a sharp turn towards autocracy under the BJP. Its main media channels are controlled by (or intensely favourable to) the government, and most of them gave minimal coverage to the protests, so young people resorted to sharing information and anti-government memes on social media. The party is no stranger to social media (its “troll army” is adept at smearing digital opponents, and the government tried to shut down the Cockroach party’s X account in early July), but it has lost control of the narrative.Modi’s last-ditch attempt to engage protesters with two reels he posted to his then 101 million Instagram followers on Thursday night (after which he gained over 1 million more, an impressive number, though still fewer than Beyoncé’s 299 million) seemed contrived and stilted. “He has been crucified online for those videos,” Hannah says.Is this the start of something bigger?It’s tempting to compare the Cockroach protests to otheryouth uprisingsthat have led toregime changein south Asia. But “a quick look at the outcome of people’s movements in India is not encouraging,” the novelist Arundhati Roy wrote in a recentpiecefor Equator magazine. “Revenge is surely being planned and will be visited on those [the government] sees as the main instigators.” After people took to the streets in 2019 to protest against the BJP’s controversial new citizenship act, the government swiftly outlawed gatherings in several places and detained protesters.The real test of the BJP’s power will come at election time. It is one of the world’s richest and most formidable parties, and has attempted to capture India’s electoral machinery, pushing for reforms to its voting map that would tilt power further in Modi’s favour. In West Bengal, a state the BJP had never won before, it “revised” the electoral roll and excluded more than 9.1 million voters from the register, securing adecisive victoryearlier this year.“It seems like the BJP has much less support than people actually think,” Bhatia says. But after these protests, Modi will be doing all that he can to maintain his party’s grip on power.The week to comeMonday |Andrew and Tristan Tate are due back in the Florida court where they’re fighting their extradition to the UK, to face rape and sex-trafficking charges.Tuesday |Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy are expected to be among those attending the Washington DC memorial service for the late South Carolina senator and Trump ally Lindsey Graham.Thursday |People will go to the polls to elect the next mayor of Greater Manchester, who will replace Andy Burnham.What else we’ve been enjoyingView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignTo enshittification, we can now add the idea ofdecadence without pleasure: “For anyone with an Internet connection and a little discretionary income, the contemporary moment offers a superabundance of seductive distractions.Why then the pervasive mood of emptiness?” Truly, what a time to be alive.Toby Moses, head of newslettersThe world is approaching “plutocratic collapse”. That’s the view of the French economistGabriel Zucman, and I’m inclined to agree. I enjoyed Will Dunn’srecent profileof him in the New Statesman (£).HettieAddshinglesto the long list of things millennial women need to worry about –Emily Retter has lookedat why the excruciating disease is on the rise.Tobyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSportView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar passes the basilica of Sacré-Coeur as the Tour de France finished with a thrilling final stage in Paris.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPATour de France| Tadej Pogacar took arecord-equalling fifth winin the Tour de France on Sunday, joining the all-time greats, as Mathieu van der Poel won a frantic final stage in Paris.Commonwealth Games| Adam Ramsay-Peaty isready to bounce backafter his 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games. He said: “The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind, but I’m really happy with that.”Formula One| Lando Norriswon the Hungarian Grand Prixwith an assured drive for McLaren at the Hungaroring, his and the team’s first victory of the year.The front pagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Guardian“Miliband vows to give UK ‘global leadership’ role on climate crisis”, is theGuardian’s front page today.TheTimessays “Teen anxiety pays more than job”, and theTelegraphalso has “PM to crack down on youth benefits”. Still on politics, TheMailgoes with “Streeting: I will quit if defence plan falls short”, thei Papersays “Council tax and stamp duty to be scrapped under Burnham plans”, and theExpresssplashes “Police ‘waste’ millions on diversity schemes”.TheFTsplashes “Biggest defence companies home in on start-ups for nimbler military tech”, and theMirrorleads with its water safety campaign, saying “No child should die for a day at the seaside”. Lastly,Metrosplashes “Fly and dry” on Gatwick’s water outage.Today in FocusView image in fullscreenThe tech company’s relationship with the UK’s public health service is under the spotlight.Photograph: Arnd Wiegmann/ReutersHow Palantir got into the NHSInvestigative journalist, Lucas Amin,reports on how the tech companyPalantir won a £330m contract with the NHS … and what happened once its software was introduced.Cartoon of the day | Tom GauldView image in fullscreenIllustration: Tom Gauld/The GuardianThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenThe small clinical trial run by academics at Rutgers University in New Jersey found ‘additional benefits’ beyond weight loss to restricted eating.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianRestricting eating to a nine‑hour window and avoiding food for four hours before sleepmay improve cognitive health in older adults. In a six‑month trial of 47 women who were considered overweight or obese, both groups lost similar weight, but those following time‑restricted eating performed better on spatial planning and problem‑solving tests, with hints of improved memory.Researchers suggest circadian rhythms, metabolism and inflammation may play a role. Experts stress the findings are preliminary and require larger, peer‑reviewed studies.Prof Wendy Hall, the head of nutritional sciences at King’s College London, said: “Time-restricted eating is a plausible approach to supporting cognitive health in midlife”.Sign up herefor a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.Quick crosswordCryptic crosswordWordiplyExplore more on these topicsIndiaFirst Edition newsletterNarendra ModiDelhiMumbaiSouth and central AsiaActivismnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needs | Education policy | The Guardian
description: PM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs market
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: PM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs market
Content: Under the plan, mayors and other local leaders will work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyView image in fullscreenUnder the plan, mayors and other local leaders will work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyEducation policyBurnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needsPM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs marketPeter WalkerandJosh HallidayMon 27 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will tell schools across England to adapt their curriculums to the needs of local businesses as part of a devolution drive aimed at tackling the jobs crisis for young people.By moving decision-making to local areas, the PM hopes the plan will make technical and vocational skills as valued as academic qualifications – and help cut the benefits bill.Based in part on the Greater Manchester baccalaureate that Burnham introduced as the region’s mayor, it will task schools with making their curriculums for students aged 14 and above more responsive to the local jobs market, teaching technical skills alongside traditional academic subjects.It would, Burnham said, mean the country could “value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap”.Described by No 10 as “a fundamental change to the education system”, the announcement kicks off a week of policy initiatives by Burnham, expected to also cover adult social care, defence and devolution.After last week’s succession of rapid, consumer-focused policies such as help with electricity bills, Burnham’s team aim to use the coming days to present him as a leader willing to tackle more intractable and complex political problems.Under the plan, intended to begin operating from September 2028, mayors and other local leaders would work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs.In combination, there will be prioritised funding for such technical and vocational qualifications, plus guidance to Ofsted to recognise the value of these as well as more traditional qualifications.In addition to giving local areas more control over education for the 14-16 age group, Burnham said the intention was to redress what he said was an over-simplified focus on academic routes.He said:“For too long in this country, students have been told that you must take the academic path to do well and to be respected. The whole school system has been built around it and that has let down young people seeking technical qualifications.“I want an education system based on parity between academic and technical which gives all young people a clear path in life. From today, Britain will value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap.”The intention is also to help address the worsening problem of young people not in education, employment or training, which was the subjectof a reportpublished in May by Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister.The first part of an ongoing review, Milburn’s report said the issue now affected 1 million young people across the UK, with the numbers rising fast. It cited a number of factors, including a changing job market, inequality and health problems, but also blamed a lack of focus on employability skills and non-academic qualifications.Milburn said in a statement that he welcomed the plans to overhaul and devolve education for 14-plus pupils, calling it “a big step in the right direction and consistent with the findings of my review”.Moves to get more young people into work will also be a key element of wider efforts to tackle the benefits system, due to be guided by both Milburn’s findings and a separatereview by Stephen Timms, the minister for social security, into the personal independence payment disability system.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn an interview with the BBC broadcast on Monday night, Burnham said he believed that many young people had been failed by a system that “pays for failure” rather than “sets people up for success”.Asked if he believed some people received benefits they did not need, he replied: “I wouldn’t necessarily go straight to blaming those people. What I would say is that there are people in the benefit system, young people in their 20s, who have been, I would say, quite seriously let down because the support wasn’t there for them when it should have been there.”This failure included, he said, “an education system that for a very long time has been obsessed on the university route but hasn’t done enough for young people who want technical qualifications and in many ways has treated them as second class students”.The new initiative is firmly based on Burnham’s flagship education policy as Greater Manchester mayor, introduced in September 2024.Known as the Greater Manchester baccalaureate, or MBacc, it was designed to offer courses and work experience for children aged 14 and over in key sectors in the regional economy.Alongside the traditional subjects of English, maths and sciences, schools in Greater Manchester can now offer technical lessons tailored towards employment in industries including financial services, engineering and manufacturing, construction and the green economy. There are also new routes into public services such as health and social care, education and transport.Experts say it is too soon to properly evaluate whether the MBacc has been a success – it was piloted in only 10 schools in its first academic year. However, several other of England’s regional mayors have called for greater power over the school curriculum to link it more closely with their local economy.Some mayors complain that the Department for Education has been one of the most stubborn government bodies when it comes to devolving powers outside Whitehall.Explore more on these topicsEducation policySchoolsEnglandAndy BurnhamYouth unemploymentVocational educationYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Police make inquiries after Farage reports Polanski post for ‘inciting murder’ | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotine
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotine
Content: A Green party spokesperson said that Zack Polanski ‘condemns the image on the T-shirt’.Photograph: Rich McCarthy/PAView image in fullscreenA Green party spokesperson said that Zack Polanski ‘condemns the image on the T-shirt’.Photograph: Rich McCarthy/PANigel FaragePolice make inquiries after Farage reports Polanski post for ‘inciting murder’Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotineSinéad CampbellMon 27 Jul 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are “conducting inquiries” into an image shared by Green party leaderZack Polanskion Instagram after Reform UK reported it for “inciting murder”.The image showed a man wearing a black T-shirt with the words “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, alongside a photograph of a guillotine.AGreen partyspokesperson said that Polanski “condemns the image on the T-shirt” and accepted being tagged in a post with 20 images “without realising there was more to it than he had seen”.Nigel Farage shared a screenshot of the image on X and wrote: “This is what Zack Polanski has just posted on his Instagram.“If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski.”Reform UK’s spokesperson for home affairs, Zia Yusuf, said Polanski was “inciting murder”, and that sharing the image weeks after the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe, who was murdered in her home in Devon, was “staggering”.Last week, prosecutors told a court that a man allegedly hit Widdecombe 21 times over the head with a hammer in a “planned and targeted” attack.A Green party spokesperson said: “The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself [Polanski].“He [Polanski] and the Green party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division.”A spokesperson for the Metropolitan police said: “Earlier today, we received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media.“We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting inquiries into the matter.”Yusuf wrote on social media: “Zack Polanski has posted to his 713kInstagramfollowers a photo of a man in a T-shirt calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage.“Polanski is inciting murder. It must be treated as such by the police.”The image, which has since been removed from Polanski’s Instagram account, was shared in a collaborative post with other accounts, as part of a carousel of images from a Green party event on Sunday.The words on the T-shirt come from Making Plans for Nigel, a song by English rock band XTC, which was released as the lead single from the 1979 album Drums and Wires.A post on a website that appeared to sell the T-shirt for £20 stated: “Whether it’s a nod to old punk music or a sharper bit of political satire, this design is for those who prefer their statements with a side of mystery.”Earlier this month, Andy Burnham said that a serious review is needed into MP security after the murder of Ann Widdecombe. Jess Phillips previouslytold the Guardianthat the threat to MPs must be tackled at source, amid an ongoing refusal by social media platforms to take responsibility for what’s published on their platforms.According to theBBC, Polanski has not been contacted by the police.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageZack PolanskiReform UKGreen partyInstagramnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham appoints Bridget Phillipson as Labour party chair | Bridget Phillipson | The Guardian
description: Former education secretary will take up influential role that puts her at vanguard of Labour’s battle to win next general election
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Former education secretary will take up influential role that puts her at vanguard of Labour’s battle to win next general election
Content: Bridget Phillipson. The role of party chair has been held by Labour big beasts, including Harriet Harman, Angela Rayner and Tom Watson.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreenBridget Phillipson. The role of party chair has been held by Labour big beasts, including Harriet Harman, Angela Rayner and Tom Watson.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APBridget PhillipsonAndy Burnham appoints Bridget Phillipson as Labour party chairFormer education secretary will take up influential role that puts her at vanguard of Labour’s battle to win next general electionAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentMon 27 Jul 2026 16.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBridget Phillipson has been appointed Labour party chair, putting her at the vanguard of Labour’s battle to win the next general election.The former education secretary and architect of a landmark overhaul in special educational needs and disabilities (Send) provision in England will follow in the footsteps of otherLabourbig beasts who have held the position, including Harriet Harman, Angela Rayner and Tom Watson.Phillipson, who was sacked as education secretary by Andy Burnham last week, replaces Anna Turley after last week’s government reshuffle, which saw the Labour Co-op MP for Redcar moved to a new ministerial role in the Home Office.The prime minister said the MP for Houghton and Sunderland South would drive culture change and work alongside him and Lucy Powell. “She will play a vital role in ensuring the Labour party is match fit for the next election,” he said. “I am delighted Bridget has accepted this role and I look forward to working closely with her on this vital task.”After a major cabinet reshuffle in which dozens of cabinet ministers, including several loyal to Keir Starmer, were removed from their posts, Phillipson was viewed as a rare survivor, albeit in a reduced role.In what is likely to be seen as an olive branch to members of the previous government, Labour said the appointment reflected Burnham’s “commitment to drawing on the full breadth and depth of talent across the Labour party as he builds one united team”.Phillipson said she would put “Labour values and the voices of our movement at the heart of government”. She added: “By uniting together, we will bring hope back to communities and strengthen British society against those working to divide us.”Phillipson was demoted last week when she was replaced by key Burnham ally Powell as secretary of state for education. But she maintained her position in the cabinet as women and equalities minister, the first time the traditionally more minor role has been part of cabinet in its own right.While not an overt Burnhamite, the former education secretary was not seen as overly tribal and hadwon plaudits from Labour MPs for her engagementover plans to make provision for children with Send more widely available in mainstream schools. Critics raised concerns about the plans, which will raise the bar at which children inEnglandqualify for an education, health and care plan (EHCP), which legally entitles them to get support.Phillipson has become something of a bete noire for some on the right after overseeing the Labour policy of applying20% VATto private school fees from the start of 2025, having recently been called a“spiteful class warrior”by Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch.
