Brought up in a low-income, single-parent household in the town of Washington, Tyne and Wear, Phillipson wrote a report on child poverty for Starmer and his chancellor Rachel Reeves, and argued thatabolishing the two-child benefit capwas the most cost-effective way to make lives better for young disadvantaged people.She later told the BBC she was going to have Badenoch’s insult put on a T-shirt, adding: “If being a spiteful class warrior means lifting half a million children out of poverty I’ll be wearing that T-shirt with pride.”Having held the education brief since Labour entered government in July 2024, Phillipson was replaced by Powell, who became the 11th person to hold the post in the last decade.Powell, who is also deputy leader of the Labour party, has long been a Burnhamally. A fellow Manchester MP, she played a key role in helping win the Makerfield campaign, which saw him return to Westminster, and has previously run byelections as well as having directed Ed Miliband’s 2015 national Labour campaign.Explore more on these topicsBridget PhillipsonLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew and Tristan Tate to remain in jail until next extradition hearing | Andrew Tate | The Guardian
description: Social media influencers fighting against extradition to UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Social media influencers fighting against extradition to UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegations
Content: Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan speak to the media as they arrive in Romania from US on 22 March 2025.Photograph: Daniel Mihăilescu/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndrew Tate and his brother Tristan speak to the media as they arrive in Romania from US on 22 March 2025.Photograph: Daniel Mihăilescu/AFP/Getty ImagesAndrew TateAndrew and Tristan Tate to remain in jail until next extradition hearingSocial media influencers fighting against extradition to UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegationsAssociated PressMon 27 Jul 2026 16.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 16.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSocial media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail at least two more weeks until their next hearing as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge said on Monday.US magistrate Lauren Louis set a detention hearing for 13 August to determine whether the Tates should stay in jail or be released during what could be a months-long extradition process.The brothers were not in court on Monday or required to be there and have remained in jail since making a brief court appearance two days after their 18 July arrest.The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the US, Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing.Attorneys for the brothers said on Monday that they want the US government to turn over documents that UK officials submitted to secure their arrest.“They don’t have anything but the accusations,” Joseph McBride, an attorney, said after the hearing. “It’s just their word against our word right now.”The UK has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the state department, Alejandra Lopez, a US attorney, said in court.The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes.Jackie Perczek, another one of their attorneys, said the Tates have shown they are not a flight risk by returning to Romania every month after they were accused there of luring women for sexual exploitation.“For three years they have not fled,” she said. “They’ve traveled the world and every month they return to Romania.”The former professional kickboxers, who have dual US and UK citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn’t expect any help from the president.McBride said shortly after the Tates were arrested that “they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit,” he said.McBride said the extradition attempt was politically motivated, though he provided no details.Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in south-eastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”.The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the UK between 2012 and 2015.The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case has not gone forward because of legal and procedural problems.Andrew Tate, 39, became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the UK reality television show Big Brother. He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman.He has amassed more than 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women.Explore more on these topicsAndrew TatenewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham’s Ukraine gambit is a symbolic start for PM who wants to look inward | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: New prime minister wants to focus at home, but his first week already suggests the world has other plans
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: New prime minister wants to focus at home, but his first week already suggests the world has other plans
Content: Andy Burnham told Volodymyr Zelenskyy: ‘We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.’Photograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham told Volodymyr Zelenskyy: ‘We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.’Photograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APAndy BurnhamAnalysisBurnham’s Ukraine gambit is a symbolic start for PM who wants to look inwardPippa CrerarPolitical editorNew prime minister wants to focus at home, but his first week already suggests the world has other plansMon 27 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.37 EDTShareIt took just seven days in office forAndy Burnhamto meet his first world leader. As he welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday, the new prime minister told the Ukrainian president it was “no accident” he was his first international visitor since entering No 10.“It is intended to send a very clear message,” Burnham told him. “We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” In short, the UK’s support for Kyiv would continue despite the change in leadership.ForKeir Starmer, the relationship with Zelenskyy became one of the defining ones of his premiership. He visited Ukraine four times over his two years in office, inviting the Ukrainian president back to the UK on another four occasions. They also met regularly at international summits.In a symbolic move, Starmer travelled to Ukraine during his final week in office, receiving the order of freedom medal for his role leading the coalition of the willing and helping to persuade Donald Trump back to the table on Ukraine after he flirted with siding with Putin.But over the course of his premiership, the formerLabourleader faced accusations of spending too much time on international issues instead of domestic ones, with his critics nicknaming him “never here Keir” and even his own Downing Street team complaining that he “needs to get off a plane”.View image in fullscreenZelenskyy talks to Burnham. The UK prime minister said: ‘It is intended to send a very clear message.’Photograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APBurnham, in contrast, has always been clear he would prioritise what was happening at home, reflecting his own political instincts as well as his wariness of not falling into the same trap as his predecessor. But it led some in the Labour party to worry that he would be unprepared for the global stage.“It’s a frustrating characterisation because not many incoming prime ministers, including Keir, have any experience of international affairs,” one of his inner circle said. “Andy has said that his priority will be domestic, but of course there will be moments where he’ll need to be more outward facing.”Day to day, Burnham’s allies have suggested that he will rely on delegating responsibility to his team – including his foreign secretary in Ed Miliband and senior diplomatic adviser in Jonathan Powell, whom he persuaded to stay on in No 10 from the Starmer administration.Labour MPs point out that Yvette Cooper, Miliband’s predecessor, was often left fighting for influence as there were so many other senior figures who saw themselves as the de facto foreign secretary, including the deputy prime minister, David Lammy, Powell, and Starmer himself.One senior MP said: “I suspect that Ed may be in a fortunate position where he is actually given more freedom than other foreign secretaries in the past. As long as Ed is known to have the authority of the PM and to be trusted to speak for him, then this may be his moment.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Simon Jones/The Sun/APOther Labour figures suggested that strong prime ministers should be able to delegate and rely on their teams. One said: “I don’t think Andy is particularly interested in foreign affairs. He’ll need to front some things up, but as long as he’s well briefed and charming, he doesn’t need to make the day-to-day decisions like Keir did.”But they warned there would inevitably be moments where complex international issues “crash land” on UK domestic policy – as Starmer found to his cost when dealing with Trump – and he would have no choice but to intervene.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham has already indicated he will not shy away from standing up to the US president. “Obviously, the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything that they say,”he told the Guardianlast month.There are some with experience of foreign affairs in government who believe that Starmer has already done the hard yards on foreign policy – on Ukraine, the European Union and the US in particular – so Burnham just has to stick to the same course.In his final interview in office, Starmer told his successor that he should not spend less time focusing on international affairs, in order to prioritise the situation at home. “It’s not sensible to think you can just separate these two things out,” he said.“If you’re PM and you care what bills are going to be like in any household around the country, you have to care about finding a lasting solution to the situation in Ukraine, you have to care about what happens in the strait of Hormuz.”But those around Burnham believe he can better balance them. At least for now. They have been watching events in Iran closely, mindful of the potential to cause yet more global economic upheaval should Trump take further action.“Andy has a bit of space now to prioritise policy at home – but it could all be blown off course by Iran,” one Foreign Office insider said. “He has to seize this moment to talk about the domestic, because this window might not come again.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamForeign policyLabourKeir StarmeranalysisShareReuse this content

title: Cracker Barrel CEO to step down after overseeing logo backlash last year | Business | The Guardian
description: Julie Masino faced criticism as restaurant chain was called ‘woke’ and ‘soulless’ after unveiling modernized logo
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Julie Masino faced criticism as restaurant chain was called ‘woke’ and ‘soulless’ after unveiling modernized logo
Content: Julie Felss Masino, president and CEO of Cracker Barrel, speaks during 13D Monitor’s Active-Passive Investor Summit in New York City on 21 October 2025.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreenJulie Felss Masino, president and CEO of Cracker Barrel, speaks during 13D Monitor’s Active-Passive Investor Summit in New York City on 21 October 2025.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersBusinessCracker Barrel CEO to step down after overseeing logo backlash last yearJulie Masino faced criticism as restaurant chain was called ‘woke’ and ‘soulless’ after unveiling modernized logoGaya GuptaMon 27 Jul 2026 13.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCracker Barrel’s CEO, Julie Masino, is stepping down, the restaurant announced on Monday, nearly a year after the company was swept into a political maelstrom over proposed modernizations to its branding.Criticson social media denounced the Tennessee-based rustic restaurant chain as “woke” as well as “sterile and soulless” after it unveiled an updated logo that removed Uncle Herschel, the overall-clad man leaning against a barrel in the restaurant’s original logo, last August. Donald Trumpweighed inon the updates soon after, posting: “WTF is wrong with Cracker Barrel?!” and demanding on social media that the company “admit a mistake”.The companyannouncedthat it would revert back to its old logo soon after the social media reaction exploded. Masino, who has served as the chain’s CEO since 2023, told the rightwing commentator Glenn Beck in December that she felt “fired by America” after the controversy.Cracker Barrel’s stock dropped nearly 3% after the announcement of Masino’s departure. The chain’s new CEO, David Deno, will take over on 10 August, and Masino will remain until October to help with the transition.“Cracker Barrel is a truly iconic American brand, defined by its unique combination of warm country hospitality, timeless appeal, and deep connection with guests across generations,” Deno said in a statement.Masino’s departure the latest fallout from social media-fueled backlash against brands accused of appealing to certain political ideals. The Harris Pollfound last yearthat a quarter of Americans have changed their shopping habits to align with their morals, with 50% of Democrats and 41% of Republicans responding that they stopped shopping at stores opposing their political views.Some companies have quickly felt the financial strain of these calls to action. In 2023, after Target announced a pride month collection and Bud Light aired an advertisement with a transgender influencer, both companies announced declines in sales. On the other side of the political aisle, Target was pulled as a sponsor from Minneapolis’s annual pride festival last year after it announced it was ending its diversity, equality and inclusion policies.Not all of these boycotts have been successful, though – Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey saw great success at its global box office debut, despite Elon Musk and other criticscastigating the movie’s castas part of a “woke” agenda.Cracker Barrel has had a history of discriminatory treatment against diners and staff. In 1991, the chain blocked the hiring of LGBTQ+ workers and dismissed 11 staff members, though it later backed down from that policy. In 2004, Cracker Barrel paid $8.7m tosettle discrimination allegationsfrom Black customers who said they were denied service and Black employees who said they received more “back of house” assignments compared with their white counterparts.Explore more on these topicsBusinessRestaurantsFoodDonald TrumpFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurd | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world
Content: ‘Trump is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Trump is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpTariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurdSteven GreenhouseThe president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the worldMon 27 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.15 EDTShareWith the midterm elections less than four months away, it’s a precarious time for Donald Trump and Republicans: Trump’s war against Iran is going badly, hisapproval ratings are in the toilet, gas prices are soaring and pushing up inflation, and nation after nation is furious about Trump’s insults, bullying andugly American unilateralism.So amid all this mess, what does Trump do? He turns to his favorite economic plaything: tariffs. On Monday, Trump signed orders to slap a50% tariff on many Canadian goods, and four days later, he imposedacross-the-board 10% or 12.5% tariffson goods from more than 80 countries. Trump was no doubt thumping his chest, while millions of people overseas were dumping on him for yet another unnecessary, hostile act.Too bad for Republicans, and most Americans, though, because Trump’s fixation on tariffs will only worsen their troubles. Trump’s new tariffs will push up prices – let’s not forget that tariffs are taxes on imports, and US consumers will pay those taxes. A corollary of that: Trump’s tariffs will worsen AmericansNo 1 economic concern: affordability. In bad news for typical Americans, the Yale Budget Lab estimates that Trump’s tariffs will increase costs for the average UShousehold by $1,100 each year. The tariffs are also likely to push Trump’s approval ratings deeper into the sewer. If Trump thinks these tariffs are going to distract Americans from thinking about the Epstein files or the disastrous mess he’s made with his Iran “excursion”, he’s deluding himself. The American people aren’t going to forget those things.It’s hard to tell whether Trump’s repeated use of tariffs is a fixation or an addiction. Emperor Donald I evidently loves tariffs because he can use them to clobber other countries whenever he wants. They’re a powerful cudgel he won’t let go of. Trump imposed his new tariffs on more than 80 countries on the very day that another set of tariffs he slapped on dozens of countries was due to expire. Toparaphrase the actor Charlton Heston, I can imagine Trump saying: “I’ll give up tariffs when you take them from my cold, dead hands.”With these new tariffs, Trump is again engaged in his delusional, destructive tariff tomfoolery. They’ll push up prices, squeeze Americans’ wallets and anger other countries. Trump said his tariffs would boost US manufacturing, but the US haslost 75,000 factory jobssince he returned to office, with many executives complaining about all the herky-jerky uncertainty Trump has wrought. Assessing Trump’s effects on the economy, Atsi Sheth, the chief credit officer for Moody’s Ratings, told the New York Times :“Volatility and unpredictabilityis the new normal.”What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countriesRead moreLike so much that Trump does, his new tariffs are clearly based on pique and false premises with lots of shamelessness and absurdity thrown in. After the US supreme courtoverturned Trump’s me-against-the-whole-world tariffsin February, Trump, refusing to let go of his tariff toy, turned to other strategies. To justify his new 50% tariffs against Canada – which arepiled atopnumerous other tariffs he’s imposed on a country that was long the US’s closest ally – Trump relied on a never before usedprovision of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, a widely derided 1930 law that greatly worsened the Great Depression of a century ago. With this new tariff, placed on hockey sticks, paper, plywood, dairy products and many other Canadian goods, Trump invoked a Smoot-Hawley provision that allows retaliation against countries that engage in trade discrimination against the US.In making that case, Trump’s exhibit No 1 is something rather preposterous, or should I say rather shameless? After Trump imposed high, punitive tariffs on Canada last year, 11 of Canada’s 13 provinces and territories halted liquor imports from the US because they were so irate about those tariffs along with Trump’s outlandish and belittling statements that he wanted to make Canada the 51st state. The White Housecalled this ban on US liquor illegal discrimination, while Canadians view it as a type of traditional trade retaliation that countries engage in when another country – here the US – slaps tariffs on them, a situation made worse by the fact that Trump’s tariffs against Canada arean egregious violationof the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.Trump also insists that Canada has improperly discriminated against the US because Canada imposed a 25% tariff on select US-made cars after Trumpslapped a 25% tariffon Canadian-made cars.He is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US. That’s the logic of America’s leading stable genius, who also offered another far-fetched justification for his decision: “We’re going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke,” hetold reporterson Friday, referring to wildfire smoke that has crossed the US border.Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, isn’t happy about Trump’s painful, new 50% tariff. “We won’t back down,” he said on social media. “The fastest and only way to get US alcohol back on Ontario shelves is for the U.S. to drop its illegal tariffs on Canada.”As for the new tariffs hitting more than 80 countries, Trump, who over the years hasshown next to no concernabout worker exploitation, turned rather surprisingly to the issue of forced labor to slap on those tariffs.After the supreme court overturned his Liberation Day tariffs, Trump hit dozens of nations with a replacement tariff that would expire after 150 days. Eager to follow the boss’s wishes and impose a new tariff as soon as that one expired, Trump’s toadies uncovered a trade law provision that lets Washington punish countries that fail to take enough action against forced labor. No surprise here: Trump’s US trade representative issued a report that made the boss happy. That report found that dozens of countries, including Canada, the UK, Australia, Norway, Japan and China, plus the European Union, were not doing enough to enforce a prohibition against forced labor. That report pointed to forced labor inproducing rice in Myanmar, tobacco in Malawi, and cotton and polysilicon in China.It’s deeply perplexing that Trump is punishing some of these trading partners. Norway haspioneered lawsto crack down on forced labor in overseas supply chains, while the European Union’snew ban on goods produced with forced laborwill take effect in December 2027. Canadaalready bans imports made with forced labor, and is moving to strengthen that prohibition.If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world | Eduardo PorterRead moreIt’s not as if Trump has shown much concern before about worker exploitation or forced labor. In 1998, Trump agreed to pay$1.375m to settle a lawsuitbrought by undocumented Polish workers who said they were underpaid for their work demolishing a department store to make way for Trump Tower in New York. Sometrade experts criticize Trumpfor slamming all these longtime allies about forced labor even as he is pushing vigorously to improve ties with China, which the Biden administration found to haveserious forced labor problems in its Xinjiang region.Trump’s newfound concern about forced labor rings especially hollow considering that his administrationchopped more than $500m from the labor department’s effortsto investigate and fight against forced labor, child labor and human trafficking. “This was a completely indiscriminate meat axthat was taken to these projects, and workers will suffer,” said Thea Lee, who served as the labor department’s deputy undersecretary for international labor affairs under Biden. Bemoaning that $500m-plus in cuts, Kelly Fay Rodriguez, who was Biden’s special representative for international labor affairs, told Equal Times. “Unfortunately, it is extremely likely that child labor and forced labor practiceswill increase. We know these problems are endemic but … we’ve wiped out the resources and the prioritization for fighting them.”Imagine a world whereDonald Trumptruly cared about worker exploitation and forced labor. He would be pushing to raise the absurdly low $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage – something he has never lifted a finger to do. He would be increasing, rather than cutting, the number of safety inspectors for mines and factories. He would be pushing to strengthen – instead of repeatedly moving to weaken – the nation’s labor unions, long the most effective voice in fighting against worker exploitation. He would be pressuring China’s President Xi Jinping to stop all the forced labor in his country. But that would be a make-believe Donald Trump – he cares far more about what’s good for billionaires than what’s good for workers.Bottom line: there remains far too much forced labor in the world –more than 27 million children, women and menare in forced labor, according to the International Labor Organization. It would be great if Donald Trump sincerely seized on that issue rather than used it as an insincere pretext to clobber other nations with tariffs.Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump tariffsTariffsTrump administrationUS foreign policyCanadacommentShareReuse this content

title: Oil prices fall as US pauses strikes on Iran over strait of Hormuz | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fall
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Brent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fall
Content: The US has suspended its bombing campaign around the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/APView image in fullscreenThe US has suspended its bombing campaign around the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/APOilOil prices fall as US pauses strikes on Iran over strait of HormuzBrent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fallJasper JollyMon 27 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 04.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOil prices have dropped sharply as traders bet that a pause in US attacks on Iran could prevent an escalation in the conflict that would further restrict global supply.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, initially fell 9% to below $88 a barrel on Monday after climbing to $100 last week, when the Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea.An attempted recovery later in the day was halted by comments from Donald Trump that the US was having “good talks” with Iran, pushing Brent back down about 8%.The retreat from the short-lived return to more than $100 a barrel came as the US and Iran paused hostilities after 13 days of fighting, amid Trump’s comments suggesting that talks to end the conflict had resumed.US pauses Iran attacks after Trump advised to halt bombingRead moreIran said it hadstopped “retaliatory” attacksafter two nights without American missiles, after the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, told journalists on Sunday that Trump had decided to pause the attacks to allow more time for diplomacy. Separate reports claimed that US military officials had told Trump that the bombing campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness and warned of dwindling stocks of munitions.The comments raised hopes that a renewed focus on diplomatic solutions could de-escalate the regional conflict, which since the end of February has disrupted flows of oil and gas from Gulf states via the strait of Hormuz, and in recent weeks has interrupted vesselsleaving the Red Sea via the Bab al-Mandabstrait, too.However, the brief reprieve from rising oil prices was met with scepticism by some market observers. “We’ve been here multiple times since March,” said Ole Hvalbye, an analyst at SEB Research. “And each rally on a leak has faded as substance failed to materialise.”John Evans, an analyst at PVM, said he expected oil prices would only be able to fall further if there was a meaningful decline in demand, “not questionable mini-ceasefires”.He said: “The market seems to be forever seeking good news from an arena that really is not providing any. A stay of military strikes might seem an improvement, but it does not come with any guarantees that oil will soon flow from the area.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnalysts at Deutsche Bank led by Jim Reid said the 10% increase in Brent crude prices last week had “added to fears that the global economy was facing a prolonged inflation shock, and that the Fed might need to hike rates more aggressively in response”.The expectation of higher inflation caused by rising global energy costs has put pressure on central banks to raise interest rates. In recent weeks that has pushed up sovereign bond yields, which move inversely to prices. However, the oil price drop on Monday prompted yields to fall. The yield on UK 10-year government debt dropped below 5%, down 0.05 percentage points during the day. The rate-sensitive two-year yield fell 0.06 percentage points to 4.35%.Higher oil prices could harm Trump politically, with many members of the Republican party nervous of the effects of inflation on their prospects at midterm elections in November. Some Federal Reserve policymakers may feel the need to raise interest rates to try to counteract price increases, a move that could slow the US economy – despite Trump’s wish for lower rates.Explore more on these topicsOilEnergy industryCommoditiesInterest ratesStrait of HormuzEconomicsGlobal economynewsShareReuse this content

title: AstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’ | AstraZeneca | The Guardian
description: Europe and US risk being outpaced on innovation, as happened in the car industry, warns Pascal Soriot
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Europe and US risk being outpaced on innovation, as happened in the car industry, warns Pascal Soriot
Content: Pascal Soriot is AstraZeneca’s chief executive and the highest-paid leader of a FTSE 100 company.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/ReutersView image in fullscreenPascal Soriot is AstraZeneca’s chief executive and the highest-paid leader of a FTSE 100 company.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/ReutersAstraZenecaAstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’Europe and US risk being outpaced on innovation, as happened in the car industry, warns Pascal SoriotJasper JollyMon 27 Jul 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 15.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstraZeneca must operate at “Chinese speed” to ensure it does not suffer the fate of the western automotive industry by losing out to more innovative rivals, the drug company’s boss has said.The FTSE 100 company is watching the rise of China’s pharmaceutical industry closely and collaborating to take drugs to global markets, but its chief executive, Pascal Soriot, said the US and European pharmaceutical sectors must focus on increasing the speed of innovation.“We have to make sure we don’t fall behind,” Soriot said. “What we are learning ourselves is we have to move much faster. We always talk about Chinese speed in our company, and we want to operate in Chinese speed.”AstraZeneca said on Monday it was confident of hitting its growth targets for 2030, when itexpects to make $80bn (£60bn) in annual sales, up from $59bn last year. The British company, headquartered in Cambridge, reported revenues of £30.7bn in the first half of 2026, a 6% increase on the same period a year earlier at constant exchange rates.Soriot, thehighest-paid FTSE 100 chief executive, said the pipeline of new drugs from the company was “unmatched”, putting it on course to hit the growth targets in 2030 and beyond despite the surprise failure of Wainua, one of its major heart disease drug prospects, in clinical trials earlier this month.“We have to accept to fail some of the time,” Soriot said. “Biology is biology.”AstraZeneca makes surprise U-turn with £300m pharma investment in UKRead moreDespite confidence in growth prospects, French-born Soriot acknowledged that dominant pharmaceutical companies in Europe and the US needed to be aware of the potential challenge from Chinese competitors.He cited the automotive industry as an example, where western companies had predominantly focused on making cars with petrol engines, leaving the way clear for Chinese companiesto dominate electric car sales.“Chinese companies were focused completely on electric vehicles and batteries and those kinds of technologies,” Soriot said, adding that Chinese pharmaceutical companies were investing heavily in equivalent novel technologies such as antibody drug conjugates, which deliver chemotherapy agents directly to cancer cells, and cell therapy, in which live cells are injected into the body to help fight diseases.Sorit also played down the risk to jobsposed by AI, which he said could increase the speed of drug development, particularly in the design of trial protocols.He said he believed AI tools would help improve productivity in the pharma industry, allowing for economic growth rather than meaning fewer people would be needed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This story about AI killing jobs is a bit of a fake story,” Soriot said. “I can tell you it makes me faster and smarter,” he added, of his experience interacting with AI tools.Soriot said that AstraZeneca would engage with the UK government under its new leader, Andy Burnham, to seek clarity on adeal with the USthat could result in the NHS paying billions of pounds more for medicines.He said it was too early to say whether the change in leadership would have any effect on the deal – struck under pressure from Donald Trump, who threatened to impose heavy tariffs on UK drug exports to the US – which analysis has suggested could lead to229,000 excess deaths in England.“We need to understand their priorities and where the priorities are,” Soriot said. “You have to establish your priorities and then fund them.”Explore more on these topicsAstraZenecaPharmaceuticals industryDrugsEuropenewsShareReuse this title: The lessons of the WNBA’s triumphant All-Star Weekend: ‘get off the ’net’ and lean into the joy | WNBA | The Guardian
description: The buildup to this All-Star Game had some headaches, but the festivities in Chicago – with a Barack Obama cameo and a record crowd – were a rousing high
Author: Stephanie Kaloi
Headline: The buildup to this All-Star Game had some headaches, but the festivities in Chicago – with a Barack Obama cameo and a record crowd – were a rousing high
Content: Jonquel Jones celebrates with Team Spoon teammate Caitlin Clark after their win in Saturday night’s WNBA All-Star Game in Chicago.Photograph: Sage Zipeto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJonquel Jones celebrates with Team Spoon teammate Caitlin Clark after their win in Saturday night’s WNBA All-Star Game in Chicago.Photograph: Sage Zipeto/Getty ImagesWNBAThe lessons of the WNBA’s triumphant All-Star Weekend: ‘get off the ’net’ and lean into the joyThe buildup to this All-Star Game had some headaches, but the festivities in Chicago – with a Barack Obama cameo and a record crowd – were a rousing highSign up for our free weekly WNBA 30 newsletterStephanie Kaloiin ChicagoMon 27 Jul 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf your perceptions of what theWNBAis like in 2026 are largely shaped by narratives derived from and driven by social media, the scene in Chicago at WNBA All-Star Weekend would have proved a surprise.The mood Friday morning at the Barack Obama Presidential Center was downright ebullient. And, sure, to a degree that was because No 44 himself clocked in for about an hour of practice. The former president briefly showed off some moves in his jeans and loafers afterhe was surprise-attackedby the New York Liberty’s Jonquel Jones.But there was something else in the air: everyone was just excited to be there. All-Star provides a brief respite from the slog of the regular season, a couple of days of either total rest for those who aren’t playing or the chance to spend time alongside friends they don’t usually play with for those who are.Sign up for WNBA 30: a limited run women’s basketball newsletterRead moreLast year’sAll-Star Gamewas held in Indianapolis under a cloud of tension. The players were preparing for what would prove to be a months-long period spent negotiating terms for a new collective bargaining agreement. Fans, who often get their WNBA news from social media, made their support for the athletes known; the game ended with chants of“Pay them!”ringing out in Gainbridge Fieldhouse.A year later, theCBA is doneand players are getting paid, but the weeks preceding this summer’s All-Star Game were filled with no shortage of headaches and problems. An offseason taskforce designed to improve foul calls and officiatingresultedin changes in policy and practice that are still being rolled out; incidences ofhard fouls, such as when Alyssa Thomas accidentally pushed her fist into Caitlin Clark’s throat during a game last month, were handled through the proper league channels but were inflamed online, by people genuinely invested in the league but also those who just want to stir up problems.And that’s not all: the week before the All-Star Game saw two incidents that went against the spirit of theleague’s “No Space For Hate” platform, which was unveiled last year and “reflects the WNBA’s unwavering commitment to protecting its players and upholding the values of inclusion, respect, and unity”. The Toronto Tempo’s head coach Sandy Brondello wascaughton a hot mic calling Atlanta Dream star Angel Reese a “protected species”, and Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham brazenly used transphobic language in an apparent attempt to defend herself against the nickname “Maga Barbie”.Brondelloissued a heartfelt apologyto Reese and was suspended for one game. Cunningham told ESPN she wants to “protect young girls in the locker room” from “biological men” – a phrase thatGLAAD has identifiedas a hate term – and then doubled down on her stance.Coverage of those events (and more) appeared to have reached even Obama himself. “You’re great. You’re fantastic. Don’t let all this nonsense get you down,” Obama told Clark. “To have that much immersion in nonsense ... don’t lose that joy. The game’s the game, and you’re a hooper. You’re always hooping, and you’re on a nice little run right now.”(“My hands were getting a little bit sweaty, and I don’t really get nervous for anybody,” Clark told reporters after the interaction. “But that’s somebody like, just his presence commands a room.”)View image in fullscreenFormer president Barack Obama met the WNBA All-Stars on Friday.Photograph: Paul Beaty/APIn other words, this year’s All-Star Game could have been messy. Instead, it was one of the best weekends in league history, and ended with a historic attendance (19,783 people showed up for the game at United Center) and a series of announcements from Commissioner Cathy Engelbert – including a replay center that should make for stronger officiating next season – that indicate things are only getting better for the WNBA.Throughout the weekend, players and coaches embraced the success of the league while acknowledging there’s room for more. Speaking to reporters Friday, Minnesota Lynx guard Courtney Williams emphasized staying positive when she can. “I lean into the love, for sure. I feel in the W, as opposed to men’s sports, there’s more pressure to be online,” she said. “I feel it just depends on who you are. If you like to be on the ’net, be on the ’net. If you don’t like the ’net, get off the ’net.”Las Vegas Aces head coach Becky Hammon echoed that sentiment. When it comes to how stories about the WNBA reverberate through the media and social media, Hammon said: “I think the biggest mistake is maybe the people that talk the most know the least on some of these topics. They don’t have a good pulse on our league at times.”“Honestly, I don’t really pay attention so much to what everybody else is saying either. I’m busy trying to win games … and put a great product on the court,” she continued. “And, hopefully, as many people as possible want to come to see great basketball.”Not everyone in the league is as offline. Theaverage age of WNBA playersis approximately 27; adults in their 20s havenearly universal internet use. The StudBudz – the duo of Williams and Seattle Storm guard Natisha Hiedeman – ran a 24-hour Twitch livestream of the weekend’s events, and plenty of people use Threads and Instagram to speak to and interact with fans. The internet can be a dark place, but it’s also one that can be a lot of fun.“There’s a lot of great players here with different backgrounds, different stories,” Dallas Wings forwardJessica Shepard told the Guardian on Friday. Those differences only make the league stronger, she added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I think anytime you have diversity, anytime you have people who have different stories, it definitely creates a nice environment,” Shepard said of the league. “I think also for the younger generation, it gives everyone someone to look up to that maybe has a similar story to them.”That’s what “All-Star is really all about,” Las Vegas Aces center and four-time MVP A’ja Wilson told the Guardian. “We come together in this place.”View image in fullscreenGabby Williams and Paige Bueckers during Saturday’s All-Star Game, which drew a record crowd of 19,783.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APIf there’s one person in the WNBA who can’t avoid the internet, it’s Engelbert. As the head of the league, Engelbert bears the brunt of joy and disappointment from fans, coaches, owners, and, most importantly to her, the players.While addressing the media on Saturday, Engelbert admitted her leadership could improve. She acknowledged there are “processes around fines, suspensions, and investigations,” and dismissed the idea that the league only looks into certain instances in response to social media outcry. The CBA negotiations were “contentious”, she added, but Engelbert said that this year “we’re in a really good place.”She also explained player safety is constantly top of mind, and that includes what happens on and off the court.“The internet is a very complicated place,” Engelbert said, a sentence that practically vibrates with relevance in 2026. “And, someone gave me this term, keyboard warriors are very, very adamant to get their messages through to our players, whether it’s through DMs, whether it’s through other means.”One way Engelbert personally plays to continue to nurture a safer environment for the league’s athletes is to reach out directly more frequently. The commissioner said she believed “players don’t want to hear from us all the time”, but learned at a meeting with the WNBPA last week that crucial league communications are often missed by players who didn’t receive them or aren’t reading articles about those announcements. When it comes to that two-way street between the league and players, “there’s no doubt I need to be better,” Engelbert said. “Everybody needs to be better at communication, I think, all the time.”The city of Chicago and maybe even the WNBA (including Engelbert, who oversaw it all) can bask in a job well done and a weekend where joy and celebration of30 seasonsof WNBA was the mission. The entire league gets back to work this week, but will do so after riding a very singular, and very special, kind of high.Explore more on these topicsWNBAUS sportsCaitlin ClarkBarack ObamafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Son of Kansas City Chiefs assistant Eric Bieniemy charged in shooting of his mother | Kansas City Chiefs | The Guardian
description: Authorities in Loudoun County, Virginia, have arrested Elijah Bieniemy, the son of Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Authorities in Loudoun County, Virginia, have arrested Elijah Bieniemy, the son of Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy
Content: Eric Bieniemy is the offensive coordinator for the Kansas City Chiefs.Photograph: Charlie Riedel/APView image in fullscreenEric Bieniemy is the offensive coordinator for the Kansas City Chiefs.Photograph: Charlie Riedel/APKansas City ChiefsSon of Kansas City Chiefs assistant Eric Bieniemy charged in shooting of his motherVirginia authorities arrest 27-year-old Elijah BieniemyMia Bieniemy is stable after multiple gunshot woundsKansas City OC was at team camp in Missouri on SundayAssociated PressMon 27 Jul 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe son of Chiefs assistant coach Eric Bieniemy has been arrested and charged with the shooting of his mother, Mia Bieniemy, the wife of the Kansas City offensive coordinator, authorities in Virginia said Monday.The Loudon county sheriff’s office said deputies responded late Sunday to a shooting in Ashburn, Virginia, where the couple still had a home from Bieniemy’s time with the Washington Commanders. They found the 57-year-old Mia Bieniemy with multiple gunshot wounds, and she was transported to a hospital where she was in stable condition MondayElijah Zion Bieniemy, the 27-year-old son of the couple, was arrested in connection with the shooting. He has been charged with malicious wounding, use of a firearm in commission of a felony and discharge of a firearm inside a dwelling, and is being held without bond at the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center.The sheriff’s office said the investigation was ongoing.Eric Bieniemy was with the Chiefs at their practice in St Joseph, Missouri, earlier Sunday. He was not present for Monday’s workout, which was closed to the public. The team did not plan any media availability afterward.“The club is aware of the incident involving Eric Bieniemy’s family,” the team told the Associated Press in a statement. “Out of respect for their privacy, we won’t have a comment at this time. Our thoughts and prayers are with them.”Eric Bieniemy was part of Chiefs coach Andy Reid’s initial staff in Kansas City in 2013, and spent five seasons as the running backs coach before he was promoted to offensive coordinator. Over the next five seasons, the demanding but popular Bieniemy helped the Chiefs reach three Super Bowls and win two of them while helping to direct one of the NFL’s best offenses.He interviewed for several head-coaching jobs but was continually skipped over, so Bieniemy went to the Commanders in 2023 in hopes of burnishing his résumé. But the team struggled and coach Ron Rivera’s staff was let go, and Bieniemy spent one season as the offensive coordinator at UCLA before spending last season as the running backs coach with the Chicago Bears.Bieniemy returned to the Chiefs this season to replace Matt Nagy as the offensive coordinator. He was present for offseason workouts in Kansas City over the summer, and he was with the team when they began to report to training camp last week.The Chiefs are off Tuesday. The first full-squad workout at Missouri Western State University is Wednesday.“It’s great to have [Bieniemy] back in the building,” Reid said last week. “He always brings great energy. I’ve told you, he’s one of the more phenomenal guys I have been around at being a leader of men. He is doing that. He’s in there cranking – works his tail off, and I appreciate that. Doesn’t let anything slide by. Does a good job with that.”Explore more on these topicsKansas City ChiefsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mind the ever-growing gap: the Premier League keeps spending big | Premier League | The Guardian
description: English clubs have spent more on players this summer than the other four major European leagues combined
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: English clubs have spent more on players this summer than the other four major European leagues combined
Content: Bradley Barcola could be the next expensive import to move to the Premier League.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenBradley Barcola could be the next expensive import to move to the Premier League.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyPremier LeagueMind the ever-growing gap: the Premier League keeps spending bigEnglish clubs have spent more on players this summer than the other four major European leagues combinedAndrew BeasleyMon 27 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe financial power of thePremier Leagueis unmatched. The teams in England’s top division have collectively invested more than £1.4bn in new players already this summer (through disclosed fees alone), around £303m more than the 76 clubs from the Bundesliga, La Liga, Ligue 1 and Serie A combined.These figures are the gross spend, so take no account of players sold to help balance the books. Factoring this in only increases the divide. The clubs of Ligue 1 and the Bundesliga are £203.4m and £72.2m in credit from their transfer dealings respectively. While La Liga (£163.1m) and Serie A (£124.1m) have spent more than they have earned, they are an ocean adrift of the Premier League’s net spend of £523.6m.None of this is new; it has been the trend for many years. The worrying aspect for teams across the continent is that the gap between the Premier League and the rest may grow wider before the summer is out.Chart showing net transfer spend in Europe’s big five leagues in summer 2026Despite their enormous outlay, top-flight English teams have spent about £230m less than Premier League clubs of 2025-26 had at this point last year. But only 25 deals were completed by the end of 1 July (which is when new contracts usually start, explaining why pre-arranged moves are often finalised then). It’s roughly half as many as the 47 that occurred by that date last summer. The expanded World Cup will probably have delayed some deals, creating a potential backlog of transfer spending that will soon hit the books.Assessing clubs individually highlights why most might continue spending. Aston Villa, Brighton and Tottenham have already spent more in gross terms than in the entirety of the summer 2025 transfer window. Unai Emery has a net £109.6m burning a hole in his pocket following business which includes the departures of Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans. Brighton will need a larger squad as they have a Conference League campaign on the horizon while Tottenham are hoping to improve upon consecutive 17th-place finishes. Their trading may not be complete even though they’ve already outspent their efforts from last summer, with Spurs’ net spend of £149.7m the highest in Europe’s big five leagues.Chart showing net transfer spend by Premier League clubs in summer 2025 and summer 2026Chelsea also have a higher net spend than last year, even before their reportedly agreed deal for Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix goes through. Even if that transfer is not completed, would you bet against BlueCo throwing more money around, especially with a new manager to back?Danny Welbeck is the latest to emergeon the Stamford Bridge radar. Either way, Chelsea have already invested more in new talent than they had on this day last year. The same is true for Everton, Fulham, Manchester City and Newcastle, all of whom may have further incomings in the pipeline, too.There are other clubs with work to do. The three promoted teams have only spent £8m more between them than Sunderland alone had at this point in 2025. Régis Le Bris added a total of 18 new players to his squad last summer, with fellow promoted sides Burnley (15) and Leeds (11) also hitting double figures for incomings. By these standards, Ipswich (with seven new players), Hull (four) and Coventry (three) must recruit further.At the opposite end of the Premier League scale, Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have collectively spent two-thirds of a billion less on new talent than they did last summer.The latest rumour millgossip says the champions may make a move for Vinícius Júnior. If not the Brazilian then perhaps Bradley Barcola, though Liverpool are also said to be pursuing the Paris Saint-Germain winger. Neither player will be remotely cheap. United are believed to be targeting Ollie Watkins – he wouldn’t cost Vinícius or Barcola money, but neither would Villa sell to a rival at a reduced fee.The Premier League also has clubs who have yet to make an outlay. It is unlikely Crystal Palace, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland end the summer without spending a transfer fee as is now the case. It would be remiss of Palace and Sunderland not to invest when they are in European competition this season. As for Forest, like Chelsea they have had an insatiable thirst for player turnover in recent times. With Elliot Anderson having left for an enormous fee, replacements will surely arrive soon.It is remarkable to think the Premier League may not be halfway through its summer outlay when £1.4bn has already been used for recruitment. The top-flight English clubs collectively spent £3.1bn on players last summer, with over £600m in the final week of dealing alone. That figure may be blown away by the time the transfer window closes on 3 September.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTransfer windowfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fifa president Gianni Infantino called to appear before Congress over Trump ties | World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Democrat Jamie Raskin pushes Fifa to release records of contact with Trump, administration and family business
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: Democrat Jamie Raskin pushes Fifa to release records of contact with Trump, administration and family business
Content: Donald Trump joins Fifa president Gianni Infantino on the field for the trophy presentation at the World Cup final.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenDonald Trump joins Fifa president Gianni Infantino on the field for the trophy presentation at the World Cup final.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto/AllstarWorld Cup 2026Fifa president Gianni Infantino called to appear before Congress over Trump tiesDemocrat Jamie Raskin pushes Fifa to release records of contact with Trump, administration and family businessElla BrockwayMon 27 Jul 2026 16.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, has launched an investigation into Fifa presidentGianni Infantino, seeking documents that would detail the ties between soccer’s governing body and Donald Trump and his administration.In a Sunday letter, Raskin wrote to Infantino and called forFifato provide any documents and communications related to gifts, payments or benefits provided to Trump and his associates, as well as the visitor logs for Fifa’s office space in Trump Tower, which it acquired last year. The committee also requested that Infantino sit for a transcribed interview.Infantino’s relationship with Trump came under scrutiny in the lead-up to this summer’s World Cup. In December, at the World Cup draw in Washington, Trump was awardeda newly created “Fifa peace prize”at the Kennedy Center, where renovations were allegedly “rushed” on theadministration’s ordersto prepare for the event. Fifaopenedits office in Trump Tower in midtown Manhattan last July.Fifa president Gianni Infantino accuses critics of spreading hate at World CupRead moreSuch scrutiny intensified during theWorld Cup. Trump made several calls to Infantino to lobby for a review of US striker Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before the Americans’ last-16 match against Belgium. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team and drew the ire of other teams and associations from around the world.Alongside the leaders of Canada and Mexico, TrumpjoinedInfantino for the World Cup trophy presentation after Spain beat Argentina in the final. The pair, who watched the final together in a glassed-in section of luxury seats, were met with boos from the New York New Jersey Stadium crowd when they took the field.Raskin’s letter references the Department of Justice’s decision to “dismiss the indictments” of defendants in US government investigations into corruption in global soccer, including the 2015 prosecution of more than 20 high-level Fifa officials and sports-marketing executives.“[Y]our election as Fifa president was supposed to mark a red-card break from a decades-long culture of corruption and scandals that dressed down world soccer’s reputation,” Raskin wrote to Infantino in the letter. “Instead, at the start of your tenure, you dismantled Fifa’s ethical guardrails and disabled the organization’s ethics committee by pushing out most of its members. This lack of transparency and oversight has since paved the way for you to ingratiate yourself with the Trump administration via tactics that a New York University law professor and one of your former ethics committeemen described as ‘legal bribery’.”The letter also addresses Fifa’s World Cup ticketing policy, which is already the subject ofinvestigationsby several attorneys general in the United States. The use of dynamic pricing drew much criticism during the tournament, leading to massive surges and pricing out many fans from attending games.“The most recent quid pro quo that Fifa and President Trump orchestrated is not a victimless crime. It hurts Americans. Fifa has taken its newfound favored status in the Trump administration as a sign that it may rip off its consumers, most notably, by employing illegal price-gouging and fraudulent sales tactics for the World Cup,” Raskin said in the letter.The letter gives a deadline of 9 August to provide the requested documents and schedule the interview. Raskin does not have the power to compel Infantino to appear, given that Democrats do not hold the majority in the House, unless he garners Republican support.Fifa’s interactions with the US government did not end with this summer’s World Cup. The US is expected to be the primary host of the Women’s World Cup in 2031, and the success of this year’s tournament has led many to speculate thatthe 2038 men’s World Cupcould be hosted by the US. Fifa has been approached for comment.Earlier on Monday, Infantinoused a 15-part messageon Instagram to denounce his critics, accusing them of spreading hate and false narratives. He touted the World Cup as a success.More than 200 Fifa members haveendorsedInfantino ahead of the presidential election in March, but some associations have stood in opposition. The Norwegian football federation isplanningto submit a formal complaint to Fifa ethics investigations over Trump’s role in the reversal of Balogun’s ban.Explore more on these topicsWorld Cup 2026World CupUS sportsGianni InfantinoFifaDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: North Carolina place GM Michael Lombardi, Belichick’s right-hand man, on paid leave | College football | The Guardian
description: The university announced on Monday it had put Lombardi, a former NFL general manager who was an immediate hire by Belichick, on paid administrative leave
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The university announced on Monday it had put Lombardi, a former NFL general manager who was an immediate hire by Belichick, on paid administrative leave
Content: Michael Lombardi, left, joined Bill Belichick at North Carolina when the six-time Super Bowl-winning coach was hired in late 2024.Photograph: Lance King/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMichael Lombardi, left, joined Bill Belichick at North Carolina when the six-time Super Bowl-winning coach was hired in late 2024.Photograph: Lance King/Getty ImagesCollege footballNorth Carolina place GM Michael Lombardi, Belichick’s right-hand man, on paid leaveFootball program does not provide details for moveLombardi had pledged to make UNC ‘the 33rd [NFL] team’Associated PressMon 27 Jul 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorth Carolina football general manager Michael Lombardi has been placed on paid administrative leave.The school announced the move with a statement Monday morning, days before the Tar Heels open preseason camp. The school didn’t provide details as to the reason, noting that employees and athletes aren’t permitted to address the topic “as is standard procedure with personnel matters”.Lombardi joined Bill Belichick in making the NFL-to-college move when the schoolhired the former New England Patriots coachin December 2024. Lombardi’s career as an NFL executive had included being the general manager of the Cleveland Browns in 2013, and he was an immediate hire by the six-time Super Bowl-winning coach in Chapel Hill.The school had hired Belichick to jolt a football program that had largely been an Atlantic Coast Conference also-ran while making periodic but unsustained climbs into national relevance.A few months into Belichick’s tenure, Lombardi said the goal was running a college program in a way similar to the NFL, saying the Tar Heels “consider ourselves the 33rd [NFL] team” due to the staff connections to the pros.The Tar Heels went just 4-8 in Belichick’s first season. They open his second season against TCU in Dublin, Ireland, on 29 August.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballUS sportsCollege sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tadej Pogacar’s ability to win unopposed stands champion out among Tour legends | Tadej Pogacar | The Guardian
description: The Slovene is the youngest of the five riders to win five Tours de France and few would bet against him claiming a sixth victory next year
Author: William Fotheringham
Headline: The Slovene is the youngest of the five riders to win five Tours de France and few would bet against him claiming a sixth victory next year
Content: Tadej Pogacar ends his long journey on the streets of Paris.Photograph: Garnier Etienne/ReutersView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar ends his long journey on the streets of Paris.Photograph: Garnier Etienne/ReutersTadej PogacarTadej Pogacar’s ability to win unopposed stands champion out among Tour legendsWilliam FotheringhamSlovene is youngest of riders to win five Tours de France and few would bet against him claiming sixth victory next yearMon 27 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.07 EDTShareThe 2026Tour de Franceserved up an epic battle that lasted for day after day between two protagonists of the highest calibre with different skillsets, a tale of epic breakaways, intriguing team tactics and reversals of fortune, building to a spectacular climax on the race’s toughest stage. The contest for the green jersey of points winner between Mads Pedersen and Jasper Philipsen was a classic.Those hoping for something similar in the race for the yellow jersey of overall winner were disappointed,and rapidly. Any suspense was eliminated with 42km of stage six remaining, high above the ski village of La Mongie, when Tadej Pogacar dislodged Jonas Vingegaard and the other putative race favourites on the Col du Tourmalet. It was a familiar stinging attack, and a familiar outcome, with the Slovene opening a lead that looked insurmountable, as indeed it was.Analysing the race for themaillot jauneto the RMC radio station, the former FDJ United manager Marc Madiot did not mince his words: “There was one single rider who attacked in this Tour:Tadej Pogacar. He attacked once, and everyone understood it was finished.”Unfortunately for the neutrals, the art of cycling’s greats boils down to this: they don’t so much kill suspense as tie it up and eviscerate it before jumping up and down on its steaming remains. The neutrals have to make do with Pedersen and the green jersey, or Richard Carapaz and the polka dots.From that moment on the Tourmalet, the chances of Pogacar joining Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin as a five-times Tour winner were nailed on, and on Sunday evening, the world champion duly entered the record books. Even with the rise of Paul Seixas and Remco Evenepoel’s confirmation as a man of the Tour, few would bet against “Pogi” taking the absolute record in 2027 if he chooses to do so.View image in fullscreenFive-time winner Bernard Hinault (right) challenges Greg Lemond in the 1986 Tour.Photograph: Lionel Cironneau/APPogacar is exceptional in many areas, but in the elite club of quintuple Tour winners he also stands out: he is younger than the other four and, unlike all those who have stood in Paris as a five‑time winner of the world’s greatest bike race, there were no glitches or question marks to disrupt his serene progress to the record books. Unlike all the previous true greats, at no point in the past few weekscould Pogacar wonder if victory might slip away.Speculation that he might have switched to black shorts in the final week to disguise stomach issues doesn’t cut it as a glitch – not compared with the broken nose that left Hinault looking like a boxer who’d had a bad night in the final week of win number five after a finish-line crash at Saint-Étienne. Or with the open wound on the crutch that dogged Merckx throughout the 1974 race, needing “constant care, bathing, the application of cream and sterile plasters, and cushioning with bits of foam and plasters”. Merckx did win eight stages in that Tour, but he was close to collapse on the mountain-top finish at Pla d’Adet and was never the same athlete again.Similarly, although he was eventually stripped of the victory for doping, 2003 was the only Tour when Lance Armstrong did not have the race sewn up until the final time trial, while in 1995, “Big Mig” Induráin and his Banesto team had to cope with a day of crisis in the Massif Central en route to Mende. Anquetil, famously, was run close by Raymond Poulidor in 1964, and could thank his lucky stars that “PouPou” suffered a puncture in a key time trial.View image in fullscreenMiguel Indurain was renowned as a Grand Tour specialist.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianIn the pantheon of cycling’s greatest champions, Pogacar has long since outstripped Big Mig, physically impressive but essentially a Grand Tour specialist who shied away from one-day Classics and never won a world road race title. He is far above the calculating but charismatic Anquetil, another who never shone in the Classics, although Pogi will never have the chance to match “Master Jacques” most insanely quixotic career challenge, winning the Dauphiné Libéré stage race (now known as the Tour Auvergne Rhone Alps) and the Bordeaux‑Paris motorpaced marathon without a day off.Quick GuideCycling all-time greats' prizesShowEddy Merckx11 Grand Tours, 3 world road titles, 1 Hour Record, 19 Monument ClassicsBernard Hinault9 Grand Tours, 1 world road title, 6 Monument ClassicsTadej Pogacar6 Grand Tours, 2 world road titles, 13 Monument ClassicsWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.When you get to Hinault, the statistical game becomes more nuanced, the debate more interesting. Pogacar has forged ahead of the “Badger” in major one-day wins – 13 Monument Classics and counting, plus two world road titles – but Hinault has won more Grand Tours, having won the Vuelta and Giro twice each, to Pogacar’s single Giro win. As for Merckx, the Slovene has won fewer Grand Tours, fewer world titles and fewer Monuments than the “Cannibal”, who also, famously and painfully, claimed the world one-hour record.The debate over who is the greatest will continue and could well take a further twist if Pogacar rides the Vuelta and world championships later in the year, because if he starts those races, the chances are he will win both. Only when Merckx and Hinault were in their absolute prime could that be written, and that is the best reflection of where the past three weeks have put him.Explore more on these topicsTadej PogacarTour de France 2026Tour de FranceCyclingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The 2026 World Cup is over, but the onslaught of soccer relentlessly rolls on | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The supply of soccer seems to be enormously exceeding demand. It’s made the sport feel utterly overwhelming
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The supply of soccer seems to be enormously exceeding demand. It’s made the sport feel utterly overwhelming
Content: Liverpool supporters during a preseason friendly in the US; a Premier League ball; Rodri holding the World Cup.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskView image in fullscreenLiverpool supporters during a preseason friendly in the US; a Premier League ball; Rodri holding the World Cup.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskSoccer with Jonathan WilsonSoccerThe 2026 World Cup is over, but the onslaught of soccer relentlessly rolls onLeander SchaerlaeckensThe supply of soccer seems to be enormously exceeding demand. It’s made the sport feel utterly overwhelmingMon 27 Jul 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.11 EDTShareOn Friday, the Scottish Premiership kicks off its 2026-27 season. The following Friday, the Dutch Eredivisie begins anew, and England’s Carabao Cup sets off on its ponderous journey. The various European club competitions have already begun their qualifying rounds – and did so on 7 July, in the case of the Champions and Conference Leagues. Liga MX is two rounds into its Apertura season; Major League Soccer resumed its regular season on 16 July. Other soccer is available elsewhere and at other times.It has been only a week since theWorld Cupended.The sense of relentlessness that soccer impels is never more obvious than in the wake of its signature event, when we are reminded that the sport didn’t stop even as the world sort of did. There is no off-season, no respite. One season just bleeds into the next between postseasons and preseasons and the transfer market. Soccer is a permanent condition.From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World CupRead moreThe World Cup derives its power from the feeling that it is possibly the last global piece of monoculture. In another time, the moon landing, or a heavyweight boxing title bout or the crowning of a monarch – back when people cared about such things – might have compelled much of the planet to sit and watch and engage with the same thing, more or less together. In our increasingly fractured experience of the world, it’s sometimes nice to share something in common.Its absence for 47 months out of 48 makes the World Cup rare and allows for anticipation to build. The forces of the sport are arrayed against this moderation, of course, and indeed winning that battle. This World Cup grew by 50% from the last one, to 48 teams. If Fifa had its druthers, it would have a biennial tournament with 64 teams.After all, the only idea in the sport’s executive class is more soccer. The one lesson it seemsnotto have taken from American sports, is that the National Football League retains its status as the sector’s hegemonic power because its product is scarce. Its games feel like events, rather than a routine you can opt out of today and simply make up tomorrow, in spite of the NFL’s own ongoing efforts to lengthen its regular season playing schedule.For a month and change, once every four years, nearly the whole planet watches the same games. Aside from the final days of the group stage, the matches do not overlap, do not conflict, do not counterprogram. During that time, we entertainment consumers inhabit a largely unified reality.And now we shall return to the endless silos dictated algorithmically by our past tastes and behaviors or to our own bespoke suite of players and teams and leagues we currently care about.Outside the World Cup, pro soccer can feel like the Facebook feed you stopped paying attention to years ago because it is just filled with relentless AI slop. Very little seems to be hugely relevant to you, and much of it might not even feel real at all, making it just so very easy to scroll past. It all feels amorphous, a shapeless static creeping about that roughly coalesces into something like soccer when you look up from your other screen.The supply of pro soccer seems to so enormously exceed demand that the market for our attention spans is forever flooded. There’s never a breather. There’s never any anticipation. Very anecdotally, it may be that others are feeling this as well. On Saturday, Liverpool and Sunderland didn’t come close to filling an MLS stadium in Nashville for their preseason friendly. Wrexham and Leeds United, meanwhile, drew a sparse crowd to Tampa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut in a sense, this onslaught has always existed. There is more soccer than there used to be, starting earlier and ending later on whatever calendar it goes by, but there are roughly the same number of domestic competitions. It’s just that they didn’t used to be so readily available across borders. Growing up in Belgium, I had access to a French Ligue 1 highlights show on Sunday mornings, Belgian and Dutch highlights on Sunday evenings and the BBC’s Match of the Day Premier League highlights at night. Every now and again, I’d chance upon a Serie A game on the Italian national broadcaster. Today, sitting in my den in New York, there is seemingly no limit to the games I can access from anywhere in the world.This is not a worse way to live, but it is a more muddled one. And it can make the sport feel utterly overwhelming, like a lone man standing before a tsunami of, and we must invoke the dreaded term … content. Another season has already started, as we still consider and process and digest the last one. Thoughts aren’t fully formed on the World Cup yet, what it meant, how it shifted the sport’s assorted paradigms.We need a break. Yet there is always more soccer.This is an extract from Soccer with Jonathan Wilson, a weekly look from the Guardian US at the game in Europe and beyond, helmed this week by Leander in Jonathan’s absence.Subscribe for free here. Have a question for Jonathan? Emailsoccerwithjw@theguardian.com, and he’ll answer the best in a future edition.Leander Schaerlaeckens is a Guardian US contributor whose book on the US men’s national soccer team, The Long Game, is out now.
