title: ‘It’s human first, then athlete’: Ramsay-Peaty happy with second bronze in new reality | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Adam Ramsay-Peaty said: ‘It’s human first, then athlete, which is a fair price to pay,’ while Scotland’s Archie Goodburn was racing despite his brain cancer diagnosis
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Adam Ramsay-Peaty said: ‘It’s human first, then athlete, which is a fair price to pay,’ while Scotland’s Archie Goodburn was racing despite his brain cancer diagnosis
Content: South Africa’s Michael Houlie (left), Sam Williamson of Australia (centre) and Adam Ramsay-Peaty of England after the 50m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSouth Africa’s Michael Houlie (left), Sam Williamson of Australia (centre) and Adam Ramsay-Peaty of England after the 50m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026‘It’s human first, then athlete’: Ramsay-Peaty happy with second bronze in new realityFormer Olympic champion admits ‘superpower’ waningScotland’s Archie Goodburn in final despite brain cancerSean Ingleat the Tollcross Swimming CentreMon 27 Jul 2026 16.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly after Adam Ramsay-Peaty had battled desperately to snatch another bronze medal at theseCommonwealth Games, it was put to him that he was no longer a winning machine.Once upon a time, Britain’s greatest swimmer might have bristled. Instead he nodded – before pointing out that, at 31, he was now winning in an altogether different way.English part-time sprinter bursts with ‘national pride’ and slams Games no-showsRead more“That period of time where I was undefeated for eight years, whatever it was, it was athlete first, then human,” Ramsay-Peaty said. “Now it’s human first, then athlete, which is a very fair price to pay.”He was then asked whether he could get his superpower back. “My superpower looks very different now. I think juggling babies with milk and having a toddler around is, I guess, a different superpower when that time comes. But as a professional athlete, I’m still committed. I’ve still got that mentality. We just had to approach it very differently because I’ve been that person who wins all the time, and it costs you pretty much everything, and I won’t say it’s worth it now.”Ramsay-Peaty was smiling as he spoke. And he was also smiling after a 50-metre breaststroke final in which he needed a dramatic finish to even get on the podium. He alsowon bronze in the 100m breaststrokeat the weekend.View image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty in the men’s 50m breaststroke.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianNormally Ramsay-Peaty’s best part of his race is the first 30m. At his best, he has already established clear blue water by then. Not this time. He was fighting the water, and his opponents, and it needed a late surge to take him into bronze in 26.94sec – just 0.01 clear of Chris Smith of South Africa. That time was 0.99sec off Ramsay‑Peaty’s world record – and well behind Australia’s Sam Williamson who took gold in 26.50, adding to his 100m breaststroke triumph, with South African Michael Houlie winning silver in 26.77.But while Ramsay-Peaty may be more zen these days, he admits that he is still frustrated with his recent performances. “We weren’t good enough, and we have to look at why because the data in training, the data this whole season, has been tracking on an upward trend, and I can’t really put my finger on it where I’ve just lost that power per stroke,” he said.“I’m not going to lie, it’s very frustrating. Something is not clicking. But it is my first championship since Paris to get two bronzes. You know, we’ve still got relays to go. I’d say that’s success. I’m not going to be too hard on myself, not any more. Let’s keep it in perspective.”That refreshing attitude came to mind as Scotland’s Archie Goodburn received the biggest roar of the night in the same race despite finishing tied last. And no wonder, given the 25‑year‑old was competing here having been diagnosed with terminal brain cancer two years ago.View image in fullscreenArchie Goodburn received a diagnosis of terminal brain cancer two years ago.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA“The reception was monumental,” said Goodburn, who was strikingly positive afterwards. “I tried to prepare myself for it. But that was the next level.”Doctors have diagnosed oligodendrogliomas, which accounts for roughly 3% of all primary brain tumours, and means he may have only a decade to live. But Goodburn has made it his mission to raise as much awareness as possible about the condition.“Every athlete talks about tough times, but there’s been some really tough times,” he said. “And the shoes I was in, or the position I was in this time last year, it was a dark spot.“So looking back on where I am now 12 months later, and everything we’ve managed to achieve over the year, thanks to the support of my friends, family and the University of Edinburgh. I can’t say a big enough thank you. And long may that continue.”Last year, Goodburn started using Vorasidenib – a breakthrough new treatment designed to slow the spread of cancer. That has delayed the prospect of chemotherapy. But there are plenty of tough times ahead.When asked how he remained positive, he was powerful and direct. “I advocate because I believe that my own advocacy can make a difference to my own life. And the best way I can do that is to be positive about the situation and positive for change.“But I also advocate for the future Archies. I swim for future Archies that want to succeed on an international level. But also young patients and people with brain cancer under the age of 40.“Brain cancer is the biggest killer of all cancers for people under the age of 40 in the UK. And I do believe that our advocacy groups are making a difference to that. That we’ll hopefully see over the next few years.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Adam Ramsay-PeatySwimmingCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boss of startup hacked by rogue OpenAI agent urges ‘radical transparency’ in investigation | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Artificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face CEO
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Artificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face CEO
Content: Hugging Face’s boss said the attack by the OpenAI agent deserved an ‘unprecedented response’.Photograph: Andre M Chang/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHugging Face’s boss said the attack by the OpenAI agent deserved an ‘unprecedented response’.Photograph: Andre M Chang/Zuma Press/ShutterstockOpenAIBoss of startup hacked by rogue OpenAI agent urges ‘radical transparency’ in investigationArtificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face CEODan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 27 Jul 2026 08.15 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 08.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of the startup hacked by an OpenAI agent has called for the investigation intothe incidentto show “radical transparency”.Clément Delangue, the chief executive of Hugging Face, said the “unprecedented” attack on his business required a similar response.Writing on X afterOpenAIrevealed that its technology had gone rogue during a cybersecurity test, Delangue also called on the company to provide $100m (£75m) worth of computing power to help build defences against such attacks.Be skeptical of OpenAI’s rogue hacker agent story | John ThickstunRead more“The first autonomous agent cyber-attack is an unprecedented event. It deserves an unprecedented response!” he wrote.OpenAI revealed on Wednesday last week that Hugging Face had been hacked by an agent – an AI tool that can carry out a series of tasks autonomously – powered by a combination of its latest publicly available model,GPT-5.6 Sol, and an even more capable model that was yet to be released. This occurred during a test of the models’ hacking abilities, which included deploying them in a supposedly safe “sandbox” – an enclosed digital laboratory – with lower safety guardrails.Once they had gained the open internet access needed to exit the sandbox, the models targeted Hugging Face, according to OpenAI, because they “inferred” that the startup had the information needed to “cheat the evaluation”. Hugging Face first reported the hack on 16 July and at the time was not aware OpenAI had inadvertently carried out the attack.Delangue, whose company provides a database of AI models to developers, called for a fully transparent review of the incident, which has led to expressions of concern over safety standards at OpenAI and within frontier AI labs.Writing that he had asked for “radical transparency” from OpenAI, Delangue said: “Let’s release the traces from the ‘rogue’ agents so the entire research community can study what happened.” Calling for extra funding from OpenAI to build protection against AI, he added: “Let’s commit $100M in compute from OAI to help the Hugging Face community build powerful cyber defenses with the best open and closed models.”Reuters reported last week that the agent spent days hacking Hugging Face without OpenAI noticing. It also reported an OpenAI agent had left notes for future versions of itself should it require tips on breaking free from internal constraints, although Reuters was unable to verify whether that incident was related to the Hugging Face agent. Time magazine reported that agent-related safety incidents had been “happening for a while”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said Delangue’s call should be heeded. “It’s too easy to ‘blame’ the AI as having gone rogue whereas this is all about how OpenAI were running the tool. What is required is that OpenAI give full details of their setup and how that failed,” he said.OpenAI was approached for comment and referred the Guardian to its initial statement last week in which it said it was investigating an “unprecedented security incident” with Hugging Face.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)HackingInternetTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Honor Magic V6 review: sleek foldable phone lacking a bit of polish | Android | The Guardian
description: Super-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by software
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Super-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by software
Content: Slim, light and long-lasting, the Magic V6 goes the distance while fitting a tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSlim, light and long-lasting, the Magic V6 goes the distance while fitting a tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianAndroidReviewHonor Magic V6 review: sleek foldable phone lacking a bit of polishSuper-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by softwareSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Honor’s svelteAndroidphone-tablet has been given a glow-up for its sixth version, offering a great alternative to Samsung for a fancy foldable with a red suede-like back framed in gold.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Magic V6 continues the Chinese challenger brand’s strategy of taking a razor-thin device and slapping a giant circular lump on the back to fit in top-class cameras, something others often forgo. It costs a not inconsiderable £1,500 (€1,700/A$2,999) but only until August when the price jumps to a cool £2,000 (€2,300) – a solid £300 more than last year’s model as the cost ofRAMageddon continues to bite, even at the very top end of the market.Other than a new red-backed version, the Magic V6 is almost indistinguishable from the greatV5 from last year. It is one of the thinnest and lightest foldable tablets on the market, has a great fingerprint scanner in the power button and has a proper IP68 water resistance rating matching the best slab phones, making it easy to use as a daily driver. When closed it handles just like a regular flagship Android phone with a great, crisp and smooth OLED display.View image in fullscreenThe red fabric back adds texture and grip to the Magic V6, offering something a bit different from standard glass or metal.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOnce opened, the internal screen is one of the best available, ready for all your media-watching or multitasking needs. But the crease down the middle that allows the screen to fold is slightly more noticeable than some rivals and the integrated screen film is a fingerprint magnet, so it will need cleaning regularly to make the best of it.SpecificationsMain screen:7.95in (403ppi) 120Hz OLED flexible displayCover screen:6.52in (406ppi) 120Hz OLEDProcessor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5RAM:16GBStorage:512GBOperating system:MagicOS 10 (Android 16)Camera:50MP + 50MP ultrawide + 64MP 3x tele; 2x 20MP selfieConnectivity:5G, dual sim + esim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, GNSSWater resistance:IP68/69(1.5 metres for 30 minutes)Dimensions folded:156.7 x 74.5 x 8.75-9mmDimensions unfolded:156.7 x 145.6 x 4.0-4.1mmWeight:219-224gTwo-day battery lifeView image in fullscreenA full charge takes 59 minutes using a standard 100W USB-C charger (not included) hitting 50% in 25 minutes.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Magic V6 has Qualcomm’s top Android chip for 2026, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, making it one of the best performers on the market, rivalling top slab phones such as theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.However, by default the Magic V6 uses a “balanced” battery mode, which significantly inhibits the phone’s top performance. It isn’t noticeable in day-to-day messaging and browsing but it was in games and other high-intensity tasks. Switching the phone to its “performance” battery mode significantly improved things at the expense of heat and battery life.The Honor has a very large battery compared with most foldable phone rivals, which helps it last almost two full days between charges while actively using a mixture of the screens for more than eight hours for general browsing, messaging, work and media consumption. Playing games drains the battery a bit faster but the Magic V6 should outlast even the heaviest of usage days.MagicOS 10 software still needs workView image in fullscreenUp to three apps can be used in split-screen, including the ability to push one mostly off the screen for maximising useful space.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe phone runs Honor’s version of last year’s Android 16,MagicOS 10, which means it isn’t as up to date as some rivals runningAndroid 17. Honor will provide seven years of Android version and security updates for devices sold within Europe.MagicOS has improved since last year. It looks quite nice, has plenty of customisation options and tools for making the most of the folding screen, including the excellent ability to split-screen three apps beyond the bounds of the physical display,which was introduced last year.Various AI tools are strewn throughout the operating system, including Google’s Gemini, which you can set to open in split-screen next to whatever app you are using at the time by quickly flexing the tablet. Many of the tools work as shortcuts for performing tasks such as saving screenshots, editing photos and changing settings on your phone.The “AI button” is meant to launch actions such as turning on the torch or opening an AI tool by double-tapping, though not depressing, the power button, but it doesn’t work. There are various other parts of the operating system that are unpolished. A bug prevents Google’s Chrome browser from opening in split-screen. Apps that are out of date are described as having a “low version” by Honor’s App Market, which also insists on trying to update apps installed from Google Play, bringing the two app stores into conflict. The Honor lacks the ability to have a different home screen layout for the inside and outside screens, and messaging apps such as WhatsApp routinely insist on opening as small floating windows if you tap a message notification, even on the outside screen.These little niggles could be overlooked on a significantly cheaper phone, but not on a £1,500-£2,000 device. You can and should expect better.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app is easy to use and has most of the tools you would want. You can shoot with the Magic V6 open or closed.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe enormous circular bump on the back houses three cameras, with a 20MP selfie camera in each of the two screens for a total of five cameras.The cameras have changed little since last year’s V5 and perform very similarly. The main 50MP camera shoots great photos at 12MP as standard with good detail and range with its cropped 2x zoom, though it can notably suffer frommoiréon stripped textures. The 50MP ultra wide camera has been improved since the V5, solving some of thedistortion problems. The 64MP 3x telephoto is the best of the bunch, capturing excellent detail, even with its 2x crop zoom for an effective 6x magnification. Its digital zoom remains good to 30x before becoming obviously blown up.Low light photography is pretty good across all the lenses, while the camera app has tons of features, including many AI tools and a good manual mode for more creative photography. The Magic V6 shoots decent video up to 4K at 60 frames a second and can be used in various partly folded orientations.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe Magic V6 is easy to use like a regular medium-sized slab phone when closed.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery will maintainat least 80% capacity after 1,200 full-charge cycles. The phone is generally repairable and Honorpublishes pricing for spare parts, including £609 for an internal screen and £152 for the external screen, plus labour and shipping. Honor offers a free screen repair (Care+) for 24 months if bought before 2 August.The device contains limited recycled materials, which Honor breaks down in the phone’senvironmental impact report. The company offerstrade-inandrefurbished products.PriceThe Honor Magic V6 has an introductory price of£1,499.99(€1,699.90/A$2,999), which will increase to £1,999.99 (€2,299.90) from August 2026 in some regions.For comparison, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs£1,899and theGoogle Pixel 10 Pro Foldcosts£1,749.VerdictThe Magic V6 is another very attractive book-style foldable from Honor, but it fails to move things on from last year in an increasingly competitive category.It has really great battery life, matching some of the best slab phones. The outside screen is great, while the inside screen is good but has a more visible crease than some recent rivals. The Magic V6 feels particularly good when used as a phone, while the massive bump fits in some great cameras and means it doesn’t rock around on a table like some others.But it is the software that continues to let Honor down. It just isn’t as up to date or polished as it needs to be on a device this expensive.As good as the Magic V6 is, it lacks a compelling reason to buy it over more complete rivals from Samsung, Google and others.Pros:slim, light, just like a normal phone when closed, great performance, very long battery life, good internal screen, decent camera, good fingerprint scanner, IP68/9 water and dust resistance rating.Cons:very expensive, software not as refined as needed, more fragile than a regular device, costly to repair, not much of an upgrade on previous model.View image in fullscreenThe Magic V6 is about as thin and svelte as a regular flagship Android phone, complete with huge camera cluster on the back.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsAndroidTablet computersMobile phonesSmartphonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: AI can fuel biological weapons. We must harness its power for defense | Annie Jacobsen | The Guardian
description: The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design
Content: ‘The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties, and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives.’Photograph: APView image in fullscreen‘The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties, and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives.’Photograph: APOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI can fuel biological weapons. We must harness its power for defenseAnnie JacobsenThe offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological designMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 06.17 EDTShareAs artificial intelligence rapidly transforms the biological sciences, it is pushing the future of biology in two opposing directions. AI can help bad actors generate recipes for biological weapons with just a few keystrokes and computational prompts. At the same time, AI can track disease outbreaks and deliver critical public health information to millions of people in real time – potentially stopping a deadly outbreak in its tracks. What we are dealing with in this moment is profound: a race between offense and defense. Between the proliferation of dark biology, where deadly pathogens are engineered in secret, and the promise of a new era of collective global health.Every infectious disease outbreak begins with a handful of cases. Public health wins by learning about an outbreak before it spreads wide, before hospitals fill and a crisis starts to spiral out of control. As transmission rates explode, options shrink. One of AI’s greatest values is its ability to compress the timeline between outbreak and detection. Speed can mean the difference between containing an outbreak and confronting an epidemic, or another global pandemic.The WorldHealthOrganization (WHO) now uses AI to track the spread of infectious disease. At the WHO’s Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, in Berlin, Germany, computational systems leverage artificial intelligence and pathogenic surveillance to track and monitor infectious disease outbreaks around the world. At the center of this new way forward sits a computer-based system called Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources, or Eios (“EE-oss”), which acts as a giant filter for the world’s minute-by-minute health information.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dutton/Penguin Random HouseFor decades, traditional epidemic intelligence has relied on official case counts. But data from hospitals, labs, research groups and other formal reporting systems takes days or weeks to register and input into official databases. Eios leverages the colossal power of modern computing and social media to get a more immediate picture of a disease outbreak. Eios focuses on unofficial reports, citizen chatter, local news reports, social media posts and more. Proficient across multiple languages, Eios scans millions of websites, feeds and platforms, searching for outbreaks as they happen. It scrapes, filters and ranks information. The goal of Eios is to pull signal from noise.AI is a force multiplier, changing the biological sciences every day. The real question is not whether AI can do catastrophic harm in the realm of biological sciences – it most certainly can – but whether public health officials can figure out how to deploy AI as a defensive tool faster than malicious actors deploy it as an offensive one.The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. AI systems can already help researchers navigate enormous bodies of biological knowledge that once required years of specialized training. They can explain complex laboratory techniques, locate obscure scientific literature, troubleshoot technical problems and suggest experimental designs. None of these capabilities is inherently dangerous. Together, however, they lower the barrier to entering what was once a highly specialized field.AI may help us cure countless diseases – and usher in a new golden age of medicine | Samuel HumeRead moreThe greatest concern is that AIs can help humans create genuinely novel, or new, forms of biology. Scientists are already exploring these possibilities, from mirror-image life to organisms designed with capabilities that do not already exist in nature. Until recently, these possibilities were largely confined to theory or science fiction.Biologyis unlike any other technology because what it produces can reproduce, spread across borders, mutate, and evolve on its own. A software bug crashes a computer. A biological mistake can become self-propagating. Once a living organism is released into the world, it cannot simply be switched off or recalled. That biological weapons are alive is what makes them fundamentally different from every other class of weapon, from the arrow to the ICBM.The race has already begun. As I cover in my forthcoming bookBiological War, and this recentNew York Timesarticle outlines, biological weapons have an extremely low barrier to entry. Unlike nuclear weapons, which require tightly controlled fissile material and complex delivery systems, biological weapons can be built with widely available laboratory tools, aided by increasingly powerful AI systems.The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives. The point is pressure, not panic. We need to develop AI systems to strengthen public health, accelerate disease detection and help build biological defenses as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design. Because once biology outruns our ability to contain it, there is no recalling what has already been unleashed upon the world.Annie Jacobsen is the author ofBiological War, to be published on 28 July by Dutton. She also wrote the Pulitzer prize–finalist in history The Pentagon’s Brain and the New York Times bestsellers Nuclear War, Area 51 and Operation PaperclipExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionBiologyWeapons technologyComputingHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: AusAlert blared around parks, libraries and cinemas for a few seconds, but some didn’t get the alert at all  | Technology | The Guardian
description: Federal government touts emergency warning alert test as a success and says no approach works 100% of the time
Author: Kat Wong
Headline: Federal government touts emergency warning alert test as a success and says no approach works 100% of the time
Content: Australia underwent a nationwide test of a new warning system called AusAlert, which will be deployed in October to prepare Australians for fires, floods, terrorist incidents or health emergencies.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenAustralia underwent a nationwide test of a new warning system called AusAlert, which will be deployed in October to prepare Australians for fires, floods, terrorist incidents or health emergencies.Photograph: Darren England/AAPTechnologyAusAlert blared around parks, libraries and cinemas for a few seconds, but some didn’t get the alert at allFederal government touts emergency warning alert test as a success and says no approach works 100% of the timeFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKat WongMon 27 Jul 2026 02.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 06.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA blaring emergency warning alert Australians had been warned about was anti-climactic for some – and totally missed by others.Almost every phone in the country, alongside some smartwatches and tablets, was supposed to let off a loud noise at about 2pm AEST and receive a pop-up notification with the text “TEST MESSAGE” and “NO ACTION IS REQUIRED”.The event was the first nationwide test of a new warning system called AusAlert, which will be deployed in October to prepare Australians for fires, floods, terrorist incidents or health emergencies.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe federal government has spent the past week telling the public about this test alert.But for many, it came and went in just a few seconds.Indigo Miller was working from home in Canberra when her colleagues reminded her of the notification.“I was counting down for two minutes before,” she said.“But it was pretty anti-climactic and I think I accidentally clicked it away. Mine also wasn’t super loud so if I was outside and my phone was inside, I don’t know if I would hear.”Miller had attempted to film herself recording to try to capture the sound of the alert, but her phone cut out as the siren went off.Busker Dani Bainbridge was about to start performing at Sydney’s Hyde Park when the alert began pinging.“It did the job, I think,” she said.But others did not receive an alert at all.Guardian Australia received reports of mobile users whose phones got a notification but did not blast a sound.Before the test, the National Emergency Management Agency received advice that 80% of Apple iPhones would ring, as well as 16m Android devices.It also said the alert would go to iPhone models 11 and up running iOS 26.4 or later, Apple Watch models SE2, SE3, Series 6 and up running watchOS 26.4 or later, and Android devices running Android 12 or later.Guardian Australia was told of an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 12, a Samsung phone and other devices not receiving a notification despite being on.The federal emergency management minister, Kristy McBain, said 94% of targeted cell towers had successfully broadcast the alert.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAusAlert test: what time will national emergency warning siren sound on phones in Australia today? Here’s what to knowRead more“Don’t worry if you did not receive an alert – this could be because you were not in a coverage area, your software was not up to date or your device was incompatible,” she said.“Nema will continue to analyse the technical and performance data and engage with emergency service organisations around the country.”Asked if it would ever be completely successful, McBain said “there is no one avenue of communication that is 100% successful”.“This technology is more reliable than the current text-based technology,” she said.“But as I said, this is just another tool in the toolkit for emergency service agencies, who are doing a really good job in communicating to communities that are at risk during a natural disaster.”ABefore the AusAlert test, domestic and family violence advocates raised concerns about the risk of the notification exposing “safe phones” and urged people to keep devices hidden for safety reasons.AusAlert interim coordinator general Pat Hetherington said the advice for people who have safe phones and hidden phones is for them to be switched off for a 24-hour period.Businesses and people going about their daily lives reacted to the impending alert in different ways.Before the alert, those who had bought Imax tickets for Christopher Nolan’s much-anticipated The Odyssey at the 1.50pm session in Sydney were told by workers to switch off their phones.Though some still went off, they rang out during the ads that played before the film, according to people present in the theatre.At the State Library of NSW, the siren cut through the typical wall of silence, offering some reprieve to cramming Year 12 students and even waking up one high schooler who was nodding off at his laptop.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyEmergency planningnewsShareReuse this content

title: Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Research shows AI-generated physicians are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice
Author: Joe Pinner
Headline: Research shows AI-generated physicians are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice
Content: An AI-generated image of a doctor giving advice online.Illustration: TikTokView image in fullscreenAn AI-generated image of a doctor giving advice online.Illustration: TikTokAI (artificial intelligence)Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’Research shows AI accounts are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health adviceJoe PinnerMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMisleading health claims online pose a “huge danger to public safety”, experts have warned, after research has shown that AI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views onTikTokby spreading dubious health advice.The British Medical Association council deputy chair, Dr Emma Runswick, flagged the risks posed by AI accounts that “peddle medical myths and promote so-called miracle cures”.“Platforms like TikTok must do more to stop the rise of dangerous fake medical advice … otherwise, it is the public who could be paying the price with their health and perhaps even their lives,” she added.AI-generated physicians were found to have spread disproven myths about cancer, including that microwaving food in plastic, using deodorants and sleeping next to your phone could all cause cancer – all claims which have been refuted by Cancer Research UK.The research was published this month by Hallam, a digital marketing agency. It follows warnings by the NHS that health misinformation on social media was a “real threat to public health”.The research found that AI-generated content appeared in 40% of top health-related TikTok videos, with most posted by a growing number of deepfake influencer accounts designed to resemble real doctors. For some specific search terms, such as “health tips”, 84%of videos were classed as AI-generated or AI-assisted content.According to Hallam, top AI-generated doctor and health videos in their search received an average of 2.5m views. TikTok took down examples of the videos that were sent to the platform by the Guardian.Google AI Overviews put people at risk of harm with misleading health adviceRead moreThe accounts also promoted bizarre remedies for various health problems, including Coca-Cola mixed with onion as a pain-relief remedy and a fake product called “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” as an anti-ageing solution.One avatar claimed he had recommended “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” to his patients for years, and that it could combat “hair loss, skin weakening, brittle nails and joint pain” by helping the body produce “anti-ageing molecules naturally”. The Guardian could not find evidence of “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” products online.In response to the findings, Prof Frankie Swords, the national medical director at NHS England, said it was concerning to see a rise in online medical misinformation. “Many clinicians are reporting an increasing number of patients who feel worried and confused due to false advice that has been made solely for clicks,” she added.Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, the president of the Royal College of GPs, said she was also concerned by the research, adding that misleading AI content carried a “real risk” of harm.Hallam analysed 1,198 videos, selecting the top 50 videos across a series of search terms including “health tips” and “doctor advice”. It also looked for general “life-impacting” advice on issues such as personal finance and education.Alex Ruani, health misinformation researcher at UCL, said the rise of AI doctor videos represented a “frightening amount of exposure to fake medical content”.“We’re looking at industrialised exploitation of trust,” she added.Last year, a poll conducted by Savanta on 3,575 men and 3,832 women aged 18 and above in England on behalf of patient champion Healthwatch England found that about one in five people were using social media for health information.William Pett, interim director of policy and public affairs at Healthwatch England, said: “Without the skills to distinguish reliable information from commercial hype or misinformation, [people] risk being misled in ways that can seriously affect their health.”A TikTok spokesperson said: “These findings from a marketing agency with commercial interests are not an accurate reflection of our platform.”“The facts are that we remove harmful health misinformation, including when it’s AI-generated, we partner with the World Health Organization and the NHS on providing reliable health information in-app, and we continually invest in AI literacy resources and labelling technologies.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Internet safetyHealthTikTokSocial mediaDeepfakenewsShareReuse this content

title: I risk losing my livelihood because Nissan failed to repair my car | Motoring | The Guardian
description: I’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicle
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: I’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicle
Content: Delays in getting spares to repair a dual-controlled Nissan threatened a driving instructor’s livelihood.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyView image in fullscreenDelays in getting spares to repair a dual-controlled Nissan threatened a driving instructor’s livelihood.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyConsumer championsMotoringI risk losing my livelihood because Nissan failed to repair my carI’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicleAnna TimsMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy livelihood as a self-employed driving instructor is under threat owing to Nissan’s failure to repair my leased dual-control car.It has been off the road awaiting a spare part for three months, and I’ve now been told it will take at least a further month to arrive.In order to continue working I have had to hire a dual-control vehicle at a cost of more than £2,500 so far, while also continuing to pay PCP finance of about £1,500 on a car I can’t use.I have had to borrow more than £1,000 from relatives to extend the hire of the dual-control vehicle. After that, I will have no remaining funds to renew the hire, and will have to stop teaching and lose my customers and my income.CW,EastbourneYou contacted me in mid-March when the latest estimated repair date had been postponed for the third time, until the end of April. Since your hire contract was due for renewal on 15 April, and you had no money left to extend it, time was of the essence.There was no sense of urgency at Nissan, however. You complained that it had continuously kept you in the dark about timescales and reimbursements, and I had to repeatedly chase it for information.Meanwhile, you were forking out £490 a month in PCP payments and a monthly hire fee of £952.I managed to get the company to agree to reimburse you for the hire car costs up to the (as yet unspecified) repair date, but agreeing and paying are different things. Days passed, no money came.Two weeks after I waded in, Nissan told me the spare part had been sourced and the repair was planned for 15 April, the day your car hire contract ended.Your reimbursement for the hire, it said, should be paid within 10 days. This meant it would not be with you in time to pay to renew the car hire if the repair was delayed again.When I pointed this out, the company said it would fund any further hire contracts directly, then refused to put the promise in writing. In the event, your car was repaired in the nick of time.Next began the battle for compensation. You calculated that, apart from the hire charges, the delays and uncertainty had cost you nearly £900 in lost earnings and other expenses.Nissan’s response was to offer you two years of free servicing, then it ignored your protest that you had already paid in advance for a service plan and that you were due to replace the car in 12 months.Back I went to Nissan, and this month it apologised for ignoring you and agreed to pay you compensation, the value of which you have agreed not to disclose.It says: “We are sympathetic to the customer’s experience, which fell below the high standards Nissan and its dealer partners strive to deliver.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. title: Haex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventure | Games | The Guardian
description: The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes
Content: Growing fascination … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsView image in fullscreenGrowing fascination … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsSummer games previewsGamesHaex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventureThe debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyesLewis GordonMon 27 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wilds of the sub-Arctic north: towering pine trees, flashes of psychedelic-yellow lichen, and a sun that never wholly sets during the summer months. This land is gorgeous, yes, but also unforgiving, yet in Haex (pronounced “hex”) you have an unusual tool at your disposal to make it a little more hospitable: a cube that fits snugly in the palm of your hand out of which grows a plant. You plant this so-called Seed in the earth and – voilà – the world around you transforms: new vegetation and topography but also narrative threads to follow, and, naturally, enemies. Wield these small-but-mighty kernels of change at your own peril.“Your adventure and your world is player-shaped,” says Haex’s creative director Tobias Nyman. He explains that everyone starts a campaign with a unique, procedurally generated world. Each Seed then contains further procedural data that causes it to terraform before your eyes. “You change the world as you go,” he says. “It becomes even more unique.”The singularity of each game world is crucial for keeping not just you but other players on their toes. That’s another of Haex’s wrinkles: it is an online co-operative game, meaning your friends may join you on this ever-transforming survivalist adventure.View image in fullscreenRoom for more … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsTeaming up, you play as a group of research scientists sent to investigate an anomaly in the rugged Scandinavian landscape. You come across odd, shapeshifting objects and beasts: for example, an ash-grey humanoid creature with spikes protruding from its face that would make even Pinhead from Hellraiser wince; also, a sentient wall so supermassive that it scrapes the clouds. There is a further layer to these spatial and, perhaps, alien mysteries: an unknown language of arcane sigils that must be decoded.Nyman talks effusively of influences: sci-fi movies such asAnnihilationandArrival(as is clear from the trailer); the weird fiction thrillers of author Jeff VanderMeer, too. Unexpectedly, the creative director cites the niche music genre known ascosmic black metalas a touchstone. “There is the wild, grim, frostbitten north, an extraterrestrial entity and a thing that traverses the mist,” says Nyman, hinting at a shared emotional effect between his beloved music genre and the game: a mingling of dread and awe, and of seeking transcendence in nature.Nyman co-founded Haex’s studio Dead Astronauts (anothernod to VanderMeer), in 2024, having previously worked at Ubisoft Massive, where he helped make recent open-world blockbusters,Avatar: Frontiers of PandoraandStar Wars Outlaws. Yet where those titles’ settings are gorgeous and gigantic (“monumental,” stresses Nyman), they are also somewhat static. By contrast, Haex’s game world is more dynamic, and it is being made by just 12 developers. The theory is that its morphing, geo-engineered space should foster more fluid, interesting experiences, despite Haex’s focus on somewhat familiar-feeling shooting and survival mechanics.Taking the leap to independence has also enabled Nyman to make a game that is more personal to him. As a youngster, he split his time between Stockholm and the far north of Sweden. He recalls looking up at the night sky blanketed with constellations as his father explained Einstein’s theory of relativity. Another memory: gazing out at an expansive crop of cloudberries – a “field of gold,” says Nyman, by virtue of the small fruit’s colour. What has stuck with him most, however, is the region’s silence – a silence so great that it was “almost screaming at me”, he says. That feels like an apt summation of Haex’s aims: an experience that is miraculous and malicious; a setting that is beautiful yet can feel as if it is bearing down on you with cruel intensity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaex is due for release onPCin 2027.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Glitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the Backrooms | Games | The Guardian
description: The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
Content: Interior landscape … the 2022 game Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeView image in fullscreenInterior landscape … the 2022 game Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeGamesGlitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the BackroomsThe horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spacesAlex SpencerMon 27 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future$262mA24movie sensation.“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in theBackrooms,” the post begins. For the uninitiated, “noclip” refers to a game mode in which collision with solid objects is disabled, allowing players to move freely through walls and floors. Think of Chiwetel Ejiofor’s character in the film, finding a permeable wall in the basement of his furniture store and passing through to the world on the other side.Backrooms review – Kane Parsons’ icily disturbing horror rewrites the genre rulebookRead moreIn games, noclip is intended for use by developers testing out their creations – but for decades now, players have been finding ways to access it themselves and reach hidden places they were never intended to see. It’s a phenomenon that Studio Chyr creative director William Chyr is intimately familiar with, both as a maker of games and as a player.View image in fullscreenChiwetel Ejiofor in a scene from Backrooms the film.Photograph: A24/AP“Going behind the scenes, noclipping, and seeing the logic of the space, it’s like this Wizard of Oz moment of pulling open the curtain,” Chyr says. He remembers an early encounter with this inBatman: Arkham City:“There was this glitch that allowed you, if you kept spamming one of the grenades, to keep going higher and higher.” From there, the caped crusader could soar outside the level, into sections of Gotham that were only ever intended as a backdrop. “The streets had these cars that moved, but it was just a flat texture.”Watching Backrooms, Chyr was also reminded of a similar bug in the notoriously jankySkyrim, where holding a wooden plate provided a quick way of noclipping out of the world. Looking at it from the outside in, players discovered that many of the game’s “tables” were in fact just bookcases embedded deep in the ground – just like the memorable Backrooms shot of a room in which the furniture is clipping through the floor. All these things that, in video games, the player is never meant to see.The feel ofKane Parsons’ filmis actually closer to these experiences than any of the many “official” Backrooms games that have popped up. The open-source nature of this mythos (as well as 4chan and Reddit, there are sprawling fan wikis cataloguing and expanding the lore) means that it’s possible to release your own game set in the Backrooms, using the name and iconography, in a way you couldn’t with another horror movie.View image in fullscreenPlaces you weren’t meant to see … Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeThe most high-profile of these games, Escape the Backrooms, was first available in early-access form in August 2022, just months after Parsons’ first video. It offers a perfectly faithful recreation of the Backrooms aesthetic, from the yellow hallways to the yellow hazmat suits worn by agents of Async, the mysterious organisation only introduced towards the end of the film but a mainstay of the online incarnations. But all this is just wallpaper applied over the blueprint of a multiplayer survival horror game.At its best, Backrooms taps into a sense of a place being “off”, in a way that’s unsettling but hard to pin down. It’s a delicate sensation, easily shattered (as it is in the film, I’d argue) by the presence of killer monsters. Even more so by the sight of another player in their gas mask and reindeer onesie, bunny-hopping through the hallways ahead.Thankfully, there’s another stripe of Backrooms-inspired games offering nothing more than a self-guided tour through environments with a growing sense of weirdness and the constant suggestion of a threat lurking out of view.View image in fullscreenEndless halls… Hotel Infinity.Photograph: Studio ChyrPools and Dreamcore both shine a spotlight on Poolrooms, an infinite swimming-baths dimensionfirst glimpsed in one of Parsons’s videosand codified by the fandom asLevel 37of the Backrooms, with a similarly alien approach to architecture. In Dreamcore, it’s just one of a selection pack of realms to explore. You’ll also explore a “dead mall” and the looping corridors of a hotel: both abandoned and seemingly endless, like the spaces explored in the film, but with less of an obvious supernatural edge.These malls and hotels are prime examples of a larger online taste for liminal spaces from which Backrooms is just one offshoot.“These spaces always feel like they’re past their prime,” says Chyr. “It’s clear there was human activity here, at one point, but no longer.” His 2025 game Hotel Infinity is steeped in all these ideas, to the extent that at one point Hotel Liminal was considered as a title, Chyr says. “But I thought that was just too on the nose!”Set in the lifeless corridors of a hotel seemingly designed by MC Escher, it’s a VR game that uses some clever spatial trickery to fold its endless halls into a 2x2m square of your living-room floor. One particular sequence late in Backrooms made me think of Chyr’s game – he confirms that he thought the same thing. “I was like, damn, I wish we’d done that!” he laughs.View image in fullscreenImpossible architecture …  Exit 8.Photograph: Kotake CreateHotel Infinity is primarily focused on the impossible architecture of these places, something it shares withExit 8(also adapted into a film this year), a Japanese-made game that traps you in an infinitely looping section of a Tokyo metro station. The other side of the liminal coin is the sensation summoned by that original 4chan image: the eeriness of an empty place that no longer has any obvious function, or perhaps never did.One game exploring this aspect is Interior Worlds, a “liminal photography” game in which you explore such spaces armed only with an SLR camera. The game’s developer, who goes by the moniker Sodaraptor, remembers first encountering the concept of liminal spaces “back in 2020, when the original Backrooms post on 4chan started going viral.”It was an emotion they’d felt in such places but never previously had a name for. “A strange liminal discomfort”, Sodaraptor says, mixed with pangs of “anemoia”: nostalgia for an era that predates your own experience.View image in fullscreenShelf discovery … Interior Worlds.Photograph: Raptorsoft GamesSo it’s only fitting that the phenomenon’s virtual inspirations are now, in video game terms, as ancient as all those dead malls.The aforementioned Arkham City and Skyrim both came out in 2011. The same year, Valve released Portal 2, the mind-bending first-person puzzler which Parsons has repeatedly cited as his biggest influence. The director even made a couple of Portal fan-videos;the last onewas uploaded to his YouTube channel in 2021, just months before the first Backrooms clip.It is probably inevitable that the aesthetics of these 15-year-old games would just now be beginning to seep through into the cinematic mainstream. Parsons was a young child when Portal 2 came out, and it’s only natural that he – and the generation of film-makers just now coming of age – would make things informed by the dark rooms they got lost in as kids.A Minecraft Movie may already exist (unfortunately) but what will be much more interesting are the films and other artworks shaped by the experience of playing Minecraft at a formative age. Those dark caverns, the endless mines, the sounds of the zombies, the threat of the creepers – once those strange experiences have sunk into internet lore, who knows what will emerge and where it will take us.Explore more on these topicsGamesIndie gamesBackroomsSkyrimfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypse | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answers
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answers
Content: Eleanor Drage, senior research fellow at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.Photograph: Apple Photos Clean UpView image in fullscreenEleanor Drage, senior research fellow at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.Photograph: Apple Photos Clean UpScience and nature booksReviewWhat If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypseThe academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answersSophie McBainMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe AI ethicist Eleanor Drage believes that to thrive alongside artificial intelligence, humans need to recognise AI’s “humanity”. She means that while we often speak of AI as though it were some mystical, formless thing, it is the product of hours of human labour, in silicon and quartz mines, microchip factories and data labelling centres. If citizens want to wrest power from the tech companies that are building AI, it helps to understand clearly what they are selling us. This also means seeing through the marketing and hype: “the cloud”, that nebulous, distant place where your photos are stored, is just someone else’s computer; an AI “hallucination” is a system error or data labelling mistake; intelligence is a very broad – and potentially misleading – term.The story in Silicon Valley is that AI will either save us, ushering in a new era of prosperity and human longevity, or it will wipe us all out. Drage argues, convincingly, that big tech cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises while it continues to chase profit and power above all else, and while it serves the interests of a narrow few. Meanwhile, the cultural obsession with the AI-induced apocalypse conveniently redirects attention from the practical conversations we could be having about how to make AI safer – by ensuring citizens have more power over how their information is used, and how AI models are trained and regulated, for example. Tech titans’ apocalyptic visions also create the false impression that AI safety is more important than climate change, geopolitical tensions and inequality, three problems that are already causing a huge amount of suffering and that, if addressed, would reduce many AI-linked risks too.Drage, an assistant research professor at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, has conducted research that debunks AI-powered recruitment processes, and exposes the dangers of incorporating AI into law enforcement. Many of her criticisms of big tech will be familiar: that AI algorithms perpetuate and entrench pre-existing biases; that for all their bland, generic promises to be “transparent” and “accountable”, tech giants have become too big to care about ethics; that a handful of executives have amassed far too much power; and that the rollout of AI is happening without our consent and without consideration for planetary health. But her writing has intellectual heft, and her philosophical explorations of, for example, how we define intelligence and why this matters, are very interesting.Occasionally, however, Drage’s arguments seem rushed and become sloppy. “It’s merely an illusion that the labour force is disappearing: work is simply shifting, from artists to data labellers and from marketeers to engineers,” she writes at one point. But it’s not clear that artists and “marketeers” will become redundant in the coming AI era. It’s also not as though the data labellers working for poverty wages in Kenya would have been artists 10 years ago. Equally, given the importance she rightly places on promoting diversity in AI, it’s disappointing that she dismisses unconscious bias as “merely another way of taking the perspective of the perpetrator rather than the recipient of harm”, as though intention is completely irrelevant. She writes that people are ready for “less placid” conversations about equality, I’d add that these conversations also demand accuracy and nuance.The book’s title suggests Drage wants to offer an alternative vision of what AI could be. She gives a few examples of the kind of ethical, community-based AI projects she thinks should be replacing top-down big tech products, and many of them are strangely underwhelming. They include an app called Mumkin designed to facilitate difficult conversations about female genital mutilation (FGM) in India, and Kuini, an AI chatbot built to help Māori women quit smoking. In both instances I found myself wondering what value AI brings to these endeavours – particularly given all that Drage has discussed about its environmental impact and exploitative supply chains. Is an app more effective than training community members to act as counsellors, or funding support groups and peer support workers?Drage describes a toolkit she co-designed to help AI companies act ethically and comply with EU regulations as a “cornerstone of utopianism”, because it shifts the focus on to how AI is built and made. In her view, utopia is not a destination but the “process of working together to develop a fairer world”. Maybe it would be unfair to expect too specific a utopian vision, but I’d nonetheless be interested to know how AI, specifically, can help us build a better future. She does not mention the things that many of AI’s biggest critics nonetheless welcome, such as its potential to improve drug discovery and disease detection. What if we got AI right, this book asks. After reading it, I can’t say I really know.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Guardian view on Europe’s wildfires: politics must catch up with the new reality | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: At a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritised
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: At a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritised
Content: A pyrocumulonimbus, a giant cloud created by a large wildfire, seen in the Fontainebleau forest region of France.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APView image in fullscreenA pyrocumulonimbus, a giant cloud created by a large wildfire, seen in the Fontainebleau forest region of France.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APOpinionWildfiresThe Guardian view on Europe’s wildfires: politics must catch up with the new realityEditorialAt a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritisedMon 27 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.43 EDTShareAnew and ominous word has entered the vocabulary of firefighters struggling to cope with the vast wildfire sweeping through south-west France. Apyrocumulonimbusis a fire-generated thunderstorm that can whip up winds in unpredictable ways, making the containment of a blaze and assessment of its likely course far more difficult. A known phenomenon in North America and Australia, firefighters believe France is suffering its first in the Bordeaux region, as the country endures the consequences of the third major heatwave of the summer and prepares for a fourth.The direstatisticsof the ongoing fires in France and Spain tell a story of deepening devastation and human misery. A far greater expanse of French land has already been burnt this year, compared with the 30,000 hectares during the whole of 2025, while 220,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the Gironde. In Spain, the environment ministry has calculated that over 170,000 hectares have been affected, compared with 29,000 last year. Over 100,000 people have been forced to flee.View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez greeting emergency service workers.Photograph: Eva Manez/ReutersAs climate scientists long warned would be the case, Europe’s wildfires are worsening in intensity, scale and duration as the planet heats up. When the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez,attributedthe current crisis to the effects of the climate emergency, he was stating the obvious. But to his great credit, Mr Sánchez has been among the few leaders toarguethat the European Union’s green transition should be accelerated accordingly. Whether on funding adaptation efforts, or driving the macro changes needed to slow the rate of global heating, far too many others appear happy to fiddle while the continent burns.In June, for example, with spectacularly badtiming, Emmanuel Macron’s government sought savings by announcing steep cuts to a Green Fund designed to help local authorities address climate and environmental challenges. Across Europe more generally, amid persistent low growth and the fallout from Donald Trump’s war on Iran, a false dichotomy is increasingly being drawn between green ambition and competitiveness. This month, underpressurefrom countries such as Giorgia Meloni’s Italy, the European Commission unveiled proposals toweakenthe EU’s emissions trading system, its flagship climate policy. If adopted, heavy industry would receive free polluting permits for longer and at lower cost.Calls for the dilution of green measures are generally accompanied by the assertion that Europe needs to take a more pragmatic approach, at a time of geopolitical uncertainty and aggressive economic competition. The argument is wrong twice over: the faster the EU moves towards net zero, the better it will consolidate Europe’s position in the global markets of the future. More fundamentally, as the appalling impact of this summer’s wildfires vividly illustrates, the notion that climate measures are a kind of optional add-on, appropriate only when times are good, is wildly at odds with the developing reality.As a fourth heatwave hits Europe, temperatures in south-west France are predicted to hit 40C on Wednesday. According to a recentstudy, if the warming rate of the last decade continues, the 1.5C limit set by the Paris agreement will be redundant by 2030. Yet, far from seeking to catch up with the pace of change, too many governments and leaders are seeking to put their foot on the policy brake. That is not realism; it is a dereliction of duty.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresOpinionExtreme weatherFranceSpain (World news)Spain (Weather)Pedro SánchezEmmanuel MacroneditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The 2026 World Cup is over, but the onslaught of soccer relentlessly rolls on | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The supply of soccer seems to be enormously exceeding demand. It’s made the sport feel utterly overwhelming
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The supply of soccer seems to be enormously exceeding demand. It’s made the sport feel utterly overwhelming
Content: Liverpool supporters during a preseason friendly in the US; a Premier League ball; Rodri holding the World Cup.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskView image in fullscreenLiverpool supporters during a preseason friendly in the US; a Premier League ball; Rodri holding the World Cup.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskSoccer with Jonathan WilsonSoccerThe 2026 World Cup is over, but the onslaught of soccer relentlessly rolls onLeander SchaerlaeckensThe supply of soccer seems to be enormously exceeding demand. It’s made the sport feel utterly overwhelmingMon 27 Jul 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.11 EDTShareOn Friday, the Scottish Premiership kicks off its 2026-27 season. The following Friday, the Dutch Eredivisie begins anew, and England’s Carabao Cup sets off on its ponderous journey. The various European club competitions have already begun their qualifying rounds – and did so on 7 July, in the case of the Champions and Conference Leagues. Liga MX is two rounds into its Apertura season; Major League Soccer resumed its regular season on 16 July. Other soccer is available elsewhere and at other times.It has been only a week since theWorld Cupended.The sense of relentlessness that soccer impels is never more obvious than in the wake of its signature event, when we are reminded that the sport didn’t stop even as the world sort of did. There is no off-season, no respite. One season just bleeds into the next between postseasons and preseasons and the transfer market. Soccer is a permanent condition.From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World CupRead moreThe World Cup derives its power from the feeling that it is possibly the last global piece of monoculture. In another time, the moon landing, or a heavyweight boxing title bout or the crowning of a monarch – back when people cared about such things – might have compelled much of the planet to sit and watch and engage with the same thing, more or less together. In our increasingly fractured experience of the world, it’s sometimes nice to share something in common.Its absence for 47 months out of 48 makes the World Cup rare and allows for anticipation to build. The forces of the sport are arrayed against this moderation, of course, and indeed winning that battle. This World Cup grew by 50% from the last one, to 48 teams. If Fifa had its druthers, it would have a biennial tournament with 64 teams.After all, the only idea in the sport’s executive class is more soccer. The one lesson it seemsnotto have taken from American sports, is that the National Football League retains its status as the sector’s hegemonic power because its product is scarce. Its games feel like events, rather than a routine you can opt out of today and simply make up tomorrow, in spite of the NFL’s own ongoing efforts to lengthen its regular season playing schedule.For a month and change, once every four years, nearly the whole planet watches the same games. Aside from the final days of the group stage, the matches do not overlap, do not conflict, do not counterprogram. During that time, we entertainment consumers inhabit a largely unified reality.And now we shall return to the endless silos dictated algorithmically by our past tastes and behaviors or to our own bespoke suite of players and teams and leagues we currently care about.Outside the World Cup, pro soccer can feel like the Facebook feed you stopped paying attention to years ago because it is just filled with relentless AI slop. Very little seems to be hugely relevant to you, and much of it might not even feel real at all, making it just so very easy to scroll past. It all feels amorphous, a shapeless static creeping about that roughly coalesces into something like soccer when you look up from your other screen.The supply of pro soccer seems to so enormously exceed demand that the market for our attention spans is forever flooded. There’s never a breather. There’s never any anticipation. Very anecdotally, it may be that others are feeling this as well. On Saturday, Liverpool and Sunderland didn’t come close to filling an MLS stadium in Nashville for their preseason friendly. Wrexham and Leeds United, meanwhile, drew a sparse crowd to Tampa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut in a sense, this onslaught has always existed. There is more soccer than there used to be, starting earlier and ending later on whatever calendar it goes by, but there are roughly the same number of domestic competitions. It’s just that they didn’t used to be so readily available across borders. Growing up in Belgium, I had access to a French Ligue 1 highlights show on Sunday mornings, Belgian and Dutch highlights on Sunday evenings and the BBC’s Match of the Day Premier League highlights at night. Every now and again, I’d chance upon a Serie A game on the Italian national broadcaster. Today, sitting in my den in New York, there is seemingly no limit to the games I can access from anywhere in the world.This is not a worse way to live, but it is a more muddled one. And it can make the sport feel utterly overwhelming, like a lone man standing before a tsunami of, and we must invoke the dreaded term … content. Another season has already started, as we still consider and process and digest the last one. Thoughts aren’t fully formed on the World Cup yet, what it meant, how it shifted the sport’s assorted paradigms.We need a break. Yet there is always more soccer.This is an extract from Soccer with Jonathan Wilson, a weekly look from the Guardian US at the game in Europe and beyond, helmed this week by Leander in Jonathan’s absence.Subscribe for free here. Have a question for Jonathan? Emailsoccerwithjw@theguardian.com, and he’ll answer the best in a future edition.Leander Schaerlaeckens is a Guardian US contributor whose book on the US men’s national soccer team, The Long Game, is out now. You can buy ithere. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsFootballSoccer with Jonathan WilsonWorld Cup 2026World CupUS sportsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Tariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurd | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world
Content: ‘Trump is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Trump is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpTariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurdSteven GreenhouseThe president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the worldMon 27 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.15 EDTShareWith the midterm elections less than four months away, it’s a precarious time for Donald Trump and Republicans: Trump’s war against Iran is going badly, hisapproval ratings are in the toilet, gas prices are soaring and pushing up inflation, and nation after nation is furious about Trump’s insults, bullying andugly American unilateralism.So amid all this mess, what does Trump do? He turns to his favorite economic plaything: tariffs. On Monday, Trump signed orders to slap a50% tariff on many Canadian goods, and four days later, he imposedacross-the-board 10% or 12.5% tariffson goods from more than 80 countries. Trump was no doubt thumping his chest, while millions of people overseas were dumping on him for yet another unnecessary, hostile act.Too bad for Republicans, and most Americans, though, because Trump’s fixation on tariffs will only worsen their troubles. Trump’s new tariffs will push up prices – let’s not forget that tariffs are taxes on imports, and US consumers will pay those taxes. A corollary of that: Trump’s tariffs will worsen AmericansNo 1 economic concern: affordability. In bad news for typical Americans, the Yale Budget Lab estimates that Trump’s tariffs will increase costs for the average UShousehold by $1,100 each year. The tariffs are also likely to push Trump’s approval ratings deeper into the sewer. If Trump thinks these tariffs are going to distract Americans from thinking about the Epstein files or the disastrous mess he’s made with his Iran “excursion”, he’s deluding himself. The American people aren’t going to forget those things.It’s hard to tell whether Trump’s repeated use of tariffs is a fixation or an addiction. Emperor Donald I evidently loves tariffs because he can use them to clobber other countries whenever he wants. They’re a powerful cudgel he won’t let go of. Trump imposed his new tariffs on more than 80 countries on the very day that another set of tariffs he slapped on dozens of countries was due to expire. Toparaphrase the actor Charlton Heston, I can imagine Trump saying: “I’ll give up tariffs when you take them from my cold, dead hands.”With these new tariffs, Trump is again engaged in his delusional, destructive tariff tomfoolery. They’ll push up prices, squeeze Americans’ wallets and anger other countries. Trump said his tariffs would boost US manufacturing, but the US haslost 75,000 factory jobssince he returned to office, with many executives complaining about all the herky-jerky uncertainty Trump has wrought. Assessing Trump’s effects on the economy, Atsi Sheth, the chief credit officer for Moody’s Ratings, told the New York Times :“Volatility and unpredictabilityis the new normal.”What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countriesRead moreLike so much that Trump does, his new tariffs are clearly based on pique and false premises with lots of shamelessness and absurdity thrown in. After the US supreme courtoverturned Trump’s me-against-the-whole-world tariffsin February, Trump, refusing to let go of his tariff toy, turned to other strategies. To justify his new 50% tariffs against Canada – which arepiled atopnumerous other tariffs he’s imposed on a country that was long the US’s closest ally – Trump relied on a never before usedprovision of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, a widely derided 1930 law that greatly worsened the Great Depression of a century ago. With this new tariff, placed on hockey sticks, paper, plywood, dairy products and many other Canadian goods, Trump invoked a Smoot-Hawley provision that allows retaliation against countries that engage in trade discrimination against the US.In making that case, Trump’s exhibit No 1 is something rather preposterous, or should I say rather shameless? After Trump imposed high, punitive tariffs on Canada last year, 11 of Canada’s 13 provinces and territories halted liquor imports from the US because they were so irate about those tariffs along with Trump’s outlandish and belittling statements that he wanted to make Canada the 51st state. The White Housecalled this ban on US liquor illegal discrimination, while Canadians view it as a type of traditional trade retaliation that countries engage in when another country – here the US – slaps tariffs on them, a situation made worse by the fact that Trump’s tariffs against Canada arean egregious violationof the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.Trump also insists that Canada has improperly discriminated against the US because Canada imposed a 25% tariff on select US-made cars after Trumpslapped a 25% tariffon Canadian-made cars.He is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US.
