That’s the logic of America’s leading stable genius, who also offered another far-fetched justification for his decision: “We’re going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke,” hetold reporterson Friday, referring to wildfire smoke that has crossed the US border.Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, isn’t happy about Trump’s painful, new 50% tariff. “We won’t back down,” he said on social media. “The fastest and only way to get US alcohol back on Ontario shelves is for the U.S. to drop its illegal tariffs on Canada.”As for the new tariffs hitting more than 80 countries, Trump, who over the years hasshown next to no concernabout worker exploitation, turned rather surprisingly to the issue of forced labor to slap on those tariffs.After the supreme court overturned his Liberation Day tariffs, Trump hit dozens of nations with a replacement tariff that would expire after 150 days. Eager to follow the boss’s wishes and impose a new tariff as soon as that one expired, Trump’s toadies uncovered a trade law provision that lets Washington punish countries that fail to take enough action against forced labor. No surprise here: Trump’s US trade representative issued a report that made the boss happy. That report found that dozens of countries, including Canada, the UK, Australia, Norway, Japan and China, plus the European Union, were not doing enough to enforce a prohibition against forced labor. That report pointed to forced labor inproducing rice in Myanmar, tobacco in Malawi, and cotton and polysilicon in China.It’s deeply perplexing that Trump is punishing some of these trading partners. Norway haspioneered lawsto crack down on forced labor in overseas supply chains, while the European Union’snew ban on goods produced with forced laborwill take effect in December 2027. Canadaalready bans imports made with forced labor, and is moving to strengthen that prohibition.If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world | Eduardo PorterRead moreIt’s not as if Trump has shown much concern before about worker exploitation or forced labor. In 1998, Trump agreed to pay$1.375m to settle a lawsuitbrought by undocumented Polish workers who said they were underpaid for their work demolishing a department store to make way for Trump Tower in New York. Sometrade experts criticize Trumpfor slamming all these longtime allies about forced labor even as he is pushing vigorously to improve ties with China, which the Biden administration found to haveserious forced labor problems in its Xinjiang region.Trump’s newfound concern about forced labor rings especially hollow considering that his administrationchopped more than $500m from the labor department’s effortsto investigate and fight against forced labor, child labor and human trafficking. “This was a completely indiscriminate meat axthat was taken to these projects, and workers will suffer,” said Thea Lee, who served as the labor department’s deputy undersecretary for international labor affairs under Biden. Bemoaning that $500m-plus in cuts, Kelly Fay Rodriguez, who was Biden’s special representative for international labor affairs, told Equal Times. “Unfortunately, it is extremely likely that child labor and forced labor practiceswill increase. We know these problems are endemic but … we’ve wiped out the resources and the prioritization for fighting them.”Imagine a world whereDonald Trumptruly cared about worker exploitation and forced labor. He would be pushing to raise the absurdly low $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage – something he has never lifted a finger to do. He would be increasing, rather than cutting, the number of safety inspectors for mines and factories. He would be pushing to strengthen – instead of repeatedly moving to weaken – the nation’s labor unions, long the most effective voice in fighting against worker exploitation. He would be pressuring China’s President Xi Jinping to stop all the forced labor in his country. But that would be a make-believe Donald Trump – he cares far more about what’s good for billionaires than what’s good for workers.Bottom line: there remains far too much forced labor in the world –more than 27 million children, women and menare in forced labor, according to the International Labor Organization. It would be great if Donald Trump sincerely seized on that issue rather than used it as an insincere pretext to clobber other nations with tariffs.Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump tariffsTariffsTrump administrationUS foreign policyCanadacommentShareReuse this content

title: The US agency that fights workplace discrimination just voted to stop measuring it | Jamil Smith | The Guardian
description: Republicans have moved to dismantle a 60-year-old demographic reporting system. Now the agency wants to choose what it sees
Author: Jamil Smith
Headline: Republicans have moved to dismantle a 60-year-old demographic reporting system. Now the agency wants to choose what it sees
Content: ‘The federal government wants to stop keeping the count it created to tell whether employers obey the law.’Photograph: Mariam Zuhaib/APView image in fullscreen‘The federal government wants to stop keeping the count it created to tell whether employers obey the law.’Photograph: Mariam Zuhaib/APOpinionTrump administrationThe US agency that fights workplace discrimination just voted to stop measuring itJamil SmithRepublicans have moved to dismantle a 60-year-old demographic reporting system. Now the agency wants to choose what it seesMon 27 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTShareWorkplace discrimination isolates. When a Black manager is passed over for a promotion, or a pregnant worker is quietly sidelined, they are left with a polite excuse and a lingering suspicion. They cannot see the company-wide spreadsheet. They cannot know if others are hitting the same invisible wall. For 60 years, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has kept a spreadsheet of its own: an annual demographic snapshot compiled from employer reports. That nationwide record lets the agency see beyond any one complaint.Last Tuesday, however, the EEOC’s Republican majorityvoted 2–1to begin dismantling that reporting system. Two days later, the proposalentered the Federal Register, arguing that requiring employers to classify workers by race and sex may itself violate the constitutional guarantee of equal protection. The rule is not final: comments are due on 24 August, and a hearing is set for 11 August.In plain English: the federal government wants to stop keeping the count it created to tell whether employers obey the law.The Civil Rights Act will remain on the books, helping this change slip past notice – and perhaps outlast those behind it. An administration does not have to repeal a civil right if it can blind the agency charged with enforcing it. You cannot prove a pattern the government has chosen not to see. Yet blindness is not quite the plan. The EEOC would stop looking routinely across the workforce while keeping the power to examine particular employers when its leaders choose. That is not colorblindness. It is selective attention.Since 1966, private employers with at least 100 workers, andcertain federal contractors with at least 50, have reported employees by race or ethnicity, sex and 10 job categories. Today, those reports typically cover more than 50 million people at roughly 73,000 employers. A company’s submission is confidential; the public dataset identifies no one. It sounds like paperwork until you consider that it shows the agency what no single worker can see. A complaint identifies a wound. Data reveals the system that made it.double quotation markFor an agency built to find discrimination, that is a remarkable turn: a tool it has used for six decades is now framed as a possible civil-rights injuryThere are fair objections to these reports. They require employers to sort workers into demographic categories even when no one has alleged discrimination. The categories are broad and sometimes dated. A numerical imbalance can be mistaken for proof of a problem, or used to defend preferences the law forbids. The EEOC estimates employers spend$273ma year complying. All of that is worth taking seriously. It sounds like a case for updating the form and enforcing the law carefully, not abandoning the system itself. Yet the proposal suggests that compulsory collection of this race and sex information may itself be unconstitutional. For an agency built to find discrimination, that is a remarkable turn: a tool it has used for six decades is now framed as a possible civil-rights injury.Employers would still keeprecords of hiring, promotion, pay and termination. The required demographic categories that let investigators compare those decisions across groups would disappear. The commission could still demand demographic information after a charge or lawsuit begins, but it could no longer assume employers had collected the same information in the same form. The subpoena survives; the evidence thins.Routine reports arrived whether or not the agency suspected anyone. Without them, its leaders would gain more control over when – and whose workplaces – the government examines for discrimination. This isn’t an agency going blind. It is choosing what it wants to see.The EEOC chair, Andrea Lucas, has already shown us whose allegations she finds urgent. In December, sheinvited white menwho believed they had suffered race or sex discrimination to come to the EEOC. She hasdescribed diversity programsas producing widespread, systemic discrimination, primarily against them.Look no further than Nike. No employee complaint set that investigation in motion; Lucas did,through a commissioner’s chargein May 2024. The charge itselfcites Nike’s publicly disclosed EEO-1 data– a product of the very reporting requirement she now proposes to eliminate. The agency later subpoenaed extensive records, including demographic data, while investigating alleged bias against white employees. The investigation remains open. The need for a charge is no real limit when a commissioner can issue one herself.The latest public national count, from 2023, offers a useful check on Lucas’s claim of systemic discrimination in the US. White men were about a third of the surveyed workforce, yet held52.7%of executive and senior-management jobs – the only group in the Associated Press’s analysis overrepresented at that level.That does not mean white men cannot be wronged at work. Title VII protects them, and the EEOC should enforce the law for them. But that is one thing a nationwide record is good for: letting evidence test an official’s theory. Lucas wants to end the measurement best able to complicate a conclusion she has already reached.Public transit is a lifeline for countless Americans. Trump is derailing our protections | Lateefah Simon and Guillermo MayerRead moreThe same selective attention governs the administration’s foreign policy. ProPublicareported this monththat appointees in the state department’s human rights bureau sought to fund an Afrikaner group, Lex Libertas, to study crimes against South African minorities. The idea later became an invitation-only competition for a $1m grant, still undecided. By then, Trump hadreserved 10,000 additional refugee slotsfor Afrikaners. Through June,7,727 of the 7,730 refugeesadmitted this fiscal year were South African –up from just one in the last full fiscal yearbefore Trump took office.Some Afrikaners may have legitimate claims, as some white men face workplace discrimination. But the double standard is hard to miss: the government treats one collective grievance as settled and may spend public money documenting it while abandoning standardized evidence about the whole workforce. You cannot prove a pattern the government refuses to measure. The government can, however, commission the search for a pattern it has already chosen to believe.Employers filedtheir 2024 numbers, but the commission has not published them; the 2025 collection may never open. A later administration could restore the form; it could not go back and take the picture. The years without a count will remain years without a count. Title VII will still forbid discrimination at work. But without that nationwide record to reveal the system, the government is leaving workers alone with their wounds.Jamil Smith is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionRaceGenderRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers? | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists
Content: ‘Just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right does not mean that it is popular with the public.’Photograph: Inquam Photos/Eduard Vinatoru/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right does not mean that it is popular with the public.’Photograph: Inquam Photos/Eduard Vinatoru/ReutersOpinionDemocratsWhy are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers?Moira DoneganThe party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategistsMon 27 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.10 EDTShareIt’s not exactly strange thatelements of the Magaversehave embracedAndrew Tate. What’s strange is that theDemocratsdo not seem interested in holding the Trump movement to account for it.Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer who is accused by numerous women around the world andnow by British prosecutorsof rape andstrangulation, as well as assault, sex trafficking,possession ofchild abuse images and extreme pornography, and various other forms of gender violence and exploitation, was arrested in Miami last week, along with Tristan, his brother and sidekick. Or I should say, they were rearrested: the men were previously charged in Romania, where they were under house arrest until, following some conveniently timed diplomatic moves from the Trump administration, they were allowed to leave the country andresettled in the US. When asked if the Trump administration had secured their release from Romania back then, theTates’ lawyer said: “Do the math. These guys are on the plane.” Now, finally, they are awaiting extradition to the UK, where they are dual citizens.The Tate brothers have long made their living by making provocative, contemptuous statements about women online. But in June, the New Yorker’s Heidi Blake published along investigationthat centered not on what the Tates have said, but on what they’re said to have done – detailing a long and documented history of alleged sex trafficking, violence and sexual assault along with a disturbing pattern of police mismanagement, incompetence and indifference that allowed the men to go free. The Tates denied wrongdoing in that piece; their lawyer called the new British charges against them “garbage”. But if anyone thought the Tates’ misogynistic influencer career was mere bluster, the Blake investigation offered a formidable bit of counterevidence: she painted a picture of the men acting exactly the way that they talked.In a world where people take misogyny as seriously as they claim to, the Tates would long ago have been ostracized, and condemned, for their hatefully sexist rhetoric and alleged violence against women. In this world, they got rich, and ingratiated themselves to powerful figures in the Republican party.Tate is a natural fit on a Maga right that has served to unite its many different factions – from Christian conservatives to Silicon Valley eugenicists, to beer-chugging barstool denizens, conspiracy mongers, and the male hosts of multi-hour podcasts – around a foundation of male supremacy. Contempt for women is the uniting force on the American right, more uniform across the competing styles within the movement even than the hatred of immigration or devotion to the prerogatives of capital. Donald Trump cemented the presidency, after all, when he was revealed to have bragged about “grab[bing]” women “by the pussy” and still maintained his base of support. In the decade that followed, his domineering, narcissistic, vulgar style of masculinity, and the alternately belittling and hateful treatment of women that accompanies it, have come to be seen on the right as a feature, not a bug. Other men within the Maga movement now imitate Trump’s style of misogyny with a gleeful competitiveness; the coalition welcomes men who collect harems of women to breed their children, those who have been multiply accused of sexual abuse and those whodecry our right to vote. Andrew Tate, in this milieu, is not an exception. He is the rule.But just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right – in which sex is seen to elevate men’s status at women’s expense, in which women’s aspirations to education, skilled work, dignity, public participation, or even mere decency are mocked; and in which men’s mistreatment of women is the key way for them to gain the esteem of other men – does not mean that it is popular with the public. Tate’s version of vulgar, avowed, preening misogyny has a constituency of Republican politicians and unlikable teenage boys; it does not have a constituency among the majority of the American public.Why areDemocratsnot making the Tates into symbols of Maga’s hateful and bizarre cultural project, of Trump’s personal alleged affinity for sexual misconduct, or of the antisocial, anti-democratic and anti-equality stances of the Maga movement?Rape, after all, might be the most quintessentially anti-democracy act: a violent refusal of equality in the most intimate terms. One could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that built from anti-rape principles into pro-democracy ones; less ambitiously, one could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that merely drew a link between Trump’s pathetic narcissism and that of the sleazeball Tates and their manosphere ilk. It seems like an easy win.That the Democratic party is not taking it shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists, and how anathema even the most basic and remedial feminist claims are now understood to be by those same forces. Because one explanation for why the Democrats are not taking advantage of the Tates’ links to Trump is as simple as it is dark: they do not want to alienate the Tates’ base of manosphere content consumers.It is by now a cliche to say that Democrats arelosing men, a demographic reality that is treated as a much greater emergency than the GOP’s parallel loss of women. Sects within the Democratic consultant class have made the recruitment of manly men candidates into their singular mission. Following the 2024 election, major party players fundraised a massive$20mfor a “Speaking with American Men” project, meant to lure men back to the party; the California governor,Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 presidential candidate, has forged his own podcast project, in which he has taken to embracing some rightwing cultural positions on things like trans rights. The party is running white male candidates who saycartoonish thingslike it’s OK “to be a manly man” – as if anyone was confused.It is this desperate and frantic effort to re-masculinize the party at any cost that led to the recruitment ofGraham Platner, the ex-marine who dropped out of the Maine Senate race earlier this month after being accused of rape (he has denied the allegations). Major players in the Democratic party did the right thing in that case, calling on Platner to drop out en masse. But many of them still believe in the strategy that elevated him in the first place: that of prizing men over women, of coveting men’s votes and men’s support as somehow more legitimate, more valuable, than women’s.In this sense, there is another reason that some in the Democratic party won’t seize upon the Tate issue: even if they don’t condone his alleged violence, on his most fundamental principle – that men are better and more important than women are – they may not entirely disagree.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionWomenGenderAndrew TateUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: AI can fuel biological weapons. We must harness its power for defense | Annie Jacobsen | The Guardian
description: The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design
Content: ‘The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties, and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives.’Photograph: APView image in fullscreen‘The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties, and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives.’Photograph: APOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI can fuel biological weapons. We must harness its power for defenseAnnie JacobsenThe offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological designMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 06.17 EDTShareAs artificial intelligence rapidly transforms the biological sciences, it is pushing the future of biology in two opposing directions. AI can help bad actors generate recipes for biological weapons with just a few keystrokes and computational prompts. At the same time, AI can track disease outbreaks and deliver critical public health information to millions of people in real time – potentially stopping a deadly outbreak in its tracks. What we are dealing with in this moment is profound: a race between offense and defense. Between the proliferation of dark biology, where deadly pathogens are engineered in secret, and the promise of a new era of collective global health.Every infectious disease outbreak begins with a handful of cases. Public health wins by learning about an outbreak before it spreads wide, before hospitals fill and a crisis starts to spiral out of control. As transmission rates explode, options shrink. One of AI’s greatest values is its ability to compress the timeline between outbreak and detection. Speed can mean the difference between containing an outbreak and confronting an epidemic, or another global pandemic.The WorldHealthOrganization (WHO) now uses AI to track the spread of infectious disease. At the WHO’s Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, in Berlin, Germany, computational systems leverage artificial intelligence and pathogenic surveillance to track and monitor infectious disease outbreaks around the world. At the center of this new way forward sits a computer-based system called Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources, or Eios (“EE-oss”), which acts as a giant filter for the world’s minute-by-minute health information.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dutton/Penguin Random HouseFor decades, traditional epidemic intelligence has relied on official case counts. But data from hospitals, labs, research groups and other formal reporting systems takes days or weeks to register and input into official databases. Eios leverages the colossal power of modern computing and social media to get a more immediate picture of a disease outbreak. Eios focuses on unofficial reports, citizen chatter, local news reports, social media posts and more. Proficient across multiple languages, Eios scans millions of websites, feeds and platforms, searching for outbreaks as they happen. It scrapes, filters and ranks information. The goal of Eios is to pull signal from noise.AI is a force multiplier, changing the biological sciences every day. The real question is not whether AI can do catastrophic harm in the realm of biological sciences – it most certainly can – but whether public health officials can figure out how to deploy AI as a defensive tool faster than malicious actors deploy it as an offensive one.The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. AI systems can already help researchers navigate enormous bodies of biological knowledge that once required years of specialized training. They can explain complex laboratory techniques, locate obscure scientific literature, troubleshoot technical problems and suggest experimental designs. None of these capabilities is inherently dangerous. Together, however, they lower the barrier to entering what was once a highly specialized field.AI may help us cure countless diseases – and usher in a new golden age of medicine | Samuel HumeRead moreThe greatest concern is that AIs can help humans create genuinely novel, or new, forms of biology. Scientists are already exploring these possibilities, from mirror-image life to organisms designed with capabilities that do not already exist in nature. Until recently, these possibilities were largely confined to theory or science fiction.Biologyis unlike any other technology because what it produces can reproduce, spread across borders, mutate, and evolve on its own. A software bug crashes a computer. A biological mistake can become self-propagating. Once a living organism is released into the world, it cannot simply be switched off or recalled. That biological weapons are alive is what makes them fundamentally different from every other class of weapon, from the arrow to the ICBM.The race has already begun. As I cover in my forthcoming bookBiological War, and this recentNew York Timesarticle outlines, biological weapons have an extremely low barrier to entry. Unlike nuclear weapons, which require tightly controlled fissile material and complex delivery systems, biological weapons can be built with widely available laboratory tools, aided by increasingly powerful AI systems.The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives. The point is pressure, not panic. We need to develop AI systems to strengthen public health, accelerate disease detection and help build biological defenses as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design. Because once biology outruns our ability to contain it, there is no recalling what has already been unleashed upon the world.Annie Jacobsen is the author ofBiological War, to be published on 28 July by Dutton. She also wrote the Pulitzer prize–finalist in history The Pentagon’s Brain and the New York Times bestsellers Nuclear War, Area 51 and Operation PaperclipExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionBiologyWeapons technologyComputingHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: He’s commander-in-chief of chaos. Now we’re all victims of Trump’s wars | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: New tariffs, gas price rises, the deaths of thousands, insecurity … We’re living at the whim of one capricious, vain, easily bored man and his gang of stooges, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: New tariffs, gas price rises, the deaths of thousands, insecurity … We’re living at the whim of one capricious, vain, easily bored man and his gang of stooges, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Composite: Guardian Design, Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design, Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionDonald TrumpHe’s commander-in-chief of chaos. Now we’re all victims of Trump’s warsNesrine MalikNew tariffs, gas price rises, the deaths of thousands, insecurity … We’re living at the whim of one capricious, vain, easily bored man and his gang of stoogesMon 27 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 09.29 EDTShareYou would be forgiven, as the US and Iran traded strikes over the past few days, for thinking that it was only last month that the two signed the Islamabad Memorandum, which formalised the process of ending the war and established a 60-day period to negotiate the final terms of a deal. That’s because itwasonly last month. But there has been so much talk and bluster and strike and turn tail that the conflict feels like it has started and ended several times already. The whole war is only five months old but is already settling into a sort of permanent feature of life, one that is all repetitive theatre now, each act indistinguishable from the one before it to all but the most plugged-in observers. The war is over. The war is at its peak. The Iranians arebrave people. The Iranians arescum, not least their leaders. The Iraniansdon’t want a ceasefire. The Iranians arebegging for one. The strait of Hormuz is open, it is shut, it is partly open.To recap, where we are now in the war that was only supposed to last a few weeks but is now entering its sixth month is that the US has expanded airstrikes on Iran in a “major military punishment”. Iran has once again struck US base targets located across the region. TheHouthis have claimed their own blockadeover a second shipping chokepoint – the war now extends from the Gulf to the Red Sea. Trump can’t get out. Iran now understands the powerful leverage of the strait and its geographical, and therefore military, advantage in controlling it. Trump cannot end the war with that bargaining chip in its hands and the Iranians will not end the war without it. He can’t withdraw on terms that merely restore the prewar status quo. And Trump can’t go all in. Boots on the ground would be an extended bloody campaign that would claim many lives. In the US, the deaths of 18 troops so far and how the Pentagon appears to be trying to undercount that number hastriggered outrage.So what now? A sunk-cost logic that will continue to throw more money, and more bodies, into the quagmire. The war has already cost the US almost $40bn. And the Pentagon is asking for another $67bn. The White House’s request for Congress for the fiscal year is acolossal $1.5tn. The implications of this profligacy for the US are the choking of domestic spending. “We’re fighting wars,” Trump said earlier this year. “It’s not possible for us to take care of daycare, Medicaid, Medicare … We have to take care of one thing: military protection.” For what? A war that the US itself launched, that nobody asked for, that has no defensive features at all, and which is run by a frat house of bullies and lickspittles.Everything into the furnace for Trump’s adventures:Iranian childrenand civilians and infrastructure; Gulf countries’ economies and political stability and even their drinking water, as Iran strikes desalination plants upon whichseveralare heavilydependent. And almost every household in the world. Oil broke $100 a barrel last week andenergy prices are higheracross the board. Brent oil prices are now almost 40% higher than before the war. A gallon of gasoline in the US now also costs 37% more than it did and diesel is 40% higher.Gas prices have soared again in the UK, up nearly 50% just this month, and the lag between the new raised oil prices and what you pay at the pump will show up in a fortnight. And the story is replicated all over the world,slamming energy consumptionand government budgets. These are not just statistics: together they constitute nothing short of a global energy re-configuration as the Iran war beds in. One that heaps pressure on economies all over the world in various states of distress, whether it is wealthy capitalist ones creaking under the weight of privatisation,price gougingand profiteering, or poorer ones where governments cannot absorb more pain for already stressed consumers. Protests over rising costs and fuel prices have flared up and paralysed transport fromIrelandtoKenya.View image in fullscreenProtesters set tyres alight during a nationwide transport strike over rising fuel prices in Nairobi, Kenya, 18 May 2026.Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPAWhich makes this volatile moment a perfect time to pass some stabilising measures and increase confidence in economic stewardship. Something, perhaps, like a swap ofTrump’s tariff regime, which expired last week, with a new one, imposed on the grounds that countries were not doing enough to “tackle forced labour”. If you think that this is a risible excuse, and that the Trump administration does not harbour a deep moral concern about poor working conditions across the world, then this is sadly a symptom of Trump derangement syndrome. You should get that looked at.There is no amelioration of the cumulative impacts of this vandalism, no subsidy or cap that can soak up a colossal shock at the heart of global energy transit channels and oil production. We are all held hostage by a regime in the US that has pressed its military and economic prowess in service of ego and ignorance; tethered to an administration that runs the country as it runs in the world, in pursuit of point-scoring in a game where no play is too small or too big. Whether it isadding warning signs outside the Smithsonianto alert that exhibits are “inaccurate”, initiating crude tariff policies, or dragging a whole region into war because he thought it would be easy and look cool, Trump is wildly casual, cavalier, one moment bored and the other vexed. As if the whole world were a plaything to be toyed with and discarded, then picked up again and shaken and prodded.And it all shows no signs of abating. Yoked to US hegemony, we all count the pennies, the bodies, the ever-escalating tithes of the election of a single man and the willingness of careerists and cowards who enable and support him. The more it carries on, the more these costs will be recounted in a sort of background noise to our existence and what was previously unthinkable will become the new normal, again and again. TheIranwar is the most hazardous manifestation of this. Phantom breakthroughs, threats of final decisive escalations, all have given way to a chilling reality. An exorbitant war that is with each day rearranging geopolitics, domestic budgets and household ones, is once again, a new normal. Trump is stuck. Unable to swallow the unpalatable price of peace. And everyone else pays the cost.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranTariffsGasOilIrancommentShareReuse this content

title: The patient who loves buying lettuce for his daughter-in-law – and what his case teaches us about shared decision-making in medicine | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: Doctors should recommend treatment accompanied by conversations about the pros and cons for the individuals who are in front of them
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: Doctors should recommend treatment accompanied by conversations about the pros and cons for the individuals who are in front of them
Content: ‘Patients often worry about “dying on the table” but that’s rare – it’s the aftermath that matters.’Photograph: Chinnapong/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Patients often worry about “dying on the table” but that’s rare – it’s the aftermath that matters.’Photograph: Chinnapong/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionHealthThe patient who loves buying lettuce for his daughter-in-law – and what his case teaches us about shared decision-making in medicineRanjana SrivastavaDoctors should recommend treatment accompanied by conversations about the pros and cons for the individuals who are in front of themMon 27 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 19.05 EDTShareWeeks before major surgery, a patient cancels his appointment with our geriatric oncology service, declaring it unnecessary. An astute nurse convinces him otherwise.In his mid-80s, the patient has been diagnosed with an early cancer. The surgeon advises that surgery would be the only cure but, noting the lack of urgency, sends him to see me. I can see why. The proposed procedure is long and complicated; in elderly people, even temporary setbacks can result in long-term effects.I start by asking the patient to describe his day.Each morning, he tends the garden before having coffee with old friends. He returns home with the fresh salad leaves his daughter-in-law relishes. After dinner, which sometimes includes the grandchildren, he retires early. His son adds that his father’s memory is beginning to falter but an established routine keeps him functional. They both praise his quality of life as being ideal.My patient hates the notion of an “intruder” in his body.“I just want it gone,” he says.At a dying man’s bedside, I see something much rarer than grief: the courage to include the young | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreI reassure him that this is understandable but we should discuss in some depth his decision to undergo surgery. The patient balks, his son is eager to talk.I explain that hisrisk of any complicationis high and even reversible events such as delirium, infection and electrolyte imbalance can cause prolonged difficulties. Patients often worry about “dying on the table” but that’s rare – it’s the aftermath that matters.The surgeon and I estimate the early cancer is unlikely to cause problems during his lifetime. I say we are not opposed to the surgery itself, rather we want to make sure he understands its ramifications.But by now, the patient has tuned out.“I know you’re tired, so here’s a simple question,” I try. “At this point in your life, what matters to you?”His face lights up. “Meeting my friends. And buying salad leaves for my daughter-in-law.”The son is visibly surprised by this beautiful sentiment.“And if you were no longer able to do this independently?”“Then it’s not a life I would want.”This one articulation becomes the turning point that allows an honest discussion about what he values and the perceived cost of lost independence. I can’t help but notice that the patient who engages in this more personal conversation is entirely different from the patient who had lost interest in a generic discussion of the benefits and risks of an operation.double quotation markIn advising that a particular intervention ‘might help’, doctor and patient might sit at opposite ends of hope and realityI ask the pair to reflect on our talk. Later, when they cancel surgery, their explanation is telling – making a fast initial decision, even the inappropriate one, had relieved the distress of indecision. But once the patient had voiced what mattered to him, the right decision was clear.I recalled this encounter as I heard a thoughtful talk at a conference aboutshared decision-making in healthcare.At its simplest, this involves equal parts doctor and patient – the doctor bringing medical knowledge and the patient contributing personal preferences to reach a collaborative decision that is right forthatpatient inthosecircumstances.Doctors might say it’s what they do but, far too often, patients report not understanding that they have a real choice, which includes saying no. This is reflected in decisional regret:“If only I had known then what I know now.”This is not a result of either party’s motivations, “care factor” or even attention to detail. How can doctors and patients make a shared decision if they don’t speak a shared language?This is the first challenge of shared decision-making. Words like rare, likely and tolerable are subjective. In advising that a particular intervention “might help”, doctor and patient might sit at opposite ends of hope and reality.Time is another challenge. Pressed doctors can be tempted to “do” informed consent from a bygone era: speed through a list of risks and say, “Sign here.” Most people will.But a thorough discussion of risks should contain risks specific tothatperson.No doctor wants to have this conversation with a patient. For everyone’s sake, we must | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreAnother challenge is a knowledge gap. Exhorting shared decision-making as a tenet of good medicine but not explicitly teaching how to go about it leaves doctors to construct their own definition. Variation in practice is inevitable. A recommendation should be accompanied not only by the scientific evidence (notably derived from highly selected patients) but also a deliberate discussion of the pros and cons forthatpatient withthosegoals.Given this, how should patients better advocate for themselves when it comes to important healthcare decisions?Spearheaded by a geriatrician, anAustralian websitecontains a plain-language (and translated) guide designed with the patient for the patient. A one-page “before your appointment” sheet contains questions every patient or carer should consider. I routinely recommend it to my family. The clinician section has nuanced questions that all doctors can learn to ask. I use it myself to keep me on track.Another useful site comes from theNHSin the UK.For an ageing population with multiple conditions and a banquet of interventions – often pricey, not always friendly and sometimes downright dangerous – shared decision-making must go from idea to reality.The tools are free; if patients insist on using them, doctors will follow.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionDoctorsHospitalsCancerAgeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Here’s why India’s cockroach protests were such a success – and why the Mamdani effect means more to come | Mukul Kesavan | The Guardian
description: The young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra Modi, says Dehli-based essayist and author Mukul Kesavan
Author: Mukul Kesavan
Headline: The young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra Modi, says Dehli-based essayist and author Mukul Kesavan
Content: Celebrations in Mumbai on 26 July after the resignation of  education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.Photograph: Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCelebrations in Mumbai on 26 July after the resignation of  education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.Photograph: Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOpinionIndiaHere’s why India’s cockroach protests were such a success – and why the Mamdani effect means more to comeMukul KesavanThe young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra ModiMon 27 Jul 2026 05.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.32 EDTShareThe rebellion in India of the young, led by theCockroach Janta party (CJP),unfolded against a backdrop of large, abstract, geometrical structures – arcs, planes, hemispheres – that together make up an observatory called Jantar Mantar, built in the early 18th century to refine almanacs and tell time. Jantar Mantar has been a byword for political protest for decades: it marks the space that the Delhi police assigns to the politically disgruntled so they can vent in a contained way. But it had never before hosted a political insurgency that started from scratch and forced the Indian state to back down in less than eight weeks.When its founder,Abhijeet Dipke, brought the CJP to Jantar Mantar, it was a social media hashtag with 20 million followers. While he was studying in Boston, Dipke took the remarks of chief justice Surya Kant, who is accused of referring to the swathes of unemployed young people and activists as “parasites” and “cockroaches”, and turned them into a here-we-come meme. When he brought the CJP home to Delhi on 6 June to make it real, people were intrigued. Given the mostly dismal fate of civil society movements during prime minister Narendra Modi’s time in office, no one anticipated the David and Goliath contest that came to a head last Saturday.Like other political tourists, I visited Jantar Mantar on 6 June out of curiosity. On that inaugural day it was modestly crowded and not that different from the dozens of demos I had attended over 50 years. The one difference was how young these so-called cockroaches were. I had seen young people mobilise against Modi’s government at close quarters before when the students ofJamia Millia Islamia, the university I taught in, came out against a pernicious citizenship bill. Their courage and idealism was defeated by a combination of police repression and organised rioting. This government’s willingness to use police brutality, vigilante violence and a pliant judiciary to snuff out protest hung over the fledgling CJP campaign like a shadow.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) celebrate the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, Mumbai, India, 26 July 2026.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPABut when I returned a month and a half later on 20 July, the scheduled day for the march to parliament, Jantar Mantar was unrecognisable. A hunger strike had raised the political temperature of the protest. The government had forcibly removed the main hunger striker,Sonam Wangchuk, from the site and detained him in a hospital. The calculation was that his absence would defuse the tension and demoralise the protesters. That didn’t happen.India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for ModiRead moreThere were tens of thousands of people crammed into the barricaded space and thousands of police officers in attendance. The government had underestimated the size of the crowd that poured in by bus, train and car from Delhi and beyond. In the afternoon the Delhi police force and its masters compounded its miscalculation by attacking this giant gathering of young people withlathis(bamboo sticks) and teargas.This tableau of brutality was shocking enough in real life, but in the hands of young digital natives, whose phone cameras were extensions of themselves, it became a gush of online content that brought the violent drama of this confrontation into every home. The callous violence of the police and the raging, mocking, laughing defiance of the young protesters played out on every mobile phone.The cockroaches won where other protesters, not unlike them, such as Jamia’s students, had lost. They won, in part, because they weren’t visibly Muslim. There were Muslims among them, but this was a protest about the corruption of competitive examinations, an issue that concerns every middle-class family inIndia. It couldn’t easily be tarred as an anti-national conspiracy in the way that the struggle for secular citizenship led by Jamia’s mainly Muslim students was. This didn’t stop India’s mostly tame mainstream media from trying, but the scandal of the medical school examination was so egregious that no one gave them a hearing.Also, this was in the heart of New Delhi, a stone’s throw from parliament. Once the government had made, from its point of view, the cardinal error of letting gen Z occupy the commanding heights of the capital, every day of the protest produced hundreds of new episodes of a national drama – a digitalMahabharat– in which the vulnerable and charismatic children of light faced off against the armed and uniformed enforcers of darkness. Bharatiya Janata party governments have sanctioned massive police violence against minorities in India’s borderlands, in Manipur, Assam and Kashmir. But this was Jantar Mantar, the sacred centre of the republic.View image in fullscreenCJP spokesperson Saurav Das (left) and founder and president Abhijeet Dipke at a demonstration at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, India, 25 July 2026.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAThe leaders of the movement, Abhijeet Dipke andSaurav Das, had set themselves up for success by demanding a difficult but doable concession: the sacking of the education minister. It was difficult because Modi had never dismissed a cabinet minister in response to political pressure; this stubbornness was central to his strongman persona. It was doable because there were precedents in the history of the republic for a minister taking responsibility for a disaster and resigning.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionModi did everything he could to wriggle out of this standoff. He even produced a comically inept Instagram video promising fast-track courts to address the corruption in the examination system. When that didn’t work, his government capitulated and Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister,departed. There was an assembly election scheduled in Uttar Pradesh next year and Modi knew that the BJP would haemorrhage political support if the Jantar Mantar impasse wasn’t resolved.The quarrel that some commentators on the left have with the CJP is that Pradhan’s dismissal was a symbolic victory but not a substantial one.Pralhad Joshi, the man who has replaced Pradhan as education minister, is not an improvement. Like Pradhan he is a member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the BJP’s far-right parent body. He publicly defended the premature release in 2022 of 11 men convicted for rape in the notoriousBilkis Bano gang-rape case.The CJP’s argument is that Pradhan was always a proxy for Modi. The point of the protest was to diminish Modi by forcing him to back down publicly. Also, it isn’t clear what a systemic victory would look like or how it would be achieved.The striking thing about the CJP’s leadership is its youth and poise. Zohran Mamdani, the youthful mayor of New York, now seems a template. He is 35. Dipke, the CJP’s Dalit leader, is 30 years old.Ashutosh Ranka, who negotiated the end of the protest with the BJP’s leadership, is about the same age. Das, the other negotiator and spokesperson, is all of 26.Neha Bora, the president of a leftwing student organisation, the All-India Students’ Association, is 25. It’s hard to know how their politics will evolve. What they have in common is eloquence, message discipline, all-round unflappability and the potential to leave a legacy. They may be an enduring problem for this government. Jantar Mantar may have just produced an echelon of homegrown Mamdanis.Mukul Kesavan is an essayist and author based in DelhiExplore more on these topicsIndiaOpinionNarendra ModiProtestSouth and central AsiacommentShareReuse this content

title: Amid the social and political panic about falling birthrates, why not ask new mothers what they think? | Lucy Jones | The Guardian
description: Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the priority is for policy that addresses women’s real concerns, says author and journalist Lucy Jones
Author: Lucy Jones
Headline: Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the priority is for policy that addresses women’s real concerns, says author and journalist Lucy Jones
Content: Mothers with young children carry an expectation to ‘do it all’: to work, manage the household and raise children.Photograph: Natalia  Lebedinskaia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMothers with young children carry an expectation to ‘do it all’: to work, manage the household and raise children.Photograph: Natalia  Lebedinskaia/Getty ImagesOpinionChildbirthAmid the social and political panic about falling birthrates, why not ask new mothers what they think?Lucy JonesNew research reveals deep anxieties. Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the priority is for policy that addresses women’s real concernsMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.30 EDTShareIt seems as though every week brings another news story on declining global birthrates. A number of political leaders have been panicking for a while, of course, instructing citizens to reproduce in tones so beguiling, who could possibly resist? JD Vance: “I want more babies”; Jacob Rees-Mogg: “We need more babies”. While in France this year, a government direct-mailing campaignurged 29-year-oldsto have a baby before it’s too late.People are busily scratching their heads and trying to work out why this is happening. The trend is described as a catastrophe for civilisation, with leaders drumming up incentives and policies in response, from medals (Russia) and a €1,000 birth bonus (Italy) to expanding access to IVF (the US, with Donald Trump crowing – and if you’re eating you may want to skip the rest of this sentence – he’ll be known as the “fertilisation president”).We hear ever-multiplying theories, from housing costs, contraception, education for women andsmartphone addictionto lower rates of hooking up,problems with car seats,global heatingand urbanisation. But something is missing in these discussions. Here’s a clue. It begins with M and it has seven letters.In all the panic about falling birthrates, the experiences of the people actually doing the births and those parenting infants – most often mothers – are strangely absent. We hear about the ruinous effect of low birthrates, but comparatively little of the difficulties mothers face, such as maternity discrimination and mental health issues. It’s as though there is something about the way we organise society that means new mothers, caregivers, are unseen.Thank goodness, then, for amajor new reportfrom the thinktank Theos – for which I wrote the foreword – which aims to make the experience of becoming a mother more visible. It is rich, fascinating and in depth, covering subjects such as mortality and tax, sleep and debt, the body and politics. While the experience of becoming a mother is obviously individual, there are recurring themes that should make us, as a society, take notice.One of the most striking findings is that many mothers feel “undervalued”. What does it mean to organise society in a way that people who are growing and raising new humans feel like this? It can’t be good. But perhaps it is convenient. While most people in the study thought that childcare was as vital to the economy as paid work, the maximum state maternity pay in the UK – from six weeks to 39 weeks after giving birth – is £6,412.56, far below the minimum wage. It is no surprise, then, that in a society where value is priced against profit mothers feel undervalued.What is it like to be a mother today? While many found childcare rewarding and enjoyable, the study also points to data showing that 48% found it stressful and 40% found it overwhelming. Perhaps this has something to do with the finding that mothers with young children carry an expectation to “do it all”: to work, manage the household and raise children. Many mothers also felt “invisible” once they had their babies. “You sort of cease to exist as a person, and you just become a mum,” said one.Another talked about people giving up their seat on the tube when she wore a badge in her pregnancy. But “it’s very rare for people to offer you a seat once you have a baby and a pram, which is funny, because I actually feel like, particularly after my C-section, I probably needed it a bit more”. This oversight should be easy to address, with a fuller rollout of priority seats on public transport for parents travelling with babies and young children, or even – as many European countries have – specific areas on trains for prams and families.What was birth and its aftermath like for the women in the study? Many described it as a time of “overwhelming exhaustion, sleep deprivation and anxiety”, with some finding postnatal visits rushed and “tick-box”, overlooking the mother, with the same at the routine six-week check. Experiences of maternal healthcare during birth and post-partum support were mixed: one woman spoke of “being handled like a piece of meat”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPeople keep asking me why I’m choosing to have a caesarean – here are my reasons | Sharon GaffkaRead moreThe study found that the interviewees were nervous or scared of sharing feelings of overwhelm after giving birth, because of the stigma attached to struggling in new motherhood. The focus on perinatal mental illness is obviously important, but it’s not the whole story. A better understanding about the dimensions of ordinary matrescence would help. The report’s recommendations also include enhancing the six-week check and improving care for new mothers in the immediate hospital stay.When we had our first child, I had never really thought about “motherhood”. I imagined my body – because I carried our kids, though of course not all mothers do – would be like a box or a flowerpot, and that when she was born I’d return to who I was, more or less. Instead, I soon realised the biological, socio-political and psychological experience of becoming a mother was a lot more complicated and intense than I’d been led to believe, from the messaging of antenatal care to the philosophy, politics and culture I had absorbed through my life.There are two intersecting problems. First, there is a lack of recognition of the heft of the experiences of pregnancy, birth and new motherhood. Second, there is a lack of social support in the perinatal period. Both are needed to improve the experience of people becoming parents.More widely, we need to understand how and why new mothers are feeling like this, what it reveals about our current value system, and how we might evolve a culture and society that is able to value birth and care, for all people. No need for any medals.Lucy Jones is a journalist and the author ofMatresenceand Losing EdenExplore more on these topicsChildbirthOpinionHealth & wellbeingMental healthHealthWomenFamilyChildrencommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham is master of his message for now. But he should know this: media foes will offer no respite | Tom Baldwin | The Guardian
description: While the new PM’s slick social media operation can help him bypass the hostile press that devoured Starmer, he will still need friends in the fourth estate, says former Labour party adviser Tom Baldwin
Author: Tom Baldwin
Headline: While the new PM’s slick social media operation can help him bypass the hostile press that devoured Starmer, he will still need friends in the fourth estate, says former Labour party adviser Tom Baldwin
Content: Illustration: Ellie Foreman-Peck/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ellie Foreman-Peck/The GuardianOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham is master of his message for now. But he should know this: media foes will offer no respiteTom BaldwinWhile the new PM’s slick social media operation can help him bypass the hostile press that devoured Starmer, he will still need friends in the fourth estateMon 27 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 13.29 EDTShareAfter a week in Downing Street where Labour’s previously flatlining position inthe polls has at least showed signs of having a pulse,Andy Burnham is still just about enjoying a prime ministerial honeymoon. But he has been in politics long enough to know that the largely friendly media coverage that he has received so far won’t last for ever.Indeed, within hours of becoming prime minister, some familiar predators were circling as they tried to decide whether to attack him for being too leftwing, too insubstantial or simply offering more of the same.The Mail accused him of embarking on an unfunded“spending spree”, the Sun highlighted a series of“embarrassing”and “humiliating” moments that marred his first days in office, while the Telegraph declared he stood for nothing except “gimmicks” and“rehashing failed ideas”. Much of this, of course, goes with the territory, because Labour leaders always face the unyielding hostility of a rightwing press.But this grim process, one I have witnessed close-up both as apolitical “lobby” journalistand as a communications director for Labour, has accelerated and become ever more gory as new adversaries emerge online. Orderly old methods of managing the news cycle with “a grid” of stories for newspapers and broadcasters have been replaced by the mayhem of a zombie movie. In the past couple of years, Keir Starmer was demonised out of all recognition and beyond reason by platforms such as Elon Musk’s X. AndAI-generated imagesthat purport to show Burnham promising that his new constituency of Makerfield will house more asylum seekers, orcompletely false claimsthat he once gave a public contract to his wife, have already circulated widely on social media.In private, the new prime minister is intensely critical of this toxic and sometimes terrifying media environment. Over the nine years he spent away from Westminster as mayor of greater Manchester, Burnham is said to have watched – with a sense of dismay, disorientation and maybe dread – how social media algorithms fuel an individualist briefing culture that portrays politics as a shallow game of “who’s up and who’s down”. This has infected the mainstream press, which, by consistently elevating drama and unfolding chaos over policy and substance, gives alienated or angry voters the impression of politicians being more interested in themselves than people like them.View image in fullscreenDaily Mail, 18 July.Photograph: Daily MailAnd, perhaps because Burnham has so recently benefited from the resulting instability, many restlessLabourMPs now hope that Britain’s fifth prime minister in four years will be better suited to dealing with such challenges than his immediate predecessors. Certainly, he appears comfortable with modern forms of communication and to prioritise content for platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram and X. While retaining some of Starmer’s politically appointed press advisers, Burnham has brought his own digital team into Downing Street with him.His willingness to take risks with social media, from self-deprecating dad jokes and dressed-down selfiesto a videodiscussing the merits of different pub snacks with his new chancellor, has helped him make a much-prized connection with voters on the platforms where most of them get their information. Admirers hope this strategy means he can tell a story about himself and his programme that resembles not so much Donald Trump or Nigel Farage but that of another progressive mayor – New York’s Zohran Mamdani. In a recent post where Burnham was shown with a sign saying“Ask Andy Anything”and taking questions from passersby in Cardiff, he mentioned to one of them that his father had Alzheimer’s before going on to explain that this was why he cared so deeply about reform of the social care system. By contrast, Starmer, who appeared uneasy with social media and, for principled reasons, generally shied away from opportunities to explain policy through personal experiences such as his late mother’s disability or his brother’s cancer diagnosis, which was kept secret until after he had died.Yet the new PM’s apparent openness to people he meets on the street has not, so far, been extended to lobby journalists. Between winning the Makerfield byelection a month ago and becoming prime minister, he made two speeches and took no questions at either of them from the media, while doing just three interviews, which included a podcast mostly about football with Gary Lineker. Although political editors invited to join him in the Downing Street garden on Monday afternoon included one from the Sun, a newspaper that Burnham has previously shunned for its coverage of theHillsborough disaster, the whole lot of them were limited to a total of four questions.View image in fullscreenA selfie with Mo Farah shared by Andy Burnham on Instagram.Photograph: Andy BurnhamAides insist there is no deliberate effort to avoid scrutiny and can point to how he spoke at lengthto the BBC’s Laura Kuenssbergover the weekend, on issues ranging from social care to his approach to President Trump. They promise that other journalists will get their chance before long as part of a new “integrated” communications strategy. And, for what it’s worth, I sympathise with his desire to have important speeches covered in their own right rather than be overshadowed by journalists grandstanding with “gotcha” questions afterwards. Nor can those outlets, such as the Mail or GB News, that are so obviously intent on throwing rocks at him really whinge too loudly if Downing Street decides to limit their access and opportunities to do so.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDaily Telegraph, 22 July 2026.Illustration: The TelegraphThere is more justifiable concern, however, about the build-up to last week’s reshuffle, which ultimately shed much blood but little light. In what appeared to be a coordinated operation by those claiming to know Burnham’s mind, multiple journalists were told this would be Shabana Mahmood, along with some disobliging remarks about Ed Miliband that appeared all too reminiscent of the anonymous factional briefing that too often characterised Starmer’s government.Even the Financial Times, a newspaper that treads very carefully because it has the capacity to move markets, was confident enough to declare Mahmood was“set to” get the jobafter being told this by three separate sources. It is possible, of course, that Burnham really had not made any decision at the time, or that he changed his mind in the days before John Healey was appointed. And yet there appears to be more than a little satisfaction about the lobby’s humiliation within the prime minister’s wider circle, with one member of it suggesting that journalists had “learned the hard way only to trust official spokespeople in future”. There may also have been an effort to work out who was responsible for leaks by giving those suspected of unauthorised briefing false information that then appeared in the newspapers. Either way, these are dangerous tactics from a new administration that will need to be trusted by the more responsible end of the Westminster media when, inevitably, the going gets rough.One journalist who covered Burnham for many years in Manchester says he can get “prickly” in such circumstances. And there is scepticism that the PM’s “blokey” – if slightly one-geared – social media personality will always work so well when the algorithms of such platforms are tuned more to “rage bait” than a reasoned explanation about the long-term benefits of devolution. And, if the “medium is the message”, Burnham cannot allow his communications to become too reliant on these new forms of media that are so often open sewers of hate and lies. One of his closest advisers in No 10 acknowledges the current good vibes will inevitably fade, and indicates his team are preparing for tougher times ahead by studying ways of “inoculating ourselves” against online disinformation, before adding: “What can I say? We will do our best.”Perhaps the best thing Burnham can do now is just grow a thicker skin. He will need it.Tom Baldwin is a former assistant editor of the Times and a former senior adviser to the Labour party. He is the author of Keir Starmer: The BiographyExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that | Benedict Cumberbatch, Alan Cumming and Benedict Wong | The Guardian
description: The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should, say actors led by Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong
Author: Benedict Cumberbatch
Headline: The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should, say actors led by Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionTelevision industryA TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop thatThe Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought in the US and UK. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She shouldBenedict Cumberbatch,Alan CummingandBenedict WongMon 27 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.40 EDTShareView image in fullscreenThough it has yet to become front-page news in the UK, you should know about the proposedParamount-Warner Bros merger. It threatens to inflict immense harm on the British public. As actors and public figures who have spent our careers in the arts in Britain – working with British crews, on British stages and sets – we have a responsibility to the public who support, enjoy and consume the art we make.The UK is being threatened by a media merger that would harm our workers, our culture and the public – but we can stop it. We are encouraged by Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, who recently sent letters toParamount SkydanceandWarner Bros Discovery, as well as a statement toparliament, indicating that she is “minded to intervene” in Paramount’s$110bn takeoverof Warner Bros.She is correct to investigate this major threat to the UK’s public interest. And she will not be acting alone. This month, 12 US states, led by California,sued in federal courtto block the merger, warning that it would raise prices, shrink the number of films made and degrade the quality of what audiences see. And they just won a major victory: on Friday, Paramount agreed todelay the mergeruntil trial, which could be months. These states acted even after Washington’s own justice department – despitethe reported reservationsof career staff –waved the deal through.Their lawsuit confirms the danger; it cannot, however, do the UK’s work for it. US courts fight on the antitrust front for US markets. The EU, which last weekconditionally backed the merger, also makes its own decisions. The UK’s public interest, our public service broadcasting, our news plurality, the plurality of voices British audiences hear, can only be defended here, by our own secretary of state and the Competition and Markets Authority.The fight against this merger now runs on two fronts, and Nandy commands one of them. Should her department decide to intervene, it may prove one of the most important decisions any culture secretary has taken for UK film, television and media in a generation.This is why. We have spent our lives working in this industry. We know what it looks like from the inside: the sound stages at Leavesden, the crews who move from production to production, the editors and camera operators and costume designers whose names scroll past in the credits at the end of a film. These are our cherished friends and colleagues, who create the shows we all love, who produce the news that educates the public and film the sport events we enjoy together. UK film and television are not just images on your screens; they are the lives and livelihoods of thousands of workers and families, whose work supports local economies. The industry supportsmore than 180,000 jobs, generated£6.8bn in production spendlast year alone and adds roughly£12bn a yearin value to our economy. It is one of the things the UK still does better than almost anyone, and a cultural heritage we must protect.We have watched, with growing alarm, what consolidation does to the breadth and depth of the work we produce: independent film acquisitions at the leading independent film festival Sundancefell by halfbetween 2019 and 2025. Award-winning documentaries – films thatwon Oscarsandtopped festival juries– havestruggled to find commercial distributionbecause they touched subjects the remaining handful of buyers found inconvenient. Every merger of this kind narrows the funnel through which stories can reach audiences.That is precisely what makes the Paramount-WBD merger so dangerous. It’s why the intervention of Nandy and her department matters so much.Paramount proposes to swallow Warner Bros Discovery in one of the largest leveraged buyouts ever attempted, loading the combined company withan estimated $84bn in debt. To service it, executives have promised investors around $6bn in “synergies”. In plain English, that means redundancies, cancelled productions, fewer films commissioned and fewer risks taken.We have seen this before. When Discovery merged with WarnerMedia in 2022, it shelved finished films andcut thousands of jobs; when Skydance merged with Paramount last year, itlaid off about 2,000 people. Now the same executives are making the same promise, and UK crews, producers, talent and audiences will pay when the bill comes due.But jobs are mostly a matter for the Competition and Markets Authority,whose reviewshould end in a full phase 2 investigation. The job of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport goes further: to determine whether the merger is in the public interest. It most certainly is not. Inher statement to British MPs, Nandy cited the need for a sufficient plurality of views in news media and a sufficient plurality of individuals controlling media enterprises. She has also highlighted the potential impact on streaming services, content homogenisation and children’s television. TheEnterprise Actprotects something we should all care about: who decides what we get to watch, and what we get to know.Consider the breadth of what this single company would hold. Channel 5, one of our fivepublic service broadcasters, which serves the evening news to people without the cost of a subscription. CNN International, whichOfcom research in 2018 foundUK viewers rated above every other TV news source for quality, accuracy, trustworthiness and impartiality. The CNN and CBS news archives – among the world’s most important broadcast news collections, withmore than 4.25mvideos, images and media spanning nearly half a century of history. If one commercially interested owner controls access to both, they control the raw material of our historical memory.One owner controlling this much of the news, and the truth, endangers the public in a way no ordinary consolidation does. When separate owners run separate newsrooms, a story judged inconvenient by one can still reach audiences through another. Fold those newsrooms into a single company, and one boardroom’s commercial anxieties – or political debts – determine what millions of people see and what they never learn existed.And we know something about this particular proprietor’s intentions. Paramount’s chief executive reportedly told Donald Trump that he would make “sweeping changes” to CNN if the deal went through. When the buyer of the world’s most trusted international news channel makes editorial promises to a politician, a British secretary of state is entitled – and, really, obliged – to ask questions before the ink dries.Nandy has been scrupulous in noting that no final decision has been taken. Good. It is important to take the time to get this right. But the case for a full public interest intervention, with Ofcom assessing plurality and reporting back, is overwhelming.Actors are often told to stay out of legal arguments. We understand the instinct. But we have spent our lives on enough UK sets, worked alongside enough UK crews and watched enough brilliant work from the UK struggle to find a buyer to know that this is not someone else’s argument. It is ours. Nandy has opened the door to intervention. Shemustwalk through it, for the sake of everyone who makes UK television and film – and everyone who watches it. If she does not, we will be left without the ability to protect our industry and our culture from this consolidation. We must not push the public’s interest aside; we must stand up for it and block this merger.Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong are actors working in the UK and Hollywood

title: Sweet, fragrant, impossible to resist – south Asian mangoes in Australia’s winter summon memories and unite historic enemies | Shadi Khan Saif | The Guardian
description: At a party in Melbourne hosted by a cricket mate we celebrate this summery delight of a fruit that transcends borders
Author: Shadi Khan Saif
Headline: At a party in Melbourne hosted by a cricket mate we celebrate this summery delight of a fruit that transcends borders
Content: ‘I saw boxes of mangoes selling like hotcakes at a price  I hesitated to pay. I had a lifelong privilege of enjoying the finest of them back in Pakistan at a much cheaper rate.’Photograph: Syed Mehdi/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘I saw boxes of mangoes selling like hotcakes at a price  I hesitated to pay. I had a lifelong privilege of enjoying the finest of them back in Pakistan at a much cheaper rate.’Photograph: Syed Mehdi/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionFruitSweet, fragrant, impossible to resist – south Asian mangoes in Australia’s winter summon memories and unite historic enemiesShadi Khan SaifAt a party in Melbourne hosted by a cricket mate we celebrate this summery delight of a fruit that transcends bordersSun 26 Jul 2026 21.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 02.34 EDTShareIwas grabbing my post-workout shake from a juice shop when the lady behind the counter announced, to the delight of everyone, that mangoes were due to arrive soon. I was already surprised to see this place open late in suburbanMelbourne– the joy of the crowd intrigued me even more.The following week, I saw boxes of mangoes selling like hotcakes at a price I hesitated to pay. I had a lifelong privilege of enjoying the finest of them back in Pakistan at a much cheaper rate. I asked the lady if they were indeed “chaunsa” mangoes – theultra-sweet aromatic variety from Pakistan. She checked the labels, replied, “Yes, they are,” and passed one to me – knowing that they are impossible to resist.It was worth every dollar given the nostalgia associated with that honey-like sweetness, buttery flesh and almost addictive taste of these species thousands of miles away from here in Australia. Behind me in the queue were two young people. We struck up a conversation about summers and monsoons, mangoes eaten over kitchen sinks and family gatherings. They insisted that alphonso mangoes from Mumbai were the superior variety. I disagreed, just as passionately.Beneath the mock rivalry was something deeper: a shared love that ignored borders.It took me down memory lane to Jakarta more a decade ago where I was visiting with other cadet journalists from the Asia-Pacific as well as India,Pakistanand Afghanistan. It was just months after the horrible Mumbai attacks that left scores of innocent people dead. Fingers were being pointed at Pakistan for orchestrating it.
