But even then I remember colleagues from the two countries coming together in defence and praise of their mangoes during drinks and fruits breaks.At my friend’s citizenship ceremony, I was moved by the quiet pride in the faces of new Australians | Shadi Khan SaifRead moreLater, when I moved to Germany, a colleague from Lahore at the public broadcaster Deutsche Welle invited me to join an amateur theatre club of a few local, British, Greek and south Asian enthusiasts to stage some German adaptations. My cherished memories from there are the rehearsals we did with slices of chaunsa and alphonso on the side.Ages before modern borders, mangoes trace their origins back more than 4,000 years to the Indian subcontinent, where they were cultivated and revered as symbols of love and prosperity.Now, living in Melbourne, I still love them. A cricket mate from New Delhi threw a mango music party. In the Australian winter it could have not got any better than gathering to enjoy this summery delight of a fruit that transcends boundaries. The historic animosity between nuclear-armed neighbours India and Pakistan remains. But if there is one sweet thing between them, it is definitely a mango!In the home countries of many of those at the mango party, politics and the vicious cycle of death and destruction has pushed people into silos. Millions of people have grown up hating each other without knowing enough about each other. Over time, some move to places like Germany, Australia or elsewhere where they get better opportunities to meet people from across the border – at a mango party, for example.Here, feelings and behaviours might soften given common interests and values. Of course, the chances of this changing the course of history and politics are slim but for a few moments it liberates people from the weight of their bitter past.At this Melbourne party, the lovely music was one binding force but the host’s idea of adding a mango flavour made it one to remember.Shadi Khan Saif is an editor, producer and journalist who has worked in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Germany and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFruitOpinionPakistanIndiaFoodSouth and central AsiaAustralian food and drinkMelbournecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on ancient DNA: a female shaman exposes our flawed assumptions about the past | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Thanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly know
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Thanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly know
Content: We Go Way Back, an exhibition exploring how ancient DNA is revealing new insights into human evolution, migration, culture and disease, is at the Francis Crick Institute in London.Photograph: Martin Stacey/Easy Animal StudioView image in fullscreenWe Go Way Back, an exhibition exploring how ancient DNA is revealing new insights into human evolution, migration, culture and disease, is at the Francis Crick Institute in London.Photograph: Martin Stacey/Easy Animal StudioOpinionArchaeologyThe Guardian view on ancient DNA: a female shaman exposes our flawed assumptions about the pastEditorialThanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly knowMon 27 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 19.34 EDTShareArchaeologists believe the Upton Lovell Shaman, who lived in what is now Wiltshire 4,000 years ago, was an important religious leader and metalworker because of the artefacts and tools buried with the body. Until very recently it was also believed, on considerably slimmer evidence, that this shaman was a man: it was simply assumedthat someone of such status must be male, and the view was barely questioned over the years. Now ancient DNA analysis performed at the Francis Crick Institutehas revealedthat the body, held by the Wiltshire Museum, is in fact a woman.That should cause a stir in bronze-age studies. But it is also yet another example of how many of our assumptions about human history have been upended by the rise of ancient DNA analysis over the past two decades. Others include the revelation that there were (frequent) liaisons between humans and Neanderthals just 50,000 years ago, a reconstruction suggesting that thefirst modern Britonshad “dark to black” skin, and the closing of longstanding mysteries such as what really killed two members of Italy’s powerful Medici family in the 16th century (probably malaria, not murder as was often believed). Every time we widen our keyhole view of the past even slightly, we are confronted by how many of our seemingly grounded assumptions are, in fact, wrong.These insights have emerged because the technology to extract and read DNA from ancient, poorly preserved samples has improved exponentially since around 2010. DNA analysis hardly provides a total picture of the past, but it has been useful for mapping migrations, sexual relations and family structures, as well as tracking plagues and diseases. For instance, it has told us that groups of ancient humans moved around and intermixed with each other far more often than previously thought, allowing us to imagine a more dynamic, less lonely ancient world.It also suggests that the replacement of one group with another, such as evidence of thenear-total disappearanceof the Stonehenge-building Neolithic Britons, just a few centuries after the arrival of the Bell Beaker people around 2400BC, was relatively common. But it cannot answer why or how that replacement took place. These are big questions that will keep scientists, anthropologists and archaeologists busy for decades.Alongside a deeper and richer view of the past, we should take a lesson from the constant stream of debunking and myth-busting emerging from this research. The politics behind assuming a shaman is male are obvious, but last year a studytook on more subtle biasesby proving that famous plaster casts of citizens of Pompeii long believed to show a mother and child locked in a final embrace were in fact two people who were not related, and the adult was male. The authors note that there was no published evidence suggesting the sex or family relations of these bodies, but both scholars and the public found the romantic (and very modern) interpretation irresistible.We will probably always try to see something of ourselves in our ancestors. But the past is more interesting when we consider it on its own, often bracingly foreign, terms. DNA evidence will not conveniently overturn every one of our biased judgments about the ancient world, but each case does make it easier to recognise how readily it happens, and to be humble about how little we really understand.Explore more on these topicsArchaeologyOpinionMalariaeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s so much magic!’: how we made Harry Potter and the Cursed Child  | Harry Potter and the Cursed Child | The Guardian
description: ‘The ripple of energy and anticipation from the audience was almost visual. It was like opening a new Star Wars film – I didn’t hear a phone go off once’
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: ‘The ripple of energy and anticipation from the audience was almost visual. It was like opening a new Star Wars film – I didn’t hear a phone go off once’
Content: ‘Bringing something new to audiences’ … the final battle scene in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at the Palace theatre in London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreen‘Bringing something new to audiences’ … the final battle scene in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at the Palace theatre in London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanHow we madeHarry Potter and the Cursed Child‘There’s so much magic!’: how we made Harry Potter and the Cursed Child‘The ripple of energy and anticipation from the audience was almost visual. It was like opening a new Star Wars film – I didn’t hear a phone go off once’Interviews byImogen TildenMon 27 Jul 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamie Parker, played Harry PotterMy initial response when I was asked if I was interested in the role was confusion – I felt a bit long in the tooth to play a teenager. I had read the firstHarry Potterbook and seen a few of the movies, but was just past the right age when it was all kicking off. I didn’t know that there was the coda in the final book that places the action 19 years later, and that’s where the play would be picking up from.I’m happy to admit now that I thought the show was a terrible idea. But a lot of hit showsareterrible ideas on paper. And I’m used to eating my own words – which began the moment I saw the team involved – producers Sonia Friedman and Colin Callender, and so many of the other creatives I would have taken a contract blind just to work with them, not leastJack Thorne. I thought, if this is as close as I get to being in This Is England, I’ll do it.Of course, once I took the role, I had Stephen Fry’s readings of the books on a loop. By the time I got through the rehearsals, the year in London, and then the year in New York when it went to Broadway, I had listened to the entire series seven times and was a bit of a Potterhead.View image in fullscreen‘By the end I was a Potterhead’ … Jamie Parker as Harry with Noma Dumezweni as Hermione and Paul Thornley as Ron.Photograph: Manuel Harlan/PR Company HandoutThe two parts of the play are the story of the next generation coming up, and of chickens coming home to roost, but it wasn’t a one-man show and the pressure felt shared. Everything you do ends up being a crucible for your own neuroses that you pestle and mortar into some kind of grit that you use as part of making the theatre piece. Like Harry, I was barely 12 when I also got on a train and went to a boarding school in Scotland. I also had round glasses!double quotation markMy wand helicoptered downstage right. I launched myself after it with half my torso off the stage in the auditoriumI’m always looking for things that challenge me, and I had never done anything like this with all the magic. I thought, I hope I can learn how to do that … I don’t know, but let’s find out! Playing various musical instruments helped – there’s a musicality built into the rhythm of the illusions. But, as anyone in my life will tell you, I can’t walk through a doorway without banging the back of my hand against the latch – my spatial awareness is dreadful. That I went through all those tight entrances and exits, and around all those bits of heavy moving machinery at speed, in the dark, without ever doing myself or anyone else serious mischief is a miracle.There were occasional moments when things didn’t go as planned. One night in the duel scene with Alex Price (Draco), I gesticulated and my wand caught on part of my clothing. It skittered out of my hand, and helicoptered downstage right. Without thinking I launched myself after it and blindly reached into the dark with half my torso off the stage in the auditorium. Somehow I caught it. Alex just went, “Yes!” – like he was watching the cricket!During the first preview, the ripple of energy and anticipation that went through the theatre was almost visual. It was put to us that this was like opening the new Star Wars film but in one cinema worldwide – we had audiences coming from Australia to the Philippines to Canada. But, outside of the big commercial opening aspect, there was a real sense of this place being a precious, even dare I say, sacred space. Audiences were in their seats 10 minutes before the start and I didn’t hear a phone go off once. I’ve never known attentiveness in an audience like it.Jamie Harrison,illusionsdesignerI got into magic as a child and for a while made a living out of it, but later, studying acting at drama school, I was told by some of the lecturers that it was vaudevillian and that I should hide it from my CV. I set up my own theatre company, Vox Motus, and began introducing illusion into our shows without really knowing what I was doing, but it was a safe environment to explore new things.When I got the first draft, I couldn’t sleep for three nights thinking, “What have I done? This is so full on. There’s so much magic!”There were moments that Jack had written into the script – ”and they vanish” or “a spell happens here” – and it was up to me to decide what to do. Then there were other points where we knew exactly that it had to be a Patronus charm, or the Polyjuice potion that turns one character into another.View image in fullscreenShadows and light … Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.Photograph: Manuel HarlanPeople often think that magic and illusion are off-the-shelf. They say, “Who invented that?” But I’ve always tried to draw on the work of brilliant illusionists of the past, while reworking them so that we’re bringing something new to audiences.Audiences particularly love the phone box and the entry to the Ministry of Magic by dialling “MAGIC”. That almost didn’t happen at all. John [Tiffany, the director] was trying to give the show its own identity and make it distinct from the films. He said, “I don’t want to a big red phone box on stage … can we think of a different way of doing it?” Christine Jones, the designer, and I looked over old photographs of King’s Cross and we spotted an emergency telephone on a wall in one of those small booths.I made it out of cardboard and bits and pieces in fabric, and we started to re-create a famous trick called the mascot moth that a magician called David Devant created 120 years ago – a person comes on stage with big moth wings on, folds them around himself and vanishes. It was terrible to begin with but we developed it and brought in clever makers to make different iterations. We got it working and it looked fantastic – I was really proud. Then we did the first preview in front of a test audience of Harry Potter superfans. And one of the main bits of feedback was: “You can’t do the Ministry of Magic without a phone box!” So Sonia and John said, “We know we said we didn’t want a phone box, but we need one by this time next week!”I’m not going to reveal any of our secrets. Absolutely not! I can say that people often think there are trapdoors being used in sequences where there aren’t. The show uses shadows and light in ingenious and incredibly precise new ways. It might look very organic and handmade, but there is an absolute wodge of technology involved and a huge crew. There are a lot of computers – it looks like a spaceship.View image in fullscreen‘There’s a wodge of technology involved’ … Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, at London’s Palace theatre.Photograph: Manuel HarlanThe Expelliarmus spell (where a wand jumps from one person’s hand into another’s) is a highly skilled effect that the performers have to start practising on day one – there’s a real knack to getting it right. There are now probably hundreds of actors who have toiled away and have an insight into what life could be like to be a magician. That was the first thing that I had to showJK Rowling. She was really interested to see that and the Time Turner when she came to one of the early workshops. We set up a presentation, but none of the performers were confident enough to do it yet. So John said, “You’re going to have to perform it.” I was more nervous than the flipping actors! I demonstrated it and she went, “Oh! Do that again!” You know you’ve got somebody if they ask to see it again. I was thrilled. I wanted to say no, a magician never repeats his tricks, but it was JK Rowling, so, yes, we did do it again.The original two-part production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child celebrates its 10th anniversary on 30 July and is at the Palace theatre, London until 20 September; theone part production opens on 9 October.Explore more on these topicsHarry Potter and the Cursed ChildHow we madeHarry PotterTheatreJK RowlingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBC | Bill Oddie | The Guardian
description: The beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he loved
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he loved
Content: TV’s signature birdwatcher … Bill Oddie at home in his garden.Photograph: Vicki Couchman/Camera PressView image in fullscreenTV’s signature birdwatcher … Bill Oddie at home in his garden.Photograph: Vicki Couchman/Camera PressBill OddieBill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBCThe beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he lovedBill Oddie, naturalist and broadcaster, dies aged 85Bill Oddie – a life in picturesMark LawsonMon 27 Jul 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 21.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Oddie,who has died aged 85, had two separate, substantial TV presences – as a comedy actor and an ornithologist. Both roles brought him fame but also pain. The peak of the former career was 76 episodes from 1970-82 of The Goodies, which he co-wrote and co-starred in with Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor. They played an eccentric trio of investigators and fixers who rode into action on a three-seater bicycle called a “trandem”.As a birdwatcher, his onscreen zenith was Springwatch, which he initially co-hosted with Kate Humble, from 2005. It began a BBC Two natural history franchise marking the change of seasons, its success leading to wintry, autumnal and summery spin-offs. Binoculars lowered to show eyes awed or enthused, and Oddie became TV’s signature birdwatcher.Bill Oddie – a life in picturesRead moreBorn in Rochdale, he came early to both comedy and ornithology. He was a teenager when his sightings first appeared in the annual report of the West Midland Bird Club. In his early 20s, he appeared in the West End and on Broadway in transfers of the Cambridge University revue in which he first worked professionally with Brooke-Taylor and Garden, who is now the only survivor of the three. Oddie wrote the music for the revue and then The Goodies, who released five spin-off singles in 1974-75, spending a combined 38 weeks in the pop charts, with Funky Gibbon, an anthropomorphic jungle dance number, reaching four in the Top 10.Each of Oddie’s TV hits, though, was overshadowed by sadness. In the case of Springwatch, it was personal. Particularly bad incidents of the bipolar condition he experienced throughout his life led him to miss a number of episodes. He returned to the programme, but his departure in 2008 – which he made clear was not voluntary – was triggered, by his account, by another serious depressive downturn.In the case of The Goodies, there was an underlying resentment shared by Brooke-Taylor and Garden relating to the show’s treatment by the BBC. The series attracted 12 million viewers at its mid-70s peak – very high for a BBC Two show – and won the Silver Rose of Montreux, the second prize at Europe’s leading TV festival. The gong was for Kitten Kong, an inspired movie spoof in which a massive moggy terrorises London using some special effects impressive for the period.View image in fullscreenThe Goodies in 1973, from left: Tim Brooke-Taylor, Graeme Garden and Bill Oddie.Photograph: South Coast Press/ShutterstockHowever, The Goodies was never valued by many corporation executives who – due to the relatively high quotient of slapstick, puns and visual gags involving animals – designated it a “children’s show”, which was intended as an insult and taken as such by two of the creators. For what proved to be the final series, the trio moved to London WeekendTelevision.Unlike most hit shows of its period, The Goodies has not been regularly repeated on terrestrial TV, any re-airings by the BBC largely in archive slots. This upset and frustrated Oddie, Brooke-Taylor and Garden. During the home video and DVD boom, when it sometimes seemed that the BBC was systematically releasing all material ever shown, the threesome negotiated a box set release with a commercial outfit, which did something to redress the neglect.A few other shows from the era have also been denied repeats and releases because they contain language or attitudes now considered unacceptable. BBC off-the-record briefers have sometimes suggested that this was why The Goodies has been so difficult to watch or buy. There is an occasion on which the three men start to apply blackface, but it occurred in an extraordinary 1975 episode called South Africa. This begins with the Goodies undertaking an advertising campaign to attract Britons to South Africa and ends in a Britain with a Black Enoch Powell presiding over a regime of reverse apartheid.Although there is some silly wordplay – at one point, a regime of “apart-height” requires the diminutive Oddie to become a slave to his taller colleagues – the broadly progressive politics and complexity of the storyline make the “children’s television” tag seem particularly absurd. Indeed, absurdity is a more fitting label for South Africa and many other editions.In The Goodies, the writer-actors played exaggerations of aspects of their character: Garden (a qualified doctor) professorial and absent-minded, Brooke-Taylor posh and patriotic, and Oddie sulky and scrappy. Those characteristics meant that some colleagues found him hard to work with – which may have contributed to his departure from Springwatch – but some such behaviour was explained, if not entirely excused, by his mental health issues.Oddie was quite right, though, to be annoyed by the diminishment in BBC and TV history of The Goodies, memories of which will make its viewers smile amid the sadness at his death. His admirers will also hope that any afterlife contains a chorus of birdsong.Explore more on these topicsBill OddieTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The greatest album never made’: the untold story of George Michael’s secret, star-packed duets project | George Michael | The Guardian
description: Suing his record label and sick of being a sex symbol, the singer spent 1992 working on the Trojan Souls for stars including Aretha Franklin and Bryan Ferry. Now, newly released studio footage shows him in his creative prime
Author: Dorian Lynskey
Headline: Suing his record label and sick of being a sex symbol, the singer spent 1992 working on the Trojan Souls for stars including Aretha Franklin and Bryan Ferry. Now, newly released studio footage shows him in his creative prime
Content: ‘The best time of our lives’ … Michael at LAX in October 1992.Photograph: Ron Galella Collection/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The best time of our lives’ … Michael at LAX in October 1992.Photograph: Ron Galella Collection/Getty ImagesGeorge Michael‘The greatest album never made’: the untold story of George Michael’s secret, star-packed duets projectSuing his record label and sick of being a sex symbol, the singer spent 1992 working on the Trojan Souls for stars including Aretha Franklin and Bryan Ferry. Now, newly released studio footage shows him in his creative primeWham! special: read Andrew Ridgeley on their bizarre 1985 trip to ChinaDorian LynskeyMon 27 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheGeorge Michaelalbum that never was began in defiance and ended in grief. It was 1992. Mired in a toxic dispute with Sony Records, Michael chose to keep busy and declare his independence by making an album of songs to be sung by several of his musical heroes, including Aretha Franklin, Janet Jackson and Sade Adu, under the alias the Trojan Souls. Michael worked on the album for months until his Brazilian boyfriend Anselmo Feleppa died of Aids in March 1993 and he lost interest in music. It was never revived.Tracks from the sessions have since leaked, along with some of the fly-on-the-wall footage filmed by Michael’s close friend and informal adviser Andros Georgiou, who has spent years trying to get unauthorised clips removed from YouTube and TikTok. Now, months before the 10th anniversary of Michael’s death, he is releasing 90 minutes of unedited video as Trojan Souls – not exactly a film but an unfiltered view of Michael in his creative prime. “I thought these fans were making money from my rights so I decided to stop fighting and get it out there,” Georgiou says. He hopes it will open a door on what he calls, with characteristic hyperbole, “the greatest album never made”.Georgiou called his self-published 2012 memoir Rock: The Luckiest Man in Pop, the luck being that his father and Michael’s father were cousins who emigrated to England from Cyprus together in 1953, so he grew up alongside one of the greatest artists of his generation. They remained close until a bitter falling out in 1998, of which more later.View image in fullscreen‘He had a 48-track studio in his mind’ … Michael at work.Photograph: Courtesy Andros GeorgiouEver loyal to his childhood friends (another, David Austin, now runs his estate), Michael gave Georgiou creative opportunities. They first collaborated as Boogie Box High, whose cover of the Bee Gees’ Jive Talkin’ was a Top 10 hit in 1987, and co-founded Aegean Records in 1996. Georgiou was also a regular on-the-road companion. When they were in Tokyo during the Faith tour, Sony gave Georgiou a state-of-the-art Hi8 video camera which enabled him to make high-quality home movies.Georgiou makes the origins of the Trojan Souls sound as a dramatic as a heist. When Michael released Listen Without Prejudice Vol 1 in 1990, he was so sick of his sex-symbol image that he disappeared from view: no appearances in videos or on record sleeves, no interviews, no concerts. “He wanted to make music but he didn’t want to play the lying game any more,” says Georgiou. Michael believed that Sony then punished him by underpromoting the album. The singer felt trapped.double quotation markBeing arrested was the beginning of the end. He laughed it off but it seriously affected himIn January 1992, he and Georgiou flew to LA for some winter sun but Michael soon got bored and suggested going to Dave Stewart’s Chapel Studios in Encino to bang out a quick cover in the spirit of Boogie Box High. The 1979 disco hit Ain’t No Stoppin’ Us Now was a symbolic choice because Gene McFadden and John Whitehead originally wrote it to rebuke their own label, Philadelphia International. Michael decided they should return in July to start an album, recruiting vocalists he had loved growing up. According to Georgiou, only David Bowie politely declined. He says the name came to him in a dream: The Voice of Reason by the Trojan Souls. “From the Trojan horse,” he says. “The soldiers came in and then came down fighting.”Back in London, Georgiou was contractually obliged to offer it to Sony first, despite the bad blood. “Of course they said no. I called George and he said, ‘Fuck Sony!’ I went, ‘I’ll be home in two hours with a deal, trust me.’” Georgiou called an A&R at Warner and dashed over. “Rob Dickins, the chair, was there. He said, ‘What do you want?’ I said a million pounds. He goes, done.” In October, Michaelfiled a lawsuit against Sony, alleging that his contract was unreasonable restraint of trade. “He wanted to get back at Sony any which way he could,” says Georgiou.Despite the project’s bitter origins, the three songs in the film have a sunny, funky dynamism. “He was so happy,” Georgiou says. “For the first couple of months we probably had the best time of our lives making this record.” The lush ballad One Day I’ll Know was destined for Stevie Wonder and the shimmering Maybe It’s Not Your Time for Bryan Ferry. The instrumental track Wendy Melvoin’s Song featured virtuosic rhythm guitar by one half of Wendy and Lisa, in the hope that she would lure her former employer Prince on board.Obsessed with protecting his mystique, Michael was never officially filmed handling an instrument or building a track. “If you’re a fan,” says Georgiou, “this is your first chance to see how he directs everyone in the studio.” It’s fascinating to watch how precisely Michael drills his world-class musicians – Melvoin, keyboardist Chris Cameron, bassist Deon Estus and Lynn Mabry’s backing singers – through take after take, even grabbing Estus’s bass guitar at one point to show him what he means. To the viewer the takes may sound identical but Michael was always chasing the perfect sound he heard in his head.View image in fullscreenCollaboration … Elton John and Michael in the early 1990s.Photograph: Photoshot/Getty Images“He had a 48-track studio in his mind,” says Georgiou. He recalls how, even when they were kids, Michael used to deconstruct songs by their favourite artists and explain how he would have changed this or that. Or how, when they were working at Sarm West in Notting Hill, Michael would get in the car with a cassette of a skeletal backing track and have a melody written by the time he got home to Hampstead.“He was quite a frustrating person to work with because he had quite a strange creative process,” says Sathnam Sanghera, author of Tonight the Music Seems So Loud: The Meaning of George Michael. “He would often sing at musicians and say, ‘This is what I want it to sound like.’ I’ve talked to a lot of musicians who worked with him and almost all of them said the same thing: ‘At the time it drove us fucking mad.’ But looking back they can see that of all the people they’d worked with he was the most talented. He just had these amazing ears.”double quotation markThis is just the beginning of something that could have been amazingThe fragments heard in Trojan Souls are tantalising but only the Elton John collaboration This Kind of Love was ever completed. By the start of 1993, Feleppa was fading fast. “It was terribly difficult for him to finish anything so we went from track to track,” Georgiou says. “And then it got too much for him.” Leaving work unfinished was not unusual for Michael, though. “George had a history of losing interest,” says Sanghera. “A lot of projects never came to fruition: Listen Without Prejudice Vol 2, the Daft Punk collaboration, the duets album …”A few years later, Georgiou’s friendship with Michael ended, too. On 7 April 1998, Michael was arrested for “engaging in lewd conduct” in a public toilet in LA’s Will Rogers Memorial Park and the closeted star was outed to the world. “Basically it all went wrong when he was arrested,” Georgiou says. “He laughed it off but it seriously affected him mentally and that was the beginning of the end.”When I interviewed Michael in 2004, he connected the incident to losing his mother to cancer a year earlier. Having finally worked through the creative drought occasioned by Feleppa’s death to make 1996’s Older, he was poleaxed by grief once again. “Really since 1991, when I found out [Feleppa] was HIV positive, all I’d done was either wait for someone to die or grieve,” he told me. “It was just so easy to feel picked on and angry and nihilistic.”View image in fullscreenClose before a bitter falling out … Georgiou and Michael.Photograph: Courtesy Andros GeorgiouMichael’s compulsive cruising on Hampstead Heath created a rift. Georgiou thought it was self-destructive; Michael resented his friend’s judgment. “I couldn’t understand the risks he was taking,” Georgiou says. “He was loud and proud, which I absolutely respected, but you can’t carry on doing what you’re doing.” He claims that the final straw was Michael suddenly ordering him to drop Aegean’s entire roster. “The next day I was just like, you know what? Fuck you. And I walked out.”An alternative account is that Georgiou crossed a line by telling his story, and giving family photographs, to Hello! magazine. Either way, Michael told me, “losing that relationship absolutely devastated me. Everything I took for granted in my 20s I lost.” Georgiou says that they tentatively reconnected in 2016 and planned to meet up in the new year. “It took a lot. We’re both Greeks at heart and have our arrogance and pride. And then he died. Even talking about it now, I can’t believe it.”The Trojan Souls material wasn’t mothballed entirely. Ain’t No Stoppin’ Us Now was released on Aegean Records in 1998, as one of the first ever commercially available MP3s, and Michael rerecorded This Kind of Love, sans Elton, not long before his death – Sanghera calls it “his one great unreleased song”. As for the rest, we can only imagine. Could The Voice of Reason ultimately have been a triumph?“I think it could have worked as a duets album, because 90% of George was his voice,” Sanghera says. “He was at his creative peak. This could have been Listen Without Prejudice Vol 2 if his lover wasn’t dying, if he hadn’t sued Sony. But I think he would have needed another two years for a fully realised album. This is just the beginning of something that could have been amazing.”Georgiou has often been regarded with suspicion by Michael’s fans for monetising his proximity to pop genius. Now he is preparing a rewritten memoir, an accompanying film, the release of more footage on his website, and even a duet version of This Kind of Love if he can get Elton John’s blessing. Then again, these are his videos and Trojan Souls was his project, too. Given his long estrangement from Michael, the home movies document not just an unfinished album but a much-missed friendship. “It’s my legacy in a way,” he says. “I was there for nearly 40 years. What a time!”Trojan Souls is available for streaming attrojansouls.comExplore more on these topicsGeorge MichaelPop and rockDocumentary filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Haex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventure | Games | The Guardian
description: The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes
Content: Growing fascination … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsView image in fullscreenGrowing fascination … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsSummer games previewsGamesHaex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventureThe debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyesLewis GordonMon 27 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wilds of the sub-Arctic north: towering pine trees, flashes of psychedelic-yellow lichen, and a sun that never wholly sets during the summer months. This land is gorgeous, yes, but also unforgiving, yet in Haex (pronounced “hex”) you have an unusual tool at your disposal to make it a little more hospitable: a cube that fits snugly in the palm of your hand out of which grows a plant. You plant this so-called Seed in the earth and – voilà – the world around you transforms: new vegetation and topography but also narrative threads to follow, and, naturally, enemies. Wield these small-but-mighty kernels of change at your own peril.“Your adventure and your world is player-shaped,” says Haex’s creative director Tobias Nyman. He explains that everyone starts a campaign with a unique, procedurally generated world. Each Seed then contains further procedural data that causes it to terraform before your eyes. “You change the world as you go,” he says. “It becomes even more unique.”The singularity of each game world is crucial for keeping not just you but other players on their toes. That’s another of Haex’s wrinkles: it is an online co-operative game, meaning your friends may join you on this ever-transforming survivalist adventure.View image in fullscreenRoom for more … Haex.Illustration: Dead AstronautsTeaming up, you play as a group of research scientists sent to investigate an anomaly in the rugged Scandinavian landscape. You come across odd, shapeshifting objects and beasts: for example, an ash-grey humanoid creature with spikes protruding from its face that would make even Pinhead from Hellraiser wince; also, a sentient wall so supermassive that it scrapes the clouds. There is a further layer to these spatial and, perhaps, alien mysteries: an unknown language of arcane sigils that must be decoded.Nyman talks effusively of influences: sci-fi movies such asAnnihilationandArrival(as is clear from the trailer); the weird fiction thrillers of author Jeff VanderMeer, too. Unexpectedly, the creative director cites the niche music genre known ascosmic black metalas a touchstone. “There is the wild, grim, frostbitten north, an extraterrestrial entity and a thing that traverses the mist,” says Nyman, hinting at a shared emotional effect between his beloved music genre and the game: a mingling of dread and awe, and of seeking transcendence in nature.Nyman co-founded Haex’s studio Dead Astronauts (anothernod to VanderMeer), in 2024, having previously worked at Ubisoft Massive, where he helped make recent open-world blockbusters,Avatar: Frontiers of PandoraandStar Wars Outlaws. Yet where those titles’ settings are gorgeous and gigantic (“monumental,” stresses Nyman), they are also somewhat static. By contrast, Haex’s game world is more dynamic, and it is being made by just 12 developers. The theory is that its morphing, geo-engineered space should foster more fluid, interesting experiences, despite Haex’s focus on somewhat familiar-feeling shooting and survival mechanics.Taking the leap to independence has also enabled Nyman to make a game that is more personal to him. As a youngster, he split his time between Stockholm and the far north of Sweden. He recalls looking up at the night sky blanketed with constellations as his father explained Einstein’s theory of relativity. Another memory: gazing out at an expansive crop of cloudberries – a “field of gold,” says Nyman, by virtue of the small fruit’s colour. What has stuck with him most, however, is the region’s silence – a silence so great that it was “almost screaming at me”, he says. That feels like an apt summation of Haex’s aims: an experience that is miraculous and malicious; a setting that is beautiful yet can feel as if it is bearing down on you with cruel intensity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaex is due for release onPCin 2027.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The plane movie I’ll watch anytime’: why Up in the Air is my feelgood movie | Up In The Air | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers’ most pleasurable comfort films is a journey through US airports with George Clooney
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our series of writers’ most pleasurable comfort films is a journey through US airports with George Clooney
Content: George Clooney in Up in the Air,Photograph: Dale Robinette/APView image in fullscreenGeorge Clooney in Up in the Air,Photograph: Dale Robinette/APMy feelgood movieUp In The Air‘The plane movie I’ll watch anytime’: why Up in the Air is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers’ most pleasurable comfort films is a journey through US airports with George ClooneyJoe EllisonMon 27 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirports have always been my happy place. From shiny citadels jutting out of the desert to shoddier European hubs located 120 miles outside the city they’re designated to serve; I love them all. With so many stories to be told, all those connections and people colliding, it’s a first-class seat to life itself. Which should go some way to explaining why I hold such a deep admiration for 2009’s comedy-dramaUp in the Air.‘Justice, morality and triumph’: why Matilda is my feelgood movieRead moreDirected by Jason Reitman and based on the book of the same name by Walter Kirn, it stars an Oscar-nominatedGeorge Clooneyas Ryan Bingham, a US corporate downsizer who spends 322 days a year flying state to state doing the job cowardly employers prefer to outsource, leaving him with “43 miserable days at home”. That is until graduate Natalie Keener (Anna Kendrick) enters the firm with a cost-saving idea of firing people by video call, and hits the road with her older colleague, who is suddenly forced to grapple with the future of his own industry while re-evaluating his nomadic lifestyle.Clooney’s hatchet man is closing in on 10m frequent flier miles – a feat he gleefully reveals has been achieved by fewer people than have set foot on the moon – and has managed to get air travel down to an exact science: flexing his airline Concierge Key like Patrick Bateman might a business card, and rolling his (perfectly sized) suitcase through the minefield of departures with panache, this is a traveller who stacks security trays withconviction. It’s infectious to watch, truly.In my early 20s (around the time of the film’s release) I would often travel to far-flung places on somebody else’s dime, preferring lonely barstools, a buzzy career and fleeting relationships abroad over any real adult responsibility that lay back home in London’s tricky rental market. Though I was two decades younger than its central character, Up in the Air connected with me in such a way that I would watch the movie near religiously during those trips, screening it on any device possible for that extra hit of wanderlust. It remains the plane movie I’ll watch anytime, anywhere.What keeps me coming back to this movie isn’t some inner desire to travel – it’s the heart. For all his commitment issues, Bingham is pretty empathetic when he’s on the clock. Fortune 500’s answer to Freddy Krueger at least does his best to connect with the staffers he’s letting go, cutting the bullshit when necessary and reminding Kendrick’s eager bee that in this line of work they’re meeting people on the worst day of their lives. Firing people from thousands of miles away, he tells her, is morally wrong on every level (this from a guy she accuses of living in “a cocoon of self-banishment”, no less) but most of all it lacks a real duty of care – and as we hurtle ever closer towards workplaces being ruled by big AI, I find this message more prescient than ever.Another plotline that yanks at the heartstrings is Bingham’s romance with a similarly well-travelled businesswoman, played by Vera Farmiga. Kindred spirits? Not quite. Late in the movie, he makes a surprise dash to her home only to realise that their love story has been about as transactional as room service when he sees signs of a husband and kids through the door frame. Clooney’s wide-eyed expression as he backs away into the snowy Chicago night never fails to floor me.And there is a happy ending – just not for the reasons you might think. By far the biggest masterstroke of this movie is Reitman’s decision to cast real people who had recently been fired, instructing them to talk to the camera crew as they would their ex-employer, providing an unfiltered snapshot of the casualties on the frontline of a recession. The director found these talking heads by pretending to cast for a documentary – and it really shows, feeling part-HBO doc and part-episode of NBC’s The Office as real faces (and tears) are intermingled alongside stellar performances from the likes of JK Simmons and Zach Galifianakis, as employees who bite the dust.Throughout the runtime these genuine voices turn from collective anger to dumbfoundment and even optimism, reminding us just how unbreakable the human spirit can be. In fact, by the movie’s finale you’ll find it so uplifting that you may have the urge to put a tray table up.Up in the Air is available on Kanopy or Hoopla, to rent digitally in the US, on YouTube, to rent digitally in the UK and to rent digitally in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsUp In The AirMy feelgood movieGeorge ClooneyAnna KendrickComedy filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Glitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the Backrooms | Games | The Guardian
description: The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
Content: Interior landscape … the 2022 game Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeView image in fullscreenInterior landscape … the 2022 game Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeGamesGlitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the BackroomsThe horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spacesAlex SpencerMon 27 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future$262mA24movie sensation.“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in theBackrooms,” the post begins. For the uninitiated, “noclip” refers to a game mode in which collision with solid objects is disabled, allowing players to move freely through walls and floors. Think of Chiwetel Ejiofor’s character in the film, finding a permeable wall in the basement of his furniture store and passing through to the world on the other side.Backrooms review – Kane Parsons’ icily disturbing horror rewrites the genre rulebookRead moreIn games, noclip is intended for use by developers testing out their creations – but for decades now, players have been finding ways to access it themselves and reach hidden places they were never intended to see. It’s a phenomenon that Studio Chyr creative director William Chyr is intimately familiar with, both as a maker of games and as a player.View image in fullscreenChiwetel Ejiofor in a scene from Backrooms the film.Photograph: A24/AP“Going behind the scenes, noclipping, and seeing the logic of the space, it’s like this Wizard of Oz moment of pulling open the curtain,” Chyr says. He remembers an early encounter with this inBatman: Arkham City:“There was this glitch that allowed you, if you kept spamming one of the grenades, to keep going higher and higher.” From there, the caped crusader could soar outside the level, into sections of Gotham that were only ever intended as a backdrop. “The streets had these cars that moved, but it was just a flat texture.”Watching Backrooms, Chyr was also reminded of a similar bug in the notoriously jankySkyrim, where holding a wooden plate provided a quick way of noclipping out of the world. Looking at it from the outside in, players discovered that many of the game’s “tables” were in fact just bookcases embedded deep in the ground – just like the memorable Backrooms shot of a room in which the furniture is clipping through the floor. All these things that, in video games, the player is never meant to see.The feel ofKane Parsons’ filmis actually closer to these experiences than any of the many “official” Backrooms games that have popped up. The open-source nature of this mythos (as well as 4chan and Reddit, there are sprawling fan wikis cataloguing and expanding the lore) means that it’s possible to release your own game set in the Backrooms, using the name and iconography, in a way you couldn’t with another horror movie.View image in fullscreenPlaces you weren’t meant to see … Escape the Backrooms.Photograph: Fancy Games, Blackbird Interactive, Secret ModeThe most high-profile of these games, Escape the Backrooms, was first available in early-access form in August 2022, just months after Parsons’ first video. It offers a perfectly faithful recreation of the Backrooms aesthetic, from the yellow hallways to the yellow hazmat suits worn by agents of Async, the mysterious organisation only introduced towards the end of the film but a mainstay of the online incarnations. But all this is just wallpaper applied over the blueprint of a multiplayer survival horror game.At its best, Backrooms taps into a sense of a place being “off”, in a way that’s unsettling but hard to pin down. It’s a delicate sensation, easily shattered (as it is in the film, I’d argue) by the presence of killer monsters. Even more so by the sight of another player in their gas mask and reindeer onesie, bunny-hopping through the hallways ahead.Thankfully, there’s another stripe of Backrooms-inspired games offering nothing more than a self-guided tour through environments with a growing sense of weirdness and the constant suggestion of a threat lurking out of view.View image in fullscreenEndless halls… Hotel Infinity.Photograph: Studio ChyrPools and Dreamcore both shine a spotlight on Poolrooms, an infinite swimming-baths dimensionfirst glimpsed in one of Parsons’s videosand codified by the fandom asLevel 37of the Backrooms, with a similarly alien approach to architecture. In Dreamcore, it’s just one of a selection pack of realms to explore. You’ll also explore a “dead mall” and the looping corridors of a hotel: both abandoned and seemingly endless, like the spaces explored in the film, but with less of an obvious supernatural edge.These malls and hotels are prime examples of a larger online taste for liminal spaces from which Backrooms is just one offshoot.“These spaces always feel like they’re past their prime,” says Chyr. “It’s clear there was human activity here, at one point, but no longer.” His 2025 game Hotel Infinity is steeped in all these ideas, to the extent that at one point Hotel Liminal was considered as a title, Chyr says. “But I thought that was just too on the nose!”Set in the lifeless corridors of a hotel seemingly designed by MC Escher, it’s a VR game that uses some clever spatial trickery to fold its endless halls into a 2x2m square of your living-room floor. One particular sequence late in Backrooms made me think of Chyr’s game – he confirms that he thought the same thing. “I was like, damn, I wish we’d done that!” he laughs.View image in fullscreenImpossible architecture …  Exit 8.Photograph: Kotake CreateHotel Infinity is primarily focused on the impossible architecture of these places, something it shares withExit 8(also adapted into a film this year), a Japanese-made game that traps you in an infinitely looping section of a Tokyo metro station. The other side of the liminal coin is the sensation summoned by that original 4chan image: the eeriness of an empty place that no longer has any obvious function, or perhaps never did.One game exploring this aspect is Interior Worlds, a “liminal photography” game in which you explore such spaces armed only with an SLR camera. The game’s developer, who goes by the moniker Sodaraptor, remembers first encountering the concept of liminal spaces “back in 2020, when the original Backrooms post on 4chan started going viral.”It was an emotion they’d felt in such places but never previously had a name for. “A strange liminal discomfort”, Sodaraptor says, mixed with pangs of “anemoia”: nostalgia for an era that predates your own experience.View image in fullscreenShelf discovery … Interior Worlds.Photograph: Raptorsoft GamesSo it’s only fitting that the phenomenon’s virtual inspirations are now, in video game terms, as ancient as all those dead malls.The aforementioned Arkham City and Skyrim both came out in 2011. The same year, Valve released Portal 2, the mind-bending first-person puzzler which Parsons has repeatedly cited as his biggest influence. The director even made a couple of Portal fan-videos;the last onewas uploaded to his YouTube channel in 2021, just months before the first Backrooms clip.It is probably inevitable that the aesthetics of these 15-year-old games would just now be beginning to seep through into the cinematic mainstream. Parsons was a young child when Portal 2 came out, and it’s only natural that he – and the generation of film-makers just now coming of age – would make things informed by the dark rooms they got lost in as kids.A Minecraft Movie may already exist (unfortunately) but what will be much more interesting are the films and other artworks shaped by the experience of playing Minecraft at a formative age. Those dark caverns, the endless mines, the sounds of the zombies, the threat of the creepers – once those strange experiences have sunk into internet lore, who knows what will emerge and where it will take us.Explore more on these topicsGamesIndie gamesBackroomsSkyrimfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Furious review – a proper grownup thriller that’s powered by sheer female rage | Television | The Guardian
description: This crime drama about a female serial killer is enormously entertaining TV that demands you pay attention
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This crime drama about a female serial killer is enormously entertaining TV that demands you pay attention
Content: Emmy Rossum as FBI agent Alice Black in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyView image in fullscreenEmmy Rossum as FBI agent Alice Black in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyTV reviewTelevisionReviewFurious review – a proper grownup thriller that’s powered by sheer female rageThis crime drama about a female serial killer is enormously entertaining TV that demands you pay attentionLucy ManganMon 27 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFurious is well named. It is powered throughout its eight-episode run by an unfaltering current of female rage. It is the creation of Elizabeth Meriwether, who gave uslast year’s astonishing Dying for Sex(starringMichelle Williamsas a woman with terminal cancer discovering the range and depth of her sexuality for the first time) and 2022’s brisk, brilliantThe Dropout(the tale of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder ofblood-testing company, Theranos). They were both based on true stories. Furious was apparently inspired by the 1987 film Black Widow, starring Theresa Russell and Debra Winger, but it has jettisoned the marry-and-murder-for-money plot and contemporised the rest so thoroughly that the result hardly seems to merit the dutiful hat-tip the publicity has given it.Meriwether is the writer of the first three episodes, the rest are divided among four women and one man. The drama itself is dominated by three complicated and fascinating female characters, played by Emmy Rossum, Lola Petticrew (who gave an extraordinary performance in2024’s Say Nothing) and Quincy Tyler Bernstine. A fantastic supporting cast and a dense, lean, evocative script make this television for grownups, television to pay attention to and to entertain you enormously.Furious opens with a man crawling across an apartment floor. A tiny, childlike woman (Petticrew) in a Halloween cat mask watches him as she gathers sweets for a child at the door. “I’ll be back in a minute,” she says. Candy corn dispensed, she returns just as he has made it to the stairs. She injects him with something and lies down next to him to watch him die. We eventually learn that her name is Catherine.View image in fullscreenLola Petticrew in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyRossum plays Alice Black, a former NYPD officer who left the force after her childhood sweetheart-turned-fellow-cop-boyfriend-turned-violent-drunk assaulted her so badly that she was hospitalised. When she reported him to their lieutenant, virtually the whole department turned against her. Now she is manning the FBI tip line while she waits for a spot to open up for her in the sex crimes unit.She gets a call from her one remaining friend, Danny Kelly (Scoot McNairy) – who has suffered the consequences for supporting her - at her old job. He needs her help investigating the case of the body on the stairs. The body is that of Caleb Easton, scion of local billionaire Jay Easton, and it is clear that his apparent overdose was staged. Alice notices similarities with an old case and, as further clues and bodies accrue, the detectives conclude that they are on the hunt for that rare thing – a female serial killer.Alice uses this as an in with the sex crimes unit boss, Nora Washington (Bernstine), who becomes a sort of unofficial mentor to the new FBI agent, in part as an act of self-salvation. What follows is partly a standard thriller, as they discover a sex trafficking ring implicating the great and the good who have been helping themselves to young women and children with impunity for years. But it’s also a Killing Eve-like cat and mouse game between a detective who, against her better instincts, is gradually coming to bond with her quarry. And, not least, it’s a character drama that explores the different ways in which reactions to similar traumas can manifest themselves.There are plenty of harrowing scenes, but not the ones you would expect. There is no lingering on the murders. There is little gore. But there is an early moment – not much more than a look, really – between Alice and her sister at the latter’s hen party that speaks to a heartbreakingly unbridgeable chasm between them. There is an awful, shocking scene when one of the few people Alice loves and trusts suddenly turns screamingly against her. And a quietly magnificent, quietly terrible scene by a hospital bed involving a monologue from Nora that distills the revulsions and the bone-deep despair of her years spent watching children being abused and “never,never” really being able to make a difference to the amount of evil in the world. “You think you’re ever going to catch anyone who matters?” she says to Alice. It is rhetorical and Alice knows better than to answer.With Furious, I think we might be seeing the birth of a new subgenre of television drama; call it the Epstein thriller. Pre-him, the files and revelations about the depth and breadth of his network of suppliers, enablers and willing (rich, male) participants, we might have thought the plot of Furious preposterous, sitting uneasily with the series’ grimly realistic tone and emotional palette. Now it is an organic, seamless, horrifying whole that asks how individuals survive such predators and how society survives such knowledge. And when we are going to become furious enough to do something to make a difference.Furious is on Disney+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTV crime dramaDramareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rienzi review – Wagner’s early opera makes its Bayreuth debut as a frenzied contemporary election drama  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Alexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production swaps 14th-century Rome for an abstract near future in an over-busy staging . Jennifer Holloway’s Adriano is a standout in a strong cast
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Alexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production swaps 14th-century Rome for an abstract near future in an over-busy staging . Jennifer Holloway’s Adriano is a standout in a strong cast
Content: Too much happening … Rienzi at Bayreuth festival.Photograph: Enrico NawrathView image in fullscreenToo much happening … Rienzi at Bayreuth festival.Photograph: Enrico NawrathOperaReviewRienzi review – Wagner’s early opera makes its Bayreuth debut as a frenzied contemporary election dramaBayreuth festival theatre, BayreuthAlexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production swaps 14th-century Rome for an abstract near future in an over-busy staging . Jennifer Holloway’s Adriano is a standout in a strong castFlora WillsonMon 27 Jul 2026 08.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 08.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was Adolf Hitler’s favourite opera – and thus vital to a historical chapter that Germany’sBayreuth festivallong preferred to avoid. But Rienzi has finally arrived atWagner’s symbolic HQ, opening the 150th anniversary season as an exception to the festival’s rigid canon of his 10 “mature” works.Rienzi’s problems are unavoidable. Since the complete handwritten score was given to Hitler and subsequently disappeared, no authentic version of Wagner’s longest opera exists. Aesthetically, Rienzi shares the vast scale of French grand opera but sounds broadly Italian. Flashes of chromatic ambition hint at a Wagnerian language to come. Yet there are endless repetitions and the sense of an epic both overcompressed and underpowered.Bayreuth’s acoustic worked its magic, lending even four-square passages a diffuse luminosity. But this performance’s sporadic momentum was down to conductorNathalie Stutzmann, who found moments of pure chamber-music tenderness, majestic poise and vast surges of bass amid the military marches and rousing choral outbursts.View image in fullscreenAbstract near-future … Rienzi at Bayreuth festival.Photograph: Enrico NawrathInAlexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka’s production, 14th-century Rome becomes an abstract near-future (smartphone-like devices for all, screens everywhere, dystopian concrete) that also references recent political events in the US and beyond. One political faction brandishes placards screaming “lock him up” and “bringing Rome back”; Rienzi’s supporters insist they’re “stronger together”. Events onstage are filmed and projected, labelled “live from theCapitol”. Rienzi’s narrative becomes an election drama incorporating psychosis and incest. Bayreuth itself gets a cameo in the act two ballet, a madcap compilation of Wagner’s operas directed by a child dressed as the composer. At one point, Bible verses spool across the stage. We see numerous video clips of pigeons. There is, in short, too much happening.Leading the cast,Andreas Schagerwas characteristically high-wattage in the title role, his clarion tenor thrilling if unvaried, his gentleness in act four a rare instance of poignancy.Andreas Bauer KanabasandMichael Nagywere persuasive as his political rivals Colonna and Orsini whileGabriela Scherergleamed as his sister Irene. Best of all wasJennifer Holloway’s Adriano – now a soft-butch lesbian rather than Wagner’s trouser role – whose desperation and torn loyalties remained sympathetic, her singing searing, as catastrophe raged around her.Rienzi continues at the Bayreuth festival until 26 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaRichard WagnerClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I would be ashamed to have written any part of this’: Odyssey translator Emily Wilson attacks Nolan blockbuster | Movies | The Guardian
description: Wilson, whose work on Homer’s epic was praised by Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with ‘nothing convincing to say’
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Wilson, whose work on Homer’s epic was praised by Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with ‘nothing convincing to say’
Content: ‘Underdeveloped’ … Matt Damon and Charlize Theron in The OdysseyPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Underdeveloped’ … Matt Damon and Charlize Theron in The OdysseyPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMovies‘I would be ashamed to have written any part of this’: Odyssey translator Emily Wilson attacks Nolan blockbusterWilson, whose work on Homer’s epic was praised by Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with ‘nothing convincing to say’Peter Bradshaw reviews The Odyssey‘At times I felt I’d bitten off more than I could chew’: Christopher Nolan interviewedWhat Nolan’s Odyssey changed, invented – and left outAndrew PulverMon 27 Jul 2026 10.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 21.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmily Wilson, the classicist whose 2017 translation of Homer’s Odysseywas cited by Christopher Nolan in early publicityfor his hugely successful adaptation of the poem, has roundly criticised the film, saying “it has nothing convincing to say” and that it “lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth”.Go woke, get rich: why rightwing hate campaigns don’t affect the box officeRead moreIn a scathing essay for the London Review of Books, Wilson writes: “I had hoped that Nolan’s affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters. But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality … the film’s vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants.”Wilson adds: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great. It has nothing convincing to say about time, memory, history, war, or about the relationship between one warrior’s glorious return and the lives of his family, adversaries, comrades, friends and neighbours. It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth. Its narrative structure is gimmicky. The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.”View image in fullscreen‘And all the food looks horrible’ … Emily Wilson.Photograph: Elijah EllisWilson also noted Nolan’s admiration for the opening line of her Odyssey translation: “Tell me about a complicated man” – but added: “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”Wilson, who is department chair and professor of classical studies at the University of Pennsylvania, also went on the attack inan interview with the Sunday Times, saying: “It didn’t land emotionally for me at all. Which I think is partly about the fact that, unlike Homer, it’s not very well written.”The music in Nolan’s Odyssey is as well-crafted – and bloodlessly forgettable – as the film itselfRead more“The characters don’t have the kind of depth the Homeric characters have. I felt, ‘Do I really care if this guy gets back to his wife?’ You haven’t given me any reason to.”Why is it so hard to translate The Odyssey?Nevertheless, Wilson acknowledged the impact the film is already having on cultural awareness of ancient Greek literature as well as cinema itself. Saying “the release ofThe Odysseyis still an event to celebrate,” she suggests: “This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas … translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves … [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments.”“Nolan,” Wilson says, “is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful.”Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyHomerClassicsChristopher NolannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance Again | Boy George | The Guardian
description: Culture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attack
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Culture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attack
Content: Boy George performs on stage in Hamburg this month.Photograph: Tristar Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBoy George performs on stage in Hamburg this month.Photograph: Tristar Media/Getty ImagesBoy George‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance AgainCulture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attackBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 27 Jul 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoy George has released a new song entitled We Will Dance Again, which voices support for Israel’s military action in Palestine.Posted on X and Instagram with the Hebrew title עוד נרקוד alongside its English translation, the song features a pop-reggae backing. The opening lyrics are: “You say genocide, I say war / When you’re attacked, that’s what the army’s for / Does it get ugly? You bet it does / When I know you wanna kill every last one of us.”Boy George cites theattack by Hamas at the Nova music festival in October 2023, saying the civilians killed there were “murder[ed] … for the crime of dancing”. A total of 344 civilians and 34 security personnel were killed and 44 people were taken hostage.The overall Palestinian death toll since the war started ismore than 73,000.The title phrase We Will Dance Again, repeated for the song’s chorus, has been used by Israelis to express hope and solidarity in the wake of the 7 October attack, and was used as the title of an acclaimed documentary about it.Elsewhere in the chorus, Boy George asserts: “There will be no war / But if you’re ever confused / I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human.”He also criticises the pro-Palestinian movement, including musicians who have condemned Israel: “You condemn the Jews, with selective memory / Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet feels so weak.” Musicians who have supportedPalestineinclude Stormzy, Damon Albarn, Clairo and Brian Eno, the latter of whom conceived an all-star charity single, Lullaby, which vied for Christmas No 1 in 2025.Boy George, who is not Jewish, has recently voiced support for Jewish communities. In an interview with the Telegraph, when discussing his admiration for Jewish peers in the 1980s during his time fronting Culture Club, he said: “Over the years it’s been a really personal thing. It doesn’t mean that I don’t have compassion for Palestinians, it doesn’t mean that I agree with what’s going on in Israel, but I am always going to defend the people that I love. I have a lot of Jewish friends and there would never be a situation where I’d turn my back on them.”He also voiced his support after theknife attack in Golders Green in April which left two Jewish men injured, saying: “We need to make our Jewish community know we support them.”His new song marks an intensification of his support for Israel, having said earlier in the year that he didn’t have an opinion on the country.View image in fullscreenBoy George with San Marino contestant Senhit at the Eurovision song contest in Vienna in May.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APSpeaking ahead of an appearance with San Marino for their Eurovision song contest entry (which didn’t reach the contest’s final), he was questioned about the boycott of Eurovision from countries opposing Israel’s inclusion in the contest. “I have many Jewish friends, whom I’ve known since I was 15 or 16 years old,” he replied. “Are people asking me, as someone with principles, to turn my back on my Jewish friends? That is not going to happen – it will never happen. From the beginning of my career, I wore the Star of David … I feel very connected to the Jewish people. I’m not necessarily connected to Israel. I don’t really have an opinion on that. But the mission of music is to unite people.”His characterisation of Israel’s action against Palestine as a legitimate military response rather than genocide runs counter to aUnited Nations inquiry, which stated in 2025 that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel’s foreign ministry called the report “distorted and false”. Last month, anotherindependent UN inquiryfound that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by targeting children. That report was dubbed a “libellous sham” by Israel.Boy George was one of the most flamboyant and recognisable pop stars of the 1980s, with Culture Club scoring four UK Top 10 albums including 1983’s chart-topping Colour By Numbers. Hit singles include Do You Really Want to Hurt Me? and Karma Chameleon, which were both hugely successful in the US as well as UK, and have endured as staples on oldies radio.The band also had a hit with an anti-war track, The War Song, which reached UK No 2 in 1984 and featured the chorus: “War is stupid and people are stupid / And love means nothing in some strange quarters.”Last month, Boy George launched a new company called Artist Included, which will use AI to allow artists to create new versions of earlier songs which resemble the originals, as a way of wresting back control of master recordings. It launched with a new version of Karma Chameleon, which Boy George recorded then de-aged. “When I heard it, I was absolutely gobsmacked,” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “It sounds like another take from that original session.”Explore more on these topicsBoy GeorgePop and rockIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Carly Simon shares Parkinson’s disease diagnosis and says music has ‘rescued’ her | Carly Simon | The Guardian
description: Singer-songwriter also had surgery to treat carcinoma on her face, leading her to ‘withdraw from public view’
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Singer-songwriter also had surgery to treat carcinoma on her face, leading her to ‘withdraw from public view’
Content: Carly Simon performs in New York in 2008.Photograph: Joe Kohen/WireImageView image in fullscreenCarly Simon performs in New York in 2008.Photograph: Joe Kohen/WireImageCarly SimonCarly Simon shares Parkinson’s disease diagnosis and says music has ‘rescued’ herSinger-songwriter also had surgery to treat carcinoma on her face, leading her to ‘withdraw from public view’Owen MyersMon 27 Jul 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 16.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe musicianCarly Simonhas revealed that she hasParkinson’s diseasein a statement shared on Monday.“So many people have written to me, kindly wondering about my relative silence, asking how I am and what I have been doing,” Simon said. “The truth is, I’ve been learning how to live with Parkinson’s disease.”Simon’s music career has endured for many decades since she won the Grammy award for best new artist in 1972, with beloved hits including You’re So Vain, Let the River Run and Nobody Does It Better.Carly Simon’s 20 greatest tracks – ranked!Read more“It has taken me some time to understand the diagnosis, to adjust to it and to decide how much I wanted to say about it,” said Simon, who turned 83 last month. She said that she was still in the process of accepting the condition “without feeling that I have surrendered something essential”.“Parkinson’s is different for everyone, and it can be unpredictable,” she said. “Some days I’m so tired I can’t get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work, and feel like myself.”Parkinson’s disease affects more than 10 million people worldwide, with 90,000 people diagnosed every year in the US alone per the Parkinson’s Foundation. Common symptoms include tremor, stiffness, slowed movement and balance issues, as well as depression, anxiety and feelings of apathy. There is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms and restore quality of life.“There is no tidy or predictable schedule to the illness,” Simon said. “It does not consult my calendar before deciding what kind of day I am going to have.”The singer said that her health issues began after she had a knee and hip replacement due to arthritis. She was diagnosed with Parkinson’s in a consultation at the Mayo clinic, a private US healthcare facility.Simon said that her feelings of apathy brought on by the condition had been particularly challenging. “It is not simply sadness or laziness,” she said. “It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list.”During the same period, Simon said that she underwent treatment for basal cell carcinoma on her face. The cancer was removed, but the surgery altered her appearance and made her self-conscious about being seen in public.“Between my mobility issues, the Parkinson’s diagnosis, the surgery and the emotional effects of it all, withdrawing from public view was the most palatable reaction,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe artist added that the recording process for her new album, Comes in Waves, had given shape to her days. The record is scheduled for release on 14 August.“It gave me somewhere to go without having to leave the room,” she said. “It reminded me that illness can change your life without becoming the whole of your life.”Music “has rescued me more times that I can count”, she said.Simon ended her statement by thanking her doctors, family and friends for their support. “These days I move more slowly, I lean on others more than I once did, and I have learned to accept that every day will look a little different,” she concluded. “But I am still very much here.”Explore more on these topicsCarly SimonParkinson's diseaseHealthPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Gunther von Hagens, creator of Body Worlds and plastination, dies aged 81 | Science | The Guardian
description: Controversial anatomist’s body ‘will definitely be plastinated’ in line with his wishes, a spokesperson said
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Controversial anatomist’s body ‘will definitely be plastinated’ in line with his wishes, a spokesperson said
Content: Gunther von Hagens with a plastinated human body, displayed as part of a touring Body Worlds exhibition in 2007.Photograph: LM Otero/APView image in fullscreenGunther von Hagens with a plastinated human body, displayed as part of a touring Body Worlds exhibition in 2007.Photograph: LM Otero/APScienceGunther von Hagens, creator of Body Worlds and plastination, dies aged 81Controversial anatomist’s body ‘will definitely be plastinated’ in line with his wishes, a spokesperson saidPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorMon 27 Jul 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 14.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGunther von Hagens, who developed a technique for permanently preserving human bodies in rigid states and toured the world with his controversial Body Worlds exhibition, has moved closer to fulfilling a long-held wish to be sliced up and displayed in a museum after dying aged 81.“It is with deep sadness that the family and the Institute for Plastination announce the passing of Dr Gunther von Hagens, inventor of plastination and creator of the Body Worlds exhibitions,” the German anatomist’s institute said in a statement on Monday.Von
