Hagens, who was diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2008, died in a hospital in Heidelberg on 24 July, a day after suffering a cerebral haemorrhage.He frequently said he wanted his own body to be preserved after his death, though he wavered on his preferred mode of presentation.“I could envisagemy plastinated body standing in a welcoming pose at the entrance of an exhibition, or rendered into slices and distributed across various sites,” he wrote in the Guardian in 2018.On Monday, a spokesperson for the Plastinarium – a museum von Hagens founded in Guben,Germany, in 2006 – said the anatomist’s body “will definitely be plastinated, as this was always a long-held wish of his”, though where it would be put on display had not been determined.View image in fullscreenA plastinated body posed as if playing chess, on show in 2001.Photograph: Jockel Finck/APVon Hagens was born Gunther Gerhard Liebchen in January 1945 in Skalmierzyce, Poland, then under German occupation and named Alt-Skalden. He grew up in socialist East Germany and took part in protests against the violent Soviet suppression of the Prague Spring in 1968. The following year, he was imprisoned after trying to flee into the west.In 1970, West Germany paid 40,000 deutschmarks for him to be released to its care as a political prisoner. In the west, he met and married his first wife, Cornelia von Hagens, adopting her surname and its connotations of nobility.Von Hagens came up with his technique for preserving bodies in 1977, while working as a research scientist at the University of Heidelberg’s institute of pathology and anatomy. “Looking at specimens embedded in plastic – the most advanced preservation technique then available – I wondered why the plastic was poured around bodies rather than into them,” he wrote in the Guardian.Plastination involves extracting bodily fluids and soluble fat from a dead body and replacing them with resins, silicon rubbers and epoxies. The technique lends a high degree of rigidity to the tissue, enabling bodies to be displayed in upright, lifelike poses.From 1995, von Hagens’ plastinated bodies were displayed in travelling exhibitions. Some were sliced up to reveal internal organs, while others were posed playing chess, doing physical exercise or having sex. Called Body Worlds, the displays became a global phenomenon, attracting more than 50 million visitors globally.Von Hagens curated the shows in tandem with his second wife, Angelina Whalley, and said they were driven by a desire to “democratise anatomy” and shatter taboos around death.But many critics felt the exhibitions deliberately tried to titillate audiences with exhibits such as a series of foetal specimens at various stages of gestation.View image in fullscreenVon Hagens with his wife and co-curator, Angelina Whalley, at the opening of a Body Worlds exhibition in London in 2018.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe anatomist insisted the bodies displayed in the shows belonged to people who had authorised the use of their bodies after their deaths for educational benefit, though the use of infant and animal bodies raised difficult moral questions.In 2004 German news magazine Der Spiegel published documents appearing to show that von Hagens’ plastination facility in Dalian, northern China, had purchased “ownerless bodies” from police, some of which had been executed and bore bullet holes. After the expose was published, he reportedly instructed his employees not to accept executed bodies anymore.Von Hagens’ fedora-and-leather-vest wearing public persona – “a cross between evil scientist and the television cliche of ghoulish murder-scene pathologist”,according to one review– may not have helped dispel questions about his motives.After Parkinson’s disease left him with reduced motor skills and limited speech, von Hagens transferred organisational and financial duties to his wife and son, Rurik.“Sometimes, at this stage of my life and illness, I wish I could suspend my convictions and embrace the idea of a divinity and an afterlife,” he wrote in 2018. “But I don’t think there is a continuum beyond death. Every deceased body I have seen has shown me the absence of the soul. I don’t believe anything is left of us after we die.”Explore more on these topicsScienceAnatomy and physiologyExhibitionsGermanyDeath and dyingMuseumsParkinson's diseasenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tom Holland says some of his films are ‘shit’ and people shouldn’t see them | Movies | The Guardian

Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Speaking to the Dish podcast, it is unclear which films he was referring to, though the Spider-Man and Odyssey star said he was ‘super proud’ of both of those
Content: Really proud of this one … Tom Holland promoting Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Eloisa Sanchez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReally proud of this one … Tom Holland promoting Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Eloisa Sanchez/Getty ImagesMoviesTom Holland says some of his films are ‘shit’ and people shouldn’t see themSpeaking to the Dish podcast, it is unclear which films he was referring to, though the Spider-Man and Odyssey star said he was ‘super proud’ of both of thoseAndrew PulverMon 27 Jul 2026 06.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 07.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpider-Man and Odyssey starTom Hollandsays that some of his films are “shit” and that people “shouldn’t” see them.Holland was speaking on the Dish podcastand was asked by co-hosts Nick Grimshaw and Angela Hartnett about his experiences promoting his movies. Holland responded by saying: “When you’re doing press for movies that you’re really proud of it’s really easy because when they ask you questions about why should people go and watch this movie, you’re not lying to anyone.”He added: “I’ve had experiences before when people say like, ‘Why should you see this movie?’ And in the back if your mind you’re like, ‘You shouldn’t. Because it’s shit.’”13:13The Odyssey: is Nolan adaptation worth the hype? - The LatestIt is not clear which films Holland is referring to, having starred in three hugely successful Spider-Man features, with a fourth, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, shortly to be released. Holland has also appeared in a number of related films as Peter Parker, including Captain America: Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War, Avengers: Endgame and Venom: Let There Be Carnage. Outside superhero films, Holland has starred insouthern gothic noir The Devil All the Time, theRusso brothers’ crime thriller CherryandYA sci-fi Chaos Walking.Holland is currently appearing as Odysseus’s son Telemachus in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of Homer’sThe Odyssey. Commenting on promoting both The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Holland said: “It’s felt really like a bit of a victory lap, to be honest. And I’ve really enjoyed it. You know, I’m super proud of both of the films.”Explore more on these topicsFilmTom HollandThe OdysseySpider-MannewsShareReuse this content

title: Charli xcx portrait added to National Portrait Gallery collection | Charli xcx | The Guardian
description: Pop star is celebrated as ‘one of the defining cultural figures of her generation’ by gallery, which acquires Brat-era portrait by Harley Weir
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Pop star is celebrated as ‘one of the defining cultural figures of her generation’ by gallery, which acquires Brat-era portrait by Harley Weir
Content: Harley Weir’s 2024 portrait of Charli xcx.Photograph: Harley Weir/PAView image in fullscreenHarley Weir’s 2024 portrait of Charli xcx.Photograph: Harley Weir/PACharli xcxCharli xcx portrait added to National Portrait Gallery collectionPop star is celebrated as ‘one of the defining cultural figures of her generation’ by gallery, which acquires Brat-era portrait by Harley WeirBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 27 Jul 2026 06.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA portrait of Charli xcx has been added to the National Portrait Gallery’s collection, in the week that she hopes for a No 1 chart position for her new album Music, Fashion, Film.The photograph by Harley Weir was taken in 2023 and became one of the key images associated with Charli’s Brat era: the 2024 album that became a pop cultural phenomenon for its candour and debauchery.Brandei Estes, the National Portrait Gallery’s senior curator of photographs, said the gallery was “delighted” with the acquisition. Charli is “one of the defining cultural figures of her generation”, she said, and Weir “has developed a distinctive photographic language that combines intimacy with a powerful sense of presence”.The photo is exhibited in the gallery’s History Makers Now space, and its acquisition was funded by a gift from the Bukhman Foundation.Charli’s album Music, Fashion, Film has been a critical and commercial success since its release on Friday, with the Guardian describing her as “our most consistently bracing pop star” ina five-star review. It could become her fourth UK No 1 and second this year, after her soundtrack to Wuthering Heights topped the chart in February. It is at No 1 in the midweek chart ahead of new releases by Snow Patrol, Shania Twain and the Strokes.Over the weekend she released three additional songs not included on Music, Fashion, Film, described as B-sides of the album tracks, and titled I Keep on Thinking Bout You Every Single Day and Night, Playboy Bunny and If You Take Away the Music Then What Has She Got? “I felt adamant I wouldn’t put them on streaming because it sort of felt counterintuitive to the whole ethos of those songs, but I know you all really wanted them so I’ve begrudgingly put them on iTunes lol,” she said on Instagram.Charli xcx: Music, Fashion, Film review – slippery search into selfhood that hits just as hard as BratRead moreOne song from the album, Camera, documents Charli’s recent forays into film acting: she has recently appeared in the Polish arthouse drama Erupcja, the fantastical 100 Nights of Hero, and opposite Anya Taylor-Joy and Chris Evans in Sacrifice, plus she starred as herself in the mockumentary The Moment.She’ll next be seen in Gregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex, comedy thriller The Gallerest, and the remake of 1978 horror movie Faces of Death. She is starring in and producing the untitled next film by Takashi Miike, the Japanese director of Audition and Ichi the Killer.Her next major live shows are headlining the Reading and Leeds festival, before a North American tour in September and October.Explore more on these topicsCharli xcxPop and rockNational Portrait GalleryPhotographynewsShareReuse this content

title: CBSO/Yamada review – Poulenc and Adams pairing is stylish, witty and thrilling | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lucas and Arthur Jussen brought fun and energy to Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos, and John Adams’ Harmonium was monumental and moving in the City of Birmingham Orchestra and Chorus’ Prom under their chief conductor Kazuki Yamada
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Lucas and Arthur Jussen brought fun and energy to Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos, and John Adams’ Harmonium was monumental and moving in the City of Birmingham Orchestra and Chorus’ Prom under their chief conductor Kazuki Yamada
Content: Lucid and urbane … Kazuki Yamada and the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenLucid and urbane … Kazuki Yamada and the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewCBSO/Yamada review – Poulenc and Adams pairing is stylish, witty and thrillingRoyal Albert Hall, LondonLucas and Arthur Jussen brought fun and energy to Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos, and John Adams’ Harmonium was monumental and moving in the City of Birmingham Orchestra and Chorus’ Prom under their chief conductor Kazuki YamadaAlexandra CoghlanMon 27 Jul 2026 07.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 07.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican minimalism can punch and thrill, hypnotise and slow your pulse, but how often does it make you laugh? What a brilliant idea, then, from Kazuki Yamada and theCity of Birmingham Symphony Orchestrato pair John Adams’ formative 1980 epic Harmonium – a sonic wrestle with love and death and desire – with music by the wittiest, slipperiest, most self-puncturing composer in the business, an artist who will break your heart with the cheekiest of grins: Francis Poulenc.It’s entirely typical that Poulenc can’t even bring himself to call a symphony a symphony. Any delusions of grandeur are seen off at the pass by diminutising his 1948 “Sinfonietta”, which duly unfolds in a series of impeccably shaded and textured dances, marches and melodies that thumb their nose at anything so dutiful as development.Lucid and urbane, Yamada’s Poulenc was impeccable – a crisp musical suit, an Hermès pocket-square of whimsy just visible in silky woodwind solos and harp, always undercut by clean architectural lines. When the music has this many punchlines you have to play it absolutely straight; all the more essential, because there was a riotous coda to come in the form of Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos.View image in fullscreenFingers flying as one … the Jussen brothers.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouDutch duo theJussen brothers(who’ve been playing this since they were teenage prodigies) bounded on for their Proms debut in matching suits and flung themselves at this naughty musical satire – whose target is modernism as much as a Mozart piano concerto – with irrepressible rhythmic energy. Two heads nodded vigorously from either side of the stage, fingers flying absolutely as one: enormously stylish fun.A performance of Harmonium at home in Birmingham a few weeks ago lacked choral welly, but with the CBSO Chorus now bolstered by the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs we had the rippling textural canvas the Adams demands for this quasi-choral-concerto – voices treated as pulsing points of light inNegative Love; as an explosive, ululating jangle inWild Nights. Central movementBecause I could not stop for Deathwas the only sticking point, sagging where it should have held us rapt. But to demand electricity here is rather like asking for more pace in mile 22 of a marathon – a quibble in a frankly monumental achievement.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicCity of Birmingham Symphony OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot review – Anne Enright celebrates a landmark feminist novel | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Half a century on, this tale of a woman who abandons her children in search of her self remains thrillingly original
Author: Anne Enright
Headline: Half a century on, this tale of a woman who abandons her children in search of her self remains thrillingly original
Content: ‘Joan Barfoot understands the inside-out logic of maternal obligation.’Photograph: eyevine/Chloë Ellingson/The Observer/eyevineView image in fullscreen‘Joan Barfoot understands the inside-out logic of maternal obligation.’Photograph: eyevine/Chloë Ellingson/The Observer/eyevineBook of the dayFictionReviewGaining Ground by Joan Barfoot review – Anne Enright celebrates a landmark feminist novelHalf a century on, this tale of a woman who abandons her children in search of her self remains thrillingly originalAnne EnrightMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 05.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a growing literature of maternal flight: novels about women who leave not just their husbands but also the children they have made. In the real world, men are the more frequent deserters; the connection of the father to family life is seen as contingent, while motherhood is revered as an intrinsic state. This means that women who “un-mother” themselves are doing something impossible: the connection between a woman and her child is not just emotional, but also creational. Joan Barfoot understands the inside-out nature of the logic involved in maternal obligation: “she created these other people and their need for her,” says Abra, the abandoning mother of Gaining Ground, “and now she must fulfil them.”Abra neglects to fulfil her children or their needs. The novel is rigorously and meditatively about the business of separation, which is also the business of becoming a single and undivided self.Gaining Ground came out in Canada in 1978, under the title Abra, before it was published in the UK under the current title by the Women’s Press in 1980. This was around the time Barfoot’s fellow Canadian Alice Munro began to write her adulterous, runaway women, whose instinct for freedom chimed so well with the feminism of the day. Abra is not sprung from domesticity by her desire for another man, however, nor does she return to her children, as Leda inElena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughterdoes, after years spent regaining what she had lost. Abra is closer to the protagonist in Cathy Sweeney’s recentBreakdown, who has no single answer to the question of why she left her former life: In Japan, Sweeney writes, “So many people disappear that there is a word for them –johatsu. It translates as evaporated people.”These novels cannot fully resist the question of whether the bolting mother is a monster or a victim of societal expectation. Gaining Ground was written before any of them and, already, Barfoot was wise enough to refuse the terms of the debate: Abra never questions the morality of becoming her true self.The novel begins with the arrival of a young woman at Abra’s cabin in the woods, nine years after she drove away from her old life. Abra feels her presence as a pressure, an expectation, but can barely remember who the girl is, or who she herself used to be. Then, a moment of recognition – it is her 18-year-old daughter, Katie: “I know her now, and it locks me to her.”double quotation markBarfoot was wise enough to refuse the terms of the debate: Abra never questions the morality of becoming her true selfKatie’s arrival tips Abra into a recollection of her lovely, ordered home in Toronto; her marriage, in which there would sometimes be “late movies and making love on the couch and popcorn”; and her two children. Her first baby, a son, provoked a fierce sense of attachment: “I didn’t even want to talk about him, although he so completely occupied my mind, because I felt somehow that talking about him took him a distance away, made him separate, gave a piece of him to someone else.” Her second child seemed less of a miracle: “she was a baby, beautiful, and she was mine and Stephen’s and we had created her, but it seemed natural now”.The story may be about maternal ambivalence, depression, the loss of meaning, but it always revolves around ideas of truth and pretence. Abra’s life does not feel “real”. Barfoot delivers about 16 different kinds of dissociation without going over her own footprints or saying the same thing twice. The build to Abra’s departure has a cumulative, relentless modernist effect, but she manages to keep it human, or within the human, and we are fully convinced, when Abra sees the cabin for the first time, that this is her “home”.She has brought no clocks and no mirror, and is at pains to avoid talking to other people. On her first day of digging a vegetable garden her hair proves bothersome and so she lops it off, blind. Abra works to grow food, gather wood and keep herself alive through the long Canadian winter. She thinks only about what is in front of her. The descriptions of work, the natural world and the changing seasons recall the self-reliance of Annie Dillard or Thoreau, who write in a transcendent spiritual tradition. Abra’s revelation is not about God’s infinite majesty, however, but about a kind of unbecoming. She wants to make a life in which she can slowly lose “my name, my memory, the labels I’d used, and so my sense of all words”, to arrive at a place of joy.When Katie arrives from a world where “there are motives and angers everywhere”, Abra tries to share what she has discovered about “blankness”. She considers the way she once saw her husband and wonders, “Did I make him up?” The answer is that she invented everyone: “I simplified them. And then I reacted to what I had made up, behaved as if what I had invented was real.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is hard to find an ending for a book that is trying to be about nothing, so it is considerably to her credit that Barfoot manages an affecting, dramatic conclusion to Katie’s visit. Gaining Ground is a wonderful slow burn of a book and Barfoot’s originality and control remain exciting, nearly half a century on. It is great to see this reissue put the novel at the centre of things, where it belongs.Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot is published by Faber (£9.99). title: What If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypse | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answers
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answers
Content: Eleanor Drage, senior research fellow at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.Photograph: Apple Photos Clean UpView image in fullscreenEleanor Drage, senior research fellow at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.Photograph: Apple Photos Clean UpScience and nature booksReviewWhat If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypseThe academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answersSophie McBainMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe AI ethicist Eleanor Drage believes that to thrive alongside artificial intelligence, humans need to recognise AI’s “humanity”. She means that while we often speak of AI as though it were some mystical, formless thing, it is the product of hours of human labour, in silicon and quartz mines, microchip factories and data labelling centres. If citizens want to wrest power from the tech companies that are building AI, it helps to understand clearly what they are selling us. This also means seeing through the marketing and hype: “the cloud”, that nebulous, distant place where your photos are stored, is just someone else’s computer; an AI “hallucination” is a system error or data labelling mistake; intelligence is a very broad – and potentially misleading – term.The story in Silicon Valley is that AI will either save us, ushering in a new era of prosperity and human longevity, or it will wipe us all out. Drage argues, convincingly, that big tech cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises while it continues to chase profit and power above all else, and while it serves the interests of a narrow few. Meanwhile, the cultural obsession with the AI-induced apocalypse conveniently redirects attention from the practical conversations we could be having about how to make AI safer – by ensuring citizens have more power over how their information is used, and how AI models are trained and regulated, for example. Tech titans’ apocalyptic visions also create the false impression that AI safety is more important than climate change, geopolitical tensions and inequality, three problems that are already causing a huge amount of suffering and that, if addressed, would reduce many AI-linked risks too.Drage, an assistant research professor at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, has conducted research that debunks AI-powered recruitment processes, and exposes the dangers of incorporating AI into law enforcement. Many of her criticisms of big tech will be familiar: that AI algorithms perpetuate and entrench pre-existing biases; that for all their bland, generic promises to be “transparent” and “accountable”, tech giants have become too big to care about ethics; that a handful of executives have amassed far too much power; and that the rollout of AI is happening without our consent and without consideration for planetary health. But her writing has intellectual heft, and her philosophical explorations of, for example, how we define intelligence and why this matters, are very interesting.Occasionally, however, Drage’s arguments seem rushed and become sloppy. “It’s merely an illusion that the labour force is disappearing: work is simply shifting, from artists to data labellers and from marketeers to engineers,” she writes at one point. But it’s not clear that artists and “marketeers” will become redundant in the coming AI era. It’s also not as though the data labellers working for poverty wages in Kenya would have been artists 10 years ago. Equally, given the importance she rightly places on promoting diversity in AI, it’s disappointing that she dismisses unconscious bias as “merely another way of taking the perspective of the perpetrator rather than the recipient of harm”, as though intention is completely irrelevant. She writes that people are ready for “less placid” conversations about equality, I’d add that these conversations also demand accuracy and nuance.The book’s title suggests Drage wants to offer an alternative vision of what AI could be. She gives a few examples of the kind of ethical, community-based AI projects she thinks should be replacing top-down big tech products, and many of them are strangely underwhelming. They include an app called Mumkin designed to facilitate difficult conversations about female genital mutilation (FGM) in India, and Kuini, an AI chatbot built to help Māori women quit smoking. In both instances I found myself wondering what value AI brings to these endeavours – particularly given all that Drage has discussed about its environmental impact and exploitative supply chains. Is an app more effective than training community members to act as counsellors, or funding support groups and peer support workers?Drage describes a toolkit she co-designed to help AI companies act ethically and comply with EU regulations as a “cornerstone of utopianism”, because it shifts the focus on to how AI is built and made. In her view, utopia is not a destination but the “process of working together to develop a fairer world”. Maybe it would be unfair to expect too specific a utopian vision, but I’d nonetheless be interested to know how AI, specifically, can help us build a better future. She does not mention the things that many of AI’s biggest critics nonetheless welcome, such as its potential to improve drug discovery and disease detection. What if we got AI right, this book asks. After reading it, I can’t say I really know.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
