title: A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that | Benedict Cumberbatch, Alan Cumming and Benedict Wong | The Guardian
description: The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should, say actors led by Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong
Author: Benedict Cumberbatch
Headline: The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should, say actors led by Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionTelevision industryA TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop thatThe Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought in the US and UK. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She shouldBenedict Cumberbatch,Alan CummingandBenedict WongMon 27 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 10.40 EDTShareView image in fullscreenThough it has yet to become front-page news in the UK, you should know about the proposedParamount-Warner Bros merger. It threatens to inflict immense harm on the British public. As actors and public figures who have spent our careers in the arts in Britain – working with British crews, on British stages and sets – we have a responsibility to the public who support, enjoy and consume the art we make.The UK is being threatened by a media merger that would harm our workers, our culture and the public – but we can stop it. We are encouraged by Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, who recently sent letters toParamount SkydanceandWarner Bros Discovery, as well as a statement toparliament, indicating that she is “minded to intervene” in Paramount’s$110bn takeoverof Warner Bros.She is correct to investigate this major threat to the UK’s public interest. And she will not be acting alone. This month, 12 US states, led by California,sued in federal courtto block the merger, warning that it would raise prices, shrink the number of films made and degrade the quality of what audiences see. And they just won a major victory: on Friday, Paramount agreed todelay the mergeruntil trial, which could be months. These states acted even after Washington’s own justice department – despitethe reported reservationsof career staff –waved the deal through.Their lawsuit confirms the danger; it cannot, however, do the UK’s work for it. US courts fight on the antitrust front for US markets. The EU, which last weekconditionally backed the merger, also makes its own decisions. The UK’s public interest, our public service broadcasting, our news plurality, the plurality of voices British audiences hear, can only be defended here, by our own secretary of state and the Competition and Markets Authority.The fight against this merger now runs on two fronts, and Nandy commands one of them. Should her department decide to intervene, it may prove one of the most important decisions any culture secretary has taken for UK film, television and media in a generation.This is why. We have spent our lives working in this industry. We know what it looks like from the inside: the sound stages at Leavesden, the crews who move from production to production, the editors and camera operators and costume designers whose names scroll past in the credits at the end of a film. These are our cherished friends and colleagues, who create the shows we all love, who produce the news that educates the public and film the sport events we enjoy together. UK film and television are not just images on your screens; they are the lives and livelihoods of thousands of workers and families, whose work supports local economies. The industry supportsmore than 180,000 jobs, generated£6.8bn in production spendlast year alone and adds roughly£12bn a yearin value to our economy. It is one of the things the UK still does better than almost anyone, and a cultural heritage we must protect.We have watched, with growing alarm, what consolidation does to the breadth and depth of the work we produce: independent film acquisitions at the leading independent film festival Sundancefell by halfbetween 2019 and 2025. Award-winning documentaries – films thatwon Oscarsandtopped festival juries– havestruggled to find commercial distributionbecause they touched subjects the remaining handful of buyers found inconvenient. Every merger of this kind narrows the funnel through which stories can reach audiences.That is precisely what makes the Paramount-WBD merger so dangerous. It’s why the intervention of Nandy and her department matters so much.Paramount proposes to swallow Warner Bros Discovery in one of the largest leveraged buyouts ever attempted, loading the combined company withan estimated $84bn in debt. To service it, executives have promised investors around $6bn in “synergies”. In plain English, that means redundancies, cancelled productions, fewer films commissioned and fewer risks taken.We have seen this before. When Discovery merged with WarnerMedia in 2022, it shelved finished films andcut thousands of jobs; when Skydance merged with Paramount last year, itlaid off about 2,000 people. Now the same executives are making the same promise, and UK crews, producers, talent and audiences will pay when the bill comes due.But jobs are mostly a matter for the Competition and Markets Authority,whose reviewshould end in a full phase 2 investigation. The job of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport goes further: to determine whether the merger is in the public interest. It most certainly is not. Inher statement to British MPs, Nandy cited the need for a sufficient plurality of views in news media and a sufficient plurality of individuals controlling media enterprises. She has also highlighted the potential impact on streaming services, content homogenisation and children’s television. TheEnterprise Actprotects something we should all care about: who decides what we get to watch, and what we get to know.Consider the breadth of what this single company would hold. Channel 5, one of our fivepublic service broadcasters, which serves the evening news to people without the cost of a subscription. CNN International, whichOfcom research in 2018 foundUK viewers rated above every other TV news source for quality, accuracy, trustworthiness and impartiality. The CNN and CBS news archives – among the world’s most important broadcast news collections, withmore than 4.25mvideos, images and media spanning nearly half a century of history. If one commercially interested owner controls access to both, they control the raw material of our historical memory.One owner controlling this much of the news, and the truth, endangers the public in a way no ordinary consolidation does. When separate owners run separate newsrooms, a story judged inconvenient by one can still reach audiences through another. Fold those newsrooms into a single company, and one boardroom’s commercial anxieties – or political debts – determine what millions of people see and what they never learn existed.And we know something about this particular proprietor’s intentions. Paramount’s chief executive reportedly told Donald Trump that he would make “sweeping changes” to CNN if the deal went through. When the buyer of the world’s most trusted international news channel makes editorial promises to a politician, a British secretary of state is entitled – and, really, obliged – to ask questions before the ink dries.Nandy has been scrupulous in noting that no final decision has been taken. Good. It is important to take the time to get this right. But the case for a full public interest intervention, with Ofcom assessing plurality and reporting back, is overwhelming.Actors are often told to stay out of legal arguments. We understand the instinct. But we have spent our lives on enough UK sets, worked alongside enough UK crews and watched enough brilliant work from the UK struggle to find a buyer to know that this is not someone else’s argument. It is ours. Nandy has opened the door to intervention. Shemustwalk through it, for the sake of everyone who makes UK television and film – and everyone who watches it. If she does not, we will be left without the ability to protect our industry and our culture from this consolidation. We must not push the public’s interest aside; we must stand up for it and block this merger.Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong are actors working in the UK and Hollywood

title: ‘My mother was 4ft 11in and scared the hell out of people’ – Sean Astin on child stardom, The Lord of the Rings and surviving 45 years in Hollywood | Movies | The Guardian
description: His mother was an Oscar-winning actor who had been exploited from a young age; Astin appeared in The Goonies at just 13. Now, he has followed in his mother’s footsteps again as a union leader. He talks Stranger Things, AI and why playing Samwise Gamgee cost him his house
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: His mother was an Oscar-winning actor who had been exploited from a young age; Astin appeared in The Goonies at just 13. Now, he has followed in his mother’s footsteps again as a union leader. He talks Stranger Things, AI and why playing Samwise Gamgee cost him his house
Content: ‘I’ve been number one on the call sheet and number 247’ ... Sean Astin in his Sag-Aftra office in Los Angeles.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The Guardian; photographer's assistant: Jhovany QuirozView image in fullscreen‘I’ve been number one on the call sheet and number 247’ ... Sean Astin in his Sag-Aftra office in Los Angeles.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The Guardian; photographer's assistant: Jhovany QuirozThe big interviewMoviesInterview‘My mother was 4ft 11in and scared the hell out of people’ – Sean Astin on child stardom, The Lord of the Rings and surviving 45 years in HollywoodSteve RoseHis mother was an Oscar-winning actor who had been exploited from a young age; Astin appeared in The Goonies at just 13. Now, he has followed in his mother’s footsteps again as a union leader. He talks Stranger Things, AI and why playing Samwise Gamgee cost him his houseMon 27 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 06.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSean Astin is showing me around his new office. There’s framed movie prints on the walls, piles of paperwork and a stack of boxes of Stranger Things Funko Pops. “If you were here, you could look out this window and see a 10-storey building with our iconic Sag-Aftra logo on it,” he says proudly on video call, gesturing out of the window to the Los Angeles skyline. “But you just have to trust me that it’s there.” He shows me a framed photo of his mother, Patty Duke, aged 16, with the best supporting actress Oscar she won in 1963 (for playing Helen Keller in The Miracle Worker), and even more proudly, a framed copy of Duke’s business card from when she was president of the Screen Actors Guild in the mid-80s – the role he now occupies (Sag merged with the American Federation ofTelevisionand Radio Artists in 2012). The 10 months of his presidency “has been a whirlwind”, he says.It’s still slightly jarring to see Astin in a suit and tie, lanyard around his neck. We’re more accustomed to seeing him in the handwoven cloak and hairy feet of Samwise Gamgee, loyally accompanying mister Frodo into Mordor in The Lord of the Rings. Or as Winona Ryder’s short-lived partner in Stranger Things (before a Demodog got to him). Or as never-say-die college football underdog “Rudy” Ruettiger in the 1993 biopic. Or, for viewers of his own vintage, as plucky leader Mikey in The Goonies. Astin has been a member of the union he now represents for 45 of his 55 years, but he seems to have survived the perils of child stardom and a Hollywood upbringing remarkably unscathed. In fact, you could see it all as preparation for the role.He certainly honed his negotiating skills early. “I learned at a very young age, how to speak different languages. I could speak the language of my mother, I could speak the language of father and my brothers and I had a peacemaker role in our five-boy family.”But there’s also an overlap between Astin’s roles on screen and off. “The parts I get are the ‘working man’ parts,” he says. “Rudy comes from a steel mill, Samwise is a gardener, he’s hands in the soil. There’s just something physically about me. I don’t know whether it’s my height and weight or whatever my internal life became with my parents and my wife and children and everything, but I’m just appropriate for those parts.”View image in fullscreenPlucky leader ... from left: Astin, Kerri Green, Ke Huy Quan, Josh Brolin, Martha Plimpton and Corey Feldman in The Goonies.Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyThis was his pitch to Sag-Aftra’s 160,000 members – not just actors but also dancers, stunt performers, broadcast journalists and DJs: “I said I want to lean into the parts of my personality that are depicted in The Goonies and Rudy and Stranger Things and The Lord of the Rings, on behalf of the members.” He was elected last September with nearly 80% of the vote.Astin was born into what some might term “Hollywood royalty”, though on paper it sounds less like a head-start than a curse. Duke, his mother, was groomed as a child star and acquired considerable commercial clout, including her own TV show, which ran for three years in the 60s. But she suffered the worst of the industry in the process. She was taken into the care of talent agents John and Ethel Ross when she was eight, given drugs and alcohol and exploited and abused, sexually and financially. As well as eating disorders there were “suicide attempts, violent outbursts, and long stretches of depression,” Astin says. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in 1982.When Duke became pregnant with Sean in 1970, aged 23, it was not clear who his father was. She had been in a relationship with 17-year-old Desi Arnaz Jr (which apparently infuriated his mother, the comedian and actor Lucille Ball). Duke then fled to Las Vegas and hastily married Michael Tell, a rock promoter (the marriage lasted 13 days), then a year after Astin was born, she married the actor John Astin, best known for portraying Gomez in the original Addams Family television series. John and Duke were married until 1985, and he became Sean’s adoptive father, although a DNA test in 1994 revealed that Tell, who died last year, was his biological father. Astin maintained good relationships with all of these men, he says, including his stepfather, Duke’s fourth husband, Michael Pearce. He calls Arnaz Jr his “godfather”. Astin senior is now 96 and happily retired. Sean credits him for somehow making this complicated, potentially traumatic setup work: “He always wanted to do the right thing, and for him the right thing was humanity, and to put yourself in the other guy’s shoes, and two wrongs don’t make a right.”The same goes for his mother, who died in 2016. To classify her as a casualty of the entertainment industry is too reductive, Astin suggests, “because she was so smart. She was brilliant. My dad had all this academic training, but if you watch the gameshows that they were on in the 70s and 80s, she’d wipe the floor … so I feel like it’s a trope to lean into the melodrama and the pop culture.” Still, Duke’s level of child stardom cannot have been healthy, he acknowledges, “when you have money and that level of impact on other people, it can be destabilising for everyone involved.”View image in fullscreenAstin with his mother, Patty Duke, in 2004.Photograph: David S Holloway/Getty ImagesHis parents never discouraged Astin from following the same path, although his mother was fiercely protective of him. He hesitates to psychoanalyse her, but says, “I think she wanted to rectify the pain and trauma of her childhood by raising a child who could have a similar experience absent that trauma.”He remembers a time as a teenage actor when she was on set, and a sound engineer made a disparaging comment about his braces. “He mumbled something about ‘the kid’s got fucking marbles in his mouth.’ And my mom flipped out. Her upset was way more traumatic than me not having even heard this mildly disparaging thing that this guy had whispered to himself. But that is the level of mama-bear protection that she had. She was only 4ft 11in, but she scared the shit out of people.”For similar reasons, Duke was also a formidable union leader. “She was, from everything I’ve heard, a beloved figure.”Being a child star in the 80s certainly had its dangers. Astin was 13 when he starred in The Goonies. His co-star Corey Feldman, and Feldman’s friend Corey Haim, both later alleged childhood sexual abuse within the industry – and struggled with substance abuse and other issues in adulthood (Haim died in 2010). His near-contemporary Drew Barrymore was in rehab by the time she was 13. Astin remembers meeting her in a nightclub around that time. “I saw her and gave her a big hug. We kind of liked each other … But I remember thinking: ‘Boy, is it OK that she’s in that experience?’” Astin didn’t do that kind of stuff, he says. “I was never interested in drugs and alcohol or like wild promiscuity or those kinds of things. I got married very young, at 21. We just had our 34th wedding anniversary.”If there was one time the industry started to get to him, it was during The Lord of the Rings movies, in the early 00s. Astin was a key member of the huge cast, arguably the story’s moral centre, but “I was not prepared for that level of visibility and access,” he says. “And there was a disconnect between the attention that I was getting and how much money we had. It was not a lot of money! In fact, I had to sell my house because I negotiated such a small amount on the trilogy.” He’s “very comfortable financially now”, he says.View image in fullscreen‘I was not prepared for that level of visibility’ ... with Elijah Wood in The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyHe has also had the very 21st-century experience of seeing Samwise Gamgee as the subject of erotic fan fiction, endless memes and now AI-generated fan slop, where his character meets his older or younger self, or dies and has a funeral, or does things with Frodo that would make Tolkien turn in his grave. “So far I haven’t been bothered by it,” he says, “but what happens when it truly is indistinguishable from yourself?”He still sees his fellow hobbits – Elijah Wood, Billy Boyd and Dominic Monaghan – regularly, at conventions all over the world. “We have a great time. We go to fancy dinners together. We really enjoy the fellowship. We’ve probably done a dozen of them, we’ve got more planned.” And a return to Middle-earth is still possible. Andy Serkis is now in New Zealand filming in-between movie The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum, with Wood and Ian “Gandalf” McKellen reprising their roles. And director Peter Jackson recently announced another project after that, co-written by Tolkien superfan Stephen Colbert. It’s very early days, says Astin, who has spoken to Colbert about it, but he could see himself returning. “I don’t think anybody is opposed to it. We’d all love to connect to those characters, particularly if it’s done with such sensitivity as we heard.” And better paid this time? “Goddam right.”View image in fullscreenAstin poses for a portrait at the SAG-AFTRA officePhotograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianFor the time being, though, acting is not really the priority. There’s no shortage of issues in Astin’s in-tray, uppermost of which is the looming spectre of artificial intelligence. Under his predecessor, Fran Drescher, Sag-Aftra went on strike in 2023 for 118 days, partly over studios’ use of AI-created “digital doubles” of performers, but also over residual fees from streaming services. Deepfakes and other AI image technology have become more sophisticated and widely available since.Sag-Aftra has been campaigning for the past three years to pass theNo Fakes Act, alongside a coalition of politicians, and tech and media companies such as Disney and Google. “The premise of this law is, it’s going to establish for the first time an individual intellectual property right in name and likeness. So this is the silver-bullet fix,” Astin says. Earlier this month he warned the House judiciary committee of the threat, but he did not dismiss the technology wholesale: “We don’t want to stop progress, we need to civilise it.”View image in fullscreenBefore a Demodog got him ... with Winona Ryder as her short-lived partner in Stranger Things.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThere are myriad complications to this issue. He was a month into the job when AI-generated actor Tilly Norwood arrived on the scene, for example. Big tech is moving in on Hollywood, as with the Paramount-Warner Bros merger, bankrolled by the Oracle-owning Ellison family, which threatens further job losses on top of a downturn in US film and TV production of as much as40% in recent years(Sag-Aftrarecently announcedits opposition to the merger).At the same time, elder statesmen such asMartin ScorseseandGeorge Lucashave openly embraced AI, and urged the industry to do likewise. Astin gives a measured response: “I would ask these legends in the industry to speak thoughtfully and carefully about this technology. I get the sense sometimes that some of the commentary is not well thought-out. And I think that audiences really need their leadership in navigating this space.”If Astin seems comfortable in the role, it’s partly because he has been a local Sag-Aftra delegate and sat on its committees for several years now. He’s still learning, he says, but he seems to relish it. “I gotta say, it’s a much more enjoyable existence than feeling buffeted by the winds of a trillion-dollar industry that has just foisted itself on the public without any real concern for the safety and wellbeing of people who are going to use this technology.”His career has had ups and downs. “I’ve been number one on the call sheet and I’ve been number 247,” he says.“Even at the height of any of these movies, including Lord of the Rings, I’ve never been on the A-list.” He’s always had a steady stream of work, but he’s been turning down offers recently because he doesn’t want to step out of Sag-Aftra negotiations, he says.View image in fullscreen‘The parts I get are the working man parts’ … Astin in biopic Rudy.Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyGiven that past presidents of Sag include Ronald Reagan, I wonder if he has considered getting into politics. He has supported Democrat politicians in the past, including Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. Well-known and liked, scandal-free, diplomatic, a family man, with a record of standing up for the little guy and vanquishing evil (on film at least) – it feels as if he’s got all the attributes.“I appreciate that,” he replies. “I certainly have the interest, but my wife and I have talked a lot about the porch with the rocking chairs …” She has been very patient through his various exploits, he says. Not just acting and union work, he’s also done a master’s degree (in public administration and policy), completed an Iron Man triathlon, hosted a podcast … he’s always busy. “So at a certain point, it’s just not very courteous to not honour the family.”So he has thought about it? “Well, I’ve always fantasised about it. You know, actors love politics. We want to play congressmen and senators and presidents.” He deflects, pointing out that thanks to social media, everyone has a platform these days, not just actors and celebrities, and that we should all be participating in the political process and making our voices heard, especially given the threat big tech poses, not just to Hollywood, but to all of us.But Astin is also smart enough, and modest enough, not to get ahead of himself. “I’m a straight shooter and I’m honest. There are certain things about my value system that are unimpeachable. But I’m also, you know, a fuck-up sometimes,” he says. Being president of the actors union is plenty enough for now. “I feel equal to the task of accepting the responsibility of this job and the constitutional requirements that come with it … I don’t expect that anyone would look at me and think he’s, you know, unflappably perfect, but I like the idea that people would look at me and go: ‘Wow, he sort of put his shit together.’ That’s pretty good.”This article was amended on 27 July 2026. An earlier version said Sag-Aftra had not taken a position on the Paramount-Warner Bros merger; in fact, they announced its opposition on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe big interviewTelevisionFilm industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Valentina and the MUOSters review – US military surveillance in Sicily triggers family discord on the ground | Movies | The Guardian
description: A young woman strives for self-reliance as local people protest the US military communications system that has landed in their rural town
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: A young woman strives for self-reliance as local people protest the US military communications system that has landed in their rural town
Content: Aliens out of thin air … Valentina and the MUOSters.Photograph: True StoryView image in fullscreenAliens out of thin air … Valentina and the MUOSters.Photograph: True StoryMoviesReviewValentina and the MUOSters review – US military surveillance in Sicily triggers family discord on the groundA young woman strives for self-reliance as local people protest the US military communications system that has landed in their rural townPhuong LeMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe title of Francesca Scalisi’s documentary evokes a 1950s sci-fi yarn, even if the film’s visuals are rooted in the drama of the everyday. The acronym MUOS stands for Mobile User Objective System, an advanced satellite communications system used by theUS militaryto direct drones, missiles and other kinds of attacks from a distance. One of the key MUOS ground stations is located in Niscemi, a rural Sicilian town that is also home to Valentina, a 27-year-old woman teetering on the cusp of maturity. Politically engaged yet intimate, Scalisi’s film captures two parallel struggles for autonomy: the local people’s protests against the MUOS base, and Valentina’s determination to lead an independent life.Much emphasis is placed on Valentina’s complicated relationship with her loving but over-protective parents. A sensitive introvert, she doesn’t work and still lives at the family home, unlike her older sister who has established a career elsewhere. Trying to become more self-reliant, Valentina picks up driving and applies for jobs, but her efforts are often met with harsh criticism from her father. Scalisi links these intense moments of familial discord to the atmosphere of surveillance that engulfs the area. Valentina is routinely stopped and questioned by troops stationed at the MUOS base, moments of disruption that turn her home into a land of strangers.Seen in wide shot, the massive, white MUOS antennas contrast starkly with the surrounding agricultural landscape, like aliens materialising out of thin air. Their electromagnetic waves also carry ecological and health hazards, including a negative impact on pacemaker users – including Valentina’s father. Though beginning on a note of generational confrontation, Scalisi’s film moves towards a point of solidarity and understanding. The chants of the protesters against MUOS name not just Sicily, but also Africa and the Middle East, specifically Palestine. Here is not just a local fight, but a global one.Valentina and the MUOSters is on True Story from 31 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsItalyUS militaryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Dairy Story review – giving cows and calves a happier life through progressive farming | Movies | The Guardian
description: Filled with shots of emerald pastures and gambolling animals, this documentary shows that challenging accepted practices can benefit animals and the environment
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Filled with shots of emerald pastures and gambolling animals, this documentary shows that challenging accepted practices can benefit animals and the environment
Content: Mum’s the word… at Rainton Farm calves stay with their mothers for five or six months.Photograph: A Dairy Story.View image in fullscreenMum’s the word… at Rainton Farm calves stay with their mothers for five or six months.Photograph: A Dairy Story.MoviesReviewA Dairy Story review – giving cows and calves a happier life through progressive farmingFilled with shots of emerald pastures and gambolling animals, this documentary shows that challenging accepted practices can benefit animals and the environmentPhil HoadMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnew addition to the ranks ofneo-rural cinemathat is getting its hands dirty with the realities of the modern countryside, this mellow Scottish documentary lauds the emerging practice of cow-and-calf farming. It focuses on Rainton Farm in Dumfries and Galloway where, instead of the dairy-industry norm of separating calves from their mothers a few hours after birth, owners David and Wilma Finlay allow them to stay together until the youngsters are five or six months old. Having run a fully fledged organic operation since the 1990s, the Finlays have progressive form; Rainton is thought to be the first European site where cow-and-calf has been attempted at commercial scale.This shakeup breaks dairy-farming orthodoxy, which refuses to waste lucrative milk on calves. Not only are neighbouring farmers sceptical, the cows initially are too: in the 2012 pilot, the animals were stressed out by the sudden change of routine when they were confronted with needy offspring that they had expected to disappear. Milk yields dropped, but rebounded to a 25% increase in subsequent trials, as the mums settled down and extra suckling stimulated production. An even greater revelation are the damaging routines imposed on dairy farmers by old-style methods: a stressed-out factory milking schedule that, ringfenced by intensive veterinary and crop fertilisation, has ecological repercussions in the fields.Ian Findlay’s film, filled with drone shots of emerald pastures and gambolling calves, makes a handsome case that change is possible. The animal sentience considerations that spurred the Finlays to change their ways crystallise even further – with more time to acknowledge their needs, each animal’s individual personality becomes undeniable. Staunchly proselytising as well as slightly repetitive, this manifesto film glosses over a few details: fine ones, such as the economics at the farm, which David Finlay admits are a work in progress; and the real nitty-gritty, including the fact that the milk of human kindness has its limits at a beef-producing outlet such as Rainton. All the same, this is a quiet, steadfast challenge to the industrial-agricultural complex – as well an uplifting epitaph to Wilma Finlay, who died last year of lung cancer.A Dairy Story is at Norwich Cinema City on 30 July,then tours.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsFarmingAnimalsScotlandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly 20 Georgia O’Keeffe works to go on display in UK for first time | Georgia O'Keeffe | The Guardian
description: Ghost Ranch exhibition at Courtauld in London will look at how artist’s New Mexico home shaped her life and work
Author: Lanre Bakare
Headline: Ghost Ranch exhibition at Courtauld in London will look at how artist’s New Mexico home shaped her life and work
Content: Animal skulls, like the one painted in O’Keeffe’s 1936 work Mule’s Skull with Pink Poinsettia, hung on the walls of Ghost Ranch.Photograph: Georgia O’Keeffe/© 2026 Georgia O’Keeffe Museum / DACS Courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. Photo: Tim Nighswander/IMAGING4ARTView image in fullscreenAnimal skulls, like the one painted in O’Keeffe’s 1936 work Mule’s Skull with Pink Poinsettia, hung on the walls of Ghost Ranch.Photograph: Georgia O’Keeffe/© 2026 Georgia O’Keeffe Museum / DACS Courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. Photo: Tim Nighswander/IMAGING4ARTGeorgia O'KeeffeNearly 20 Georgia O’Keeffe works to go on display in UK for first timeGhost Ranch exhibition at Courtauld in London will look at how artist’s New Mexico home shaped her life and workLanre BakareArts and culture correspondentMon 27 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 05.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs soon as Georgia O’Keeffe was shown Ghost Ranch, she knew it was her place.The remote property in the shadow of the mountains north of Santa Fe in New Mexico would become the artist’s summer residence for decades – a setting that fascinated her, inspired several paintings and is where her ashes were scattered. “I knew the minute I got up here that this was where I would live,” she once said.Now, a new exhibition at the Courtauld will shed light on O’Keeffe’s home at Ghost Ranch and how it shaped her art and life.Almost two dozen works will make up the show, titled Georgia O’Keeffe: Ghost Ranch, which opens in October 2027, with most of them having never before been shown in the UK.View image in fullscreenRed and Yellow Cliffs, 1940, is one of a number of O’Keeffe’s works explicitly influenced by the land that surrounded Ghost Ranch.Photograph: Georgia O’Keeffe/© 2026 Georgia O’Keeffe Museum / DACS Courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. Photo: Tim Nighswander/IMAGING4ARTDr Karen Serres, senior curator of paintings at the Courtauld Gallery, told the Guardian that few in the UK are aware of the role Ghost Ranch played in the development of one of the most important 20th-century American modernists.“Ghost Ranch was such an important part of her life, and it illuminates a large part of her art in general,” said Serres.“For example, in her flower paintings, where she goes really, really, really close up and says, ‘I want to do that because I want to make people look at things that are overlooked.’ She does the exact same thing for these landscapes.”O’Keeffe moved into the property, which was part of a sprawling 21,000 acre estate, in 1934, initially renting a room there before eventually purchasing it and making it her permanent home.“As soon as I saw it, that was my country,” she once said. “I’d never seen anything like it before, but it fitted to me exactly.”Ghost Ranch was one of two properties O’Keeffe lived at in New Mexico. The other was a house in the village of Abiquiú, 16 miles south of the ranch, which ispreserved and opento the public.Ghost Ranch is not open to the general public but was somewhere that O’Keeffe “always felt more at home”, according to the New Yorker’s Calvin Tomkins, who profiled her in 1974.“The solitude, the stillness and the harsh, dry, splendid landscape are more her world,” he wrote. “Animal skulls and bleached antlers hang on the walls of her patio, and rocks picked up on her walks and camping trips spill in profusion over low tables and shelves.”O’Keeffe added to the mystique around Ghost Ranch when she suggested in interviews that the home had been the scene of a murder before she bought it, and many of her most famous photoshoots – included withCecil Beaton for Vogue– took place there.View image in fullscreenGerald’s Tree I, 1937, is another piece that found O’Keeffe committing to canvas  the unique landscape in which she lived.Photograph: Georgia O’Keeffe/© 2026 Georgia O’Keeffe Museum / DACSDespite a significant international profile, O’Keeffe’s work has rarely been seen in the UK; Serres says only six out of the two dozen works on show at the Courtauld have been shown in Britain before.O’Keeffe’s reputation in the UK hasn’t always been so exalted.After her Hayward show in 1993, Britain’s male critics unleasheda torrent of dismissive reviews. She was called a “commercial illustrator”, “irredeemably amateur”, an artist who “made good monthly images on calendars” and “grossly overrated”.Two decades later, before her show at the Tate in 2016, one of the main narratives was that the show aimed to challenge the “conservative male” assumptions that her flower paintings were depictions of female genitalia.Serres said that the Ghost Ranch exhibition is another opportunity for the wider public to gain a deeper knowledge of an artist who is still often misunderstood or who has her work framed by the response of male critics.“She’s known as just this formidable female artist,” said Serres. “But actually seeing her work, understanding what she’s about, I don’t think we are there yet.”Explore more on these topicsGeorgia O'KeeffeThe Courtauld Institute of ArtArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: The No 1 Ladies Detective Agency creator makes the world happier: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Author Alexander McCall Smith’s new series is an attempt to use short fiction to make listeners feel better about the world. Plus, what happened when two London gangsters decided to make a film?
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Author Alexander McCall Smith’s new series is an attempt to use short fiction to make listeners feel better about the world. Plus, what happened when two London gangsters decided to make a film?
Content: ‘Cover a whole sweep of history’ … Alexander McCall Smith.Photograph: Simone Padovani/Awakening/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Cover a whole sweep of history’ … Alexander McCall Smith.Photograph: Simone Padovani/Awakening/Getty ImagesBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioThe No 1 Ladies Detective Agency creator makes the world happier: best podcasts of the weekAuthor Alexander McCall Smith’s new series is an attempt to use short fiction to make listeners feel better about the world. Plus, what happened when two London gangsters decided to make a film?Hannah J Davies.Alexi DugginsandHollie RichardsonMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekThe Positive Distraction PodcastWhile he is best known for his No 1 Ladies’ Detective Agency novels, Alexander McCall Smith has something of a soft spot for short stories, which can “cover a whole sweep of history in a couple of paragraphs”. Hisnew seriesfeatures a selection of short original works that he hopes will make listeners feel better about the state of the world, beginning with a pleasingly twee tale inspired by a friend’s miniature helicopter landing pad.Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyShadow World: Breakin’ the CycleIn the early 00s, two of London’s most ruthless criminals decided to escape gangsterdom by creating a movie about their lives. Thisslick showfeatures one of them, plus the film’s editor, telling the tale of how they ended up getting S Club 7’s Bradley involved – before the creators’ background threw the production into chaos.Alexi DugginsBBC Sounds, episodes weeklyYou’ve Got BrailleView image in fullscreenAlison Steadman.Photograph: Joe Maher/Getty ImagesComedy producer Reece Finnegan and writer Jack Bernhardt have written this four-partseriesfor Hat Trick and the RNIB, about an “idiot” twentysomething who also happens to be blind. While light and sitcomy, it beautifully tackles the issues that Paddy (Finnegan) faces as a result of his disability. Alison Steadman, Steve Pemberton and Chloe Petts also star.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyCome CloserIt’s hard not to be compelled by host “Aries goddess extraordinary, keeper of dark stories” Rae Review – check out her horns on theYouTube version. She tells one of history’s grimmest tales in each episode, starting with Lorena Bobbitt, who chopped off her husband’s penis.Hollie RichardsonWidely available, episodes weeklyThe Gaza Chef“How do you investigate a questionable death when you can’t go to the place it happened?” So asks thispodcastabout Mahmud, a chef who ran a Gaza soup kitchen but was killed by a projectile from the sky. It’s a grippingly told listen from Yassin Musharbash; he sets up the story by explaining the relationship he developed with Mahmud – who sent him voice messages explaining life in Gaza.ADWidely available, episodes weeklyWhat have you been listening to this week? Share all your top tips below.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioBest podcasts of the weekPodcastsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In search of Valencia’s ‘white gold’: my hunt for the perfect horchatería | Valencia holidays | The Guardian
description: Horchata, the revered creamy drink made from tiger nuts, is still served in grand Valencian parlours – always accompanied by sugar-glazed pastries
Author: Gordon Cole-Schmidt
Headline: Horchata, the revered creamy drink made from tiger nuts, is still served in grand Valencian parlours – always accompanied by sugar-glazed pastries
Content: A glass of horchata and a sweet farton at Horchatería de Santa Catalina in Valencia.All photographs: Mirja VogelView image in fullscreenA glass of horchata and a sweet farton at Horchatería de Santa Catalina in Valencia.All photographs: Mirja VogelValencia holidaysIn search of Valencia’s ‘white gold’: my hunt for the perfect horchateríaHorchata, the revered creamy drink made from tiger nuts, is still served in grand Valencian parlours – always accompanied by sugar-glazed pastriesGordon Cole-SchmidtMon 27 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a glimpse of an old couple sharing a tender moment in the bustlinghorchateríathat drew me into one of Valencia’s most storied culinary traditions. As he sipped his milkyhorchata de chufaand a white crescent moon appeared on his coiffed moustache, they shared a soft laugh and she dabbed it away from his upper lip.“There’s no fixed time to drink horchata,” the lady said. “As long we have at least one every day.”In Valencia, this refreshing, creamy, non-alcoholic drink is so beloved it is nicknamed “white gold”, and grand parlours dedicated to making it are still going strong in the city’s most sought-after locations. These often historic, traditional places are calledhorchaterías(ororxateriasin Valencian) and there are dozens dotted around the region.Production is authorised in 16 towns in the Valencia region, with the quaint town of Alboraya (Alboraia in Valencian), about 45 minutes’ walk from Valencia old town, acknowledged as its birthplace and global capital. Here, buried in the low-lying, fertile fields around the town, you’ll find the drink’s principal ingredient: thechufa.Chufas, known as tiger nuts in English, have been cultivated in Valencia for more than 1,000 years. They look like wooden raisins but taste nutty and slightly sweet when eaten raw. Tiger nuts are not actually nuts, but tubers of a grass-like plant from the sedge family. Valencia’s agricultural zone north of the city produces 5.3m to 8m kilograms of dried tiger nuts a year. Most of the harvesting takes place in spring to ensure ample supply for the balmy summer months.View image in fullscreen‘The horchata is darker, creamier and richer than most’ … a table at Horchatería De Santa Catalina in Valencia.To turn the wrinkly tubers into horchata, chufas are cleaned, soaked and crushed, then mixed with water. Nowadays, cinnamon, lemon or orange zest and sugar are added to boost the flavour.Alboraya is also the birthplace of horchata’s companion: thefarton, a long, cigar-shaped pastry glazed with sugar, created in the 1960s by the Polo family to dip in and mop up every last drop of horchata from the bottom of the glass. Some stay loyal to its humble predecessor,rosquilletas(breadsticks), which are less absorbent but an intriguingly salty, anise-flavoured counterpart to horchata’s sweetness nonetheless.Leaving Alboraya with a bellyful of the indulgent combination, I weighed the task of finding the perfect horchatería. It felt wrong to split up horchata from its farton, so I would consider both. Horchaterías tend to offer three versions of horchata:líquida(liquid),granizada(semi-frozen slush) ormixta(a blend of liquid and slush). It would be the traditional classic líquida for me.In Valencia, there are hundreds of places serving horchata and fartons, but I wanted tradition and old-world charm – places that exist only to make horchata, not as an afterthought to spiced lattes or ice-cream. After sifting out the cafes, coffeehouses and ice-cream parlours, a handwritten list on a single sheet of A4 remained.Horchatería FabiánView image in fullscreenIt’s early evening in the old town, and the narrow shopping alley leading to my first stop, family-runHorchatería Fabián, is filled with tourists and an after-work crowd. Past bustling taverns and restaurant terraces, I glimpse its entrance and the date it was founded: 1975. Sounds promising, but something is missing. Where are the customers?Although the place is empty, the staff are distracted and cold. The horchata they unwillingly produce is over-sweet, almost artificial tasting, and the farton is parched and crumbles on to the plate. Horchata seeps into its pores nicely when I dip it into the glass, but the overriding sensation is a numbing sweetness.I slink out of the unwelcoming room, back on to the busy street and into a local tavern, fearing my high expectations for this jaunt are misplaced.Horchata €3, 4/10Farton €1, 3/10Horchatería DanielView image in fullscreenThe next day, I spy the queue spilling out of the glass-panelled room atHorchatería Daniel. This is arguably the most well-known horchatería company in Valencia, founded in 1949 and still a family business, with three locations in Valencia.I visit all three. The original, and the largest, is in Alboraya, decked with wooden tables and a constant flow of regulars. In its basement, production of horchata and fartons begins at 5am for here and its other locations – one in the famous Mercado de Colón and the third in a grand parlour in the centre of the old town, near to Plaza de la Reina.That’s where I wait now, warmed by the evening sun, before I’m shuffled into a grand, airy room and handed a glass from a cluttered tray.I can barely hear myself think over the noise of chatter and glasses clinking. The horchata is creamy and only moderately sweet. Together with the traditional farton, it’s easy to see why this is still one of the most popular horchaterías in town. Giddy, I order its newest farton creation – coated in a layer of chocolate, raspberries and crushed pistachios. Its dry interior and disjointed melange of flavours bring me back down to earth. Stick with the old favourites here and you can’t go wrong.Horchata €1.95, 6.5/10Farton85 cents, 6/10Horchatería SantabárbaraView image in fullscreenSouth from the old town the streets widen out into sun-filled, palm-lined avenues leading to the suburb of Montolivet, where neighbourhood favouriteHorchatería Santabárbarahas been in situ for four years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost tables are busy, but this does not deter the manager, Rafa, from skipping between them to pat regulars on the back and run through each step of horchata production with wide-eyed tourists. By the time he reaches our table, my glass – which is refreshing but a little too sweet – is empty.“Try this,” Rafa commands, passing me a new glass. “This is the original horchata, no sugar, no nothing. Just chufa and water.” It’s a revelation. The overburdening sugary aftertaste is gone, and what’s left is a clean, refreshing natural drink that sings above the mediocrity of the sweetened version. Pair it with its spongy, glazed farton and you’ll want to join the sea of smiling regulars coming back for more.Horchata €2.50, 7/10Farton80 cents, 6.5/10Horchatería de Santa CatalinaView image in fullscreenIn the shadow of the stunning 17th-century baroque bell tower of the Santa Catalina Church in the old town,Horchatería de Santa Catalinais the grandest of them all.A tight entrance decorated with ceramic tiles from Manises opens into a grand dining room packed with marble tables. A curved wooden staircase leads into an equally beautiful room upstairs – both are heaving when I arrive in the evening.A chilled white glass and a longer farton dusted with icing sugar arrive on the table. Like the locals around me, I don’t hesitate. The farton melts in my mouth, while the horchata is darker, creamier and richer than most. It is a delightful combination. The place itself is a class act in one of the city’s most beautiful neighbourhoods.Horchata €4, 8/10Farton €1.55, 6.5/10Horchatería Mari ToñiView image in fullscreenNorth of the river in residential La Saïdia is another neighbourhood favourite, Horchatería Mari Toñi. It’s just a few minutes from artsy Benimaclet and on the way to Alboraya, if you’re leaving from the old town.Opening at 6.15am, it’s the first place in town to get a horchata and stays busy until it closes 15 hours later. Fartons are freshly made each morning and initially they look dry. The sugar glazing seems to wilt rather than crack. But the first bite proves looks aren’t everything – they are light and fluffy, perfectly porous to the creamy horchata produced in this charming, authentic location.Horchata €3, 6/10Farton80 cents, 7.5/10On the move? The takeaway alternativeView image in fullscreenHorchatería Mon Orxata.In more than 20 visits to different Valencian horchaterías, I watched as horchata was decanted into unbranded buckets and large flasks, conducted away from the main floor. In Alboraya, at bothHorchatería PanachandHorchatería El Sariers, at least 10 litres of horchata were transported out by three families in under 10 minutes.In the city, two standout takeaway alternatives emerged. Across most central plazas in Valencia,Món Orxatais bringing back a lost 400-year-old tradition of selling unpasteurised horchata from street carts. Its horchata is clean, crisp and one of the most refreshing on the hottest of days.Pair it with the orange-infused farton, made with fermented dough by award-winning Valencia-born pastry chef Migue Señorís atGelática Ice Conceptnear the coast, and enjoy both during a sunset walk along the city’s beach.Món Orxata horchata €3.30, 7/10Gelática Ice Concept farton €1.90, 8.5/10Explore more on these topicsValencia holidaysFood and drinkSpain holidaysEurope holidaysSpanish food and drinkMilkFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Quick and easy summer salad: Georgina Hayden’s grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah recipe | Salad | The Guardian
description: Sweetness and spice abound in this refreshing summer salad
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: Sweetness and spice abound in this refreshing summer salad
Content: Georgina Hayden's grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah salad.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden's grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah salad.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.Quick and easySaladQuick and easy summer salad: Georgina Hayden’s grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah recipeSweetness and spice abound in this refreshing summer saladGeorgina HaydenMon 27 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the weather is glorious, I have very little desire to do any “proper cooking”. Turning the grill on for about 15 minutes is the maximum amount of heat I want to subject my home to, which is why, in the summer months, I eat this sort of salad on repeat: stone fruit with golden slices of halloumi is my favourite pairing. Add a little freshness with some sweetness and spice, and it is a glorious thing. You could even spoon it on to slices of toasted ciabatta for an open sandwich or elegant crostini.Grilled peach, halloumi and dukkah saladWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIf you make your own dukkah, amazing; otherwise, you can pick up some pretty good mixes from most supermarkets these days. It really works here, and feel free to add more, if you like.Prep10 minCook25 minServes43 peachesSea salt andblack pepperExtra-virgin olive oil90g rocket½ bunchmint,leaves picked and torn1 tsp dijonmustardJuice of1 lemon225g block of halloumi,cut into 1cm-thick slices1 tbsp runny honey2 tbsp dukkah1 green chilli, halved and finely sliced – pith and seeds removed first, if you want less heatHeat the grill to high. Halve and stone the peaches, then cut each half in half again. Arrange the peach quarters in a small to medium roasting tray, so they don’t have too much space between them, and season generously. Drizzle with olive oil, toss to coat, then grill for about eight minutes, until the edges of the peach wedges are a little charred and gnarly.Meanwhile, put the rocket and mint leaves in a large bowl.When the peaches are done, transfer them to a platter, and reserve all the juices in the tray. Mix the mustard into the sweet peach juices, then whisk in the lemon juice and two tablespoons of olive oil. Taste and tweak the seasoning, then pour this dressing over the rocket.Lay the halloumi slices in the now empty peach tray and pop them under the grill for five minutes, turning once halfway so the cheese goes slightly golden all over.Meanwhile, toss the dressing through the rocket and mint, then place on the grilled peach platter, dotting the fruit on top and around the leaves. As soon as the halloumi is ready, drape the slices over the top of the salad, finish with a drizzle of honey, sprinkle on the dukkah and sliced green chilli and serve right away.Explore more on these topicsSaladQuick and easySummer food and drinkFoodFruitCheeseHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Vegan pho and Thai fishless cakes: Richard Makin’s southeast Asian-style tofu recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Fragrant, punchy vegan dishes that can be kept in the kept in the fridge or freezer for an easy midweek dinner
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fragrant, punchy vegan dishes that can be kept in the kept in the fridge or freezer for an easy midweek dinner
Content: Richard Makin's pho now or pho later.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenRichard Makin's pho now or pho later.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.FoodVegan pho and Thai fishless cakes: Richard Makin’s southeast Asian-style tofu recipesFragrant, punchy vegan dishes that can be kept in the kept in the fridge or freezer for an easy midweek dinnerRichard MakinMon 27 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether you love it or loathe it, tofu is one of the most versatile ingredients in any kitchen. For me, it’s the saviour of stressful dinner times, because it cooks in minutes, absorbs flavour like no other and packs a real nutritional punch. Here, it plays two very different roles: crisped until golden in a fragrant, spice-infused Vietnamese-style pho, and mashed to give body and bite to bold, punchy Thai-ish fishless cakes.Pho now or pho later (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThe best bit about pho, IMO, is the broth; unfortunately, it’s also the most time-consuming part. But don’t fret, I’ve streamlined the process for you. Once made, the broth can sit in the fridge for up to a week, ready to be reheated and poured over noodles and vegetables at a moment’s notice. And, because it’s full of spices and aromatics, it’ll taste even better with time.Prep10 minCook30 minServes21 tsp vegetable oil200g extra-firm tofu, drained and cubed2 shallots, peeled and roughly chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly crushed with the flat of a knife2½cm piece fresh ginger, roughly sliced2 star anise4cloves2 tsp coriander seeds2 green cardamom pods1 cinnamon stick½ tsp chilli flakes½ tsp fennel seeds1½ litres vegetable stock150g long-stem broccoli, ends trimmed170g flat rice noodles1 tbsp soy sauce1 tbsp brown sugar1 tsp fine sea salt2 tbsp white rice vinegarTo serve1 shallot, peeled and finely chopped1 red chilli, stalk, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely chopped1 smallcarrot, peeled and julienned or gratedFresh coriander, mint and basil2 lime wedgesPut the vegetable oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat, then fry the tofu for five minutes, turning often, until browned all over. Lift it out of the pan, stir the shallots, garlic, ginger and spices into the hot oil left in the pan and cook, stirring, for two minutes, until fragrant. Pour in the stock, bring to a boil over a medium heat, then leave to bubble for 10 minutes.Put the broccoli in a steamer basket (or sieve) and place it over the top of the simmering pot. Turn down the heat to a simmer, cover the pan with a lid and steam the broccoli for five minutes, until tender. Take out the broccoli and set aside.Strain the stock to remove the spices and aromatics, then return the clear broth to the pan and put it on a medium heat. Add the rice noodles and cook for five minutes, or until tender.Divide the noodles between two deep bowls, and top them both with half the steamed broccoli and fried tofu. Stir the soy sauce, brown sugar, sea salt and rice vinegar into the hot broth, then take it off the heat.If serving straight away, pour the seasoned broth over the noodles, broccoli and tofu in each bowl; if serving later, leave the broth to cool to room temperature, then transfer to an airtight container. Cover the noodle bowls (or transfer to a heat-proof jar) and keep in the fridge for up to a week.When ready to serve, bring the broth back to a boil, then pour it over the noodles. Garnish with chopped shallot, red chilli, julienned carrot, fresh herbs and a lime wedge.Red curry fishless cakes with peanut slawWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenThis recipe is for my mum. She went vegan not long after I did, back in 2017, and although she doesn’t say as much explicitly, Iknowthat she misses seafood. She also loves Thai food, so these fishless cakes are a win–win. They’re gently spiced and super fragrant, with a light, flaky texture; they’re also freezable and, because they’re dinky, they don’t need to be defrosted before frying.Prep15 minCook20 minServes2For the fishless cakes1400gtin hearts of palm, drained and roughly chopped150g medium-firm tofu, drained2 spring onions, trimmed and finely chopped1 tbsp vegan red curry paste1 tsp ginger paste, or 1 tsp grated fresh ginger1 garlic clove, peeled and minced1 tsp brown sugarFinely grated zest of ½ lime1 small bunchcoriander, leaves and tender stems chopped3 tbsp plain flour, plus extra for dusting1 tbsp vegetable oilLime wedges, to serveFor the peanut slaw50g shredded red cabbage50g shredded white cabbage1 small carrot, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks50g cooked edamame beans1 spring onion, trimmed and finely chopped40g salted peanuts, roughly chopped1 tbsp agave syrup1 tbsp rice vinegar, or lime juice1 tbsp olive oil1 tbsp soy sauce1 tbsp smooth peanut butter2 tsp sriracha1tsp ginger pasteWrap the chopped hearts of palm and the tofu in a clean kitchen towel and wring out as much moisture as possible. The tofu will get mushed up, but not to worry: that’s what you want.Put the hearts of palm and tofu in a large bowl, add the spring onions, curry paste, ginger, garlic, brown sugar, lime zest, coriander and flour, then mix thoroughly with your hands until well combined.Form the mixture into six patties and dust the outsides with the extra flour. If you’re making the fishless cakes in advance, put the patties on a small baking sheet and freeze until solid. Transfer them to an airtight container or zip-lock bag, and freeze for up two months.To cook, put a large frying pan on a medium heat, add the vegetable oil, then fry the patties for five to eight minutes on each side, until lightly browned (if cooking from frozen, you’ll need to add a few minutes to the cooking time ).While the fishless cakes are cooking, in a large bowl mix the two cabbages, carrot matchsticks, edamame, spring onion and chopped peanuts. In a small bowl, whisk the agave syrup, rice vinegar, olive oil, soy sauce, peanut butter, sriracha and ginger paste, pour half of this dressing over the slaw and toss to coat.Serve the fishless cakes with the peanut slaw on the side, with lime wedges alongside and the remaining dressing for dipping.These recipes are edited extracts from Stress-Free Dinners: Over 90 Quick and Delicious Everyday Vegan Recipes, by Richard Makin, published by Bloomsbury at £22. To order a copy for £19.80, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodTofuSnacksStarterVietnamese food and drinkThai food and drinkMain courserecipesShareReuse this content
